1What the Riemann Hypothesis says

A single vertical line is supposed to contain every nontrivial zero of a function built from all the positive integers. Why should estimates for primes have anything to say about a point in the complex plane?

1.1Follow one possible zero through the proof

Suppose, for the sake of following the argument, that ζ had a nontrivial zero ρ with real part 0.60. What would force a contradiction? Start with the zero, then work backwards to the arithmetic estimate needed to exclude it. The number 0.60 is an illustrative choice.

  1. A zero leaves a pole. Near a zero of multiplicity m, write ζ(s)=(s−ρ)mh(s), with h(ρ)≠0. Its logarithmic derivative therefore contains m/(s−ρ). The proof recovers this pole by integrating a function of prime powers against x−s−1. The function uses a ramp weight and subtracts an explicit main term. The arithmetic construction also introduces Dirichlet characters. When those are grouped, the multiplicities at the same zero have positive weights, so the pole survives. Compute its residue.
  2. A bound on distant intervals would exclude this pole. Choose a real exponent strictly between ½ and 0.60, for example 0.55. The analytic theorem excludes poles to its right if the real centered family sum is bounded above by a constant times x0.55 on arbitrarily distant intervals of the prescribed relative width. First fix a level whose weighted character sum sees the proposed zero. For each sufficiently small positive ε the arithmetic construction supplies auxiliary data giving windows for that same sum. Its exponent on the specialized route is ½+9ε. Taking ε ≤ 0.005, subject also to the construction’s threshold, puts the exponent at most 0.545. An exponent of 0.65 would leave a pole at 0.60 outside the reach of the theorem. The full argument makes this choice after the prospective zero. See the quantifiers and check the integral on that same interval.
  3. The interval comes from arithmetic. At one translation, subtract the predicted main term from the observed prime-power count and sum over sampled indices and chain stages. Two parts of the proof constrain this remainder. A differentiated theta coefficient gives a valuation bound on a matrix entry. The Galois representation for the row enters the choice of an arithmetic window. At a prime ℓ and twist j, write hℓ,j for the length of the group of global degree-one classes whose restrictions above ℓ vanish. Its order is ℓhℓ,j, so its logarithmic size is hℓ,j log ℓ. The relevant sum of these logarithmic sizes contributes to the finite-place cost in the lattice comparison. On the chosen window the sum is at most √b, where b is the weight of one measurement. The lattice comparison bounds the remainder from above. Its character expansion then lets us divide by the total weight and bound the same fixed family sum as in step 2. Choosing the chain length near √x balances terms of order x/m and m.

The contradiction rules out the proposed 0.60. Repeating it for every real part above ½ and using the functional equation excludes the other side of the strip. For characters the functional equation changes which character occurs. Follow the reflection step.

For a first reading, the prime-power calculation, the window theorem and reflection explain exactly what the arithmetic must deliver. The reconstruction record gives their current scope. To see the two arithmetic inputs meet in one inequality, follow a single measurement.

Read the arithmetic through two finite counts

In the theta chain, start with two matrices with the same entry valuations. Eliminating one row reveals whether their lattice quotients have 9 or 81 elements. The length formula turns this calculation into two denominator limits for a general matrix. Once a row is fixed, its corner must satisfy a trace equation. The trace-zero calculation counts its solutions at the allowed level. Use the cell experiment to multiply the number of rows by the corners per row and subtract those already counted at shorter lengths. The shell sum weights the result by length to recover part of the Euler factor. At a real place a squared projection norm supplies the positive factor for the chosen vectors. To see how the pairing of two lifts becomes a double integral over their sources, compute it in both orders. Once the doubled theta mean has been identified and the local factors have been combined and continued, the norm identity shows why one lift survives. Keeping distinct labels independent then makes the downward map in the iterated chain surjective.

The Galois row used in choosing the arithmetic window comes from two parallel lifts in a separate construction. Cohomology controls what that window can cost in the bound for one measurement.

In the cohomology argument, average a function on the points of a finite plane over each line. The point-and-line experiment shows how much of a mean-zero function survives. The three projection estimates give a gap on the orthogonal complement of the common fixed functions. Those functions are constant almost everywhere, so the gap applies to coefficients of mean zero. It makes the mean-zero periods decay faster than a nonzero stabilized period could. The split of a finite Hecke average explains that lower limit on the decay. The central average first preserves the periods of the chosen cocycle. The mean of its coefficients gives a fully invariant form. Comparing the decay rates then proves that this form has the original periods, which bound the rank of the detected classes. Compare the two rates.

What does the lift supply, and where does cohomology enter?

In the lift chapter, a squared period is expressed using a doubled theta mean. The Fourier comparison identifies the mean with an Eisenstein value in the lower rank range. The 27 frequencies of a finite model show why equality on invertible indices alone leaves information missing. Two local calculations occur at different steps. To identify the theta mean, its Fourier coefficient uses a count of frames with a fixed Gram matrix. After inserting that identity into the paired lift and unfolding, the local zeta integral instead groups lattice cosets by length to compute an Euler quotient.

In the cohomology chapter, two different bounds protect the same period comparison. The lattice estimate helps bound a partition on the space of forms, so a representative has controlled size. Each point in the partition can have several group labels. The two-centre calculation shows how the normalization accounts for them. The calculation on translations identifies what an arithmetic unit can erase on the stabilizer cycles used in a Hecke average. These bounds enter on the analytic and homological sides of the two-rate comparison.

1.2From a series to a function

Write s = σ + it, where σ and t are real and i² = −1. In the half-plane σ > 1 the sum ζ(s) = ∑n≥1 exp(−s log n) converges absolutely, since the absolute values sum to ∑ n−σ. Multiplying the geometric series in p−s over primes lists each integer exactly once by unique factorization. This gives the Euler product. For example, multiply just the factors for 2 and 3. The term from the second power of 2 and the first power of 3 is 12−s. No other choice gives 12. Absolute convergence allows the finite prime sets to increase until every integer appears. DLMF §25.2[1]

ζ(s) = ∑n≥1 n−s = ∏p prime (1 − p−s)−1   (Re s > 1).

Could the infinite product vanish although every factor is nonzero? This can happen for products in general. Here the logarithms are absolutely summable. For σ > 1 their absolute sum is at most ∑p ∑j≥1 p−jσ/j ≤ (1 − 2−σ)−1 ∑n≥2 n−σ. Exponentiating the convergent sum of logarithms gives a nonzero product.

At s = ¾ the original series is a divergent sum of positive terms. The expression ζ(¾) nevertheless has a precise meaning. There is a unique meromorphic function on the plane agreeing with the series throughout Re s > 1. Meromorphic means holomorphic except at isolated poles. Here the sole pole is at 1, and the continued function is regular at ¾. It is this continued function that the theorem studies. DLMF §25.2, definition and continuation[1]

Theorems used. The pole of the zeta function

1.3Which zeros?

The zeros at −2, −4, −6, … are called trivial. The remaining zeros lie in the strip 0 < σ < 1. Reflection pairs zeros across the line σ = ½. A pair at σ = 0.4 and σ = 0.6 would respect this symmetry, so symmetry alone leaves the main question open. DLMF §25.10(i)[2]

If ζ(s) = 0, s ≠ 1 and s ∉ {−2, −4, −6, …}, then Re s = ½.

The exception at 1 removes the pole of ζ from the statement about its zeros. At zero the value ζ(0) = −½ eliminates another possible endpoint.

1.4Why the book follows characters

A Dirichlet character modulo a positive integer N is a multiplicative character on its invertible residue classes, extended by zero on nonunits. Its values on units are roots of unity. Inserting χ(n) in the series for ζ weights each residue class by a phase. The resulting function L(s,χ) agrees with ζ when N = 1. The principal character at a larger modulus drops all integers with a common factor with that modulus. For example at modulus 2 its series is (1 − 2−s)ζ(s) for σ > 1.

The proof first obtains right-half-plane nonvanishing for every χ and every nonzero modulus. More precisely, σ > ½ and (χ ≠ 1 or s ≠ 1) imply L(s,χ) ≠ 0. Fixing the modulus-one character gives right-half-plane nonvanishing for ζ. The functional equation deals with the other side. The hard part is producing the prime-sum inequalities that lead to this nonvanishing. Character averages enter those inequalities before the specialization to ζ.

Check the role of modulus one

What can be concluded at a hypothetical point ρ with Re ρ = ¾ and ζ(ρ) = 0? Take N = 1 and its unique character. Then L(ρ,χ) = ζ(ρ), and ρ ≠ 1 follows from its real part. The character nonvanishing theorem contradicts this zero. At Re ρ = ¼ the same substitution does not meet the right-half-plane hypothesis. The reflection chapter constructs a point with real part ¾ to which it can be applied.

2Prime powers and the Mellin transform

A prime contributes once to an Euler product, but contributes at every one of its powers to the logarithmic derivative. Follow the contribution from one prime power through a weighted sum and an integral. At the end, the multiplicity of a zero can be read from a single coefficient.

2.1How a prime power enters the sum

Write p for a prime. The von Mangoldt function Λ assigns log p to each positive power of p and zero to every other positive integer, including 1. Thus Λ(8) = log 2, while Λ(6) = 0. All logarithms here are natural. A Dirichlet character χ of modulus N ≥ 1 is a homomorphism from the multiplicative group of invertible residue classes modulo N to the nonzero complex numbers, extended periodically to the integers and set to zero on the nonunits. Its nonzero values are roots of unity because the group is finite. The principal character takes the value 1 on every unit. At modulus one the unique character takes the value 1 on every integer.

For real x ≥ 1, write t+ = max(t, 0). The smoothed sum is

Sχ(x)=∑n=1⌊x⌋Λ(n)χ(n)(xn−1)+(2.1)

The contribution from n begins at zero when x = n. After that point its slope is Λ(n)χ(n)/n. This gives a continuous, piecewise linear function on every bounded interval. The ordinary weighted count of prime powers would jump by Λ(n)χ(n) at n. The slope and the continuity here determine the two factors that will appear in the transform.

At x = 6. For the modulus-one character the active prime powers are 2, 3, 4 and 5. Their respective weights are 2, 1, 1/2 and 1/5. The sum is (5/2) log 2 + log 3 + (1/5) log 5. For the nonprincipal character modulo 3, the values on residues 0, 1 and 2 are 0, 1 and −1. In the same order the four terms now have character factors −1, 0, 1 and −1. The sum becomes −(3/2) log 2 − (1/5) log 5. Characters can remove a contribution, change its sign, or for a complex character rotate it.

2.2The transform of one ramp

Set s = σ + it, where σ and t are real, and define xs = exp(s log x) for x > 0. We use the Mellin convention ℳf(s) = ∫1∞ f(x) x−s−1 dx. With u = log x, the measure dx/x becomes du and x−s becomes exp(−su). The transform therefore studies growth on multiplicative scales as an ordinary Laplace transform in u.

One-ramp identity. Let n ≥ 1 be an integer and σ > 1. Then

∫1∞(xn−1)+x−s−1dx=n−ss(s−1)(2.2)

The integrand vanishes up to n. Above n it is the difference of x−s/n and x−s−1. Both are absolutely integrable since σ > 1. Their integrals over [n, ∞) are n−s/(s − 1) and n−s/s respectively, by evaluating the power antiderivatives at the endpoints. Subtracting gives (2.2). At s = 2 and n = 2, the two areas are 1/4 and 1/8, leaving 1/8.

The half-plane matters. For large x, the absolute value of the integrand is asymptotic to x−σ/n. The integral of its absolute value diverges for σ ≤ 1. The formula on the right continues meromorphically beyond the integration domain. In particular a later evaluation of its continuation in the critical strip does not assert convergence of this integral there.

2.3From one ramp to a logarithmic derivative

For σ > 1 define the Dirichlet L-function by the absolutely convergent series L(s, χ) = ∑n≥1 χ(n)n−s. Expanding geometric series at finitely many primes counts each integer supported on those primes exactly once. Letting the finite set grow gives the Euler product ∏p(1 − χ(p)p−s)−1, by absolute convergence. Its logarithm may be taken as the convergent series ∑p,j≥1 χ(p)jp−js/j, with p running over primes. Exponentiating recovers the product and shows it is nonzero there. NIST DLMF §25.15(i), equations 1–2[3].

Differentiate this logarithm with respect to s. The derivative of p−js supplies −j log p, cancelling j in the denominator. On every closed half-plane σ ≥ 1 + h, h > 0, the sum of absolute derivative bounds is at most ∑n≥2(log n)n−1−h < ∞ by the integral test. The differentiated series converges locally uniformly. Writing Dχ(s) = L′(s, χ)/L(s, χ), we obtain

−Dχ(s)=∑n=1∞Λ(n)χ(n)n−s(2.3)

To sum (2.2) under the integral, replace s by σ there. Since |χ(n)| ≤ 1 and the ramp is nonnegative, the sum of the integrated absolute values is bounded by

1σ(σ−1)∑n=1∞Λ(n)nσ<∞(2.4)

Indeed 0 ≤ Λ(n) ≤ log n for positive n. Fubini's theorem now permits the exchange of sum and integral. Equations (2.2) and (2.3) give the uncentered transform

ℳSχ(s)=−Dχ(s)s(s−1)(2.5)
Lean correspondence

The formal proof evaluates the integral norm at σ, sums it using absolute convergence, and replaces the Dirichlet series by its logarithmic derivative. The comparison with ∑(log n)n−σ is an elementary justification of that convergence in this exposition. Integral norm and exchange and identification of the logarithmic derivative.

2.4Why the correction terms have these signs

The raw transform has a factor 1/(s − 1). For ζ the logarithmic derivative has a pole at 1 as well. To detect zeros by their poles, we first remove the poles due to these main terms. This calculation only needs the primitive principal character (modulus one) and nonprincipal characters of positive modulus. A character is primitive if it is not induced from a character of any proper divisor of its modulus. The principal character at a higher modulus is induced from modulus one. The family used below excludes such higher-modulus principal characters.

A model for centering. A term of size xα has transform 1/(s − α) on Re s > α, by integrating xα−s−1. Subtracting this known term from a sum subtracts its pole from the transform. For example, x + x¾ has poles at 1 and ¾. Subtracting x leaves 1/(s − ¾), where the second pole is still visible. In the prime sum the known singularity at 1 includes a double pole, which calls for a second correction.

2.5The modulus-one case

Here L = ζ. Let γ = limk→∞(∑j=1k 1/j − log k), the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Put z = s − 1. The Laurent expansion ζ(1 + z) = 1/z + γ + O(z) gives an analytic function A(z) = zζ(1 + z) across 0 with A(0) = 1 and A′(0) = γ. Thus D1(1 + z) = −1/z + A′(z)/A(z) = −1/z + γ + O(z). Multiplying its negative by 1/[(1 + z)z] gives the principal part 1/z2 − (1 + γ)/z. NIST DLMF §25.2(ii), equations 4–5[4].

One coefficient is especially easy to miss here. The factor 1/[(1 + z)z] equals 1/z − 1 + O(z). When multiplied by 1/z − γ + O(z), the simple-pole coefficient receives −1 from the first factor and −γ from the second. Correcting only the double pole would leave a spurious pole with residue −(1 + γ).

Which functions of x have precisely these transforms? For Re z > 0, ∫0∞ exp(−zu) du = 1/z. Integration by parts, with u exp(−zu) vanishing at infinity, gives ∫0∞ u exp(−zu) du = 1/z2. Undo the substitution u = log x. These are the transforms of x and x log x. Hence set

G1(x)=S1(x)−xlogx+(1+γ)x(2.6)

For σ > 1 its transform is −D1(s)/[s(s − 1)] − 1/(s − 1)2 + (1 + γ)/(s − 1). The two negative-power coefficients cancel. The continuation is holomorphic at 1. This calculation uses the Laurent expansion around the pole and never substitutes a numerical value for ζ at its pole.

2.6The nonprincipal case

A nonprincipal character of positive modulus has an entire L-function, and the classical nonvanishing theorem at 1 gives L(1, χ) ≠ 0. Thus cχ = Dχ(1) is finite and Dχ(1 + z) = cχ + O(z). Equation (2.5) has principal part −cχ/z. Adding cχx to the sum cancels it. Analytic continuation[3] and

Gχ(x)=Sχ(x)+cχx(2.7)
ℳGχ(s)=scχ−Dχ(s)s(s−1)(2.8)

The numerator in (2.8) vanishes at s = 1. Dividing it by s − 1 leaves a holomorphic function there. This identifies the cancellation even when cχ happens to vanish. Neither centering formula estimates the size of the remaining error at large x.

2.7What a zero leaves in the transform

Let ρ lie in the strip 0 < Re ρ < 1, and suppose L(ρ, χ) = 0. The function is holomorphic near ρ and is not identically zero since its Euler product is nonzero for σ > 1. Its Taylor series has a first nonzero coefficient, of degree m ≥ 1. Factoring it gives L(s, χ) = (s − ρ)mh(s) with h holomorphic and h(ρ) ≠ 0. Differentiation and division give Dχ(s) = m/(s − ρ) + h′(s)/h(s). The last quotient is holomorphic on a sufficiently small disk about ρ.

Only the first term contributes a pole. In both centered formulas its multiplier is −1/[s(s − 1)], which is holomorphic at ρ since ρ differs from 0 and 1. Its value at ρ gives the coefficient of (s − ρ)−1, the residue of the continued transform Φχ.

Ress=ρΦχ=−mρ(ρ−1)(2.9)

A zero of any positive multiplicity therefore gives a simple pole. For ζ the factor s − 1 used to regularize it at 1 is a nonzero analytic factor at ρ, so the multiplicity here is unchanged.

Lean records the Laurent expansion on a punctured neighborhood, so the totalized value assigned at a pole is immaterial.

2.8Why taking real parts preserves a pole

The arithmetic estimate later controls a real sum. Let I be a finite index set. For each i in I, let χi be a character of positive modulus Ni with Ni = 1 or χi nonprincipal, and fix a real weight ai > 0. Define GF(x) = ∑i∈I ai Re Gχᵢ(x). For a character χ, its inverse χ⁻¹ on units is its complex conjugate, and both characters vanish on nonunits. Conjugating the Dirichlet series first for σ > 1 gives L(s, χ⁻¹) = conj(L(conj(s), χ)) by analytic continuation. In particular the two derivatives and values at the real point 1 are conjugate for nonprincipal χ. The ramp has real weights. Therefore Gχ⁻¹(x) is the conjugate of Gχ(x), including in the modulus-one case.

Writing Re z = (z + conj(z))/2 before taking the transform gives the holomorphic expression ∑i(ai/2)(Φχᵢ(s) + Φχᵢ⁻¹(s)) away from its poles. Taking the real part of Φχ(s) would instead conjugate the complex integration kernel and lose this identity.

For a check on the complex variable, take a real function f(x) = 1 on [1,∞). Its transform is 1/s. At s = 2 + i this equals (2 − i)/5. Taking the real part after integration would discard the imaginary part even though the integrand’s input function was real. The transform of the character average keeps s fixed in both summands.

Fix a point ρ in the strip. Let mi and mi− be the orders at this same point of the functions for χi and its inverse, assigning order zero at a nonzero value. Set

B(ρ)=∑i∈Iai2(mi+mi−)(2.10)

The family has residue −B(ρ)/[ρ(ρ − 1)]. For each zero in the family there is an index i with a zero for χi at ρ or at its conjugate. The latter gives a zero for the inverse character at ρ. At least one order is then positive. Every other contribution is nonnegative in B(ρ), so the residue is nonzero. At real 0 < ρ < 1 it is positive because ρ(ρ − 1) < 0. This is the sign of a Laurent coefficient. The example modulo 3 already shows why signs of arithmetic summands require separate attention.

Can a member that is nonzero at ρ still supply the pole?

Take one character χ of weight 1 and a nonreal ρ. Suppose L(ρ, χ) is nonzero but L(·, χ) has a double zero at conj(ρ). Conjugation gives a double zero of L(·, χ⁻¹) at ρ. At the point where we take the residue the two orders are therefore 0 and 2. Equation (2.10) gives B(ρ) = (0 + 2)/2 = 1, so the residue is −1/[ρ(ρ − 1)]. If L(·, χ) is nonzero at both points, both orders are zero and this singleton transform is regular at ρ. In each case the weight is the same. Locating the zero decides which conclusion follows.

Strict positivity of the weights alone does not produce a pole. The abstract family may even have no indices. A pole requires the witness in the zero set. In the arithmetic application the retained set includes the modulus-one character. Its weight is 1. In the finite-group coordinates of the comparison, the comparison group is a product E0 × H. A retained character has weight 1 if it is trivial on the entire factor {0} × H, and 1/(3o + 1) otherwise, where o is the order of the level. The averaging subgroup A0 can be smaller than H. In the example with four translations, take H = ℤ/4ℤ and A0 = {0, 2}. The character h ↦ (−1)h takes the value 1 on both elements of A0, so it survives the average. Its value at 1 is −1, so if retained it receives weight 1/(3o + 1). The factor 1/2 in (2.10) has the separate origin Re z = (z + conj(z))/2.

2.9What the next theorem needs

In logarithmic coordinates set g(u) = GF(eu) for u ≥ 0. For the Laplace transform it suffices to have a rough bound |g(u)| ≤ C e2u. To see why such a bound is available, each uncentered sum is bounded by x∑n≤x(log n)/n. Since (log n)/n ≤ 1, this is at most x2. On x ≥ 1 the correction terms are also bounded by a character-dependent constant times x2. Each ramp is continuous, and only finitely many contribute on every bounded interval, so the resulting g is measurable. A finite weighted sum preserves that bound.

This bound alone justifies absolute convergence of the Laplace integral in Re s > 2. The window theorem requires the integral identity on this smaller half-plane, analyticity away from the zero set in Re s > 0, isolated poles there, and their nonzero residues with positive sign at real poles. The sharper Mellin identities above hold already in Re s > 1. Every point of Re s > 0, including a point outside the zero set, has a punctured neighborhood containing no family zeros. This follows by intersecting the finitely many zero-free punctured neighborhoods for the analytic members, using the regularized function in the modulus-one case. The modulus-one singularity at 1 has been removed explicitly.

The remaining task is to exclude a pole to the right of a chosen θ with 0 < θ < 1. The window argument accepts an upper bound on selected intervals, with gaps allowed. Precisely, fix δ > 0. For every η > 0 and starting threshold Y0, it needs some Y ≥ Y0 and a function R on [Y, Y1+δ] such that R ≥ 0, GF ≤ R there, and R(y)y−θ−1 is integrable on the interval with integral at most Yη. One can take the threshold at least 1. What this chapter supplies is the transform and its pole data. Obtaining these windows is an arithmetic problem. Showing that the windows force each pole to have real part at most θ takes a further analytic argument.

2.10Two checks on the argument

1. Suppose a weight is changed to (1 − n/x)+. Compute its single-term transform for Re s > 1. Where do the denominator factors move?

Show the calculation

On [n, ∞) subtract n∫ x−s−2 dx from ∫ x−s−1 dx. The result is n−s[1/s − 1/(s + 1)] = n−s/[s(s + 1)]. In fact this calculation works for Re s > 0. Using this weight in (2.2) would change both the denominator and the centering calculation.

2. Suppose χ is real and its L-function has a hypothetical zero of order three at a real ρ with 0 < ρ < 1. For a singleton family with weight 2, what is B(ρ)?

Show the calculation

The inverse equals χ because its nonzero values are real roots of unity. Both multiplicities in (2.10) are 3, so B(ρ) = (2/2)(3 + 3) = 6. The residue is 6/[ρ(1 − ρ)]. The two appearances of χ are compensated by the half in the real-part identity.

3From formal logarithms to divisibility

The proof needs a lower bound on the powers of p dividing derivatives of a theta kernel. A derivative becomes an entry of a linear map between lattices. Divisibility of those entries at many primes contributes to the global height estimate. The local difficulty already appears for one formal variable. Differentiation supplies a factorial, and undoing the formal logarithm introduces denominators. We can calculate both at the first degree where a denominator occurs.

3.1A height-two change of coordinate

The valuation vp(a) counts the powers of p in a nonzero rational a, allowing negative counts for denominators. Set vp(0) = +∞. The inequality v(a + b) ≥ min(v(a), v(b)) will carry estimates through finite coefficient sums. An integral series has coefficients of nonnegative valuation. In formal power series, questions about composition at zero can be answered degree by degree, without an analytic radius of convergence.

A formal group describes a group law by its power series near the identity. A formal logarithm converts its composition law into addition. Complex multiplication (CM) provides endomorphisms beyond integer multiplication. For a complex elliptic curve written as a quotient of the plane by a lattice, a CM scalar preserves that lattice. Here the scalar is (1 + i√d)/2. At a suitable inert prime, the logarithm used for comparison has the following sparse shape. Put q = p².

ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 Tqʲ/pj = T + Tp²/p + Tp⁴/p² + ⋯ .

The comparison theorem assumes squarefree d ≡ 3 mod 4, CM by this scalar, prime p ≥ 5 with p ∤ d, and no square root of −d modulo p. A good model and a field identification with the completed algebraic closure of ℚp are supplied. The conclusion gives a unit ε in the closed maximal unramified field such that all coefficients of the model’s local parameter series composed with εℓ belong to that field and have norm at most one. The scalar and the direction of this composition matter.

3.2Proving the one-variable estimate

Here is an independent one-variable derivation of the loss. Take any characteristic-zero valued field extending the p-adic valuation, normalized by v(p) = 1. Since ℓ starts with T, it has a unique compositional inverse B with zero constant term and linear coefficient 1. Its coefficient bn satisfies

v(bn) ≥ −(n − 1)/(q − 1),   n ≥ 1.

Indeed B = T − ∑j≥1 Bqʲ/pj. To form degree n in a power with r = qj factors, choose positive indices summing to n. They are all smaller than n. Induction bounds their product after division by pj from below by −(n−r)/(q−1) − j. This is at least −(n−1)/(q−1) because 1 + q + ⋯ + qj−1 ≥ j. For fixed n only finitely many terms occur, and addition preserves the lower bound.

If A has integral coefficients, the degree-n coefficient of Br loses at most (n−r)/(q−1). For n ≥ 1 the constant term of A contributes nothing, so the same bound with r = 1 applies to A(B). Its n-th derivative at zero is n! times this coefficient. The exact factorial valuation is ∑j≥1⌊n/pj⌋. Each multiple of pj contributes one count at level j. Equivalently the sum is (n−sp(n))/(p−1), by expanding n in base p and summing each digit's geometric series. Since each digit is at most p−1, the deviation from n/(p−1) is at most 1 + logp n.

1/(p−1) − 1/(p²−1) = p/(p²−1) = p⁻¹ + p⁻³ + p⁻⁵ + ⋯ .

The first denominator at p = 5. Put q = 25 and choose the integral series A(T) = T. Up to degree 25, the inverse identity is B + B25/5 = T. As B starts with T, its 25th-power coefficient in degree 25 is 1. Hence [T25]B = −1/5. This attains the lower bound −(25−1)/(25−1) = −1. Its 25th derivative is −25!/5. The factorial has valuation ⌊25/5⌋ + ⌊25/25⌋ = 6, leaving valuation 5. This calculation isolates the inverse logarithm. The theta kernel also carries an exponential factor, whose mixed terms introduce the next loss.

3.3What mixed terms cost

In the multivariable estimate the derivative orders form a multi-index κ. The coefficient is multiplied by ∏i κi!. Set γp = p/(p²−1). With r coordinates and all κi ≤ a, a ≥ 1, the lower bound for the normalized valuation has the form

∑i κi(γp − σi) − r(logp a + 1).

What is a radius here? For the coefficient cν of a monomial Xν, assigning exponents ri measures its weighted valuation v(cν) + ∑νiri. A bound of zero means |cν|p ∏ |p|pνiri ≤ 1. The corresponding coordinate radius is |p|pri. Increasing ri shrinks that radius and makes the exponential easier to control. Recovering the unweighted coefficient of order κ then costs κiri. The baseline ri = 1/(p²−1) pays for the inverse logarithm. The extra σi is a choice.

The exponential explains the target weight 1/(p−1). Write its exponent as F, with F(0) = 0. If every relevant monomial of F has weighted valuation at least 1/(p−1), a term in Fm/m! has weighted valuation at least m/(p−1) − vp(m!) ≥ 0. At a given derivative order κ only monomials componentwise at most κ can enter, and the zero constant term makes the coefficient sum finite. For a mixed monomial XipαXjpβ, the extra weight contributed by the chosen radii is pασi + pβσj. The proof shows that one extra valuation unit is sufficient for each pair failing the baseline test. This gives the inequalities that the optimization below has to satisfy.

The nonnegative corrections σi pay for mixed terms of an exponential factor. Each offending monomial with exponents pα and pβ at coordinates i,j within κ requires pασi + pβσj ≥ 1. Increasing either correction helps attain feasibility and reduces the final gain by κiσi or κjσj. First bound the series at radii 1/(p²−1), increases them by the corrections to control the exponential, multiplies the two bounds, and finally uses the factorial inequality.

There are structural constraints on this optimization. The estimate assumes an odd prime, an even number of cyclic row labels ≥ 2, an ultrametric characteristic-zero field with ‖p‖ < 1, an unramified coefficient subfield, a specified primitive root, a series with coefficients in the unramified subfield, and a row-respecting integral matrix. The series must be invariant under the specified diagonal root-of-unity action. Each nonzero term has positive even-label and odd-label degree, and these two degrees cannot both be one. For each of the two prescribed additive differences of the series, exponentiation followed by substitution of the letter logarithms must give an integral series with constant coefficient one. The estimate composes an integral series with the inverse logarithms and the linear substitution, then multiplies by an exponential with sign ±1. In the frame calculation a bad pair must connect different labels with α + β odd. The radius calculation combines the bounds for individual rows, using the capacity bound on κ in the specially assigned rows. The one-variable calculation accounts for the leading gain. The next chapter identifies the global theta expansion and transfers it to these frame coordinates.

3.4Choosing correction radii on a cycle

The correction attached to a coordinate has two parts to its construction. First assign one price σs to each row label s. Then adjust individual coordinates at the rows distinguished by the frame. The first problem has an exact optimum. For the adjustment, an explicit choice with a bounded total cost suffices.

Take integers p ≥ 3 and even d ≥ 2. The optimization itself imposes no primality condition on p. Labels belong to ℤ/dℤ. Give each label a real capacity Ds ≥ 0. For each odd integer 1 ≤ j < d, an amount xs,j ≥ 0 sent from s to s + j consumes pj units of capacity at its starting point and one unit at its endpoint per unit sent. Thus the load at s is ∑j (pjxs,j + xs−j,j). Require this load to be at most Ds. Write V for the largest total ∑s,j xs,j. The zero flow is feasible. After setting unused coordinates to zero, every used coordinate lies between 0 and ∑s Ds. The continuous objective therefore attains its maximum on a closed subset of a compact box.

A feasible price vector has 0 ≤ σs ≤ 1 and pjσs + σs+j ≥ 1 on every edge. Multiply each edge inequality by the amount sent, sum, and translate the index in the incoming sum. This gives ∑s,j xs,j ≤ ∑s σs load(s) ≤ ∑s Dsσs. Equality of the optimal values yields the gain used in the coefficient estimate, with γ = p/(p²−1).

F(D) = γ ∑s Ds − V = maxfeasible σ ∑s Ds(γ − σs).

To prove equality, let C consist of pairs (b,t) for which a nonnegative flow has load ≤ b in every row and value ≥ t. This is a convex cone. It is closed because for a converging sequence of pairs, their capacities stay bounded. Truncate the witnessing flows, take a convergent subsequence in a common box, and pass the load and value inequalities to the limit. For η > 0, the point (D,V + η) lies outside C. Strict separation gives a linear functional a·b + c t which is nonnegative on the cone and negative at that point. Independent positive capacity increments belong to the cone, so as ≥ 0. Since D ≥ 0 and V + η > 0, negativity forces c < 0. Test a unit flow on each edge. Its load and value give pjas + as+j + c ≥ 0. Dividing by −c supplies prices of cost < V + η.

Clipping each price at 1 preserves every edge inequality. If either endpoint price was clipped, that endpoint alone now contributes at least 1 since pj ≥ 1. Clipping can only lower the cost because D ≥ 0. The feasible prices form a closed subset of the unit cube containing the all-ones vector, so the minimum exists. It is below V + η for every η > 0 and at least V by the load identity. Finally, every positive odd exponent j reduces modulo the even period d to another odd exponent r < d. The endpoint is unchanged and pjσs ≥ prσs. Thus the same optimizer satisfies the inequalities at all odd levels.

For example, let p = 3, d = 2 and D = (1,1). Send ¼ along each of the two edges of length one. Each load is 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. The prices (¼,¼) attain equality on both edges and cost ½, proving V = ½ and F = 2(3/8) − ½ = ¼. If D = (0,1), both flows must vanish because both use the first row. The feasible prices (1,0) have zero cost. The formula still works with a zero capacity.

From an edge to a derivative. In the two-label optimization take p = 5, a single coordinate at each label, no distinguished rows, and derivative orders κ = (500,100). The edge from 0 to 1 represents the mixed exponent pattern X₀⁵X₁. Its constraint is 5σ₀ + σ₁ ≥ 1, hence 500σ₀ + 100σ₁ ≥ 100. The symmetric prices σ₀ = σ₁ = 1/6 satisfy both directed edges with equality. Equivalently, sending 100 along the first edge consumes exactly the capacities (500,100). The minimum cost is 100. With γ = 5/24 the leading gain is 600γ − 100 = 25.

One can check that choice directly on the factorial-weighted coefficient. Suppose its series and frame hypotheses hold for this two-coordinate calculation. Including the baseline 1/24 gives weight 5/24 on each coordinate. A weighted valuation of at least zero permits an unweighted coefficient valuation as low as −600(5/24) = −125. The actual factorials contribute v₅(500!) = 100+20+4 = 124 and v₅(100!) = 20+4 = 24. The derivative therefore has valuation at least 23. The uniform estimate in the theorem gives the weaker 25 − 2(1 + log₅500) because it allows every coordinate order up to 500. The numbers in this example specialize the coefficient inequality. The kernel construction supplies its own diagram and frame.

3.5From a row price to a coefficient bound

In the frame, a coordinate has label s, row index k < N0, and a further index below N1. At each distinguished label s in a set T, the coordinates with k = 0 form its top row. Their total derivative order is ν1(s). The remaining orders sum to Ds, which equals size(s) − ν1(s) on T and size(s) elsewhere. Assume 0 ≤ ν2 ≤ ν1 ≤ size. Define the row cap Cs as ν2(s) on T and ν1(s) elsewhere. A special non-top row carries an origin u ∈ T and a signed odd shift j with s = u + j. The total order assigned the same pair (u,j) is at most Cs. Positive shifts require pj ≤ ν1(u), and negative shifts require p|j| ≤ Ds.

Let εu denote the correction on the top row at u. An ordinary non-top coordinate at s gets the optimal price σs. A special one gets max(σs, 1 − pjεu) for j > 0, and max(σs, p−|j|) for j < 0. Denote the resulting coordinate correction by ri. These maxima enforce the mixed-pair inequalities while increasing the cost only where the row price falls short.

Here is the choice of εu. Set A = ν1(u), cj = Cu+j, and let J be the least positive odd distance from u to a member of T, or ∞ if none exists. Start with the summable budget A p−j at each positive odd j, totaling Aγ. At j < J, reserve (A p−j − cj)+. At j = J reserve zero. At j > J reserve the entire budget. Write Ru for the sum of these reservations over all positive odd j. The amount left at j < J is exactly min(A p−j, cj).

Choose the first odd h < J with A p−h ≤ ch. If there is none, take h = J. Set εu = p−h for finite h, and εu = 0 for h = ∞. Positive special shifts j < h cost at most cj(1 − pjεu)+ ≤ cj, which the leftover budget covers. At finite h that budget covers Aεu, and at every j ≥ h the special surcharge vanishes. At h = ∞ the top price is zero and every used positive shift is covered individually. For finite J we also get εu ≥ p−J.

For the negative shifts out of u, let Wu be the supremum of Cu−j over positive odd j with pj ≤ Du−j, taking zero for an empty set. Each used level costs at most Wup−j. Summing over distinct levels costs at most γWu. The unadjusted non-top sum is exactly F(D) by optimality. Combining the positive and negative costs with the top contributions gives the following lower bound for the corrected gain.

F(D) + ∑u ∈ T (Ru − γWu) ≤ ∑i κi(γ − ri).

It remains to check that these corrections apply to the offending monomials. Their two exponents α, β have odd sum and their labels satisfy s + α = s′ + β in ℤ/dℤ. For two non-top coordinates with α > β, multiply the odd-shift inequality at α − β by pβ ≥ 1. Swap the coordinates when β > α. For a top and a designated non-top row, the two maxima above give the inequality for each sign of α − β. The frame’s cancellation hypothesis bounds the coefficient in the undesignated case. For two top coordinates the larger exponent includes at least the first odd distance to the other top label, and its radius alone contributes at least 1. Thus pαri + pβrj ≥ 1 for every offending pair within κ.

In the odd-prime ultrametric setting of the preceding section, the per-row cap and top-row sum bound each κi by a = max(1, maxT ν1, maxs Cs), taking the maximum over an empty T to be zero. The logarithmic factorial loss on the dN0N1 coordinates is at most dN0N1(logp a + 1). Subtract it from the left side of the displayed inequality to get the exponent in the upper bound for the norm of the factorial-weighted coefficient. This direction follows from 0 < ‖p‖ < 1. Applying this local theorem to geometric data still requires its field, series, frame and cancellation hypotheses.

The local monomial theorem next bounds a differential operator, then its frame coefficients and matrix entries. For the theta function the argument uses a decomposition with an integral factor and an inverse logarithm. It rewrites the entry in those coordinates and applies the matrix-entry theorem with sign −1. The odd-level prices therefore control the actual corrected theta series once those geometric hypotheses have been supplied.

3.6Transporting a theta function

A lattice is the integer span of linearly independent vectors in their real span. Its covolume measures one fundamental cell. A theta function on a complex vector space transforms by prescribed factors on translation by lattice points. That transformation law depends on a Hermitian form, so carrying a theta function between coordinate models requires control of both the lattice and the form.

One transport lemma takes the normalized theta function on the space associated to two admitted lattices. A complex linear isomorphism e identifies their period lattice with the target period lattice and preserves the Hermitian form. Composition with e−1 preserves holomorphicity. Pull back translation by any period x. Integrality makes its real phase parameter an integer m, so exp(πim) = (−1)m. The two translation laws then agree, including their sign. This step assumes the curve ideal, the nonzero twelfth-root normalization, the character, and the isometry. Its conclusion is membership in the target theta space. A global divisibility estimate still needs local coordinates, an integral expansion and a nonzero evaluated map.

3.7Why iterating a lift requires more than a kernel

An automorphic function is, in this setting, a function on adelic group elements with the required invariance under rational group elements and additional regularity. A theta lift integrates a function against a special theta kernel to obtain a function on another group. Write Fk for a fundamental domain and νk for its ambient invariant measure. As a model for repeated lifts, index a sequence of groups by k. One permitted step in this sequence has the form

fk+1(h) = ∫Fₖ Θk(g,h; Φ) fk(g) dνk(g).

The base function is smooth automorphic, square-integrable on the quotient, and belongs there to the prescribed starting subspace. At a step the test datum Φ must be admissible, and the integrand must be integrable for each h. Take the linear span of the resulting functions. It meets a target subspace W when it contains a member whose quotient class is outside W⊥. Even a well-defined sequence of operators can send a nonzero input to zero. This explains why a meeting or nonvanishing hypothesis is mathematically substantial. For the Galois argument one starts twice from the same source representation. In each lift a nonzero theta transform has a nonzero projection onto a target constituent. Its weight and local parameters are then read on that constituent. 4.1The normalized function on a pair of lattices

Fix a nonzero ideal 𝔠 in the imaginary quadratic field K = ℚ(√−d), with d positive and squarefree as in the host construction. Require the absolute norm of 𝔠 to be coprime to 2d. Embed it in ℂ to obtain a period lattice Λ₀. Its discriminant is Δ(Λ₀) = g₂(Λ₀)³ − 27g₃(Λ₀)². Choose a nonzero δ with δ¹² = Δ(Λ₀) and use Λ = δΛ₀. Scaling each lattice point multiplies the Eisenstein sums defining g₂ and g₃ by δ⁻⁴ and δ⁻⁶. Consequently Δ(Λ) = δ⁻¹²Δ(Λ₀) = 1. This fixes the discriminant while allowing the twelfth-root choices in the construction.

In one variable, let F(z) be the Weierstrass sigma function multiplied by exp(−s₂z²/2). Choose a representative t of a nonzero two-torsion point. Translating F shifts its argument to z + t and multiplies it by exp(−πh(z,t) − πh(t,t)/2), where h(z,t) = z conj(t)/area(Λ). Divide the translated function by its value at z = 0. The constant exponential cancels, leaving exp(−πh(z,t)) F(z + t)/F(t). Its value at the origin is 1. The denominator is nonzero since the zeros of sigma are the lattice points. In the base datum a theta vector θM satisfies a fourth-tensor-power identity with the prescribed scalar κ and fourfold kernel. The existence and nonvanishing statements use the standard model hypotheses. Form the tensor product Θ₀(z) = ∏a,b θM(z·,a,b) on a pair of standard lattices of ranks N,N′.

Let L,L′ be self-dual lattices of even ranks N,N′. Write IA,B for the operator that changes a period lattice A to B. It sums the Hermitian translates over B/(A ∩ B), weights them by the semicharacter, and divides by √[B : A ∩ B]. First move the first lattice, then the second. Write dL and dL′ for their determinant ideals relative to the respective standard lattices. Here χ acts on determinant ideals. It is multiplicative on fractional ideals whose product with their conjugates is the unit ideal. On the principal ideal of a unitary element z it takes the product of the inverses of the chosen embeddings of z. The resulting family is

eχ(L,L′) = χ(dL)N′/2 χ(dL′)−N/2 I1,2I0,1Θ₀.

Here 0, 1 and 2 denote the period lattices for (standard, standard), (L, standard) and (L,L′). It enters the jet comparison with both character powers and the two square-root index normalizations.

The logarithm substitution acts block by block, and the correcting product splits over the same four blocks. For example, choosing one column of height 1 gives ∑a Xa∂a,bΘ(0). Two such columns in the same component produce second derivatives. A repeated derivative multiplies its degree-two Taylor coefficient by 2!. The coefficient estimate holds for every permitted choice of columns and every frame monomial. The proof recovers an integral orbit factor from the established expansion, checks that each column height fits the row dimension, passes through the unit-scaled frame, and invokes the weighted bound for its product of minors. For the inert branch used in the no-extra-operator estimate, it proves an integral bound and a shape-dependent gain separately and takes the stronger of the two after the numerical comparison.

A two-row entry. Take one column of height two at one label, two source rows, two target columns, and choose the two target columns in order. The factor in the defining polynomial is det(XZ) for two 2 × 2 matrices. Since det(XZ) = det(X)det(Z), its coefficient at X₁₁X₂₂ is Z₁₁Z₂₂ − Z₁₂Z₂₁. Replacing the Z’s by derivatives and evaluating gives ∂₁₁∂₂₂Θ(0) − ∂₁₂∂₂₁Θ(0). If the two derivative valuations are ≥ B, the ultrametric inequality gives the same lower bound for this entry, including when the two values cancel. This example explains why a bound on each differentiated monomial survives the alternating signs of a minor. Establishing that a global map has nonzero image is a separate rank calculation.

The pinned proof assembles this inert calculation with different results at conjugating Frobenius, at the distinguished discriminant prime, and away from it. The resulting kernel conditions join the twisted and untwisted admissibility argument. The family-size proof uses that admissibility together with further row, counting and comparison inputs to produce the uniform divisibility hypothesis. The prime classification supplies the other local bounds. The evaluation at the base tuple uses a separate positive-dimensional quotient. The global chapter follows the remaining uniform estimates.

4.6Which estimate belongs to which prime?

Fix a word, a twist μ, a step i and adjacent lattice classes. Let p be the residue characteristic of the chosen place. The entry estimates below require the place to be free of the level. Here p differs from the word’s level prime and its two designated type primes, and lies outside the twist set Q(μ). A different condition classifies p using the arithmetic data of the host. Keeping these two tests distinct lets us apply the result to a particular matrix entry.

First come the primes dividing the host integer QS, a set which includes 2. The distinguished primes q and d each form a separate class. Outside these three classes, the Jacobi symbol (−d/p) = 1 gives the split class. Otherwise there are two inert classes, distinguished by whether the host character takes value 1. Call the first the signal class. In the last two cases the symbol equals −1 because coprimality with the prime d rules out zero.

What the integral host supplies at an inert prime

For p ≥ 5 in either inert class the construction chooses a scalar c of norm one, a good CM curve model and a Frobenius lift on its unramified coefficient field. These choices work simultaneously for every admitted pair of lattices at this prime and embedding. For each pair it then chooses an orthonormal local matrix basis. Every allowed integral linear combination of prime-to-p torsion translates has an integral power series after the formal-logarithm substitution and multiplication by the curve’s correcting exponential. This order of choices ensures that the law and correcting series agree across the summands. The proof transfers the period lattice and embedding to the curve model, obtains its Frobenius and logarithm law, and uses weak approximation to choose the local bases.

The local formulas depend on the Frobenius coordinate h in the host’s finite additive group. Write a for its additive order. If p is in the signal class, the orbit length is 2·ord(2h). In the ordinary inert class it is a. The chain assumes its split-prime bound is at least three, which puts the two inert classes in the range p ≥ 5. On level-free places the same host feeds the following calculations.

  • Signal primes, and ordinary inert primes with even a, use the all-place expansion with one correction per orbit representative.
  • At an ordinary inert prime with h = 0, a = 1. At each place label the correction begins as a two-variable series. Its variables specialize to X and εX with |ε| = 1. After substitution, one half of the signed correction contributes to the exponential, alongside a coefficientwise integral factor.
  • If h ≠ 0 has odd order a, one instead obtains an orbit product using a correction on 2a variables, a unit scale and signs at representatives. Its auxiliary root of unity has order p2a − 1. This is the odd-degree lattice-pair theorem applied to the same integral host and adapted bases.

Building the curve at an inert prime

The local theta estimate needs an elliptic curve with good reduction and a coordinate over the same ring in which to compare its formal logarithm with the height-two logarithm. Fix a prime p ≥ 5 with (−d/p) = −1 and an embedding of the algebraic numbers into ℂp. Write U for the completed maximal unramified extension of ℚp inside ℂp and W for its ring of integers. The curve construction works for this embedding and every permitted curve ideal. The global theorem uses it at inert-class and signal primes. Level freeness is an additional condition when the resulting theta estimate is applied to matrix entries.

Let 𝔠 be the nonzero ideal in the imaginary quadratic field K = ℚ(√−d), with norm prime to 2d. In the chosen complex embedding write Λ = δ𝔠, where δ12 = Δ(𝔠) and Δ denotes the lattice discriminant. The local construction first needs the ideal norm prime to p. Inertness makes (p) a prime ideal, so we can factor 𝔠 = (p)k𝔠′ with p coprime to the norm of 𝔠′. Take δ′ = pkδ. Then δ′𝔠′ = Λ exactly, and Δ(𝔠) = p−12kΔ(𝔠′) gives (δ′)12 = Δ(𝔠′). The theta section will see the same lattice.

Obtaining a good equation. Let J be the embedded j-invariant of Λ. The CM integrality theorem gives v(J) ≥ 0, where v(p) = 1. To put J in U, the proof shows inertia fixes it. A finite set of primes is discarded so that distinct roots of a monic integral polynomial for J remain distinct after reduction. Chebotarev gives a degree-one Frobenius with the same action as a specified inertia element on these roots and the same Artin class. This class is trivial on inertia. The CM Frobenius congruence at the resulting principal prime identifies the reduction of the Frobenius image with that of J. Separation makes the two roots equal.

When J differs from 0 and 1728, two CM valuation theorems give integers a,b ≥ 0 with v(J) = 3a and v(J − 1728) = 2b. Set C = 27J/(J − 1728), t = pb−a, and put

G₂ = t²C,   G₃ = t³C,   G₂³ − 27G₃² = t⁶C²(C − 27).

Since 27 and 1728 are units, v(C) = 3a − 2b and v(C − 27) = −2b. The two invariants therefore have valuations a,b, while the discriminant has valuation 6(b − a) + 2(3a − 2b) − 2b = 0. This gives the equation y² = x³ − (G₂/4)x − G₃/4 over W, with nonsingular reduction. For J = 0 and 1728 the corresponding invariant pairs are (0,1) and (1,0). In each case a change of scale over ℂp identifies the equation with the original curve. The normalized lattice has discriminant one, so this scale has norm one. The same comparison proves the normalized period invariants algebraic, ensuring that extending the given embedding to the complex numbers respects their original images.

Obtaining a coordinate over the same ring. Let LE be the curve’s formal logarithm, eE its compositional inverse and σ the unramified Frobenius. Put ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 Tp2j/pj. Inertness exchanges the CM generator ω = (1 + √−d)/2 and 1 − ω under σ. Their difference is a unit and σ² fixes ω. Using the integral CM endomorphism and a unit coefficient of multiplication by p in degree at most p², the formal-group theorem gives a unit c such that LE(T) − (c/p) · (σ²LE)(Tp²) has integral coefficients. Here σ acts on the coefficients. Choose a unit ε with ε = cσ²(ε). Dividing the logarithm by ε now gives a functional equation with factor 1/p, the same factor seen in ℓ(T) − ℓ(Tp²)/p = T. The comparison theorem gives

Θ(T) = eE(εℓ(T)) ∈ W[[T]],   Θ(0) = 0,   Θ′(0) = ε.

This Θ is a formal change of coordinate. Because its linear coefficient is a unit, its inverse also has coefficients in W. Substitution gives ℓ(Θ−1(T)) = ε−1LE(T), the isomorphism required by the genus-one datum. The host next applies its separate curve-to-theta comparison, followed by the integral expansion in an orthonormal frame. The next two arguments explain the CM Frobenius congruence and the formal-group functional equation. The CM valuation divisibilities enter the construction of the good equation.

Check the ideal and the Frobenius for discriminant −23 at 5

Take K = ℚ(√−23) and ω = (1 + √−23)/2. Its integer ring is ℤ[ω], with ω² − ω + 6 = 0. Modulo 5, the discriminant −23 is 2, a nonsquare. Thus (5) is inert and has norm 25, coprime to 46. Start with 𝔠 = (5) and δ12 = Δ(5𝒪K). The replacement is 𝔠′ = 𝒪K, δ′ = 5δ. Both choices give exactly the lattice 5δ𝒪K. In the residue field ℤ[ω]/(5) one has ω² = ω − 1, hence ω³ = −1 and ω⁵ = 1 − ω. Arithmetic Frobenius really does exchange the roots, while (1 − 2ω)² ≡ 2 mod 5 verifies the unit difference. The first terms of the matching logarithm are T + T25/5 + T625/25. The calculation uses only these local data of the host construction.

Which Frobenius fixes the invariant, and which exchanges the CM roots?

The good model and its formal coordinate use Frobenius at two different primes. To place the singular modulus J in the unramified field at the target prime p, the proof must show that inertia at p fixes J. It tests an inertia element on the roots of an integral polynomial for J using an auxiliary prime ideal 𝔮 of the quadratic field. Chebotarev selects 𝔮 outside the finite set where two distinct roots can reduce to the same value, and its residue field has prime cardinality q. The chosen arithmetic Frobenius φ agrees with the inertia element on these roots and has the same ideal class under Artin reciprocity. That class is trivial, so 𝔮 is principal. The congruence needed is Jq ≡ J at this auxiliary place. The target inert ideal (p) has residue field of size p².

How a principal ideal gives the congruence for J

Write the complex period lattice as a nonzero scalar times ℤτ + ℤ. If 𝔮 has generator α = a + bω, multiplication by α preserves the lattice. Express ατ and α in the basis (τ,1) as Aτ + B and Cτ + D. The resulting integer matrix has determinant Norm(α) = q and fixes τ under the fractional linear action. Up to a determinant-one change of basis, the q + 1 matrices indexing the degree-q correspondence send τ to qτ or to (τ + b)/q for 0 ≤ b < q. Thus one of these points τ′ has j(τ′) = j(τ) = J.

Here is why a square occurs in the calculation. Put F = E₄³ and D = Δ, so j = F/D. Form the product G over these q + 1 points of F(τ)D(τ′) − F(τ′)D(τ). The equal j-values give G(τ) = 0. To compute the product modulo 1 − ζq, use the Fourier parameter y = exp(2πiτ/q) and write B = FDq − FqD for the corresponding series. Reduction sets ζq = 1 and takes place in characteristic q, where an integral series satisfies F(yq) = F(y)q. The factor for qτ becomes B(yq). Each of the other q factors becomes −B(y), so their product is −B(yq). The two groups together give the negative square.

The modular-form expansion theorem expresses G + B² as (1 − ζq)Δ2(q+1)Q(j), with Q a polynomial over ℤ[ζq]. At τ, divide by the nonzero power of Δ. This gives the first identity below with r = Q(J) an algebraic integer. The cyclotomic binomial identity gives (1 − ζq)q = qr₀ with r₀ integral, yielding the second.

(Jq − J)² = (1 − ζq)r,   (Jq − J)2q = qr₀rq.

At every extension of the valuation at 𝔮 the right side of the second identity reduces to zero. Hence Jq − J reduces to zero there too. Arithmetic Frobenius gives φ(J) ≡ Jq, so φ(J) and J are two roots with the same reduction. The choice of 𝔮 now gives equality in characteristic zero. The original inertia element has the same action on J, as required for the good model.

At the target prime p the calculation concerns the CM endomorphism ω = (1 + √−d)/2. Let δ = 1 − 2ω, so δ² = −d. Its reduction is a unit because p ∤ d. Inertness gives (−d)(p−1)/2 ≡ −1 modulo p. The two signs remain distinct because 2δ is a unit. Thus σω = 1 − ω exactly, σ²ω = ω, and σω − ω is a unit. These last two properties enter the height-two formal-group comparison for the chosen coordinate.

Two primes for discriminant −23. At the target p = 5, δ² ≡ 2 and δ⁵ ≡ 4δ = −δ modulo 5. For an auxiliary example take τ = ω and α = 5 + 2ω. This example checks the congruence for a principal ideal. Applying it to a specified inertia element still requires the root-separation and Frobenius conditions in the first paragraph.

Why does the CM action have integral coefficients in the curve coordinate?

The Frobenius calculation distinguishes the linear multiplier α from its conjugate. The next argument uses a formal power series with this linear term. Let λ be the formal logarithm of the good elliptic curve and e its inverse. In characteristic zero, multiplication by α must act in the curve coordinate T as M(T) = e(αλ(T)). Even λ can have a denominator divisible by p. We need to know why every coefficient of this particular composition belongs to the valuation ring R = {x : |x|p ≤ 1}.

Take a CM lattice stable under ω = (1 + √−d)/2, with d ≡ 3 mod 4, and a good model at an inert prime p ≥ 5 with p ∤ d. The model supplies a rescaled lattice with the same CM action. Put n = (d + 1)/4 and let α be the image of ω. Its equation gives α(1 − α) = n. If p divided n, then −d ≡ 1 mod p, contradicting inertness. Both factors are integral roots of the monic quadratic, and their product is a unit. Thus α and 1 − α are units. Including the origin, the kernel of multiplication by ω on the complex torus has exactly n points.

What enters the coordinate formula? Choose representatives of its n − 1 nonzero points. For a representative P, ωP is a lattice point, and so is ω²P by stability. Their difference is nP. The prime-to-p torsion estimate therefore applies. In that estimate the product of max(1, |xQ|p) over the nonzero n-torsion representatives is at most 1. Every factor is at least 1, so each xQ is integral. Periodicity gives the same for xP. The good Weierstrass equation then bounds the other coordinate yP = ℘′(P)/2. For example, at d = 23 and p = 5, the five nonzero kernel points are all killed by 6. This distinction matters because the product bound uses the full 6-torsion, while the endomorphism formula sums over just those five points.

The curve’s x-coordinate has a double pole at the origin. Write A(T) = T²x(T) for the regularized coordinate, with constant term 1. The addition formula expresses the coordinate after applying the isogeny in terms of its translates by the kernel points. Clearing the pole gives an integral series V with V(0) = 1. Since M(0) = 0 and M′(0) = α ≠ 0, write M = αTg with g(0) = 1. Cancelling the common factor α²T² from the coordinate identity gives

g(T)² = A(αTg(T)) · V(T)−1.

Suppose the coefficients of g of degrees below k are integral, for k ≥ 1. The extra T in αTg means these coefficients already determine the right side through degree k. Inverting V costs no denominator because its constant term is 1. On the left the unknown gk occurs twice, each time multiplied by g₀ = 1. All remaining products have smaller indices. Thus

2gk = [Tk] A(αTg)V−1 − ∑1 ≤ i < k gigk−i.

Both terms on the right are integral, and 2 is a unit at p. This proves the next coefficient is integral and starts the induction at k = 1. Consequently M = αTg has integral coefficients.

For d = 3 the good j = 0 model has equation y² = x³ − 1/4. Its logarithm has terms only in degrees 6j + 1. The multiplier satisfies α² − α + 1 = 0, hence α⁶ = 1. The height-two proof uses two facts about this same series. Its coefficients are integral, so one can reduce it at p. Its derivative α is exchanged with 1 − α under Frobenius. The resulting difference is a unit, which is used in the two Frobenius steps.

Why the two logarithms give an integral change of coordinate

At the inert prime, the theta calculation uses the elliptic logarithm λ in one coordinate and the explicit series ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 T(p²)j/pj in another. Both have denominators. We want to match them by a substitution whose coefficients, and those of its inverse, are integral. Choose an embedding as in the good-model construction and any resulting good equation. Its invariants belong to the ring of integers W of the completed maximal unramified extension U of ℚp, with unit discriminant. Normalize the valuation by v(p) = 1. Write σ for the isometric arithmetic Frobenius on U, τ = σ² and q = p². On W, reduction of τ takes an element to its qth power.

Where the square in p² comes from. Let e(T) = [p](T) denote multiplication by p in the elliptic formal group. It has integral coefficients and λ(e(T)) = pλ(T), with λ′(0) = 1. The invariant differential λ′ has integral coefficients. Differentiation shows e′ ≡ 0 mod p, because λ′(e) has constant coefficient 1. Hence the reduction has the shape D(Tp). Let α be the image of (1 + √−d)/2. The integral CM endomorphism [α] commutes with [p]. After this first descent, D intertwines the Frobenius twist of [α] with [α] modulo p. Comparing linear terms gives (σα − α)D′(0) ≡ 0. The two roots are distinct modulo p, so D′(0) ≡ 0. For a formal group homomorphism, differentiating the addition identity transports its derivative at the origin to every coefficient of its derivative, using the unit invariant differentials. Thus D′ ≡ 0 and e(T) ≡ H(Tq) mod p. The torsion product calculation below gives a unit coefficient of e in some degree at most q. Its constant term is zero, so the first such degree must be exactly q. This degree is what height two means here.

Its formal group law gives the integral series e by adding a point to itself p times. Its constant term is zero. To bound the degree, represent the curve by the corresponding complex torus ℂ/Λ. Its p-torsion is (p−1Λ)/Λ, with p choices in each of the two lattice directions. Take one representative P of each of its p² − 1 nonzero points. Write xP for its Weierstrass ℘-value transported into ℂp by the chosen field isomorphism. The representatives P and −P each contribute a factor.

In the local parameter T = −x/y, the series A(T) = T²x(T) is integral with constant term 1. The sigma multiplication formula for the isogeny gives an integral series U with U(0) = 1 and the following factorization.

e(T)² = T²U(T)G(T),   G(T) = p² ∏P(A(T) − xPT²).

For each factor, the maximum coefficient norm is max(1, |xP|p). It is first attained in degree 0 if |xP|p ≤ 1, and degree 2 otherwise. In a product the first degrees attaining the maxima add. At their sum the product of the first maximal coefficients is the unique summand of largest norm. Thus G attains its maximum coefficient norm M = |p²|p ∏P max(1, |xP|p) by degree 2(p² − 1). Also M ≤ 1 because G = U−1(e/T)² is integral.

What forces that maximum to equal one? Choose a nonzero half-period and let h be its transported ℘-value. It solves 4h³ − g₂h − g₃ = 0. Good reduction makes h integral and 3h² − g₂/4 a unit, since the reduced cubic has distinct roots. The torsion product identity at the half-period gives |p²|p ∏P|h − xP|p = 1. Each factor is bounded by max(1, |xP|p), so 1 ≤ M. Now reduce the squared multiplication formula modulo the maximal ideal. Multiplication by U preserves the first nonzero degree, and T² adds two. Hence the first nonzero degree of the reduced e² is at most 2(p² − 1) + 2 = 2p². Squaring doubles the first degree of a nonzero series over a field, giving the claimed bound. The two descents at an inert CM prime separately force that first degree to be a positive multiple of p². Together the arguments identify it exactly.

A good curve whose first unit occurs before degree 25

At p = 5 take y² = x³ − x. Its discriminant 64 is a unit. Write x = u−2 and y = −u−3√(1 − u⁴), taking the square root with constant term 1. Comparing degree five in λ([5](T)) = 5λ(T) gives a = 2 · 5⁴ − 2 = 1248 ≡ 3 modulo 5. Here the first unit occurs at degree 5. The inert curve at the same prime reaches degree 25.

Where is the saving? The lattice estimate assumes ∏τ ‖w‖τ ≥ R > 1 for every nonzero lattice point. Use it twice. First apply it to the difference between any two points. At some place their distance must be at least 1, so the products of open radius-½ balls around distinct points are disjoint. Next put h(u) = (1 + ‖u‖)−(2n+4). Within the ball around wτ we have 1 + ‖u‖ ≤ (3/2)(1 + ‖wτ‖). This bounds the weight at the centre by (3/2)2n+4 times the weight at u. Integrate this inequality over each product of balls and add. Disjointness bounds the total by the integral over the whole space divided by the common ball-product volume.

That integral is finite in each copy of ℂn. In polar coordinates the radial integrand is r2n−1/(1 + r)2n+4 ≤ (1 + r)−5, whose integral from zero to infinity is 1/4. The one-place integral divided by the volume of a radius-½ ball is at most n4n/2. The weight W still contains one spare inverse factor per place. Here the product bound enters for the second time, now on the point itself. The product of these factors is at most 1/R. Combining the factors gives, for every finite set F of nonzero lattice points,

∑w∈F W(w) ≤ exp((6n + 9)f)/R.

Can one coordinate stay short?

In two copies of ℂ take the additive subgroup generated by (½, 12). A nonzero multiple indexed by m has product of lengths 6m², so R = 6 works. For adjacent multiples the first radius-½ disks overlap, but the second disks are 12 units apart at their centres. The product boxes are therefore disjoint. At m = 1 the spare inverse product is 1/((1 + ½)(1 + 12)) = 2/39 ≤ 1/6. This small subgroup tests both uses of the product estimate.

Return to the period. Since the summands are nonnegative, the uniform bound on finite sums passes to the sum over all nonidentity cosets. Restoring b|c|exp(Q) and using the depth condition R ≥ 2exp(Q + (6n + 9)f) bounds their total by b|c|/2. At the selected evaluation point |φ(x)| > b/2 and c ≠ 0. The identity term is strictly larger than the entire possible cancellation. This supplies the nonzero period needed at the first rung.

Which derivatives determine the lowest-type coefficient?

A matrix coefficient of an infinite-dimensional representation will be replaced by an integral on a compact group. The difficulty is to prove that the integral represents the same function. Fix G = U(p,s), m = p + s, q = min(p,s) and K = U(p) × U(s). Denote the diagonal signature matrix by J. Keep the coordinate order in which the Harish-Chandra parameters λ₁ > ⋯ > λm decrease, and record the sign of each coordinate in that order. Each λa − (m−1)/2 is integral. Suppose |λa − λb| ≥ h when the signs differ, with h ≥ 120mq3/2. When both signs occur, this gives an opposite-sign gap γ > 2m, for instance γ = h. When there is only one sign the gap condition is vacuous and any γ > 2m serves.

Let π be the unitary discrete series with these data. Denote its lowest K-type by S, with highest weight Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. Here ρn and ρc are the half-sums of the positive roots between opposite and equal signs respectively. The large-gap multiplicity-one theorem says that the sum of all copies of this lowest type is itself one finite-dimensional irreducible K-space. Write Π for the orthogonal projection onto S. We seek the operator x ↦ Ππ(g)x on S. The later branching projection in the identity term has a different target, the representation of a smaller unitary group.

Uniqueness from derivatives at the identity. Consider a smooth difference F(g) of two proposed operators on S. Suppose it transforms on both sides by K, so F(k₁gk₂) = π(k₁)F(g)π(k₂) on S, and F(1) = 0. One further set of first-order equations is required. Write Dab for differentiation along g exp(tX), extended complex-linearly to the matrix unit Eab. Arrays (vab) of vectors in S encode the noncompact first derivatives, with entries only in opposite-sign positions. Under the simultaneous compact action on the directions and the vectors, their lowering part is the sum of compact types of highest weight Λ + ea − eb with b < a of opposite signs. The first-order condition near the identity is

∑a,b Dab[F(g)vab] = 0   for every array in the lowering part.

Under these hypotheses every iterated derivative of F at 1 vanishes. The derivative of order zero is the value F(1) itself. For the coefficient below, averaging projections onto the compact translates of a highest-weight line gives I/dim S, so the normalized average and the compressed representation both start at the identity on S. Now assume all derivatives through order j−1 vanish. Commuting two adjacent derivatives replaces their difference by a bracket, a derivative of lower order. The order-j derivative is therefore symmetric in its j directions. Compact covariance removes any compact direction by differentiating the action on the input or output. The remaining derivative defines a compact-equivariant linear map T from arrays of j noncompact directions with coefficients in S to S. Applying the other j−1 derivatives to the displayed equation shows that T kills arrays obtained by inserting a lowering array in one slot with the other indices fixed.

Why must T vanish on the rest? Work in the orthogonal complement of its kernel. Permutations preserve T, so a vector f in that complement is symmetric. Orthogonality to the inserted lowering arrays says that every one-slot slice of f lies in the complementary raising part. Let CK be the compact Casimir and κ its scalar on S. The Casimir estimate on a raising slice gives a mixed term of at least (γ − 2m) times its squared norm. Summing over the slices recovers ‖f‖². There are j identical slot contributions by symmetry, each counted twice in the Casimir of a tensor product, and the Casimir on the direction indices is nonnegative. Consequently

Re ⟨f, CKf⟩ ≥ [κ + 2j(γ − 2m)] ‖f‖².

Equivariance gives T(CK − κ)f = 0, so pairing with f gives the left side exactly κ‖f‖². Since j ≥ 1 and γ > 2m, we get f = 0. This proves the induction from the assumed value F(1) = 0. The compact-type inputs here are the splitting of the one-slot array into raising and lowering types and the stated Casimir bound on each raising type.

An integral formula for the compressed operator

Choose a highest-weight unit vector w in S. Let d = dimℂ S, and give K Haar probability measure. Write Δa(Z) for the leading principal minor of size a, and put μa = λa + (m+1−2a)/2 for 1 ≤ a ≤ m, with μm+1 = 0. These are integers. Set Φ(Z) = ∏a=1m Δa(Z)−(μa−μa+1) wherever the minors are nonzero. Take a Hermitian X with XJ = −JX. Then exp X belongs to G and is positive definite, as is each compact conjugate. For arbitrary u, v ∈ S, the compression formula is

⟨v, π(exp X)u⟩ = d ∫K Φ(k−1 exp(X) k) ⟨v, π(k)w⟩ ⟨π(k)w, u⟩ dk.

Identify the value and derivatives. At X = 0, Φ(1) = 1. Averaging the projections onto the lines ℂπ(k)w gives an operator commuting with K. Its eigenspaces are invariant, so irreducibility makes it scalar. Its trace is 1, hence it equals I/d. This explains the multiplier d and makes the proposed operator agree with Ππ(1) on S.

For the comparison near 1 one uses the compact-equivariant extension from positive matrices by polar decomposition. Its local expression at a group element g uses Φ of the entrywise conjugate of k−1gk. On the positive ray the principal minors are real and this is exactly the displayed integral. Near 1 the minors are uniformly separated from zero for k in the compact group, so they may be differentiated under the integral. In the conjugated coordinates the derivative is a sum indexed by a row c and column b. Terms with b < c have zero scalar derivative coefficient by triangularity of the leading minors. For c ≤ b, the highest-weight component of a lowering array paired with the rotated vector w is zero. Thus the integral satisfies the lowering equation. The representation coefficient satisfies it as well. Indeed the map taking (vab) to ∑ dπ(Eab)vab intertwines the compact action. A nonzero image of a lowering component would give π a compact type with smaller value of ‖μ + 2ρc‖² than at μ = Λ, contradicting its minimality. The uniqueness result for derivatives now applies to the difference.

From the identity to the whole ray. Fix X and replace it by tX. On the integral side the minors depend analytically on t. At each real t their positive minimum over K permits integration of a locally convergent power series. On the representation side, the analytic-vector estimate for the lowest type gives constants B, C ≥ 0 with ‖dπ(X)ku‖ ≤ Ck(B+k)k‖u‖. Division by k! gives a Taylor series of positive radius, and unitarity gives the same derivative bound after translating along the ray. Hence the scalar difference is real analytic on ℝ. Each of its derivatives at 0 is a linear combination of the ordered derivatives already shown to vanish. The Taylor series is zero on a neighbourhood of 0. If this zero interval had a finite endpoint, continuity of every derivative and the convergent Taylor series there would extend it. The difference is therefore zero at t = 1, proving the formula.

A two-coordinate check. For U(1,1) take λ = (241/2, −241/2), so the gap 241 exceeds the required 240. The compact group U(1) × U(1) has one-dimensional types. With u = v = w, the two compact coefficients multiply to 1. Take X with zeros on the diagonal and ones off the diagonal. The leading minor of exp(tX) is cosh t and its determinant is 1, even after compact conjugation. The integral is (cosh t)−242. Its value at zero is 1, its first derivative is zero, and its second derivative is −242. At t = log 2 it equals (4/5)242. This example tests the compression formula in rank one. The subsequent period estimates impose their own dimension conditions.

Which compact types can occur in one derivative?

The uniqueness argument for the derivatives separates two kinds of noncompact directions. The distinction is visible in one derivative before we symmetrize several of them. Keep the coordinates in decreasing parameter order, and let εa be the sign of coordinate a. Put m = p + s, K = U(p) × U(s), and let S be the irreducible finite-dimensional unitary K-space of highest weight Λ. Write ea for the ath coordinate weight. The complexified noncompact directions are the matrix units Eab for which εa ≠ εb. A vector in their tensor product with S is an array ∑ Eab ⊗ vab. Set its equal-sign entries to zero.

Let this array be a nonzero highest-weight vector of weight μ. Choose a nonzero coefficient vab with maximal a − b. The diagonal action on Eab has weight ea − eb, so the coefficient has weight μ − ea + eb. To find its weight inside S, apply any compact raising operator Ecd, with c < d and equal signs. Its action on the full array vanishes. In position (a,b) that action is

Ecdvab + δac vdb − δbd vac = 0.

When a = c, the second term has index difference d − b > a − b. When b = d, the third has difference a − c > a − b. Both vanish by maximality. Thus every compact raising operator kills the selected coefficient. In the irreducible space S it has highest weight Λ. We conclude μ = Λ + ea − eb.

Finite-dimensional unitary representations split into irreducibles by successively taking invariant orthogonal complements. Group together all copies of each highest weight. The preceding calculation puts every occurring weight in one of two lists. The case a < b gives the raising part, b < a the lowering part. Distinct ordered opposite-sign pairs give distinct shifts. The two parts are consequently orthogonal and exhaust the array space. A particular candidate weight can have no summand. If one sign is absent, the noncompact direction space is zero and both lists are empty. P. Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, proposition 25.5 and corollaries 25.11 and 35.2 on highest weights and complete reducibility[5].

The Casimir on one noncompact direction

For compact matrix units write Dcd for the infinitesimal action in a representation. Fix the normalization C = ∑εc=εd DcdDdc, summing over ordered pairs, including the diagonal. On an irreducible space of highest weight η this Casimir acts by

κ(η) = ‖η + ρc‖² − ‖ρc‖².

Here ρc is half the sum of the roots ec − ed with c < d and equal signs. On a highest vector the diagonal terms give ∑ ηc². For each such pair the raising operator kills that vector, so the two orders together contribute the commutator Dcc − Ddd, with eigenvalue ηc − ηd. The sum is κ(η). This scalar holds on the entire irreducible space because C commutes with the compact action. Indeed ∑ Ecd ⊗ Edc pairs a basis of each matrix block with its dual for the conjugation-invariant trace pairing, so the sum and its product are invariant.

On the array the generator is Pcd + Dcd. The first operator acts on the matrix position by commutator and the second acts on the coefficient in S. They commute. Expanding the Casimir and exchanging c,d in one cross term gives Ctotal = Cposition + Ccoefficient + 2Ω, where Ω = ∑εc=εd PcdDdc.

To compute the position term, apply the double commutator [Ecd, [Edc, Eab]] to an opposite-sign direction. Its two middle matrix products vanish because they would require the row and column of Eab to lie in the same sign block. The outer products give EccEab and EabEdd. In the sum the first contributes once for each index in the block of a, the second once for each index in the block of b. The blocks have total size m. Thus Cposition acts by m, and Ccoefficient acts by κ(Λ). On a summand of highest weight μ the mixed operator Ω has eigenvalue

cab = (κ(μ) − m − κ(Λ))/2,   μ = Λ + ea − eb.
