How much of the weight gap survives?

For the lowest compact type, Λ = λ + ρn − ρc, where ρn is half the sum of the positive opposite-sign roots. Expanding the square in κ after adding ea − eb adds twice the difference of the two coordinates of Λ + ρc, plus 2. Hence

cab = λa − λb + (ρn)a − (ρn)b + 1 − m/2.

For a < b of opposite signs, assume λa − λb ≥ γ. Twice each coordinate of ρn counts opposite-sign indices after it minus those before it. Each coordinate lies between −m/2 and m/2. This gives cab ≥ γ + 1 − 3m/2 ≥ γ − 2m. For a general raising array, write it as the orthogonal sum of its isotypic components. The real part of its inner product with Ω applied to it is the sum of the corresponding eigenvalues times the squared component norms. It is therefore at least (γ − 2m) times its squared norm.

A check with interleaved signs. In dimension three take (+,−,+) and λ = (721,360,0). Then both half-sums equal (1/2,0,−1/2), so Λ = λ. The direction E23 tensored with a highest vector gives a highest vector of weight μ = (721,361,−1) because the only compact raising operator E13 commutes with E23. The change in the sum of coordinate squares is 722, and the change in the compact-root term η₁ − η₃ is 1. Thus κ(μ) − κ(Λ) = 723, and Ω acts by (723 − 3)/2 = 360. The two opposite-sign gaps are 361 and 360, so the uniform lower bound for γ = 360 is 354.

In a symmetric derivative of order j, fixing the other j − 1 positions gives a one-position slice. Once the lowering components have been removed, the preceding inequality applies to every such slice. Their squared norms sum to the squared norm of the whole array. By symmetry each of the j positions contributes the same lower bound, and the Casimir expansion counts each mixed term twice. This supplies the gain 2j(γ − 2m) in the uniqueness proof.

How does a gap between two weights make a matrix coefficient small?

The compression identity expresses the coefficient as an average over the compact group K. The part of its integrand that changes as we move away from K is a product of determinants. We first estimate this product at each point of the average.

Write J for the diagonal matrix of signs defining the unitary group in dimension m, and q for the smaller of the numbers of positive and negative signs. Suppose q ≥ 1. Choose a Hermitian matrix X with JX = −XJ. For k ∈ K put Y = k−1Xk and t = ‖X‖F = ‖Y‖F. The matrix Y also interchanges the two sign spaces. Let Δℓ(s) be the determinant on the first ℓ rows and columns of exp(sY), numbering coordinates in decreasing order of the weights λ₁ > ⋯ > λm. Exp(sY) is positive definite, so all these determinants are positive for real s. For consecutive weights set bℓ = λℓ − λℓ+1 + 1. Suppose the weight difference across each pair of opposite signs is at least h ≥ 0 in absolute value. Then

∏ℓ=1m−1 Δℓ(1)−bℓ ≤ exp(−(h/8) min{t², t/√(2q)}).

What one cut measures. Let P be orthogonal projection onto the first ℓ coordinates, and let A be the corresponding diagonal block of Y. Every diagonal entry of Y vanishes, so Δℓ′(0) = tr A = 0. Expanding the determinant of the block of I + sY + s²Y²/2 through second order gives Δℓ″(0) = tr(PY²P) − tr(A²). Hermitian symmetry cancels the entries with both indices in the block. What survives is the squared size of the entries crossing its boundary, Vℓ = Σj≤ℓ<i |Yij|².

To turn this derivative into a bound at s = 1, diagonalize Y in an orthonormal basis. Cauchy–Binet applied to the compressed exponential writes Δℓ(s) = ΣI wI exp(s yI), where yI is the sum of the ℓ eigenvalues selected by I. The weights are squared absolute minors of the change of basis. They sum to Δℓ(0) = 1. Thus the first two derivatives give a random variable with mean zero and second moment Vℓ. The off-diagonal sign blocks have rank at most q each. At most 2q eigenvalues are nonzero and their squares sum to t². Cauchy–Schwarz gives |yI| ≤ R = √(2q)t.

If t = 0 the product is 1. Otherwise put a = min{1, 1/R}. On [−1,1] the cubic Taylor lower bound for the exponential gives exp(x) ≥ 1 + x + x²/3. Averaging at x = a yI yields Δℓ(a) ≥ 1 + a²Vℓ/3. The added term lies in [0,1/3], where log(1+x) ≥ 3x/4 by integration of 1/(1+x). Concavity of x ↦ xa gives Δℓ(a) ≤ Δℓ(1)a. Together these give log Δℓ(1) ≥ aVℓ/4.

Why the weights add up. An entry in row i and column j with j < i contributes at cuts ℓ = j, …, i−1. The corresponding weights sum to λj − λi + i − j. For a nonzero entry the two coordinates have opposite signs, so this sum is at least h. Each conjugate pair has one entry below the diagonal, giving Σℓ bℓVℓ ≥ ht²/2. Multiplication by a/4 proves the product bound, since at² = min{t², t/√(2q)}. For example, an entry at (4,2) appears at cuts 2 and 3. The intermediate weight λ₃ cancels.

A two-cut check. In dimension three take signs (+,+,−), weights (2,1,0), and place log 2 at entries (1,3) and (3,1) of Y, leaving all other entries zero. Exponentiation gives cosh(log 2) = 5/4 on the first and third diagonal entries and 1 on the second. Both leading minors are 5/4 and both weights bℓ equal 2. Their product with negative exponents is (4/5)⁴. This small gap tests the determinant calculation before the large-gap hypothesis is needed for compression.

How many powers of the Frobenius norm are available for integration?

The integral over the stabilizer uses the ordinary Frobenius norm F = ‖g‖F. The preceding bound uses logarithms of singular values. Here is the conversion, with the constants later spent in the restricted period integral.

Lowest-type coefficient estimate. Suppose m ≥ 3 and the opposite-sign parameters of π are separated by at least h = 1000m³. For any unit vector v₀ in its lowest K-type and any g in the signed unitary group,

|⟨v₀,π(g)v₀⟩| ≤ exp(100m³) F−40m².

First take q ≥ 1. The stated h exceeds 120m q3/2 since q ≤ m. Set M = min{t², t/√(2q)}. The estimate on the compact average gives log of the upper bound equal to −125m³M. Each singular value is at most exp(t), hence F² = Σ sj² ≤ m exp(2t). Also t ≤ 1 + mM. This is immediate when t ≤ 1. For t ≥ 1 both mt² and mt/√(2q) are at least t. Using log m ≤ m, we obtain

40m² log F ≤ 20m³ + 40m² + 40m³M ≤ 100m³ + 125m³M.

Rearranging and exponentiating proves the estimate. If q = 0 the group is compact and all singular values are 1. Then F = √m, and the right-hand side is at least 1 by log m ≤ m. Unitarity bounds the coefficient by 1. This argument uses one representation. The choice of a translate with a large projection needs a second representation on the stabilizer.

Why does a translated coefficient become small away from the stabilizer?

The bottom period contains one integral for each translate. Its size depends on how far the translate moves a distinguished vector z. Start at a single real place, in coordinates where z is a positive unit coordinate vector. Write G for the unitary group of the signed Hermitian form in m = n + 1 variables, and H for the unitary group on its orthogonal complement. The embedding ι extends each element of H by the identity on z. Put ℓ(g) = ‖gz‖₂ and let ‖·‖F denote the Frobenius norm. Because g preserves the signed form, ℓ(g) ≥ 1. Right multiplication by ι(h) leaves gz unchanged.

Local coefficient estimate. Let π and σ be the discrete series on G and H in the real branching construction. Here n ≥ 3, the smaller signature has at least one negative direction and at least as many positive as negative directions. Both lists of Harish-Chandra parameters have absolute values at most B, descend in steps of at least 2 and have gaps of at least 1000m³ between entries of opposite signs within either list. The signed lists satisfy the branching condition both as given and after lowering any one entry of the longer list by 1. In decreasing order of the combined entries, successive distinct levels with no entry strictly between them obey this rule for each pair of entries at the two levels. Their signs agree exactly when the entries come from different lists.

Choose a lowest K-type unit vector v₀ in π, where K is the maximal compact subgroup fixed by the signed coordinates. Put v = π(g₀)v₀, with ‖g₀‖F ≤ (8mB)10m, and Φ(X) = ⟨v,π(X)v⟩. For the model Haar measure μ₀ on H, write V₀ = μ₀{h : ‖h − 1‖F ≤ 1/4} and ℬ(C) = exp(Cm⁴ log(8mB)). Then for every g ∈ G the restricted translate is absolutely integrable and

∫H |Φ(gι(h))| dμ₀(h) ≤ V₀ ℬ(1000) ℓ(g)−(2n+7).

Where the two powers go. The large-gap estimate for a lowest K-type bounds |⟨v₀,π(X)v₀⟩| by exp(100m³) ‖X‖F−L, with L = 40m². Unitarity replaces X by g₀−1Xg₀ for the vector v. The Frobenius norm of the inverse of a signed unitary matrix equals the norm of the matrix, since the inverse is its conjugate transpose between two diagonal sign matrices. Submultiplicativity now costs at most ‖g₀‖F2L.

Use the unitary decomposition g−1 = ι(u)b, where β = ‖b‖F satisfies β² ≤ m + 2ℓ(g)². To see the decomposition, split gz into its positive and negative parts, of Euclidean lengths a and d. Thus a² − d² = 1. Up to separate ordinary unitary rotations in these two coordinate spaces, the matrix carrying z to gz is the block with rows (a,d) and (d,a), extended by the identity. If d = 0 a rotation alone suffices. The resulting matrix T has squared Frobenius norm m − 2 + 2(a² + d²). Since T−1g fixes z, inversion gives the required factorization with b = T−1.

Where can the smaller representation be seen inside the larger one?

Its isometric intertwiner is a map i from the space of σ to that of π. Set P = i∗. Then P takes values in the smaller space, while iP is the orthogonal projection onto its copy inside the larger space.

The task is to choose a translate π(g₀)v₀ whose projection has a quantitative lower bound. Consider the nonnegative function F(g) = |⟨iw₀,π(g)v₀⟩|² and the squared column length Y(g) = ‖g−1z‖₂². Schur orthogonality says that the squared matrix coefficient of two vectors integrates to the product of their squared norms divided by the formal degree. For our unit vectors this gives ∫F dμ = 1/dπ. The model uses its fixed ambient Haar measure for the estimates below. M. Duflo and C. C. Moore, orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations[6].

∫G Y(g)F(g) dμ(g) ≤ X8m/dπ.

Here is how a column of g−1 enters. Tensor π with the dual of the defining representation. Acting on a tensor supported in coordinate l and reading its z-coordinate inserts the matrix entry (g−1)l,z. The discrete-series decomposition of this tensor on smooth vectors writes the resulting coefficient as ∑s al,s(g) over at most m summands, each with one parameter lowered by 1. In each summand, Schur orthogonality gives ∫|al,s|² ≤ X6m/dπ. Three bounds multiply here. The scalar obtained by applying the tensor projection and taking the distinguished coordinate costs at most Xm, the squared projected input with its form normalization costs X4m, and the reciprocal shifted formal degree costs at most Xm/dπ. The component estimate below derives their product.

For each l, the square of the sum costs at most the number of summands times ∑s|al,s|² by Cauchy–Schwarz. Summing over l recovers the whole squared column. The three factors from Cauchy–Schwarz, the sum over s and the sum over l are each ≤ m ≤ X. Thus the exponent is at most 6m + 3 ≤ 8m. This moment controls the mass with a large distinguished column even when left multiplication by the stabilizer makes the full matrix arbitrarily large.

The construction at a regular weight gives square-integrable models for the shifted parameters. Averaging their coefficients gives maps which together detect every smooth column. On the s-summand it has eigenvalue λs + (m − 1)/2. The eigenvalues are distinct. The product over other summands of (Ω − κt)/​(κs − κt) therefore keeps precisely the s-coordinate. This argument takes place on the smooth direct sum, where the indicated derivatives exist.

The middle bound is the one used in the moment. It counts a factor 2 whenever s is the first or second coordinate of an ordered pair. Which shifted weights give actual spaces of vectors?

In the column moment a matrix entry of the inverse of g multiplies a coefficient of π. Together they are a coefficient of X = V* ⊗ π, where V is the defining representation of G = U(p,q). To integrate its square we want to write it in terms of representations with a known formal degree. A list of candidate eigenvalues tells us how to label the pieces. We also need vectors in each piece and maps which recover every smooth column.

Regular unit shifts. Let 1 ≤ q ≤ p, m = p + q. Order the Harish-Chandra parameters λ₁ > ⋯ > λm and keep the sign attached to each position. These parameters lie on a common translate of the integers. Assume that opposite-sign entries differ by at least h ≥ 200m³. To form the sth candidate, subtract one from λs. The lattice condition is preserved. Only the gap to the next entry can close. Hence the last entry can always be lowered, and an earlier entry can be lowered exactly when its next gap exceeds one. Every opposite-sign gap after the move is at least h − 1. The analytic threshold used below is at most 43m³, so even the additional allowance m² + 3 for coefficient estimates fits inside the original gap.

The model at an allowed weight ν. Write K = U(p) × U(q) for the maximal compact subgroup. The lowest compact type is a finite-dimensional representation of K carrying a distinguished highest weight. For ν, take that type T, its unit highest-weight vector w, and its matrix kernel Ψν. The lowest-type construction gives square-integrable smooth functions g ↦ ⟨w,Ψν(g)v⟩ as v ranges over T. Start with their span, adjoin its derivatives under the complexified Lie algebra, and take the closure in L²(G). The discrete-series realization theorem for this kernel says that right translation preserves this closure, acts unitarily and irreducibly on it, and has parameter ν. Thus a regular lowering supplies an actual Hilbert space, which we call πs. The construction uses the existence and decay of the normalized kernels for the original and shifted weights.

Coefficient comparison at a regular shift. Call a vector K-finite when its compact translates span a finite-dimensional space. Let ρ(g) = (g−1)ᵗ. For K-finite v,w in π and any coordinate pair c,d, the product below has a finite expansion. In the other direction each regular model has a nonzero vector y whose diagonal coefficient ⟨y,πs(g)y⟩ is a finite sum of products of the type on the left.

ρ(g)cd ⟨w,π(g)v⟩ = ∑i ⟨bi,πs(i)(g)ai⟩.

On the space generated by derivatives, the tensor differential splits each input into finitely many eigenvectors. The central-character calculation labels their eigenvalues by shifts. The partial-trace and residue calculation removes the eigenspace of a singular shift. For a surviving eigenvector, the coefficient comparison with the model of that weight supplies one term on the right. Conversely the algebraic embedding of the shifted module realizes a pair of its vectors in tensor coordinates. Expanding the pairing over those coordinates gives the reverse identity. The embedding compares vectors in the two algebraic models before completion. G. Zuckerman, Tensor products of finite and infinite dimensional representations of semisimple Lie groups, on translation by finite-dimensional tensors[8].

How does a collision in the weights remove an eigenspace?

On the tensor columns generated by the lowest compact type, take D = −Ω, where Ω is the column differential used in the final projector. The minus sign comes from the action of a matrix on covectors. If position s survives, its candidate eigenvalue for D is as = −λs − (m − 1)/2. These numbers are distinct even when shifting a weight would create a tie. To determine which candidates are present, take the partial trace of an operator on columns, the sum of its diagonal operator entries. It acts on the original representation space.

Here are the two representation-theoretic ingredients. On the generated columns, the finite spectral decomposition of D gives projections Pb at a finite set of real values b, and each partial trace equals a scalar cb times the identity. Second, the central character prescribes the partial trace of each power Dk. Its value is the coefficient of zk+1 in ∏s(1 + z/(1 − asz)) − 1. We can compare these two evaluations using ordinary polynomials.

Introduce u = 1/z. The product becomes ∏t(1 + 1/(u − at)) − 1. Its partial fraction at as has numerator rs obtained by multiplying by u − as and evaluating there. The difference between the rational function and the sum of these partial fractions has no poles and tends to zero at infinity, so it vanishes. Expanding 1/(u − a) as z/(1 − az) now gives, for k ≥ 0,

∑b cb bk = ∑s rs ask,   rs = ∏t≠s (λs − 1 − λt)/(λs − λt).

To isolate a value v, take the union of the two finite supports. For each other value w multiply by the polynomial factor (X − w)/(v − w). The resulting polynomial is one at v and zero everywhere else on the union. Linear combinations of the power identities therefore equate the total weight at v on both sides.

One analytic fact is essential at this point. For the spectral projections here, a zero partial-trace scalar forces the entire projection to vanish. The coordinate calculation below proves this fact. In the coefficient model, testing the projection on one lowest-type vector gives the scalar as a sum of squared norms of representing vectors divided by a positive formal degree. If the scalar vanishes, all those vectors vanish. Every projected coefficient of a column supported on that test vector then vanishes. Vary the lowest-type vector and apply the commuting differential action to reach the generated columns. This positivity argument is what turns a statement about a trace into one about vectors.

If λs − 1 = λt, one numerator of rs vanishes. The interpolation and positivity show that there is no nonzero eigenvector at as. Conversely, when a lowering is regular every factor is nonzero, so the matching spectral projection is nonzero. For (6001,6000,0) the three partial-trace scalars are 0, 5999/3000 and 3001/3000. Their sum is 3, as it must be for the partial trace of the identity on three columns. Only the last two shifts contribute to the coefficient expansion.

How can a signed pairing detect every column?

To decide whether a shifted eigenspace is empty, we need a test that detects a nonzero vector even if its signed length vanishes. Write J = diag(ε₁,…,εm), where εb = ±1 records the signature of U(p,q). On an m-tuple of vectors in π put B(f,h) = ∑b εb ⟨fb,hb⟩. We take inner products linear in the second entry. For signature (+,−), the column (x,x) has signed length zero, even for a nonzero x. Pairing it with (x,−x) gives 2‖x‖².

Fix a nonzero vector y in the lowest compact type of π and its formal degree d for the chosen Haar measure. Let A(g) = (g−1)ᵗ on the dual defining representation. For derivative-generated columns define zf,b(g) = ⟨y,π(g)fb⟩ and Φ(f)(g) = JA(g)zf(g). Each coordinate is in L² by the weighted coefficient estimate for the separated original parameter. This use of the weight matters because A(g) may grow. Denote by J also the operation that changes signs coordinatewise on L²(G)m.

⟨Φ(f), JΦ(h)⟩ = (‖y‖²/d) B(f,h).

Indeed A(g)*JA(g) = J. This follows by taking inverses and conjugating the defining relation g*Jg = J, since J is real and J² = I. Thus the signed pointwise inner product reduces to that of zf and zh. Integrate and apply Schur orthogonality in π separately to each coordinate. Finally take the pair (Jf,f) in the identity. If Φ(f) vanishes, then (‖y‖²/d)∑‖fb‖² vanishes as well. This proves injectivity. Duflo and Moore, orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations, in the unimodular case[6].

Why is the partial trace a sum of ordinary squared norms?

Let P be the projector for one tensor eigenvalue. On generated columns it is idempotent, commutes with compact translations and tensor derivatives, and satisfies B(Pf,h) = B(f,Ph). Suppose its partial trace is cI. We want the sign of c. The ordinary Hilbert space where we can compute norms is the closure HP of the span of Φ(Pf). Right translation R(g) preserves this space. To see why, let V be the finite-dimensional lowest compact type. The starting space ΦP(Vm) is finite-dimensional and compact-stable. It generates every Φ(Pf) by derivatives. Indeed a tensor derivative is the sum of its actions on the matrix slot and the coefficient slot. Subtract the first action, which only mixes matrix coordinates, and induct on the number of coefficient derivatives. The tensor Casimir on these projected generators has scalar cπ+m+2z, where cπ is the original Casimir scalar and z is the tensor differential eigenvalue. Its three terms come from the coefficient slot, the matrix slot, and twice their mixed operator. Symmetry on the unitary coefficient space makes this scalar real whenever the image is nonzero. The derivative-closure theorem applies to their derivatives. In particular the ordinary orthogonal projection Q onto HP commutes with these unitary translations.

Write eby for a column with y in slot b only. Set ub = Φ(Peby), κ = d/‖y‖² and wb = κQJub. Each wb reads one coordinate of a translated vector:

vb(g) = ⟨wb, R(g)v⟩   for almost every g,   v ∈ HP.

For a generator v = Φ(Pf), its translate is the coefficient column of the translated tensor vector, since both are evaluated by replacing x with xg. The components of the translated tensor are in the closed original representation space and its coefficient functions remain in L² by right invariance of Haar measure. These are exactly the hypotheses of the signed pairing calculation. Pair this with JΦ(eby) in the signed column identity. Multiplying by κ gives exactly the value of coordinate b at g. We may first replace eby by Peby. Indeed B((I−P)η,Pf) = 0 by idempotence and signed symmetry, hence JΦ((I−P)η) is perpendicular to the closed space containing the translate. Its orthogonal projection is zero. For a limit of generators the coordinates converge in L², and along a subsequence almost everywhere. On the other side the inner products converge uniformly in g, since R(g) is an isometry. For the subsequence, choose successive L² errors at most 2−2j. The sets with error greater than 2−j then have summable measures, so their tail unions have measure tending to zero.

Computing ⟨y,(ptr P)y⟩ slot by slot gives c‖y‖² = ∑b εb B(Peby,Peby). The signed column identity makes each B on the right equal to ⟨ub,wb⟩. Expand these last inner products by coordinate. The integral comparing (ub)a and (wb)a is the complex conjugate of the integral with a,b exchanged. To see this, use the displayed coordinate formula for both functions and change g to g−1 in Haar measure. Unitarity exchanges the slots of two coordinate readers. For the mixed pair, ⟨wa,R(g)ub⟩ = κ⟨ua,R(g)Jub⟩ = ⟨ua,R(g)wb⟩. In the first equality we may drop Q because R(g)ub belongs to its range. In the second we may insert it because R(g−1)ua also belongs to its range. Conjugation then exchanges the indices at g−1. On summing, the sign εb now acts on the coordinate b inside each vector. Thus

c‖y‖² = ∑a ⟨Jua, wa⟩ = κ ∑a ‖QJua‖²,   c = (1/d)∑a ‖wa‖².

If c = 0, all coordinate readers vanish, so every element of HP has every coordinate zero almost everywhere. In particular Φ(Pf) = 0 for each generated column f. Injectivity of Φ gives Pf = 0. This proves the positivity and the vanishing criterion used at the colliding weight.

When does one shifted representation fill the projected space?

Suppose a copy of a shifted irreducible square-integrable representation has already been placed in HP. Write H′ for this nonzero closed invariant subspace, E for orthogonal projection onto it, and d′ for its formal degree in the same Haar measure as d. We can measure exactly how much of each coordinate reader lies in this copy. For v ∈ H′ every translate belongs to H′, so ⟨wb,R(g)v⟩ = ⟨Ewb,R(g)v⟩. d c − d′ = ∑b ‖(I − E)wb‖² ≥ 0.

At equality every wb lies in H′. Take v in HP perpendicular to H′. For every g we have ⟨R(g−1)wb,v⟩ = 0, so every coordinate of v vanishes almost everywhere. Hence HP = H′. For a regular lowering the formal-degree product gives d′/d equal to the residue at that shift. This proves saturation in the Hilbert coefficient space once the algebraic embedding has supplied the copy. The remaining majorant of order −(m² + 1) is integrable and its constant for fixed w is bounded by a finite sum of derivative norms of x. Since σ is unitary, the norm of the integrand is |fb,x(g)| ‖y‖. Substituting g = hu gives P A(h) = σ(h)P by left invariance. The derivative-norm estimate makes P continuous on smooth columns, so applying it to the smooth orbit of x gives the smooth orbit of Px.

Every regular model is detected. Compact-finite vectors in these discrete series are smooth, so their one-coordinate columns can enter the averaging map. Take the nonzero y in the reverse coefficient identity. Evaluate that identity at g−1 and multiply by ⟨y,σ(g)y⟩. The left side integrates to ‖y‖⁴/dσ by Schur orthogonality. Every term on the right is ⟨y,Px⟩ for one of the maps above and a column supported in one coordinate. The positive left side implies at least one such map is nonzero.

Together the maps detect every column. Suppose every map to every regular model kills a smooth column x. Choose a nonzero K-finite w in π. For a fixed coordinate c, multiply each fb,x by ρ(g)cb⟨w,π(g)w⟩ and sum over b. By the forward coefficient identity every integral is a finite sum of pairings with images of x, hence zero. Before integration, the factors ρ(g) and ρ(g−1) multiply to the identity. The single surviving coordinate gives, by mixed Schur orthogonality,

0 = ∫G ⟨w,π(g)w⟩ ⟨xc,π(g)w⟩ dg = ‖w‖² ⟨w,xc⟩ / dπ.

The common kernel is invariant. Apply the same calculation to A(h)x and multiply its vector of coordinate pairings by ρ(h)−1. This yields ⟨w,π(h)xc⟩ = 0 for every h. The closed span of the translates of the nonzero vector w is an invariant subspace, hence is the whole irreducible space of π. Each coordinate vanishes. M. Duflo and C. C. Why does one map per regular shift suffice?

Let B be the shifted model πs and T the original π. Translating B by the defining representation V raises the same coordinate back to λ. The averaging argument for this direction gives a nonzero map V ⊗ B → T. Tensor adjunction turns it into an inclusion κ from B into V* ⊗ T. In coordinates adjunction sends a map f to b ↦ ∑ded ⊗ f(ed ⊗ b), where the two bases are dual. Evaluation in each basis direction recovers f. The smooth kernel theorem makes this map injective. Indeed, if it killed a nonzero smooth vector, equivariance would kill its entire orbit span. Smooth approximation by that span controls any prescribed finite list of derivatives. Continuity in those derivative norms would then make the map zero on every smooth vector.

To bound the number of maps V* ⊗ T → B, use adjunction once more. A candidate now reads I from T to V ⊗ B. Apply I to each T-coordinate of κ. Reordering the two finite factors gives a map Φ from B to V ⊗ V* ⊗ B. Contracting the first two slots takes the trace of its matrix of vectors. This makes an endomorphism of B, hence a scalar by Schur's lemma. To see why the scalar determines I, suppose it is zero.

Write C(λ) for the scalar of the quadratic Casimir, the sum of squared coordinates of λ minus a rank-dependent constant. On Φ the total Casimir has scalar CB, and the partial Casimir on the V and B slots has scalar CT by construction of I. Expanding the square of the three-slot differential gives the sum of the two partial Casimirs, with one copy of the B-Casimir subtracted because both partials contain it, plus a cross term between the two finite slots. On a matrix of vectors that cross term is −2 times the map sending its trace to a scalar diagonal matrix. Indeed on the dual factor the generator Eab acts by −Eba. Thus on Φ the expansion reads Ctotal = CV,B + CV*,B − CB. On each row the partial Casimir for V* ⊗ B would have scalar 2CB − CT.

But the maps separating this last tensor have targets at regular second lowerings. Subtracting one in position s changes the sum of squares by −2λs + 1. A second subtraction in position t gives

C(λ − es − et) − [2C(λ − es) − C(λ)] = 2(λs − λt) + 2δst.

For t = s the difference is 2. For distinct positions it is nonzero by strict ordering. An intertwiner commutes with the Casimir, so its image of each row must be zero. Joint separation gives Φ = 0. Since κ is nonzero, one of its coordinates takes a nonzero value, which I must kill. The kernel theorem for smooth discrete-series intertwiners then gives I = 0. We have injected the space of candidate maps into the scalars. Existence from the preceding argument makes its dimension exactly one.

Choose one nonzero projection Ps per regular shift. Compositions with inclusions of other weights vanish because their central characters differ. Some projection detects a nonzero vector in the sth inclusion, hence its own projection does. Normalize that inclusion so the matching composition is the identity. Subtract ∑sκsPsx from a smooth column x. Every chosen projection kills the difference. Multiplicity one makes every map to every model a multiple of a chosen projection, so joint separation kills the difference itself. This is the smooth direct sum on which the cofactor projector is evaluated.

How large is one derivative after the vector has already been differentiated?

The projector onto a shifted summand involves a minor whose entries are differential operators. Applying the first operator can take a vector out of its lowest compact type. To estimate a product of operators, we therefore follow the spaces reached at each order.

Let π be a unitary discrete series of G = U(p,q), with m = p + q ≥ 2, and K = U(p) × U(q). Write ρ for the half-sum of the positive roots ea − eb with a < b. The same-sign roots contribute ρc and the opposite-sign roots contribute ρn. The lowest compact-type and infinitesimal-character theorems give a unique smooth compact type of highest weight Λ = λ + ρn − ρc and the full Casimir eigenvalue ‖λ‖² − ‖ρ‖². We use these statements as inputs. The discrete-series input requires a gap strictly greater than mpq + 1. Since pq ≤ m², the stipulated gap suffices. M. F. Atiyah and W. Schmid, Corollary (6.13) and Theorem (8.5), on infinitesimal characters and lowest compact types[7].

Compact derivatives preserve each layer. Each layer is finite dimensional and decomposes orthogonally into compact types. The compact weight estimate proved in the chapter on discrete-series derivatives says that each highest weight μ in Vk satisfies ‖μ − Λ‖ ≤ √2k. Each noncompact step can add a root of length √2, so the bound grows with the number of steps.

∑a,b ‖Dabx‖² ≤ 64m(B + S)² ‖x‖².

Indeed, Dab∗ = Dba on equal-sign directions and equals −Dba on opposite-sign directions, as identities of pairings on smooth vectors. Write Ω for the full sum ∑a,bDabDba and ΩK for the same-sign part. Then twice the compact sum minus the full sum gives every squared norm a positive sign. On a compact type of highest weight μ, ΩK has eigenvalue ‖μ + ρc‖² − ‖ρc‖². Thus its quadratic form on the whole layer is at most (R² − ‖ρc‖²)‖x‖² for R = ‖Λ + ρc‖ + √2k. Why do the columns of the differential minor have successive shifts?

The shifted tensor estimate needs an explicit entry of a projector. Its numerator is a determinant-like sum of differential operators. Since their order matters, begin with the exact convention. Let V be the common complex space on which the operators Eab act, for 0 ≤ a,b ≤ N. In the application V is the space of smooth vectors and the matrix size is m = N + 1. [Eab, Ecd] = δbcEad − δdaEcb.

Here [A,B] = AB − BA, and δ is the Kronecker delta. Set Tab(u) = Eab + δabu Id. For row and column lists a and b of length k, let Q(a,b∣u) be the sum over row permutations σ of their signs times the ordered product of the factors Taσ(h),bh(u − h), in the order h = 0,…,k − 1 from left to right. The rightmost operator acts first. The empty minor is the identity. Reindexing σ gives alternation in the rows.

To interchange two adjacent columns c,d, keep fixed every factor before and after these positions and pair the two assignments of their rows p,q. Write x and y for the two column parameters. The sum of the old alternating pair and the pair with its columns interchanged has the following middle factor

Tpc(x)Tqd(y) − Tqc(x)Tpd(y) + Tpd(x)Tqc(y) − Tqd(x)Tpc(y).

Expanding the factors shows exactly what the shift pays for. Put L = δpcEqd − δqdEpc − δqcEpd + δpdEqc. The purely scalar terms cancel. The mixed terms give (x − y)L. The terms with two generators give [Epc,Eqd] + [Epd,Eqc] = −L. Consecutive parameters satisfy x − y = 1, so the middle factor vanishes with the surrounding factors in their original order. Adjacent swaps generate all permutations. Thus the minor is alternating in its columns and a repeated column makes it zero. A. I. Which side of the matrix does the comatrix multiply?

Let D(u) be the full minor on the ordered lists 0,…,N. Define a matrix C(u) of operators by putting in entry (i,j) the factor (−1)i+j times the minor obtained by deleting row j and column i, keeping the remaining lists in increasing order. Its size-N minor always starts with parameter u. Let E denote the matrix with entries Ejl acting on columns in Vm. Then the identity used in the projector is

C(u) ((u − N) Id + E) = diag(D(u),…,D(u)).

Fix an output row i and an input column l. Form the full minor with its column list equal to 0,…,N with i omitted, followed by l. Group the permutations according to the row j assigned to that last column. Moving row j to the last position takes N − j switches, and the last operator stays on the right. The contribution is (−1)N−j times the minor without row j and column i, multiplied on the right by Tjl(u − N). Multiplying the whole expansion by (−1)N−i gives precisely the (i,l) entry on the left above.

If l ≠ i, the chosen column list contains l twice, so its full minor vanishes. If l = i, moving the last column back to its original position takes N − i switches. That sign cancels the factor outside the sum, leaving D(u). This proves the claimed multiplication identity without commuting the cofactor past its last factor. A. I. For a two-by-two check, the upper-right entry of the product is (u + E₁₁)E₀₁ − E₀₁(u − 1 + E₁₁) = [E₁₁,E₀₁] + E₀₁ = 0. Using u in both columns would leave −E₀₁. This is already nonzero for the defining representation.

How does evaluation select one shifted summand?

Now specialize the algebraic identity to the signed discrete series in the smooth tensor decomposition. Its infinitesimal character gives the scalar action D(u) = ∏j(u + tj) Id with tj = λj − N/2. This scalar action is the representation-theoretic input in this step. One can read off the shifts on a highest-weight vector of weight μ. In a nonidentity row permutation, take the rightmost column j whose row has moved. Its assigned row is less than j. The columns to its right have fixed rows and act diagonally on the vector. The raising operator in column j therefore kills that term. The identity permutation gives the scalar ∏j(u + μj − j). In the Harish-Chandra parameter λ = μ + ρ the jth coordinate of ρ is N/2 − j, which yields the displayed factors. The centrality of the coefficients and the infinitesimal character of the discrete series make this same scalar applicable on its smooth vectors. The tj have distinct values. A. I. On any nonzero eigenvector Y of E with eigenvalue κ, the left factor in the comatrix identity is multiplied by u − N + κ. Setting u = N − κ forces one of the factors on the right to vanish, so κ = N + ts for a unique s. On the corresponding eigenspace the identity becomes (u + ts)C(u)Y = ∏j(u + tj)Y. For u ≠ −ts cancellation gives C(u)Y = ∏j≠s(u + tj)Y. Both sides are vector-valued polynomials of degree at most N, since every cofactor contains exactly N affine factors. Their coefficients lie in a finite-dimensional span. In each coordinate these polynomials agree at infinitely many points, so they also agree at −ts.

Applied to a vector in a different shifted summand, this same product still contains u + ts and vanishes there. On the s-summand it is the nonzero scalar below. Decomposing a smooth tensor x into its summands thus gives

psx = C(−ts)x / ∏j≠s(tj − ts).

The differences are the nonzero integers λj − λs, so the reciprocal denominator has absolute value at most one. For an input supported in one coordinate the numerator is a single signed minor, the one estimated by the differential word bound. The construction uses a direct sum of eigenspaces on smooth tensors. A repeated root would invalidate this division.

A projector with a negative denominator. Take the defining two-dimensional representation, with the usual elementary matrices on basis e₀,e₁. Its full minor is (u + E₀₀)(u − 1 + E₁₁) − E₁₀E₀₁ = (u² − 1) Id. Thus (t₀,t₁) = (1,−1). On a column (v,w) the operator E gives (v₀ + w₁)(e₀,e₁), where the subscripts denote coordinates. Its eigenvalues are 2 and 0. The sum of the two diagonal elementary matrices equals Id, whence C(−1) = −E. Dividing by t₁ − t₀ = −2 gives the projector E/2. It sends (e₀,0) to (e₀,e₁)/2 and kills (e₀,−e₁).

In an orthonormal basis of the smaller space, Schur orthogonality makes the matrix coefficients of σ an orthonormal family of functions after multiplication by √dσ. This gives Bessel’s inequality and bounds the sum of squares of all entries of T by the squared L² norm of the coefficient divided by dσ. Keeping finitely many of these entries gives a finite-rank operator. By Cauchy–Schwarz the squared operator norm of the discarded part is at most the sum of its squared entries, which tends to zero. Thus T is compact.

The lower estimate is Re⟨a,Ta⟩ ≥ |⟨p,a⟩|²/dσ. One way to see why the projection appears is to average ρ against the conjugate coefficient of w₀, multiplied by dσ. This is an orthogonal projection by Schur convolution, and fixes iw₀. Its quadratic form therefore dominates |⟨·,iw₀⟩|². For a in the span of translates of w₀, a change of variables in the two coefficient integrals transfers this inequality to T. That span is dense by irreducibility, so continuity gives the lower estimate for every a.

In an eigenbasis of the compact self-adjoint T, the quadratic form at p is the sum of the eigenvalues weighted by the squared coordinates of p. If all eigenvalues were smaller than ‖p‖²/(2dσ), this sum would be at most ‖p‖⁴/(2dσ). The preceding lower estimate gives at least ‖p‖⁴/dσ. Thus there is a unit eigenvector w with eigenvalue c₁ ≥ ‖p‖²/(2dσ) > 0. Inserting b = w into the defining integral gives c₁⟨a,w⟩, the diagonal term of the period. MIT 18.102, Lecture 22, Theorem 232 (compact self-adjoint spectral theorem)[13].

The construction also gives a smooth w. The form ∫⟨y,ρ(h)v⟩⟨σ(h)w,a⟩ dν represents ⟨Ay,a⟩ for a bounded operator from the larger space to the smaller one. Its norm bound is ‖w‖(∫|⟨v,ρ(h)v⟩| dν/dσ)1/2 by the coefficient Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Schur orthogonality. Left invariance makes A equivariant. At y = v the eigenvector identity, conjugated, says Av = c₁w. Dividing the intertwiner by c₁ maps the smooth vector v to w, which is therefore smooth.

Check on a circle. To test this last operator identity, take normalized Haar measure on the unit circle, σ trivial, ρ(t) = diag(1,t) and v = (3/5,4/5). Embed σ as the first coordinate. Then Pv = 3/5 and dσ = 1. The coefficient of v is 9/25 + (16/25)t. Its conjugate integrates to 9/25, so the eigenvalue is 9/25 and the guaranteed lower bound is 9/50. This example checks the normalization of the diagonal integral independently of the large-gap estimates.

Which signed parameters give a copy of the smaller representation?

Let G = U(p,q), let z be a positive unit coordinate, and let H = U(p − 1,q) fix z. Write m = p + q = n + 1. At each position of the Harish-Chandra parameters λ of G and μ of H, record its sign in the Hermitian space and its group of origin. Merge the two decreasing lists in numerical order. The signed interlacing rule requires neighbouring entries from different groups to have the same sign, and neighbouring entries from the same group to have opposite signs.

Occurrence theorem used here. Suppose 1 ≤ q ≤ p, n ≥ 2, and each parameter is strictly decreasing in its Harish-Chandra lattice (in rank r, each entry belongs to ℤ + (r − 1)/2). Within each group require an absolute gap of at least 200m³ between entries of opposite sign. If the merged list obeys the signed rule, every pair of unitary discrete-series models π and σ with these signed parameters admits a nonzero bounded map j from the space of σ into the space of π with jσ(h) = π(h)j on H. He’s branching theorem gives the occurrence criterion for discrete series. The argument below follows the descent used for this separated range. Hongyu He, Definition 1 and Theorem 0.1[14].

Where the descent starts. Denote an entry of the merged target list by ax, and set dx = 2ax + K, choosing an integer K large enough to make all directions positive. These are distinct integers in the same order as the target. The signed frame theorem realizes the two lists of directions as an ambient diagonal operator and its compression to the smaller space after conjugation. The distant-parameter occurrence estimate then supplies an actual smaller parameter μ′ occurring under λ + t dG, with |μ′j − t dH,j| ≤ C√t for sufficiently large admissible t. Take t to be a large integer square. The displacements on the two sides are bG,i = t dG,i and bH,j = μ′j − μj. They are integers by the parameter lattices. The error from t dx is bounded by C√t + max |ax|. Consecutive predictions differ by at least t and the smallest prediction is at least t. Taking t large makes every displacement nonnegative, with bx ≤ by whenever ax < ay. Thus the offsets decrease weakly as we read the displayed lists from largest to smallest. The chosen starting pair therefore has an occurrence.

How to choose a step. The current entries are ay + by. Among the positions with bx > 0, choose the one with the smallest target entry. Lower its displacement by one. Every smaller position now has displacement zero, and every larger one has displacement at least the old bx. This proves monotonicity after the change. At either stage regularity and both gap bounds follow because monotone displacements can only enlarge a difference of target entries.

In particular, an entry from the other group cannot be the midpoint of this step. A smaller target entry has zero displacement and lies strictly below ax, the lowest possible endpoint. A larger one is already strictly above the starting value. The two ranks have opposite integral and half-integral lattices, so there are no equal target entries between groups. A step on the λ side therefore satisfies

λscurrent − ½ ≠ μjcurrent for every j.

The one-step argument below transports the occurrence across this lowering. A μ-step uses derivatives transverse to the smaller group. It assumes an occurrence before the step, admissible parameters on both sides of the step, and μj − ½ distinct from every current λs. It translates σ, proves that a projected smooth vector in the smaller tensor is nonzero by applying words in the infinitesimal operators, and uses Schur orthogonality to exclude absence of the shifted σ. At the starting pair the trial vector supplies the estimate that locates a constituent. At each smaller-group move the transverse derivative identity transfers it. Each step reduces ∑xbx by exactly one. When it reaches zero the occurrence is at the prescribed parameters.

∫H φ(h) ⟨η,π(h)y⟩ dν = κ ⟨η,iw⟩ ⟨iw,y⟩.

DsPy₀ = ΓsPη,   Ds = ∏k≠s(λk − λs),   Γs = ∏j(μj − λs + ½).

For h ∈ H, the group fixes the positive coordinate z. Evaluating the signed tensor form with first vector ezη therefore gives cs⟨b,πs(h)b⟩ = ⟨η,π(h)y₀⟩. Multiply by φ and integrate.

cs ∫H φ(h) ⟨b,πs(h)b⟩ dν = κ ⟨η,iw⟩ ⟨iw,y₀⟩ ≠ 0.

Consequently the integral itself is nonzero. Absolute convergence follows from φ ∈ L¹ and |⟨b,πs(h)b⟩| ≤ ‖b‖². The coefficient criterion below gives a bounded H-intertwiner into πs. A signed example. For G = U(3,1) and H = U(2,1), take T = 64,000 and target lists λ = (6T + ½, 4T + ½, 3T + ½, ½) of signs (+,+,−,+), and μ = (5T, 2T, T) of signs (+,−,+). The compression multiplies Pη by exactly 5/36, and the step lowers the displacement sum from seven to six.

The step from μ = 2 to 1 can now pass through 3/2 with all ambient entries clear of its midpoint.

How does a single nonzero integral produce a bounded intertwiner?

Let ρ be the restriction of the shifted representation to H. Use the Hilbert inner product linear in its second argument. For any ambient vectors a,b, write I(a,b) = ∫ φ(h)⟨b,ρ(h)a⟩ dν. Keep the irreducible square-integrable σ, its nonzero unit vector w, its integrable coefficient φ, and its Schur constant κ > 0. We construct a bounded intertwiner J with ⟨b,Jw⟩ = I(a,b).

Take the subspace of vectors y for which h ↦ ⟨σ(h)w,y⟩ is integrable. This subspace contains w, and left invariance of ν makes it stable under σ. Its closure is the whole representation by irreducibility. On this dense subspace define

Jy = ∫H ⟨σ(h)w,y⟩ ρ(h)a dν(h).

The vector integral converges since ρ is unitary. To bound its norm, expand ‖Jy‖² as a double integral and write the second group variable as ht. For each fixed h, left invariance of Haar measure leaves dν(t) unchanged. The two σ coefficients become the conjugate of ⟨σ(h)w,y⟩ and the coefficient ⟨σ(ht)w,y⟩. Their product is absolutely integrable in the original two variables and the remaining coefficient of ρ has modulus at most ‖a‖². Fubini and Schur orthogonality for σ now integrate out h, giving ‖Jy‖² = ‖y‖² κ I(a,a). This bounds J on its dense domain. Left translation in the vector integral gives Jσ(g) = ρ(g)J, and both sides extend continuously. At y = w its coefficient against b is exactly I(a,b). A single nonzero value therefore forces a nonzero bounded intertwiner. Applied to the preceding step, the two test vectors both equal the shifted vector b. How can a distant ambient representation predict a smaller weight?

The descent in the signed parameters needs a starting pair at which the smaller group actually occurs. Write G = U(p,q), H = U(p−1,q) and n = p+q−1. The subgroup fixes a positive unit vector. Choose distinct signed directions d in the big space and d′ in the small one, with the signed interlacing rule. The compression calculation below supplies a fixed g ∈ G for which the small diagonal matrix with entries d′ is the upper block of g diag(d) g⁻¹ in the subgroup coordinates.

Fix a scale t ≥ 1 at which λ + td is a regular Harish-Chandra parameter with opposite signs separated by at least 200(n+1)³. Let π be a discrete series with that parameter. Write Dab for the derived action of the matrix unit in the smaller block. For a smooth vector x define its error in following the small diagonal by

Qt(x) = ∑a,b ‖Dabx − δabtd′ax‖².

Take a unit highest-weight vector v in the lowest compact type of π. Its diagonal weights are L + td, where L = λ + ρnoncompact − ρcompact and each ρ is the half-sum of the indicated positive roots. We claim that η = π(g)v has Qt(η) ≤ C₀t for one constant independent of the scale and the chosen model. For a compact root the raising operator kills v, and commuting it with the opposite lowering operator bounds the latter’s squared norm by the absolute difference of the two weights. For noncompact roots the sum of the squared norms is the difference of the compact and full Casimir scalars. This follows by summing the signed adjoint identity for each pair of opposite matrix units. The two quadratic scalars have the same leading term t²∑ di², so their difference is affine in t. Thus every off-diagonal derivative of v has norm at most √(P+Rt) for fixed nonnegative P,R. Lowest compact type.

Conjugate the small matrix unit by g⁻¹ and call the resulting big matrix Y. Its diagonal contribution to the derivative on v is ∑ Yii(Li + tdi). The compression identity gives ∑ Yiidi = δabd′a by taking a trace. The entire order-t term is exactly the prescribed center in the displayed error. What remains has norm at most (∑ |Yij|)√(P+Rt) + ∑ |YiiLi|. Squaring, using (a+b)² ≤ 2a²+2b², and summing the n² terms proves the claim.

The density used here follows by projecting a smooth vector onto its compact types by character integration and applying the Peter–Weyl theorem. ∑i,j ‖DGijw‖² = Re ⟨(2ΩK − c)η, w⟩ ≤ A‖w‖,   A = ‖(2ΩK − c)η‖.

The superscript G includes all ambient matrix units. The corresponding sum over the smaller block is bounded by this full sum. Put B = ∑a|td′a|². For this particular scale choose F large enough that ‖w‖ is less than min(1/2, t/(4A+1), t/(4B+1)). Then the derivative sum for w and the scalar error B‖w‖² are each at most t/4. Applying the elementary square bound twice to x = η − w gives Qt(x) ≤ 2C₀t + 4(t/4) + 4(t/4). Since ‖x‖ ≥ 1/2, we obtain

x ≠ 0,   Qt(x)/‖x‖² ≤ Ct,   C = 8C₀ + 8.

Restriction to H leaves the vector and its norm unchanged and identifies the derivatives in the small block. Since its compact subgroup lies in the big compact subgroup, x is compact-finite on restriction. The approximating subspace can depend on t and π. The constant in the quotient is common to all of them.

Why does the trial vector give an actual discrete constituent?

Distant occurrence. Suppose the entries of d′ are decreasing with gaps at least one. For all sufficiently large t with λ + td admissible as above, each ambient discrete series π at that parameter contains, on restriction, a discrete series with some smaller parameter μ′ satisfying the following estimate. The constants are uniform in π. If another realization of that same smaller discrete series is chosen, it too admits a nonzero bounded intertwiner into π.

|μ′a − td′a| ≤ (√(2C) + J + n)√t,   J = ⌈C⌉ + 1.

Set ξ = td′, S = Ct and s = √(2S). The proof follows one vector through three steps. First, select a nonzero compact component whose error is at most the trial bound. Its weight ν records how the diagonal torus acts, and its compact Casimir scalar κ measures the sum of its compact derivative squares. The invariant cutoff gives the lower bound κ − 2S for the full Casimir on every unit vector in a space stable under differentiation. A vector with the original compact data survives in that space.

Next, raise the compact weight to a highest weight L at distance at most s from ξ. Now lower across opposite signs when the first derivative layer supplies the required next highest vector. Each lowering moves a coordinate by at most one and costs at least 2(t−2(s+J))−2n−2 in compact Casimir. For J = ⌈C⌉ + 1 the cost of J moves would exceed 2S for sufficiently large t. The Casimir lower bound forces a stopping type.

Finally, convert its compact weight to the parameter μ′ by the half-root shift. This costs at most n per coordinate. The three errors add to √(2Ct)+J+n, which gives the displayed estimate for t ≥ 1. At large enough separation a discrete series of this parameter exists. The isometry on translates of the terminal type puts a copy inside the restriction. The integer descent can then start at a large square scale and return to the requested pair. Hongyu He, Theorem 0.1 on signed branching[14].

Constructing a compression with the prescribed signs

Let D = diag(di) in a basis of squared lengths εi = ±1. Seek a positive unit normal z so that the compression of D to z⊥ has the specified eigenvalues d′a and signs ε′a. In the merged decreasing list all values are distinct. Multiply each sign coming from the smaller group by −1. The signed interlacing rule says these modified signs alternate. There are n+1 positive modified signs and n negative ones, so the first sign is positive.

Form the two monic polynomials P(X) = ∏i(X−di) and R(X) = ∏a(X−d′a). Canceling each pole gives the partial fractions below. After multiplication by P, both sides agree at all n+1 roots of P and have degree at most n, proving equality. Leading coefficients give ∑ ci = 1.

R(X)/P(X) = ∑i ci/(X−di),   ci = R(di)/P′(di).

The sign of ci is (−1) to the number of entries above di, by counting negative factors. Thus it equals εi. Take zi = √|ci|. Its signed squared norm is ∑ ci = 1. For each small root u = d′a put v(u) = (uI−D)⁻¹z. Its pairing with z is R(u)/P(u) = 0. Since Dv(u) = uv(u) − z, its projection onto z⊥ is uv(u). Distinct roots give orthogonal vectors by self-adjointness of the compression. Their signed squared norms are ∑ ci/(u−di)² = −R′(u)/P(u). Counting signs of factors again gives ε′a, including the minus sign for the small group. Normalize these n vectors and append z at the distinguished positive coordinate. The inverse of this isometric basis change is the g required in the moment calculation.

For U(2,1) take the big directions (5,4,3) with signs (+,−,+), and the small directions (2,1) with signs (+,−). The residues of (X−2)(X−1)/((X−5)(X−4)(X−3)) are 6, −6 and 1. The normal (√6,√6,1) has signed squared norm 1. The two vectors from the resolvent have signed squared norms 1/6 and −1/24. Thus both the eigenvalues and the signature of the compressed block can be read directly from this one rational function. For these directions take λ = (2,1,0). At every sufficiently large integer t, the ambient parameter λ + t(5,4,3) has minimum opposite-sign gap t + 1. The occurrence estimate then gives a constituent within C√t of (2t,t) in each coordinate.

Which compact component inherits the trial bound?

The trial estimate bounds the sum of the squared errors in all matrix directions at once. The first task is to find a vector with one definite weight to which the estimate still applies. Write μ = td′, S = Ct, and let Dab act in the smooth restricted representation. The full Casimir Ω sums DabDba over the smaller group. Its compact counterpart ΩK sums only over pairs with the same sign. On a finite-dimensional compact-stable space containing the trial vector x, ΩK and all diagonal derivatives are commuting Hermitian operators. A diagonal commutator assigns the opposite weights to Dab and Dba, so their product has weight zero.

Decompose x into joint eigenvectors, grouping components with identical eigenvalues. To see why their energies add, expand the sum of derivative squares as a quadratic form. Its operator on smooth vectors is 2ΩK − Ω − 2∑a μaDaa + ‖μ‖²I. The signed adjoint of each matrix unit gives the first two terms. Ω commutes with every derived matrix unit, by cancellation in the commutator with the sum defining Ω. Thus this energy operator preserves all joint eigenvalues. Different joint eigenspaces are orthogonal, so their cross terms vanish even when the energy operator takes a vector outside the finite space. Simultaneous diagonalization here follows by diagonalizing one Hermitian operator and repeating on its invariant eigenspaces for the others.

Consequently the quotient for x is a weighted average of the component quotients, with weights proportional to the squared norms. Choose a nonzero component y with quotient at most S. Write ν for its diagonal weight and κ for its compact Casimir eigenvalue. The three contributions to its quotient are

Qμ(y)/‖y‖² = ‖ν−μ‖² + (κ−‖ν‖²) + Re ⟨(κI−Ω)y, y⟩/‖y‖².

The first term is the diagonal error. The second sums squared compact off-diagonal derivatives divided by ‖y‖². The third does the same for the opposite-sign derivatives. Each is nonnegative and at most S. The last inequality gives control on this one vector. Following a sequence of derivatives will require a bound throughout an invariant subspace.

A compact calculation. In the defining action of U(2) on ℂ² take μ = (1,0). Here Ω = ΩK = 2I, because ∑a,b EabEba = 2I. Both coordinate vectors have compact off-diagonal energy 1 and noncompact energy 0. Their diagonal errors are respectively 0 and 2, giving total quotients 1 and 3. The trial vector e₁+e₂ has quotient 2. Taking its first joint component improves the bound while fixing the weight.

A bounded inverse on the Hilbert space

Fix κ from the selected component and put U = κI − Ω. Work on the dense space of smooth vectors in the Hilbert space of the restricted representation. Write R = 2S > 0. In finite dimensions the function 1/(1+(u/R)²) is large near u = 0 and small far away. To use the same idea for the possibly unbounded derivative U, first construct a bounded operator T from

B = I + U²/R²,   Re ⟨Bz, z⟩ = ‖z‖² + ‖Uz‖²/R².

The identity follows from symmetry of Ω on smooth vectors. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖Bz‖ ≥ ‖z‖, so the assignment Bz ↦ z is a well-defined contraction. Why is the range of B dense? Let M be the closure of the range of B and Q its orthogonal projection. A group translation conjugates the two matrix units in each Casimir term. The tensor ∑ Eab ⊗ Eba is invariant under simultaneous conjugation because these bases are dual for the invariant trace pairing tr(XY). Thus translations preserve the range, and their inverses do too. Unitarity gives invariance of M and its perpendicular, so Q commutes with the group. R. Melrose, Functional Analysis, §9 on closed subspaces[16].

Any bounded operator commuting with the group takes smooth orbit maps to smooth orbit maps. Differentiation shows that it commutes with each derivative, hence with B on smooth vectors. For such z this gives BQz = QBz = Bz. Injectivity of B forces Qz = z. By density, M is the whole Hilbert space. Extend the contraction Bz ↦ z by taking limits of Cauchy sequences. The resulting operator T is self-adjoint because ⟨z, Bw⟩ = ⟨Bz, w⟩, and it commutes with the group by the same dense-range argument. On smooth vectors we therefore have both TBz = z and BTz = z.

A Casimir bound on every smooth vector of the cut

In the finite-dimensional picture a derivative eigenvalue u with |u| ≤ R gives an inverse eigenvalue at least 1/2. Use this threshold on the bounded self-adjoint operator T. Let A = T − ½I, and form its positive and negative parts P = max(A,0), N = max(−A,0). The continuous functional calculus assigns operators to these scalar functions by uniform polynomial approximation on the spectrum. It respects multiplication, takes the square of a real function to the square of a self-adjoint operator, and preserves commutation with group translations. Applying these facts to the two functions and to their square roots gives A = P − N, NP = 0, and both parts positive. R. Melrose, Functional Analysis, Theorem 3.5 and Remark 3.1[17].

Let W consist of the smooth vectors killed by N. It is stable under every derivative because N commutes with the group. For z in W, also Bz belongs to W. On that vector A equals its positive part. The identity TBz = z gives ½‖Bz‖² ≤ Re ⟨z, Bz⟩ ≤ ‖z‖ ‖Bz‖. Thus ‖Bz‖ ≤ 2‖z‖. Substitution in the preceding square identity yields

‖Uz‖ ≤ R‖z‖,   Re ⟨Ωz, z⟩ ≥ (κ−2S)‖z‖²   (z ∈ W).

This lower bound will apply at every step when roots move the starting weight. The existence of a starting vector in W still requires the estimate on y.

Why a vector of the original weight survives

Restrict the calculation to the smooth eigenspace ΩK = κ. There U is nonnegative as a quadratic form because its expectation is the sum of the squared opposite-sign derivatives. Both U and T preserve this eigenspace. Put V = U/R and x = Ty, so that y = (I+V²)x. The scalar inequality 1−1/(1+v²) ≤ v/2 for v ≥ 0 follows after clearing the denominator from v(1−v)² ≥ 0. On smooth vectors there is a direct version with no choice of eigenbasis. Put w = (I−V)x. Expansion using symmetry of V gives

Re ⟨Vy, y⟩ − 2 Re ⟨y−x, y⟩ = Re ⟨Vw, w⟩ + Re ⟨V(Vw), Vw⟩ ≥ 0.

Because Re ⟨Uy, y⟩ ≤ S‖y‖² and R = 2S, we get Re ⟨Ty, y⟩ ≥ ¾‖y‖². Hence Re ⟨Ay, y⟩ is strictly positive. If Py vanished, this expectation would equal −⟨Ny, y⟩ ≤ 0. Thus Py is nonzero, and NP = 0 places it in W. Applying P to the finite compact-stable space of y gives another finite compact-stable space. Commutation with derivatives shows that Py has weight ν and compact Casimir κ. These facts supply the starting vector for compact raising.

The constant ¾ is attained when U/R = diag(0,1) and y = (1,1). The two inverse eigenvalues are 1 and ½, so their mean is ¾. The middle coordinate in the example below has U/R = 1. It is retained by the kernel condition, while the coefficient of this coordinate in Py is zero. The distinction matters because the theorem uses the entire stable space for subsequent derivatives and a single nonzero vector to start them.

A compact highest vector within square-root distance

Take the surviving vector of weight ν in the cutoff W. A compact raising move applies a derivative Dab with a < b of the same sign, provided the resulting vector is nonzero. Its new weight is ω + ea − eb when the old one is ω. This follows by commuting the derivative with each diagonal unit. If F is the finite compact span of y, the starting vector Py lies in P(F). Every subsequent compact derivative stays in that finite-dimensional compact-stable space, which is contained in W because NP = 0. They preserve the compact Casimir eigenvalue κ because ΩK commutes with compact derivatives.

At any visited weight ω, the diagonal derivative squares are part of the sum defining κ on that vector, so ‖ω‖² ≤ κ. Meanwhile ∑c cωc decreases by b−a ≥ 1 at each move. It has a lower bound on the ball ‖ω‖ ≤ √κ. The chain must end at a nonzero vector annihilated by every compact raising operator. Call its highest weight L. Each move increases the pairing with the decreasing target μ by μa − μb ≥ 0. Expanding the square now controls how far the final weight can be from μ.

‖L−μ‖² = ‖ν−μ‖² + ‖L‖² − ‖ν‖² − 2⟨L−ν, μ⟩ ≤ S + (κ−‖ν‖²) ≤ 2S.

The two terms bounded by S are precisely the diagonal and compact off-diagonal errors already available before the cutoff. Their sum was itself bounded by S in the original energy decomposition. The separate estimates suffice for the radius √(2S) used in the descent. We have found a compact highest vector at coordinate distance at most s = √(2S) from the target. Its compact Casimir scalar is cK(L) = ‖L+ρK‖² − ‖ρK‖² = κ, where ρK is the half-sum of the positive compact roots. Indeed, in the Casimir sum the diagonal terms contribute ‖L‖², and each positive compact root contributes La−Lb by commuting the raising operator to the right.

Why opposite-sign lowering must stop

A compact highest vector lies in a finite sum of irreducible compact types. Within its finite compact span, the orthogonal complement of any stable subspace is stable by the compact adjoint relations. Splitting repeatedly gives irreducible summands. Projecting the highest vector onto one where it is nonzero preserves its weight and all its raising equations. Start with this type inside the invariant cutoff W. For a type of highest weight M, its first layer is spanned by the type and the vectors obtained by applying one noncompact derivative. Commuting a compact derivative past a noncompact derivative shows this layer is compact-stable and finite-dimensional.

If the layer contains a nonzero compact highest vector of weight M − ea + eb for a < b of opposite signs, select its irreducible summand and continue. All these spaces lie in W. Each coordinate changes by at most one on each move. Assume μa − μb ≥ τ for all a < b. For up to J moves every coordinate is within s+J of μ, so Ma−Mb ≥ τ−2(s+J). On subtracting the root α = ea − eb, expand the compact scalar to obtain

cK(M) − cK(M−α) = 2⟨M+ρK, α⟩−2 ≥ 2(τ−2(s+J))−2n−2.

Here ‖α‖² = 2 and each coordinate of ρK has absolute value at most n/2 by counting compact roots. Write h for the lower bound in the display. The full Casimir expectation on every unit highest vector in W is at least κ−2S, and its compact Casimir is at least this expectation by the noncompact square identity. After J moves the compact scalar would be at most κ−Jh. If Jh > 2S this is impossible. A terminal type therefore occurs in fewer than J moves, with highest weight L′ within s+J of μ in each coordinate. For example, with n = 2, τ = 1000 and S = 2 one can take J = 1. A single lowering would decrease the compact scalar by at least 1982 while the cutoff permits at most 4. Under those hypotheses the first compact type already has the terminal property.

To recover the parameter, each coordinate of L′ is an integer. Indeed the corresponding diagonal circle acts on that weight by exp(iθL′a), which is periodic with period 2π. Put μ′ = L′ + ρK − ρnoncompact. Each half-sum has coordinates bounded by n/2, and their difference has the required parity. In coordinate a, subtracting (n−1)/2 from the difference yields minus the number of earlier coordinates of the same sign minus the number of later coordinates of the opposite sign. In particular each μ′a belongs to ℤ+(n−1)/2. The separation assumption ensures strict decreasing order and enough gap for the representation theorem.

μ′a−μ′b ≥ τ−2(s+J)−2n   (a < b),   |μ′a−μa| ≤ s+J+n.

In the distant-parameter argument τ ≥ n³ + 4n + 2 + 2(s+J). The gap in the display exceeds n³ + 2n + 1. The identification of the terminal type uses precisely the absence of these highest vectors in the first layer. Its conclusion embeds every discrete-series model at μ′. To obtain an actual constituent one also needs such a model to exist. The large-gap existence step supplies such a model once the scale is sufficiently large. A. Knapp and P. Trapa, Representations of Semisimple Lie Groups, Lecture 7, Harish-Chandra’s discrete-series theorem[18].

Which Casimir eigenvalue does the stopping type carry?

The descent inside the spectral subspace has found a finite-dimensional compact type V among the smooth vectors of the restricted representation τ. Its stopping weight L′ and the parameter μ′ constructed from it will be written L and μ throughout this identification. Write H = U(r,s), n = r+s and K = U(r) × U(s). Order the coordinates by decreasing parameter. The first derivative layer is the span of V and all EabV for coordinates of opposite signs. The stopping condition says that this layer contains no nonzero compact highest vector of weight L−(ea−eb) for any such pair a < b.

Write ρc and ρn for the half-sums of compact and noncompact positive roots, and ρ = ρc+ρn for the full half-sum. The candidate parameter is μ = L−ρn+ρc. Casimir of the stopping type. If μ is strictly decreasing and the stopping condition holds, every v ∈ V satisfies

Ωv = (‖μ‖² − ‖ρ‖²)v.

To see how the absence of a lower weight determines a scalar, introduce an exterior algebra S with a generator for each pair consisting of a positive coordinate and a negative coordinate. Exterior multiplication adds a generator and contraction removes it. The spinor highest-weight lemma for this exterior tensor supplies a nonzero tensor x ∈ V ⊗ S of compact highest weight β = μ−ρc+θ for the diagonal compact action. Here θ has value s/2 on positive coordinates and −r/2 on negative ones. The two halves of the Dirac operator pair one noncompact derivative with exterior multiplication or contraction. Both preserve the diagonal compact highest-weight equations. On the representation factor they change the sum of the positive-coordinate weights by −1 and +1 respectively.

The first-layer weight lemma used at this point is as follows. At diagonal highest weight β, a nonzero tensor in the first layer with changed positive-coordinate sum would supply a compact highest vector of weight L−(ea−eb) for opposite signs and a < b. Indeed, expand the tensor in the exterior basis and choose a nonzero coefficient whose exterior weight has least dot product with μ. The compact raising equations force this coefficient to be highest because an additional term would come from a strictly smaller dot product. The first layer allows the original weight or a change by one noncompact root. The changed positive-coordinate sum excludes the original weight. An upward change by ea−eb with a < b would put the exterior weight at θ−ρn−(ea−eb). Its dot product with μ would be smaller than the minimum ⟨θ−ρn,μ⟩. To find that minimum, sum the negative values μi−μa over positive coordinates i and negative coordinates a. These are precisely the exterior generators to include in a subset with least dot product. The surviving possibility is exactly the forbidden lowering. Applying this lemma to each half gives Dx = 0.

In this exterior model the Dirac square acts on the tensor of highest weight β by 2D²x = −(Ω ⊗ 1)x + (‖β+ρc‖²−‖ρc‖²−2⟨θ,β⟩)x. This is the compact Casimir minus the full Casimir with the displayed correction for the exterior action. Each sign block of ρc sums to zero, so ⟨θ,ρc⟩ = 0. Ordering the positive coordinates first and the negative coordinates next gives the vector ρc+θ as a permutation of ρ, so ‖ρ‖² = ‖ρc‖²+‖θ‖². Substitution gives (Ω ⊗ 1)x = (‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖²)x. At least one exterior coordinate of x is nonzero, so at least one vector of V has this eigenvalue. Its eigenspace inside V is compact-stable because Ω commutes with every compact derivative. Irreducibility of V makes that eigenspace all of V. The factor 2 and the term involving θ come from the exterior-action convention in this calculation. For the twisted Dirac square and its specialization after the weight shift, see R. Parthasarathy, Proposition 3.1[19] and Proposition 3.2[20].

For U(1,1), take signs (+,−) and μ = (41/2,−39/2). Here ρc = 0 and θ = ρn = ρ = (1/2,−1/2), so L = β = (21,−20). The compact scalar in the tensor is 21²+20² = 841. The linear correction is 2⟨θ,β⟩ = 41. The resulting 800 agrees with (41²+39²−2)/4. This checks the scalar at a stopping type of these weights. The root descent supplies the stopping condition in the occurrence proof.

Why do the two compact types have matching coefficients on the whole group?

Keep the regular parameter μ of the stopping type. First we need at least one discrete series with that signed parameter. The large-gap existence theorem for U(r,s) applies to a regular parameter on its Harish-Chandra lattice whenever its opposite-sign gaps exceed 8n²+2n. At a distant scale t, the centers of two distinct coordinates differ by at least t, and each coordinate of μ is within C√t of its center. Their gap therefore exceeds the existence threshold for all sufficiently large t. We can now fix any unitary discrete-series model σ of H with that parameter. Its lowest compact type W has the same highest weight L. The discrete-series parameter theorem gives the Casimir scalar ‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖² on its smooth vectors. On the restricted ambient representation τ the stopping-type calculation gives the same scalar on V. The highest-weight classification on the two compact unitary factors gives a compact intertwiner from V onto W. Its adjoint times itself is a positive scalar by irreducibility, so it can be rescaled to a unitary map φ. Hongyu He, signed Harish-Chandra parameters[21] · P. Etingof, highest weights for the general linear group, §27[22].

Matching the compact types has so far determined their inner products only at compact group elements. The parameter gap now does additional work. The orthogonality lemma for a separated lowest type has the following hypotheses. In a unitary representation take a smooth, compact-stable irreducible type of weight μ+ρn−ρc on which Ω has the prescribed scalar. Require every gap across signs to exceed nrs+1. If a compact intertwiner from this type into the Hilbert space has image orthogonal to the type, its image is orthogonal to every group translate of the type. The preceding descent yields gaps exceeding n³+2n+1 for μ, which suffices. The finite-layer estimate and the passage to translated orthogonality below prove the lemma from the one-position and analytic estimates.

Apply it to the direct sum τ ⊕ σ. Inside that sum take the diagonal compact type of vectors (v,φv). It has scalar ‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖² because both components do. The map (u,φu) ↦ (u,−φu) commutes with the compact action and has image orthogonal to the diagonal, since φ preserves inner products. The lemma gives orthogonality to (τ(g)v,σ(g)φv) for every g ∈ H. Taking the difference of the two component pairings gives

⟨u,τ(g)v⟩ = ⟨φu,σ(g)φv⟩   (u,v ∈ V).

At the identity this says that φ preserves inner products. At arbitrary g it describes how far translates of the compact type point in each of its original directions. Those values determine the lengths of finite sums of translates, which is what allows the compact map to extend to the required Hilbert spaces.

How do equal coefficients put the smaller representation inside the restriction?

Let Cτ be the closed span of vectors τ(g)v with v ∈ V and g ∈ H. Define Cσ in the same way using φV = W. For a finite list of pairs (gi,vi), let xi = τ(gi)vi and yi = σ(gi)φvi. By unitarity the inner product of xi and xj is the coefficient of gi⁻¹gj on vi, vj. The coefficient identity gives the same entry for the two y vectors. Write M for this common matrix of inner products. Then

‖∑ aixi‖² = a*Ma = ‖∑ aiyi‖².

A relation among the x vectors has squared norm zero, hence gives a relation among the y vectors. Subtracting two presentations shows that sending each x to its matching y defines a linear map on the span. The same identity makes it an isometry. It extends by completion to U from Cτ to Cσ. Its image is complete and contains the dense span of the y vectors, so it is onto. Left multiplication by h sends every label (g,v) to (hg,v) on both sides. Thus U intertwines on the spans and, by continuity, on their closures. This norm argument is the same one used to recover a cyclic representation from its coefficients. K. Kremnizer, Gelfand–Naimark–Segal construction, Theorem 4.1[23].

On the model side, Cσ is closed, invariant and contains the nonzero space W. Irreducibility of σ makes it its entire Hilbert space. On the ambient side, Cτ is precisely the closure generated from V by derivative words. One inclusion uses the analytic-vector invariance theorem. For these compact-finite smooth data with fixed Casimir, the derivative closure is group-invariant and contains V. For the reverse inclusion, a smooth vector in a closed invariant subspace has every real derivative in that subspace by difference quotients. Complex linearity and repetition put every derivative word on V in Cτ.

j = inclusion ∘ U⁻¹,   jσ(h) = τ(h)j.

This is the direction needed in branching. The source of j is the whole discrete series. Its image is a closed copy of that series in the restricted ambient space. The construction works for each chosen model of μ. The coefficient test can now start with this map.

Three generators of a plane. In a two-dimensional Euclidean model let y₁, y₂, y₃ be unit vectors at angles 0°, 120° and 240°. In ℝ³ take x₁ = (2,−1,−1)/√6 and its two cyclic permutations in order. Each family has diagonal inner products 1 and off-diagonal inner products −1/2. The relation with all three coefficients equal to 1 has zero norm in both families. Every permutation of the three labels acts by an isometry on each plane. The map j sends yi to xi and intertwines those permutations. In the ambient ℝ³ its image is exactly the plane of coordinate sum zero. This example isolates the role of relations, the direction of the embedding and its possible proper image.

Can the original highest weight appear again in a later derivative layer?

The comparison of compact types uses a fact about one representation. Let V be a nonzero irreducible smooth compact type of H = U(r,s), with highest weight L = μ+ρn−ρc and full Casimir scalar ‖μ‖²−‖ρ‖². Assume μ is strictly decreasing, the opposite-sign gaps are at least h, and h > nrs+1 with n = r+s. The claim is that every compact highest vector of weight L among the derivative words on V already belongs to V.

Set F₀ = V. Build Fk+1 by adding to Fk all vectors Eabu, with u ∈ Fk and a,b of opposite signs. Each layer is finite-dimensional. Commuting a same-sign matrix unit past an opposite-sign unit introduces only opposite-sign units, so induction shows that all layers are stable under compact derivatives. Every derivative word belongs to some layer. Let Pk be the orthogonal projection onto Fk. The adjoint of a compact matrix unit is again a compact matrix unit, so the perpendicular of each layer is compact-stable as well. The projections commute with the compact derivatives and preserve the highest-weight equations. P. Etingof, compact orthogonal complements, §2.1[24].

Write cK(γ) = ‖γ+ρc‖²−‖ρc‖² for the compact Casimir of highest weight γ. The quantitative estimate needed here concerns a nonzero compact highest vector w in Fk orthogonal to Fk−1, with k ≥ 1 and highest weight γ. It gives

cK(γ) − cK(L) ≥ 2k(h−n+1).

To obtain the factor k, represent w modulo the previous layer by an array A of coefficients in V, indexed by words of exactly k noncompact matrix units. Applying the words and projecting off Fk−1 maps these arrays onto the new orthogonal layer. Choose the preimage perpendicular to the kernel. The map respects the compact action, so its restriction to the kernel’s perpendicular is an isomorphism of compact modules. Hence A is nonzero and has highest weight γ.

Apply the mixed Casimir estimate for a single position. In this perpendicular space, the mixed term between the compact action on V and the action on any one word position has expectation at least (h−n+1)‖A‖². More explicitly, hold all the other positions fixed. In this one-position space the mixed operator splits into negative and positive eigenspaces, with positive eigenvalues ≥ h−n+1. The evaluation of a negative slice shows that an array with only negative components at that position evaluates into the previous layer. Test the chosen A against its own negative component, supported on just the fixed slice. This test lies in the kernel just removed. Their inner product is the squared norm of that component, hence is zero. Only positive slices remain. Summing their squared norms over all choices of the other positions gives ‖A‖². Expand the compact Casimir for the diagonal action on the array. Its part on V contributes cK(L)‖A‖². Its part on the word indices is nonnegative, being a sum of squared norms. Twice the mixed expectation occurs at each of the k positions. The total expectation is cK(γ)‖A‖² because A is highest. Dividing by ‖A‖² proves the estimate.

Now let u have weight L and satisfy the compact highest-weight equations in some Fm. Decompose it as P₀u plus the successive differences (Pk−Pk−1)u. A nonzero difference would again be highest of weight L. Its compact Casimir would have to exceed the same scalar by 2k(h−n+1). This is positive when both signature indices are nonzero, since then rs ≥ 1. If one index is zero there are no noncompact derivatives at all. In either case u = P₀u ∈ V.

A rank-two calculation. Continue the U(1,1) example with L = (21,−20) and gap 40. Take an orthonormal sequence e₀, e₁, … of weights (21+j,−20−j). Set E₁₂ej = √((j+1)(41+j)) ej+1 and E₂₁ = −E₁₂*. Their commutator on ej is (41+2j)ej, as required by the two diagonal weights. Starting with e₀, layer k is the span through ek. Its new line has compact Casimir increment 82k+2k², compared with the lower bound 78k. For k = 1 these numbers are 84 and 78. The full Casimir stays 800 because the two noncompact products cancel the growth of the compact scalar.
