How does one short representative bound the number of lines?

Let L be an integral full lattice in a totally positive definite Hermitian E-space of rank k ≥ 1. We count the rational lines U for which L ∩ U has discriminant order n ≥ 1. This intersection is a full lattice on U. It is finitely generated as a submodule of L, and clearing the denominators of any vector of U brings a nonzero scalar multiple into L. The short-vector theorem applied to the intersection gives a nonzero x ∈ L spanning U over E. Thus the number of these lines is at most the number of vectors of L satisfying the bound at all embeddings. Several short vectors can span the same line.

Use the real Euclidean norm ‖x‖2 = TrE/ℚ(h(x,x)) on the real vector space of dimension 2kf obtained from the rational lattice. For every nonzero difference of lattice vectors, its squared Hermitian length is a totally positive algebraic integer. The product of its 2f conjugates is a positive integer, hence at least one. Their arithmetic mean is at least their geometric mean. Consequently distinct lattice points are at distance at least √(2f) in this norm. Every vector with squared length at most B at all places lies in the ball of radius √(2fB).

Put disjoint open balls of radius √(2f)/2 around these lattice points. They all lie in the ball with that radius added to √(2fB). Comparing volumes bounds their number by (1 + 2√B)2kf, including the origin. Since B ≥ 1, each factor 1 + 2√B is at most 3√B. Substitution now gives

# {U of order n} ≤ (9ρ)kf nk/2.

The rank-one row bound takes n = d². The last factor becomes dk. The estimate holds for each individual lattice in the genus, so summing with weights 1/|Aut(L)| multiplies the uniform bound by the genus mass. Rank zero has at most the single zero subspace.

A line whose chosen basis vector is too long. In E = ℚ(ζ₁₂) with real field ℚ(√3), the two absolute discriminants are 144 and 12. The discriminant tower formula gives relative discriminant norm 144/12² = 1, so this example satisfies the finite unramified hypothesis. Write ε = 2 + √3, a unit with inverse 2 − √3. In the standard coordinate lattice 𝒪E² put the Hermitian Gram matrix diag(2ε²,1). On the first coordinate line the intersection is 𝒪Ee₁. Its dual is (2ε²)−1𝒪Ee₁, so n = 16. Here ρ = √12 and B = 2√12. At one place the vector e₁ has squared length 14 + 8√3, greater than B. The single vector ε−1e₁ lies in the same lattice and has squared length 2 at both places. Its trace squared norm is 8, the sum over four embeddings. Milne, §§2, 3 and 6 on discriminants and cyclotomic integers[40].

Where does the half-power of the last minor come from?

Keep one nonidentity term t that survives the character test in the diagonal subseries. Its two flags determine a positive rank j and an arithmetic list of minors δ. Consider the last minor of that list at each of the f infinite places. In the coordinates adapted to the flags, let Dτ be its positive normalized absolute size. Consequently the product P of the Dτ is positive and Δ = P² under the discriminant identity of the family. The local amplitude bound contains one inverse power of the absolute size for each of the k − 1 − j occurrences. Multiplication over the places gives

∏τ Dτ−(k−1−j) = P−(k−1−j) = Δ−(k−1−j)/2.

For an arithmetic check of the exponent, assign the two local sizes 2 and 3 and take k − 1 − j = 3. Their inverse cubes multiply to 1/216. The norm is 36, and 36−3/2 gives the same 1/216. These numbers check the product identity. A realized flag pair also has to satisfy the level, normal-form and size hypotheses. For all nonzero minors up to and including the last, divide the absolute sizes at each place by the common scale (2H₁)2r. Take their maximum and 1, whichever is larger. The representative of a term can be changed by its stabilizer. Bounding the orbital integral therefore has two costs. One measures the volume of a fundamental set for that stabilizer. The other measures the size of the integrand at the infinite places. Write a for the norm of the term vector, w for its weight, V for the volume of the word’s unipotent fundamental set (the same for every term in this word), U for the volume of the term’s stabilizer fundamental set with its adapted measures, and J for the product of the local amplitude norms. In each adapted normal form N the volume estimate gives U ≤ ωN vk(r−j)fL, where ωN is its index weight. This accounts for both copies of L in the scalar estimate. Here r is the flag dimension and v is the arithmetic volume parameter.

Each local norm also contributes the square root of a representation dimension. Their product is √dπ, where dπ is the product of those dimensions. To see one cancellation before the constants are enlarged, the common factor at each place is 2r²/vrk. Taking its f-th power and multiplying by the positive power of v from the volume leaves 2r²f/vkjf ≤ 2r²f. The scalar majorant absorbs this and the two volume losses into a family-wide cost. The resulting inequality holds for every adapted normal form. Their weights have infimum ωt. To pass to it, write c for the common nonnegative prefactor. If c > 0, the inequality makes a/c a lower bound for the weights, hence a/c ≤ ωt. If c = 0, evaluating at any adapted form gives a = 0.

‖vec(t)‖ ≤ w √dπ ωt · A(j, δ).

How can the estimate cover infinitely many lists of minors?

For a realized list δ at fixed j, write Δ > 0 for its normalized ideal norm at the last minor and S ≥ 1 for its size across the infinite places. At each place take the maximum of 1 and the normalized sizes of its nonzero leading minors, then multiply the maxima. One input bounds the amplitude for a fixed label, and another accounts for how much weight its representatives can carry. The label-dependent factors in their product are

Δ−(k−1−j)/2 Δk/2 · S−CₛkSCₚk = Δ(j+1)/2 S(Cₚ−Cₛ)k.

The minor bound Δ ≤ H S², with H independent of δ, costs Sj+1. Choose the decay parameter Cₛ ≥ Cₚ + 4. Since j ≤ r and k ≥ 2r + 2, the remaining exponent j + 1 − 4k is at most −3r. A separate arithmetic estimate bounds the sum of S−3r over every finite set of realized labels, uniformly in the set. The next calculation counts the possible entries in each size interval, then sums their weights. Multiple terms with the same list have already been paid for by the fixed-label bound.

How many lists of minors have a given size?

Fix a diagonal word u and an intersection defect j with 1 ≤ j ≤ r. Each surviving term supplies an ordered list δ = (δ₁, …, δj) of leading determinants. Two terms can supply exactly the same list. The fixed-list estimate has already paid for the terms with that list. We now count each distinct list once. Vanishing intermediate determinants retain their positions.

Both frames belong to the same self-dual Hermitian lattice. Pairing a vector in its dual with a lattice vector gives an element of the ring of integers 𝒪E. Every matrix entry therefore lies in this ring, and its determinant does too by the permutation formula. This puts each δℓ in a set whose spacing we can control.

Separation of algebraic integers. Let τ range over one embedding from each of the f conjugate pairs of the CM field E. For distinct x, y in 𝒪E, the product ∏τ|τ(x) − τ(y)|² equals |NmE/ℚ(x − y)| ≥ 1. Indeed the norm multiplies all conjugates, and each conjugate pair contributes a squared modulus. Multiplication by the nonzero algebraic integer x − y on the integral lattice 𝒪E has nonzero integral determinant. This also covers units, whose absolute norm equals one.

Divide each complex plane into half-open squares of side ½. Two points in the same square differ by less than 1 in modulus. If two algebraic integers occupied the same square at every place, their product of squared differences would be less than 1. Thus a choice of one square at each place contains at most one algebraic integer.

A list may have zero entries. In this one-place experiment, fix a single nonzero entry x in the Gaussian integers and take unit radius, so S = max(1, |x|). The shell 2 ≤ S < 4 contains 36 possible entries. For |x| < 4, the vertical lines with real part 0, ±1, ±2 and ±3 contain respectively 7, 14, 14 and 10 points in total. The smaller disk |x| < 2 contains 9, including the origin. The origin cancels in the difference 45 − 9 = 36. Any realization condition on the minor can only reduce this count.

The arithmetic family satisfies DE = DF². At each place the maximum defining στ includes Mτ/(2H₁)2r whenever x ≠ 0. Multiplying gives √Δℓ ≤ (2H₁)2rfS. A zero intermediate minor has norm zero and satisfies the squared inequality as well. The amplitude also uses an inverse power of Δ = Δj. For that step we need to know why the last minor is nonzero.

Why the last minor is nonzero. Let X and X′ be the two totally isotropic spaces in the flags. Thus the Hermitian pairing vanishes on each space separately. Write I = X ∩ X′, and let U and U′ be the spans of the first j frame vectors on each side. The normal-form theorem for a surviving term gives U ∩ I = 0 and X′ = U′ + I. It also relates the last frame vectors z and z′. Each is orthogonal to its own isotropic space, and z′ − cz lies in X + X′ for some nonzero scalar c in E. We use one more flag hypothesis. Every isotropic vector orthogonal to both X′ and z′ belongs to X′. In the arithmetic flags, a vector outside X′ meeting these orthogonality conditions has strictly positive squared length at the chosen infinite place.

If δj vanished, a nontrivial linear combination of the first j rows of the pairing matrix would be zero. The corresponding combination of frame vectors gives a nonzero x in U, because those vectors are independent. The zero row says that x is orthogonal to U′. It is already orthogonal to all of X, including I. The decomposition of X′ now gives x orthogonal to X′ as well. Since x is orthogonal to z and to z′ − cz, it is orthogonal to z′. Finally x is isotropic since it lies in X. The flag hypothesis places it in X′, so x belongs to U ∩ I = 0. This contradiction proves δj ≠ 0. Its normalized ideal norm is therefore positive.

0 < Δ ≤ (2H₁)4rf S² ≤ bCm²f S².

For the last step use H₁ = bCHm, b ≥ 2, CH ≥ 0 and m = 2r + 2. Then 2H₁ ≤ bCHm+1, while 4r ≤ 2m and CHm + 1 ≤ (CH + 1)m. Any C ≥ 2(CH + 1) works for every word and every defect. In the fixed-list estimate the ideal factor is Δ(j+1)/2. Raising the bound to this power costs precisely Sj+1.

A zero before the last position. Consider two isotropic planes with bases (e₁, e₂) and (f₁, f₂). Pair e₁ with f₁ and e₂ with f₂ with value 1, and give the other two pairs value 0. Read the second basis in the order (f₂, f₁). The resulting matrix has rows (0, 1) and (1, 0). Its list of leading determinants is (0, −1). The zero occupies the first slot in the shell count, while the inverse power in the amplitude applies to the second slot.

All the word maps take values in the same target. Its dimension D counts the independent ways the chosen archimedean representation occurs in automorphic L² after applying the finite-place projector e. The main term M for this integer is a real number. If dv is the formal degree at the real place v and V is the Haar volume of a fundamental domain F, then M = c0V, where c0 = (∏v dv) Re e(1). Why should this expression approximate a dimension? Both arise from one kernel.

Let φ be the product of the normalized archimedean matrix coefficients, their formal degrees and the finite-place function e, with the archimedean coefficients conjugated. Summing φ(x⁻¹γz) over rational group elements γ gives a kernel K(x,z). It represents an orthogonal projection of rank D. Choose continuous representatives F1, …, FD of an orthonormal basis of the range. The geometric kernel and the basis expansion give the same action on compactly supported test functions. Continuity and uniqueness of the automorphic representatives identify the two kernels pointwise. In particular,

Re K(x,x) = ∑j |Fj(x)|² ≥ 0,   ∫F Re K(x,x) dμ = D.

Each basis vector contributes one to the integral. On the geometric side the identity γ = 1 gives the constant c0 on the diagonal. Its integral is M. The real parts of the remaining summands can have either sign.

Which parameters enter the dimension comparison?

Fix a positive level-growth exponent Cg. The theorem chooses a lower bound for the ambient dimension n before varying the field and level. At each of the f infinite places the discrete series has the prescribed signature (p, q), with p + q = n and q² ≤ n. The CM field has root discriminant d with log d ≤ exp(n), and log f ≤ √n. The scale b ≥ 2 satisfies log b ≤ exp(nf log n/16). The congruence level g lies between 1 and bCg. The auxiliary rational prime exceeds 4n and splits completely in the CM field.

The absolute values of the archimedean weight entries are ≤ b². Whenever two entries at the same place have opposite signature signs, their distance is at least 8·10¹⁴(Cg + 4)n¹⁹f⁵ log(bd). This gap supplies rapid decay for the far terms. The threshold for a point to lie in the deep cusp uses the same field and level data and equals τ∗ = (nf d g b)−11q.

What does a short sublattice measure?

Let Λ be the lattice at the point and let B be a nonzero sublattice of rank s over the CM field E. Embed B at the f conjugate pairs using the positive metrics at that point. Its real covolume is taken in its own span, of real dimension 2fs. Multiply the covolume by 2fs|disc E|−s/2 and take the (2fs)th root. This is its normalized size. The least size is the infimum over all such B. The root makes it meaningful to compare different ranks. The canonical lattice filtration has a nonzero step strictly below t precisely when the least size is < t. Its step at or below t is already nonzero at equality.

For example, give the two coordinate directions of ℤ[i]² lengths ½ and 2, respectively. Here f = 1 and |disc E| = 4, so the prefactor is one in every rank. The fundamental square of the first Gaussian line has area ¼ and its normalized size is ½. The full lattice has four-dimensional covolume one. To find the least size, project a line sublattice onto a nonzero coordinate. This identifies it with a Gaussian ideal. An element of least nonzero norm generates that ideal. Round the real and imaginary parts of each quotient to integers. The remainder has smaller norm than the divisor and belongs to the ideal, so it must be zero. Thus the line has a generator (a,b) with squared length |a|²/4 + 4|b|² ≥ ¼. Every full-rank sublattice has positive integer index, hence covolume at least one. The least size is exactly ½. The strict test used in the short-flag bound therefore excludes this example at the boundary.

What can contribute close to the identity?

In the four contributions to the trace error, the first is an integral of a count with weights. At a point x of the fundamental domain, let A(x) be the sum of |φ(x⁻¹γx)| over nonidentity rational elements γ whose summand is nonzero and passes the near test. At each infinite place the Euclidean length of the vector of logarithms of the singular values of x⁻¹γx must be at most ε = 10−6n−8f−2. This test measures stretching. A unitary matrix has singular values one even when it moves vectors. The integral trace argument turns small stretching into closeness to the identity for these rational elements. The test coefficient imposes the finite lattice condition. The resulting bound is ‖x⁻¹γx − I‖HS ≤ t = 3√(nε) at every infinite place.

Near-term estimate. In signature (p, q) put n = p + q, with q ≥ 1 and q² ≤ n. Fix the level-growth exponent. Under the field, level and spectral-gap hypotheses of the dimension comparison, for all sufficiently large n one has

∫moderate A(x) dμ(x) ≤ M exp(−U/4),   U = nf log n.

Here M = c₀V is the identity contribution, with V the volume of the fundamental domain. To describe the integration region put X = nf d g b, where d is the root discriminant, g the finite-level parameter and b the height parameter. A point is moderate when its least normalized sublattice size is at least τ∗ = X−11q. This lower cutoff matters because more rational transformations can preserve a lattice with a very small subspace.

First consider a point whose least size is at least ½. Let L≤s denote the step in its size filtration generated by sublattices of largest normalized size at most s. Self-duality puts the entire lattice in L≤2. The filtration estimate for an integral near transformation gives (γ − I)L≤2 ⊆ L≤2t. Since 2t < ½, the latter step is zero. Thus γ fixes a spanning lattice and is the identity. Here A(x) = 0. At every remaining moderate point there is a nonempty canonical flag of short isotropic subspaces. Write j₁,…,ja for the successive increases in rank, and τ₁ < … < τa for the normalized sizes of the successive quotients. Then τ∗ ≤ τ₁ and τa < ½. The total rank J = ∑i ji is at most q, since projection onto the negative subspace is injective on an isotropic subspace.

Why a near term has exactly the traces of the identity

The near part of the trace count tests stretching at each archimedean place. A rotation can have zero stretching and still move every nonzero vector. To detect that motion we use the finite level of the same rational isometry. Let G be its matrix over the CM field E, of size n ≥ 1, and put f = [F ∶ ℚ] for the totally real field F below E. Take a positive integer level g0 > 4n for which (g0) in 𝒪E is radical, meaning that no prime ideal occurs twice in its factorization.

At a point x of the adelic quotient, take a rational term with nonzero test coefficient. The finite support condition says that the conjugated finite matrix preserves the reference lattice and its difference from the identity is nilpotent modulo g0 with exponent at most n. Let Λx consist of the rational vectors that enter that finite lattice after applying xf−1. It is a finitely generated 𝒪E-module spanning En. Moving the conjugation from the matrix to the vector gives

GΛx ⊂ Λx,   (G − I)nΛx ⊂ g0Λx.

For example, to check the second inclusion on a rational vector v ∈ Λx, apply xf−1 to (G − I)nv/g0. The finite support condition puts the result in the reference lattice, which is exactly the membership test for Λx.

Localize this lattice at a prime ideal 𝔭. It is free of rank n there, since it is finite and torsion free over the ring of integers. The matrix of G in a local basis is integral. Its power traces are therefore integral at every prime. For 𝔭 dividing (g0), the reduction of G is I + N with Nn = 0. In a basis adapted to the kernels of the powers of N, it is triangular with diagonal entries 1. Every power still has trace n in the residue field. Since (g0) is the product of its distinct prime divisors, these congruences give, for every j ≥ 1,

tr(Gj) − n = g0 aj,   aj ∈ 𝒪E.

The Stacks Project, lemma 15.22.11, local freeness over a Dedekind domain[32].

Now impose the archimedean test. Choose 0 < c ≤ 10−5 and set ε = c/(n8f2). At each real place the Euclidean length of the vector of logarithms of the singular values of the conjugated matrix A is at most ε. Every singular value is then at most exp(ε), so ‖Aj‖op ≤ exp(jε). Each diagonal entry has absolute value at most this operator norm. For 1 ≤ j ≤ n, we have jε ≤ 1/4 and hence |tr(Aj) − n| ≤ n(exp(1/4) + 1) < 3n. Trace is invariant under conjugation. The CM embeddings above each real place form a conjugate pair, so this bound holds for every conjugate of tr(Gj) − n.

It follows that every conjugate of aj has absolute value at most 3n/g0 < 1. A nonzero algebraic integer has a nonzero integer field norm, the product of all its conjugates. Such a product cannot have absolute value less than 1. Thus tr(Gj) = n for 1 ≤ j ≤ n.

From the power traces to a distance from the identity

Write det(I − zG) = ∑k=0n bkzk, with b0 = 1. Over a splitting field, differentiate the product of the factors 1 − λz, one for each eigenvalue λ with multiplicity. Its logarithmic derivative is −∑j≥1 tr(Gj)zj−1. Multiplication by the original polynomial and comparison of coefficients give Newton’s recursion

k bk = −∑j=1k bk−j tr(Gj),   1 ≤ k ≤ n.

The first n power traces coincide with those of I. Since the field has characteristic zero, division by k gives the same coefficients successively. The characteristic polynomial of G is therefore (T − 1)n. Cayley–Hamilton states that a matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial, giving (G − I)n = 0. This identity passes to the finite and infinite components and survives conjugation. The Stacks Project, lemma 10.16.1, Cayley–Hamilton[46].

Unipotent matrices can still have large entries. To get the distance actually needed in the count, use both the first trace and the stretching bound. In the polar decomposition write A = U exp(X) with U unitary and X Hermitian. The eigenvalues of X are the logarithms of the singular values, so its Frobenius norm is at most ε. Write B = exp(X) − I. The exponential series gives ‖B‖F ≤ exp(ε) − 1 ≤ 2ε. Since tr(A) = n, the identity A = U + UB gives n − Re tr(U) ≤ |tr(UB)| ≤ √n ‖B‖F by Cauchy–Schwarz on the diagonal. For unitary U, expanding ‖U − I‖F2 gives exactly 2(n − Re tr(U)). As √n ≤ n, this yields ‖U − I‖F ≤ 2√(nε). Adding ‖UB‖F ≤ 2ε ≤ √(nε) proves

‖A − I‖F ≤ δ = 3√(nε).

This radius satisfies δ < 1/4. For a signature index q with q2 ≤ n, substitution gives δqnf = 3√c · q/n5/2 ≤ 3√c/n2 < 1/100. The one-type count uses c = 10−6. Every contributing rational matrix now belongs to the set defined by the finite lattice condition and the archimedean δ-bound.

A Gaussian transvection. In dimension two over ℚ(i), give the basis e, f zero norms and pairing ⟨e,f⟩ = 1. The matrix G fixing e and sending f to f + ie preserves this form and the Gaussian lattice. Here (G − I)2 = 0, and the level 13 > 8 splits into the distinct Gaussian primes 3 + 2i and 3 − 2i. Its first two traces are both 2. Newton’s recursion gives b1 = −2, then 2b2 = −((−2)·2 + 2) = 2.

Take the finite coordinate of x to be the identity and its real coordinate to scale e,f by R,R−1 with R = 20,000. The upper entry of x−1Gx is now ia, with a = R−2 = 2.5 × 10−9, so its Frobenius distance to I is a. Its squared singular values have product 1 and sum 2 + a2, the determinant and trace of A*A. Thus its logarithmic singular values are ±arsinh(a/2). Their Euclidean length is less than a/√2 < 1.77 × 10−9. For c = 10−6 the permitted ε is 3.90625 × 10−9 and δ ≈ 2.65 × 10−4. This verifies the lattice and metric bounds on a nonidentity matrix. On the same space −I also has zero stretching, but its first trace differs from 2 by −4, failing the congruence modulo 13.

How many distant terms can survive at a point?

In the trace estimate, the variable x describes a lattice and γ runs over rational group elements. Fix x for now. At a real place v, take the polar decomposition of the matrix of x⁻¹γx as k exp(X), with k unitary and X Hermitian. Write zv(γ) = ‖X‖HS. This is the square root of the sum of the squared logarithms of its singular values. A nonzero summand is far when some zv exceeds the chosen radius ε. Equality with ε belongs to the inner interval. Zero summands may be dropped throughout.

Rational point count. Write tx = min(½, least(x)), where least(x) is the smallest normalized sublattice size, interpreted as an infimum. Among rational elements whose finite component after conjugation lies in the supporting compact subgroup, the number with zv(γ) ≤ Rv at every place, for prescribed nonnegative radii, satisfies

# {γ in the box} ≤ P(x) exp(κ ∑v Rv),   P(x) = (3√n/tx²)2n²f,   κ = 2n².

Here n is the matrix size and f is the number of real places. To see the lattice in this count, subtract two distinct rational elements from the box. Their finite support condition makes the difference a nonzero map from the lattice at x into itself. The lattice size inequality, using self-duality, gives a lower bound for the geometric mean of the operator norms of this difference across all places, namely tx². Thus the matrices form a separated set, even though two of them may approach one another at an individual place.

Why does the exponent contain 2n²f?

At place v the matrices lie in a ball of operator radius exp(Rv), since the largest log singular value is at most zv. Put R̄ = (∑ Rv)/f. Rescale that space of matrices by exp(R̄ − Rv). The product of the rescalings is one, so geometric-mean separation persists, while every coordinate ball now has radius exp(R̄). In the maximum norm on the product, distinct centers are therefore at least tx² apart. Open balls of radius tx²/2 around them are disjoint and fit in the concentric ball of radius exp(R̄) + tx²/2. The product space has real dimension 2n²f. Scaling its Lebesgue volume bounds the count by (1 + 2 exp(R̄)/tx²)2n²f. Since n ≥ 1, tx ≤ ½ and R̄ ≥ 0, the base is at most 3√n exp(R̄)/tx². Raising this to the indicated power yields the box bound.

How does marking a flag change the volume being counted?

Fix the positive rank jumps j₁,…,jₐ and let B be a measurable region of admissible ordered sizes. A point whose canonical flag has those ranks and sizes supplies one saturated isotropic flag. If we count all such flags over the point, the indicator of the event is bounded above by the number of markings. For instance, if three points have probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4 and carry respectively zero, one and two eligible markings, the points with a marking have probability 3/4. Counting all markings gives 1/2 + 2(1/4) = 1. This inequality permits the geometric proof to use arithmetic stabilizers.

Choose a basis adapted to a marked flag. Its data include one full lattice class for each successive quotient, of rank jᵢ, and a finite-adelic double class in the fixed residual Hermitian model supplied by the volume-ratio theorem, of signature (p−J, q−J), where J = ∑ jᵢ. On that space two finite representatives are equivalent when a rational isometry on the left and an element of the compact lattice stabilizer on the right identify them. The construction of an integral frame and the comparison of two markings put any marking with the same data into the chosen representative by these changes of basis. The archimedean flag sizes are preserved under the corresponding simultaneous change of frame. For each realized tuple of data it therefore suffices to integrate on the quotient by the subgroup preserving its marked flag. These slices cover the original event. Counting an overlap twice gives an upper bound.

The sum is countable. Each block lattice has finitely many generators in a countable number field, and the open compact subgroup at the finite places has at most countably many cosets in a second-countable group. The residual double quotient is a further quotient of that countable set.

Total isotropy means that every two vectors in it pair to zero. Put jᵢ = rank(Sᵢ/Sᵢ₋₁), d = ∑jᵢ, and suppose each real signature is (p,q) with d ≤ min(p,q).

Saturation says Sᵢ = L ∩ spanE(Sᵢ). If x ∈ Sᵢ and ax ∈ Sᵢ₋₁ for some nonzero a ∈ O, then x already lies in Sᵢ₋₁. Thus the quotient is torsion-free. It is finitely generated as an O-module. Over the Dedekind domain O it is projective, so the quotient map admits a section. Its image Aᵢ gives Sᵢ = Sᵢ₋₁ ⊕ Aᵢ. Choose a basis over E for the span of each Aᵢ, and let Λᵢ ⊂ Ejᵢ be the coefficient vectors of its integral elements. This construction also works when Aᵢ is a nonprincipal ideal and has no one-element integral basis.

Set W = spanE(Sₐ). We need a second isotropic space pairing perfectly with W and a decomposition that preserves L. Apply the same projectivity argument to L/Sₐ. If π is the quotient map and s a section, then 1 − sπ projects L onto Sₐ. Extend it by scalars to a projector P on the full rational space, with image W and P(L) ⊆ L.

How can the opposite isotropic space stay integral?

Take the Hermitian adjoint Q = P†, defined by h(x,Qy) = h(Px,y). For x,y ∈ L the right-hand side is integral, so self-duality gives Qy ∈ L. Since the image of P is totally isotropic, QP = 0. Both P and Q are idempotent. The unramified hypothesis supplies an integral w of relative trace one, as in the real-layer calculation. The corrected projector satisfies

T = Q − wPQ,   QT = Q,   T² = T,   T†T = (1 − w − conj(w))PQ = 0.

Indeed (PQ)† = PQ and PQP = 0. The last identity makes W′ = im T isotropic. On im Q the map u ↦ u − wPu has left inverse Q, so dim W′ = rank Q = rank P = d. For x ∈ W, h(x,Tz) = h(x,z). Thus if Tz pairs to zero with all of W, then Qz pairs to zero with the full space, so Qz = 0 and Tz = 0. Equal dimensions give a perfect pairing between the opposite spaces.

For an integral vector z take y = Tz and x = P(z − y). The remainder r = z − x − y lies in both ker P and ker Q. It is orthogonal to W = im P and to W′ = im T, because T†r = 0. All three summands remain in L. The perfect pairing makes their sum direct.

For a two-coordinate check, take the Gram matrix [[0,1],[1,1]]. The form takes value one on its second coordinate vector. Subtracting half of the first coordinate vector would make that value zero. In the Eisenstein integers O = ℤ[ω] with ω = (1 + √−3)/2, the integral vector (−conj(ω),1) also has form value zero, since 1 − ω − conj(ω) = 0. It still pairs to one with (1,0), and these two vectors have determinant one. This plane illustrates the trace-one correction over a ring where 1/2 is unavailable. The global theorem imposes additional unramified conditions on the field.

Why are the residual lattices equivalent at a finite place?

At an inert finite place, work first over the completed unramified quadratic extension. A self-dual lattice has an integral Gram matrix with unit determinant in an integral basis. Its reduction is a nonsingular Hermitian space over a quadratic extension of finite fields. In positive dimension it has a vector whose Hermitian value is nonzero. Otherwise, expanding the value on x + ay would give Tr(a h(x,y)) = 0 for every residue scalar a. The trace pairing of finite fields is nondegenerate, so every pairing would vanish. This argument includes residue characteristic two.

Lift such a vector. Its value is a unit of the base ring. Every unit is a norm in an unramified quadratic local extension, so scaling the vector gives Hermitian value one. Integral orthogonal projection now splits off its line and leaves a unimodular complement. Induction gives an orthonormal basis, with the empty basis as the rank-zero case. At a split place the two integral components pair perfectly and one can take an arbitrary basis on the first and its dual on the second. Thus in both cases a completed integral isometry matches any two self-dual lattices of the same rank in a common Hermitian space.

For a finite place v of the real base field, a rational vector belongs to the localized lattice when some base integer outside v takes it into the original lattice. At a split place this condition retains both primes above v. The genus comparison uses a rational isometry that matches these localized lattices. The condition on the completed lattices is open because their stabilizers are open. To see why rational isometries meet this open set, take a local isometry U. Multiply by a rational scalar λ of norm one so that 1 + λU is invertible. Only finitely many λ are excluded by the determinant polynomial, and the ratios (1 + kθ)/(1 − kθ) for integers k give infinitely many choices when θ is a nonzero purely imaginary element. Set

X = (1 − λU)(1 + λU)−1,   X† = −X,   λU = (1 − X)(1 + X)−1.

Approximate X by rational matrices Y and replace each by (Y − Y†)/2. They are exactly skew-adjoint and still approximate X. At a place above two the denominator costs a fixed precision, which can be supplied by a closer initial approximation. At a split place use simultaneous approximation in the two completions. The inverse displayed transformation is continuous on its domain and sends these rational skew-adjoint matrices to rational isometries. Undo the scalar λ. A sufficiently close choice lies in the same open lattice coset as U, so it takes the first localized lattice into the second. Duality reverses this inclusion, and both lattices are self-dual, giving equality. The rational choice here may depend on the finite place.

From the local lattices to a marked class

Each pair of opposite basis vectors contributes one positive and one negative direction at a real place, by taking their sum and difference. The residual signature is therefore (p−d,q−d). To compare it with the prescribed residual model, identify the CM fields by the given isomorphism respecting conjugation. Both forms now have self-dual lattices. At a finite place the extension is split or unramified, and local classification identifies their unimodular forms. At infinity their signatures agree. The local-to-global theorem for Hermitian forms gives a rational isometry of the residual spaces. In the resulting common space the transferred lattice is locally isometric to the reference lattice everywhere. A finite family of nontrivial local changes carries one to the other, since two full lattices agree at almost all places. Their product is the finite adelic representative of this residual lattice class.

Finally compare two markings expressed with the same coefficient lattices and residual representative. Their full frame matrices B and B′ have the same nonsingular Gram matrix, so B′B−1 is a rational unitary isometry. The coefficient description takes each integral partial sum to its namesake and gives the equality of the full lattices. Their finite representatives then differ, after this rational change of frame, by an element of the compact lattice stabilizer. The sizes of the graded pieces agree in the transported archimedean frame. This is the identification used in counting the marked slices.

From integral matrices to unitary matrices on one layer

Use orthonormal skew-adjoint coordinates on the layer. Its full lattice L lies in ℂs, with s = f dₖ, and is stable under complex conjugation. A skew-adjoint leading term has real coordinates in this basis. Put A = L ∩ ℝs and iB = L ∩ iℝs. For x + iy ∈ L, adding its conjugate gives 2x ∈ A. In the quotient by A ⊕ iB, the class of x modulo A determines the entire class. Indeed, if x ∈ A, subtraction leaves iy ∈ iB. The quotient therefore injects into (½A)/A, of order 2s. Why can we take a square root? The two covolumes are equal. In a CM extension unramified at finite places, for each rational prime p there is a purely imaginary algebraic integer whose absolute norm is prime to p. For this existence assertion write the scalar as z − conj(z). At a split pair of primes above p, choose the residues of z to be 0 and 1. At an inert prime choose a residue moved by conjugation in its quadratic residue field. The Chinese remainder theorem realizes these choices simultaneously. The difference is a unit above p. Multiplying by it exchanges the two real coordinate spaces and maps their lattices into one another. If D is the absolute determinant of this real scaling and I, J are the two indices, then I = D cov(A)/cov(B) and J = D cov(B)/cov(A). Their product D² is the dₖth power of that norm, prime to p. Consequently the positive rational number I/J = (cov(A)/cov(B))² has zero valuation at every prime. It is one. For a planar example of the index bound, the lattice of x + iy with integral coordinates of the same parity has area 2. Both axis lattices have spacing 2, attaining √(2 · 2) on the real axis.

To use the real lattice in the group, each of its leading terms must lift to an integral unitary matrix. The same unramified hypothesis gives an integral w with w + conj(w) = 1, where conj denotes conjugation. Indeed the residue trace is onto at every finite prime, both for the split pair and for the unramified quadratic residue field, including residue characteristic two. The ideal of integral traces is therefore contained in no maximal ideal and equals the base integer ring. If an integral block matrix Y has the required real leading coordinates, then X = wY − (wY)† is skew-adjoint and has the same leading coordinates. Start with g = 1 + X. Its defect D = g†g − 1 equals X†X, already in a deeper layer. Replace g by g(1 − wD). Its new defect is (1 − conj(w)D)(1 + D)(1 − wD) − 1. The linear term vanishes because w has trace one. All remaining terms lie deeper. The filtration ends after finitely many diagonals, so this produces an integral unitary lift.

Reduce the first nonzero layer modulo its real lattice, then reduce the next. A correction in a deeper layer preserves the earlier coordinates since the cross term in (1 + X)(1 + Y) lies strictly deeper. The product of the layer domains thus covers the quotient. Can one choose the block representatives at every scale at once?

For one block of rank j ≥ 1, let Γ be the group of automorphisms of its coefficient lattice Λ. Its elements act by left multiplication on tuples g of invertible complex j × j matrices, one matrix per embedding pair. We want one representative of each Γ-orbit. We also want the representative of the orbit of rg to be r times the representative of g, for every real r > 0. This lets a single unit interval of logarithmic determinants measure every other interval.

First minimize the largest absolute value of an entry, taken over all matrices in the tuple, as the tuple varies over its orbit. A minimum exists because only finitely many translates can have size bounded by any fixed number. Indeed, choose nonzero integers a, b in O with aOj ⊂ Λ ⊂ b−1Oj. For γ ∈ Γ the entries of abγ are integral. A bound on γg bounds γ after multiplication by the fixed inverse g−1. At every embedding these integral entries now lie in a bounded set. The simultaneous embedding of O is a lattice, so only finitely many entries, and hence matrices, occur.

Break a tie by dividing each matrix tuple by its size and assigning the normalized tuple a real number in a fixed, injective, measurable way. For instance, enumerate the open balls with rational centers and radii in its coordinate space and use ternary digit 2 for membership in a ball, 0 otherwise. These balls distinguish points. On the finite set of minimizers, choose the least such number. Conditions of the form “its size and tie breaker precede those of γg” are Borel, and Γ is countable, so the selected points form a measurable set D. Positive scaling multiplies all sizes by the same number and preserves all normalized coordinates. Hence D is stable under positive scalars. Left multiplication on invertible matrices is free, so the translates of D partition the matrix group.

Subtracting that multiple of x gives the integral decomposition L = 𝒪x ⊕ B, where B is the orthogonal complement in L. A vector in the rational complement that pairs integrally with B pairs integrally with the whole lattice, hence belongs to B by self-duality. Thus B is itself self-dual. The local classification of self-dual lattices identifies the complements for g and xf by an integral isometry between them. Extend it by the identity on x. Outside finitely many places the two original lattices already agree, so these maps can be chosen to be the identity there. Their product h is an adelic isometry fixing x and taking one local lattice family to the other. Then (hxf)−1g belongs to K, as claimed. Conversely, multiplying on the right by K fixes the lattice, and multiplying on the left by h preserves the condition that it contains x.

This argument also identifies the level. An isometry fixing x preserves L exactly when it preserves B. For an integral modulus c, the image of h−1 on L is just its image on B. As this lies in the perpendicular space, containment in cL is equivalent to containment in cB. This identifies the subgroup induced on the complement by a congruence condition. The double coset above uses the full lattice stabilizer. For example, −1 preserves the reference lattice. At principal level 3 it takes a primitive unit vector to a different residue class, so one may have more than one finite orbit at that finer level. The same calculation applies over the two factors at a split place and over an unramified extension in residue characteristic two.

Its complement has basis b₁ = (1,1,0), b₂ = (1,0,1). Each basis vector has norm zero and their pairing is 1. For ω²+ω+1 = 0, the norm of b₁+ωb₂ is ω+ω² = 1. On the cyclic multiplicative group of order Q²−1 it has image of order Q−1 and kernel of order Q+1. Only zero has norm zero. In both cases the number for a prescribed value b is Q−η, with an extra ηQ when b = 0. Keith Conrad, Finite Fields, Theorem 5.7 (trace and norm)[50].

The reduction of Λ is nondegenerate by self-duality. In the split case it is a pair of spaces in perfect duality, so dual bases give the sum of M products. In the field case it has a vector with nonzero norm. Indeed, if all norms vanished, expanding the norm of x + az for every scalar a would give Tr(a h(x,z)) = 0 for every a. The nondegenerate field trace pairing would then force h = 0. Scale a vector of nonzero norm to norm one by surjectivity of the field norm, split off its orthogonal complement, and repeat. In either case the reduced form is a sum of M copies of the one-coordinate norm.

Let ZM count the vectors of norm zero, including the origin. With the first M coordinates fixed, the last norm has to cancel their sum. Each choice gives Q−η possibilities for the last coordinate, plus the correction ηQ on ZM choices. Hence Z₀ = 1 and ZM+1 = Q2M(Q−η) + ηQZM. Substitution gives QZM = Q2M + (Q−1)(ηQ)M. Multiplying all coordinates by a scalar of prescribed nonzero norm permutes the nonzero fibres. Dividing the remaining Q2M−ZM vectors by Q−1 therefore gives the count for one nonzero target.

BM = Q2M−1 − ηMQM−1.   Density at β = BM/Q2M−1 = 1 − ηMQ−M.

Why does the first residue digit suffice? Given a solution x modulo πj, write a lift as x + πjz. For j ≥ 1 the next digit of its norm changes by the linear functional Tr h(x,z) on the 2M residue coordinates. Here the next digit means the coefficient of πj, viewed in k. The quadratic term in z vanishes modulo πj+1. At an inert place x is nonzero modulo π, so nondegeneracy makes h(x,·) onto the residue extension, and the trace onto k is surjective even in characteristic two. At a split place the functional is u·δv + v·δu, which is nonzero at a unit value u·v. Thus exactly Q2M−1 lifts hit each prescribed next digit. The density ratio stays fixed at every level. This extends the good-place lifting calculation for one unit target to primes above 2. In rank one, successive lifting and completeness also give an integral scalar of any prescribed unit norm. Scaling by this scalar preserves Λ and its Haar measure, so the unit fibres have equal density. This also recovers the answer by dividing the total mass of vectors of unit norm by the volume 1−1/Q of the units.

Take the base field ℚ₂ and M = 3. In the split case, each of the seven nonzero triples u admits four triples v with u·v = 1 over 𝔽₂. In the inert case every nonzero element of 𝔽₄ has norm one. An odd number of the three coordinates must be nonzero, giving 3·3 + 3³ = 36 possibilities. Thus the counts modulo 2 are 28 and 36 among 64, respectively. Modulo 4, a prescribed lift of 1 has 28·32 = 896 or 36·32 = 1152 representations among 4096 vectors. Dividing those proportions by the target mass 1/4 gives 7/8 and 9/8 again. The inert density exceeds one because the mass is measured per unit of target volume.

Why does removing a few directions cost so much volume?

Consider a short isotropic flag of total rank J in signature (p, q). Removing it and its dual changes the signature to (p − J, q − J). The flag coefficient involves a quotient of compact volumes. Its largest decrease comes from the last J sphere factors on the p side. To isolate them, write Am for the area of the unit sphere in ℂm+1 and S(r) for the product of the first r such areas, with S(0) = 1.

Am = 2πm+1/m!,   S(p)/S(p−J) = ∏m=p−Jp−1 Am.

Polar coordinates give the same value as the area times ∫₀∞ exp(−r²)r2m+1 dr = m!/2 times the area. The quotient above cancels all the lower-dimensional spheres. It is smaller than one since 2πe < 18. We may therefore replace the exponent m by its lower bound n − 2√n to get an upper bound. How can small ideals bound a regulator?

The flag coefficient contains one copy of the residue of ζE at 1 for each block of the flag. We first estimate this residue for any totally complex number field E of degree 2f. Write D for its absolute discriminant, Y = √D, h for its class number and R for its regulator. We will prove that for every real s > 1,

hR ≤ Ys (s/(s−1))2f.

Use one embedding σv from each complex conjugate pair, and write ℓv(x) = 2 log |σv(x)|. Their sum is log |NE/ℚ(x)|. On units the sum is zero. Delete the last coordinate. The unit logarithms then form a lattice Λ in ℝf−1 with covolume R, in the same normalization as the coefficient-line mass. We will cover its quotient torus once for each ideal class. Sutherland, Proposition 15.11 and Theorem 15.12, Dirichlet’s unit theorem[55].

Fix a class C and a nonzero integral ideal 𝔟 in its inverse class. For any point t of ℝf−1, append a last coordinate so that the full vector b has sum log(N𝔟 · Y). In ℂf take the product of open discs with radii exp(bᵥ/2). Its Euclidean volume is πfN𝔟 · Y. The lattice 𝔟 has covolume 2−fN𝔟 · Y. Thus the disc product has volume strictly greater than 22f times the covolume. It is convex and symmetric, so Minkowski’s lattice point theorem supplies a nonzero x ∈ 𝔟 with ℓv(x) < bᵥ for every v. The ideal 𝔞 = (x)𝔟−1 is integral and lies in C. The sum of the coordinate gaps is log(Y/N𝔞), so N𝔞 ≤ Y. Sutherland, Theorem 14.13, Minkowski’s lattice point theorem[56].

For each such 𝔞 fix a generator y of 𝔟𝔞. Since y/x is a unit, translating t by its unit logarithm and subtracting the first f−1 coordinates of ℓ(y) leaves the first f−1 gaps bᵥ−ℓv(x). They are nonnegative and their sum is at most log(Y/N𝔞). Thus one translated simplex per small ideal covers the torus. A simplex in k = f−1 coordinates given by uᵢ ≥ 0 and ∑uᵢ ≤ L has volume Lk/k!, by successive integration. In dimension zero its volume is one. Projecting a measurable simplex to the torus can only decrease its volume, as one sees by cutting it along translates of a fundamental domain. Hence R is at most the sum of these simplex volumes over the small ideals in C.

Sum over the h classes. Each nonzero integral ideal of norm at most Y enters once. For u = Y/N𝔞 ≥ 1 the exponential series gives (log u)k/k! ≤ u ≤ us. Extending the sum to all nonzero integral ideals therefore bounds hR by YsζE(s). Above a rational prime p there are at most 2f prime ideals, each of norm at least p. Indeed, the integer ring modulo p has p2f elements and maps onto the product of their residue fields by the Chinese remainder theorem. Unique factorization of ideals now bounds the Euler product by ζ(s)2f. Finally ζ(s) ≤ 1 + ∫1∞t−s dt = s/(s−1), proving the estimate.

Why is there a canonical flag below ½?

At the point x the data are a self-dual Hermitian lattice Λ in an n-dimensional space over the CM field, and a positive definite metric at each real place. A lattice size is a normalized covolume. Its rank enters the exponent so that scaling lengths by a factor c scales the size by c. For a nonzero lattice M, its largest size is the supremum of the sizes of its nonzero quotients M/K, where K is saturated and the quotient carries the quotient metric. Saturation means that the quotient has no torsion. The least size τ of Λ is the infimum of the sizes of its nonzero sublattices.

For t > 0, let F≤t be the sum of all nonzero sublattices whose largest size is at most t, and define F<t using a strict inequality. The Harder–Narasimhan filtration theorem for Hermitian lattices supplies the following size properties. Both sums are saturated. When nonzero, the closed step has largest size at most t and the open step has largest size strictly below t. Every nonzero lattice in Λ/F≤t has size strictly greater than t, and every nonzero lattice in Λ/F<t has size at least t. In positive rank the closed step is zero precisely when t < τ and the open step precisely when t ≤ τ.

A jump is a size t for which F<t ⊊ F≤t. Its quotient has size exactly t. Indeed the open-step inequality bounds its size below by t, and the largest size of the closed step bounds it above by t. Every nonzero closed step occurs at a jump. To see this, take s equal to its largest size. The lattice is included among the generators at s and s ≤ t, so F≤s = F≤t. Its largest size equals s, while a nonzero open step at s must have largest size strictly below s. The two steps at s are therefore distinct. The same argument at the largest size of a nonzero open step locates its last jump strictly below its endpoint.

At each jump the rank increases because the quotient of the two saturated steps is nonzero and torsion-free. If s < t, then F≤s ⊆ F<t. Thus distinct jumps have distinct resulting ranks in {1,…,n}. Listing the jumps below ½ in increasing order gives the finite flag. When τ < ½ the first jump is τ, since its open step is zero and its closed step is nonzero. The last lattice is exactly S = F<½. Any jump at ½ itself falls outside this list.

Why do all pairings on the short part vanish?

For a saturated sublattice M, write M⊥Λ = Λ ∩ (span M)⊥. This operation reverses inclusions and takes a step of rank r to one of rank n−r. In the self-dual lattice, successive perpendicular quotients are Hermitian duals of the original quotients, with reciprocal normalized sizes. For example, the quotient dual to M′/M is M⊥Λ/(M′)⊥Λ. The reciprocal formula follows from the determinant pairing, using the dual metrics and the integral Hermitian dual. Reversing a semistable filtration preserves semistability after dualizing its pieces. A lower bound on the size of every sublattice in a semistable piece of size s gives an upper bound s on the size of each nonzero quotient, by multiplicativity of determinant volumes. The dual sublattices consequently have size at least 1/s. Thus reversing the canonical list of sizes and inverting each size gives the canonical list again. The endpoint convention is important.

(F<t)⊥Λ = F≤1/t,   (F≤t)⊥Λ = F<1/t.

Indeed the jumps remaining after the strict step have sizes at least t, so the corresponding dual jumps have sizes at most 1/t. At t = ½ this gives S⊥Λ = F≤2. Monotonicity gives S ⊆ F≤2, so every pair of vectors of S has Hermitian pairing zero. The same implication works at any cutoff 0 < t ≤ 1. The choice ½ also ensures that the next endpoint l used in the gap estimate satisfies l² ≤ ¼.

The size inequality for a morphism answers a related question about a specified integral map. If the largest size of its domain is at most H, the least size of the target is at least L, and the map is nonzero, the geometric mean of its local operator norms is at least L/H. Thus it detects when a proposed small map must vanish. The reciprocal-step identity above identifies the whole orthogonal lattice and gives isotropy directly by inclusion.

To bound the rank, extend the rational span of S to one real place of the base field, hence to a complex Hermitian space of signature (pᵥ,qᵥ). Rationally independent vectors remain independent after this scalar extension. In coordinates in which the form is ‖z+‖²−‖z−‖², projection to either coordinate space is injective on an isotropic subspace. A vector in the kernel of either projection has zero norm also in the other coordinate, and hence is zero. Consequently

a ≤ rank S ≤ min(pᵥ,qᵥ) at every real place v.

Here a is the number of jumps below ½. This proves the inequality a ≤ q used to obtain the exponent 1/q in the orbit radius.

Why are two rounds of approximation enough?

In the filtration 0 ⊂ W ⊂ W⊥ ⊂ V, each matrix of the nilpotent Lie algebra sends a term into the preceding term. Thus all products of three vanish. The matrices sending V into W and vanishing on W⊥ form the central layer. It contains every commutator. In particular exp Y = 1 + Y + Y²/2 and log(exp B exp A) = B + A + [B,A]/2. Both formulas follow by multiplying the quadratic polynomials.

Use the coordinates of the Hermitian space at all real places to write a real orbit element as exp Y. An integral matrix here is a rational matrix preserving Λ under its linear action. Write ‖·‖x for the square root of the sum of squared Hilbert–Schmidt norms in the frames at x. The first covering-radius theorem gives an integral nilpotent matrix Y₀ and a real central matrix C approximating Y/(2g). The second gives an integral central approximation to any real central matrix. With the gap inequalities just proved, their respective radii in this norm are

r₁ = n²f d u/(8√(2f)),   r₂ = n²f d u/(16√f).

The first estimate uses the upper size h of R and the lower size l of every extension quotient. It rounds modulo the real center with error at most r₁. The second uses h² ≤ u/4 and rounds inside the center with error at most r₂. The first comes from approximating maps W⊥/W → W and lifting to the nilpotent algebra. For the second, one approximates maps V/W⊥ → W and subtracts the adjoint of an integral approximation to half the central matrix. To follow the constants, see why the first lift costs √2 and why subtracting the adjoint costs 2. With the two radius bounds in hand, combine the roundings at level g.

Why do both radii involve a ratio of lattice sizes?

Both constructions round a matrix between two lattices. Suppose the source has rank a over the CM field E and the target has rank b. Every nonzero source sublattice has normalized size at least L > 0. Every nonzero quotient of the target by a saturated sublattice has normalized size at most H > 0. The supremum over these quotients is called its largest normalized size. Use the specified Hermitian frames, let f be the number of complex places of E (one over each real place of its fixed field), and write d = |disc E|1/(2f). For any family of complex matrices Tᵥ between these frames there is one E-linear map Φ carrying the source lattice into the target, with

‖T − Φ‖ ≤ ab √f d H/(2L).

Here the norm squares and adds all matrix entries at all f places, then takes a square root. A zero source or target rank makes the error zero. For positive ranks, the integral maps form a full lattice of real dimension D = 2fab. To find an integral map near a prescribed point, use Euclidean lattice transference. In dimension D, a full lattice of dual minimum λ has covering radius at most D/(2λ). Thus it is enough to show λ ≥ 2√f · L/(d H).

What does an integral covector measure? It assigns to each integral map Φ the integer TrE/ℚ(tr(ΨΦ)) for a reverse matrix Ψ. The field trace pairing is nondegenerate, so every integral covector has this form after rational extension. If 𝔇 is the different, then δΨ sends the target lattice into the source for every δ in 𝔇. Indeed, evaluating on rank-one maps tests each scalar pairing of Ψ with a target vector and a source covector. Their traces remain integers after multiplication by every element of 𝒪E. By definition these pairings belong to the inverse different 𝔇−1. The lattice is recovered from its integral dual, giving the assertion.

Suppose Ψ ≠ 0. Its image of the target lattice is nonzero. Multiplying any nonzero sublattice of that image by 𝔇 puts it in the source and multiplies its normalized size by d. In rank r, the index factor is Norm(𝔇)r, with Norm(𝔇) = |disc E| and the size takes the (2fr)th root. Thus the least size in the image is at least L/d. For the target lattice B, put K = B ∩ ker Ψ and I = ΨB, of rank r > 0. The kernel is saturated, and B/K maps isomorphically onto I as an arithmetic lattice. In orthonormal coordinates for the quotient metric and the image metric, the real volume factor at a complex place is the square of the absolute determinant, at most ‖Ψv‖2rop. Multiplying over the places and taking the (2fr)th root bounds size(I)/size(B/K) above by the geometric mean of the operator norms. The numerator is at least L/d and the denominator at most H. This proves the lower bound L/(d H) for that geometric mean. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and the bound of operator norm by Hilbert–Schmidt norm now give ∑v ‖Ψv‖²HS ≥ f(L/(d H))².

The field trace sums twice the real part at each complex place. In Euclidean coordinates the real dual vector therefore has norm 2(∑ ‖Ψv‖²HS)1/2. Substitution into D/(2λ) gives the displayed bound. For example, over ℚ(i), multiplication by 1/2 already has integral field trace on every Gaussian integer. Its real dual vector has length one. The factor two recovers the ordinary Euclidean dual of the square lattice.

How does the map act on a quotient of the original lattice?

Let S be saturated in A, meaning that A/S has no torsion. Write a for the rank of A/S. Let the target be a sublattice R of rank b. Give the quotient its quotient metric and R its induced metric. An integral matrix on these two lattices lifts to a rational matrix on the ambient space by composing projection to the quotient, the rounded map, and inclusion of R. It kills S and sends A into R. At a real place choose orthonormal bases adapted to the source quotient and target subspace. The lifted error can be taken zero on the orthogonal complement and hence has the same sum of squared entries as its rectangular block. The bound holds for this extension of the error from the span of A. In the central application that span is the whole space. In the first layer only the error on the middle quotient is controlled at this stage.

How do we round a map on the middle quotient?

Keep the isotropic lattice R from the gap in the flag. Let W be its rational span, let Λ be the self-dual Hermitian lattice at x, and put P = Λ ∩ W⊥. Write j = dim W and n = dim V. A nilpotent infinitesimal displacement T kills W and takes W⊥ into W. Restriction to W⊥ therefore gives a map W⊥/W → W. Adding a central displacement leaves that map unchanged. The first rounding takes place in the lattice of integral maps P/R → R.

Covering estimate for maps between lattices. If R has largest normalized size at most h and every lattice M with R ⊊ M ⊆ P has quotient M/R of normalized size at least l > 0, then the restrictions of any family T as above admit one rational approximation Φ. It takes P into R and kills R. At each real place choose an extension Dᵥ of the difference (Tᵥ−Φv)|Wᵥ⊥ to the whole space. The extensions can be chosen so that

‖D‖x ≤ j(n−2j) √f d h/(2l).

This is the matrix covering bound for a quotient and a sublattice. Its dimension factor is the product of the two ranks. Nondegeneracy gives dim W⊥ = n−j, so the source has rank n−2j and the target rank j. The theorem realizes both lattices isometrically in their spans, applies a covering estimate for the pair, and carries the approximating map back by the quotient and inclusion. There is one complex place of the CM field above each real place of its totally real subfield. Thus the summed norm uses f places and the discriminant factor is the CM root discriminant d. The covering estimate for the pair of Hermitian lattices is the geometry-of-numbers input here.

Lifting the integral map. We need a skew-Hermitian matrix on all of Λ that still agrees with Φ on P. Since P is the intersection of Λ with a rational subspace, Λ/P is torsion-free. It is finitely generated over the ring of integers, a Dedekind domain, and hence projective. The quotient map therefore splits. Subtracting its splitting composed with the quotient map from the identity gives a projection π from Λ onto P which fixes P. Extend π to the rational vector space and set Ψ = Φπ. Then Ψ(Λ) ⊆ R, Ψ agrees with Φ on P, and Ψ kills W. Torsion-free finite modules over a Dedekind domain[32] · Finite locally free and projective modules[39].

Write Ψ† for the adjoint relative to the original Hermitian form. Self-duality of Λ makes Ψ† integral. Indeed ⟨z,Ψ†y⟩ = ⟨Ψz,y⟩ is integral for all y,z ∈ Λ. Moreover Ψ† kills W⊥, since Ψ has image in W. Its image lies in W⊥, since Ψ kills W. It follows that Y₀ = Ψ − Ψ† is skew-Hermitian and lowers every step of 0 ⊂ W ⊂ W⊥ ⊂ V. On P it is exactly Φ. This construction preserves integrality even at primes above two.

Why does the lift cost only √2 in norm?

At one real place, use the frame at x. In its ordinary positive definite inner product the original form is represented by a Hermitian involution J, with J² = 1. Isotropy makes W and JW orthogonal for the positive definite product. Let H be their joint orthogonal complement. Then JH = H and the original form has W⊥ = W ⊕ H. Restrict D to W ⊕ H and extend by zero on JW. The resulting matrix B has just one block, H → W, because D kills W and maps W⊥ into W. Restriction by an orthogonal projection gives ‖B‖HS ≤ ‖D‖HS.

Let B* be the adjoint for the positive definite product. The matrix A = B − J B*J is skew-Hermitian for the original form and agrees with D on W⊥. Its second block goes from JW to H. These two blocks occupy disjoint entries in an adapted orthonormal basis, and conjugation by the unitary J preserves their Hilbert–Schmidt norms. Therefore ‖A‖HS² = 2‖B‖HS². Sum over the real places and take square roots to get ‖A‖x ≤ √2 ‖D‖x. Now T−Y₀−A is a skew-Hermitian nilpotent matrix that vanishes on W⊥. Its image lies in (W⊥)⊥ = W, so it is a real central matrix C. This gives exactly the approximation T = Y₀ + C + A required by the first round.

‖A‖x ≤ r₁ = n²√f d u/(8√2),   2g r₁ = n²√f g d u/(4√2).

Indeed j(n−2j) ≤ n²/8 because the difference is (n−4j)²/8. Substitute this and h/l ≤ u in the quotient bound and multiply by √2. The orbit calculation takes T = Y/(2g), so its displacement after restoring the original scale is 2gA.

Check the two blocks in dimension four

Let J exchange the first and fourth standard basis vectors and fix the middle two. Take W spanned by the first vector and choose B with its sole unit entry in row 1, column 2. The matrix J B*J then has its sole unit entry in row 2, column 4. Subtracting gives squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm 2 and leaves the prescribed map from the second vector to the first. Here j = 1 and n = 4, so the rank factor 1·(4−2) = 2 attains the bound n²/8.

Why is the central error quadratic in the size of the short lattice?

Put j = dimE W and S = Λ ∩ W⊥. A central matrix Z is skew-adjoint and kills W⊥. It has image in W since ⟨Zv,w⟩ = −⟨v,Zw⟩ vanishes for every w ∈ W⊥. The rectangular block to round is therefore a map from V/W⊥ to W. Both have rank j. We will impose the skew-adjoint condition after rounding.

The source and target scales. The largest size in R is at most h. Self-duality of Λ and saturation identify Λ/S with the Hermitian dual of R with its induced metric. To see why this reverses the size, consider a saturated sublattice of Λ/S. Its dual is a quotient of R of the same rank, obtained by restricting the pairing. Their normalized determinant sizes multiply to one. The quotient has size at most h by the definition of the largest size of R, so the source sublattice has size at least 1/h. Passing to a finite-index sublattice can only increase that size. The ratio used in the matrix covering bound is thus h/(1/h) = h².

Apply that bound to Z/2. It gives a rational Φ killing S, sending Λ into R, and satisfying ‖Z/2 − Φ‖x ≤ j²√f d h²/2. Rational spanning extends the kernel condition to W⊥. The target condition extends to the image in W.

How can the rounded map be made skew-adjoint and integral?

Write Φ† for the adjoint with respect to the original Hermitian form. Take Z₀ = Φ − Φ†. Its adjoint is −Z₀. The kernel and image conditions on Φ give the same two conditions on Φ† by taking orthogonal complements. To check integrality, let v,w ∈ Λ. The pairing of Φ†v with w is integral because it equals the pairing of v with Φw ∈ Λ. Self-duality gives Φ†v ∈ Λ. Thus Z₀ belongs to the integral central lattice.

In each adapted frame the adjoint conjugate-transposes a matrix and multiplies its rows and columns by signs. This preserves the sum of squared absolute entries. Writing D = Z/2 − Φ, the skew-adjointness of Z gives Z − Z₀ = D − D†. The triangle inequality costs a factor of two. Isotropy gives j ≤ n/2, and the selected flag gap gives h² ≤ u/4. Consequently

‖Z − Z₀‖x ≤ j² √f d h² ≤ n² √f d u/16 = r₂.

The correction created by the first rounding has central value C′. Applying this estimate to C′/g gives the error g r₂ in the factorization below.

For a Gaussian hyperbolic plane, write E₁₂ for the matrix with a single 1 in its upper-right corner. For Z = (5i/4)E₁₂ the nearest Gaussian multiple to its half is Φ = iE₁₂. Subtracting the adjoint gives 2iE₁₂, at distance 3/4 in the ordinary matrix norm. The integral central matrix iE₁₂ is only 1/4 away. The proof needs a bound on the distance to its constructed point.

Combining the two roundings at level g

Put B = 2gY₀ and A = Y − B − 2gC, so ‖A‖x ≤ 2gr₁. Multiplying exp B by exp A introduces [B,A]/2. To cancel it, the central quantity that must still be represented is C′ = 2gC + [A,B]/2. Round C′/g to an integral central matrix Z₀, and put Z = C′ − gZ₀. Then ‖Z‖x ≤ gr₂. With E = 2gY₀ + gZ₀, the two corrections give

exp Y = exp E exp A exp Z,   ‖A‖x + ‖Z‖x ≤ n²√f g d u/4.

Indeed the two costs are n²√f g d u times 1/(4√2) and 1/16. Their sum is at most ¼ because √2 ≥ 4/3. The full two-parameter family exp(sA) exp(tZ) stays in the same real unipotent radical for all real s,t. Thus the path joining the representative to x also lies on the orbit.

It remains to check what exp E does at the finite places. A central matrix has zero product with every matrix of this nilpotent algebra. Consequently exp E − 1 = g(2Y₀ + Z₀ + 2gY₀²). This sends Λ into gΛ. Replacing Y₀ and Z₀ by their negatives checks the same condition for the inverse. This explains the factor 2 in the first rounding even when g is odd. The rational element γ represented by exp E therefore has finite component satisfying xfin−1γfinxfin ∈ K(g), the level subgroup. Its inverse k also belongs to K(g). Restoring the frames, we get

(ν,1)x = γ y (1,k),   yfin = xfin.

Here ν is the given real unipotent element and y has the two real displacements just bounded. For a general adelic element m of the radical, strong approximation gives a rational δ in the radical such that xfin−1(δ−1m)finxfin lies in the open group K(g). Left rational invariance and right level invariance therefore identify each function value at mx with its value at ((δ−1m)∞,1)x. The small real representatives now control the entire orbit used for the cuspidal average.

Why can a rational correction put the finite component in the level?

The level allows an open neighborhood of the given finite component. To find a rational point in that neighborhood, use the same nilpotent coordinates as in the rounding argument. Exponential and logarithm are inverse polynomials, exp(T) = 1 + T + T²/2 and log(1 + T) = T − T²/2. They preserve rationality and are continuous over the finite adèles. A basis of the Lie algebra over the base field F thus reduces the question to approximating one finite adèle by a number in F, independently in each coordinate.

An open condition on a finite adèle prescribes precision at finitely many primes and integrality elsewhere. Multiply by a common nonzero integer d clearing all denominators. At the selected primes prescribe the required residue of the integral numerator modulo a sufficiently high prime-ideal power. At any further prime dividing d, prescribe divisibility by the local factor of (d) to preserve integrality after division. The Chinese remainder theorem gives a single numerator in the integers of F. Dividing by d gives the required rational coordinate. Applied to all coordinates and followed by exponentiation, this supplies δ in the desired open set.

How many times can the variation estimate be applied?

Fix x and abbreviate τ(x) to τ. The unipotent orbit covering theorem supplies a neighborhood of radius ρ = n²√f g d (2τ)1/q/4. The filtered space of test vectors of order ≤ P is obtained by applying at most P archimedean derivatives to the lowest-type vectors. A derivative therefore takes a test vector to the next space. With a bound M per unit vector on that next space, the derivative estimate gives variation at most ρ√f βM on the orbit and in the neighborhood. The preceding argument replaces M by 2ρ√f βM one order lower. Use the common upper bound β = √n b² + (3/2)n3/2 + 3(8qN + N), valid at every order required here.

The initial bound at order 8qN is a local Sobolev evaluation estimate. Descend to order zero in 8qN applications. At a unit lowest-type vector, the squared norm of its vector of values is the projection diagonal. Squaring the repeated factor gives (2ρ√f β)16qN. In particular its power of τ is 16N. The initial squared evaluation bound contains (17√n/τ²)2N, which costs τ−4N. The product thus gains τ12N. As a scale check, halving τ while holding the counting data fixed multiplies this bound by 2−12N.

How large can an archimedean derivative be?

At order P, let VP be the span of vectors obtained from tensors of lowest compact-type vectors by applying at most P derivatives. A derivative in direction X is ∂Xw = (d/dt)σ(exp(tX))w at t = 0. A direction supported at one real place v belongs to the Lie algebra of its unitary group. Write ‖X‖HS for its Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Use the indefinite counting hypotheses. In particular n ≥ 8, the representations are unitary discrete series, and each coordinate of the Harish-Chandra parameter λ at each real place satisfies |λᵢ| ≤ b².

Derivative bound. The spaces VP are finite dimensional and preserved by the product of the maximal compact groups. Their vectors are differentiable along every real one-parameter subgroup, and one derivative takes VP into VP+1. For w ∈ VP and any one-place direction,

‖∂Xw‖ ≤ ‖X‖HS βP ‖w‖,   βP = √n b² + (3/2)n3/2 + 3P.

Here is why the dependence on P is linear. At one place write Eij for the operators representing the matrix units in the complexified Lie algebra. The compact roots eᵢ−eⱼ join two coordinates with the same signature sign. The noncompact roots join opposite signs. Let ρc and ρn be the half sums of the respective positive roots (i < j). The starting compact highest weight is Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. The counting hypotheses separate opposite-sign parameter coordinates by a common gap h ≥ 120nq3/2, where q is the real Witt index. The lowest-type multiplicity and infinitesimal-character theorems identify this compact type and give the scalar of the full quadratic Casimir operator on its generated module. Harris, Kobayashi and Speh, §2.3, formula (2.24)[59].

Moving a compact generator past a noncompact one adds their commutator, which is again a sum of noncompact generators. Thus words of length at most P lie in the compact-stable space obtained by applying at most P noncompact generators to the starting compact type. In one such step, the tensor-product rule with the off-diagonal block permits the old compact highest weight or a shift by a root joining opposite signs. The root eᵢ−eⱼ has Euclidean norm √2. By compact-type decomposition and induction, every highest weight μ seen by order P satisfies ‖μ−Λ‖ ≤ √2P. This bound on possible compact types holds for the entire span of words.

How does a bound on weights control every vector?

In matrix-unit coordinates let Ω be the sum of Eᵢⱼ Eⱼᵢ over all pairs and let ΩK be the same sum over same-sign pairs. On the common space of smooth vectors, unitarity gives Eᵢⱼ* = Eⱼᵢ for equal signs and Eᵢⱼ* = −Eⱼᵢ for opposite signs. Summing the squared norms therefore gives the energy identity

∑i,j ‖Eᵢⱼ w‖² = Re ⟨w, (2ΩK−Ω)w⟩.

On a compact type μ the scalar of ΩK is ‖μ+ρc‖²−‖ρc‖². On the generated module the scalar of Ω is ‖λ‖²−‖ρc+ρn‖². Put L = ‖λ‖ and A = ‖ρn‖ + √2P. The preceding weight bound gives ‖μ+ρc‖ ≤ L + A. Since the compact action is unitary, its finite-dimensional space splits orthogonally into compact types. The same upper bound for the compact Casimir quadratic form then applies to their sum, including linear combinations w.

The full half sum has coordinates (n+1−2i)/2 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n, giving squared norm n(n²−1)/12. Each coordinate of ρn has absolute value at most n/2. Thus ‖ρn‖ ≤ n3/2/2, and L ≤ √n b². For a unit vector the energy is consequently at most

2(L+A)²−L²+n³/12 ≤ (L+2A+0.3n3/2)² ≤ βP².

For the first inequality, (L+2A)² already exceeds 2(L+A)²−L² by 2A², and 0.3² ≥ 1/12. For the second, 2√2 ≤ 3 and 1 + 0.3 ≤ 3/2. This proves a bound on the sum of the squared generator norms. Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to ∂Xw = ∑ Xᵢⱼ Eᵢⱼ w gives the one-place estimate. Tensoring with the other places preserves the squared bound, as one sees by expanding in an orthonormal basis of the other factors. For simultaneous directions X = (Xᵥ), the derivative is the sum of the one-place derivatives. The product rule, the triangle inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give

‖∂Xw‖ ≤ √f (∑v ‖Xᵥ‖²HS)1/2 βP ‖w‖.

The descent in the cusp starts at order P₀ = 8qN, where N = n²f, and uses the simultaneous-direction bound. The Sobolev estimate at the starting order needs up to N more derivatives, each in a unit direction supported at a single place. Since βP increases with P, β = βP₀+N works for both steps. For example, the dimensions n = 8, f = q = 1 give N = 64 and P₀ = 512. Taking one constant through order 576 contributes 1728 to β from differentiations. This example counts orders and leaves the parameter gap and the bound b in force.

How an integral controls the starting value

The mean-zero argument starts with a bound for evaluation at every point y in a neighborhood of a deep point x. The available norm is an integral over the whole quotient. To pass from that norm to a value at y, we first average along short curves through y, then count how often their coordinate neighborhood can cover the same point of the quotient.

Evaluation along one curve. For a continuously differentiable complex function h on [0, s], integration of its derivative and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give |h(0)| ≤ |h(t)| + √s (∫ |h′|²)1/2 for every t in that interval. Square using (a + b)² ≤ 2a² + 2b² and average over t. The resulting endpoint estimate is

|h(0)|² ≤ (2/s) ∫0s |h(t)|² dt + 2s ∫0s |h′(t)|² dt.

There are N = n²f real directions, an orthonormal Lie algebra basis of size n² at each of f places. Write Fw for the continuous representative of one automorphic image of a test vector w. Along the jth one-parameter subgroup the derivative of Fw is F∂ⱼw. Differentiating raises the allowed order of the vector by one. Suppose the integral of |Fw|² on the full parameter cube is at most C(y)‖w‖² for all vectors through order P + N, and ‖∂ⱼw‖ ≤ β‖w‖ at the orders where a derivative is taken.

Use the subgroups in a fixed product order. For fixed values of the first N − 1 parameters apply the endpoint estimate in the last one, then integrate in the first N − 1. The two full-cube integrals are bounded by C(y)‖w‖² and C(y)‖∂Nw‖². Thus removing one parameter costs at most 2/s + 2sβ². The bound on the smaller cube holds through order P + N − 1. After N removals the cube is the point y, and all vectors through order P are still covered. With s = 1/β each removal costs 4β. The stated estimate rounds (4β)N up to (6β)N.

How often does the cube cover a quotient point?

Write t(y) = min(1, τ(y)), where τ is the least normalized sublattice size. Let P∞ = ∏v cv be the product of the gauge constants that specify real-place Haar measures, and let kg be the positive Haar volume of the finite level subgroup Kg.

For 12n³s ≤ 1 and 8n⁵s ≤ 1, the quantitative exponential-coordinate theorem bounds the parameter integral of any nonnegative measurable function by efP∞ times its Haar integral on a set S at the real places. Any two matrices in S differ multiplicatively by a matrix of operator norm at most 2 at each place. The factor ef allows a Jacobian loss of at most e at each place.

Extend S by Kg at the finite places. The squared representative is invariant under right translation by Kg, so this extension multiplies its integral by kg. When we fold the translate y(S × Kg) into a fundamental domain, each point z is counted once for each rational translate γz inside it. Fix one such γ₀ if any exist. The ratios γγ₀−1 are distinct rational transformations that preserve the finite lattice at y. In coordinates at y their operator norms are at most 2 at each real place.

The lattice separation inequality gives a lower bound t(y)² for the geometric mean over the real places of the operator-norm distances between two distinct such matrices. To see the two factors, take the difference of the corresponding rational transformations. It sends the lattice at y into itself and has nonzero image. For such a map between lattices, the geometric mean of its local operator norms is at least the least size of the target divided by the largest size of the source. Here the target has least size τ(y). The Hermitian lattice is self-dual, so duality reverses the filtration and replaces each size by its reciprocal. The largest size of the source is 1/τ(y). Their quotient is τ(y)², which is at least t(y)² after truncation. At least one local distance is therefore ≥ t(y)². In the maximum of the local norms, the open balls of radius t(y)²/2 about the matrices are disjoint. They lie in the ball of radius 2 + t(y)²/2. Volumes scale with exponent 2N, the real dimension of f spaces of complex n × n matrices. Their volume ratio bounds the multiplicity by (1 + 4/t(y)²)2N. Enlarging 4 to 4√n gives the bound used in the count. Dividing by the finite volume introduced above gives the cube constant

C(y) = ef (1 + 4√n/t(y)²)2N P∞/kg.

5.16Putting the words in the same row coordinates

Choose one orthonormal basis of the target, adapted to the common arithmetic row subspace, and one orthonormal basis for each full word space. Let Mu record the coordinates of Pu in those bases. In Mu∗Mv the sum over the shared row index gives exactly the inner products between the two sets of images, by Parseval. This is why the previous bounds apply simultaneously to the matrices. The unfolding volumes and dimensions give cu ≥ 0. The lower dimension proviso gives du > 0, and the scale bound gives e0 < 1. Together they force strict positivity. Indeed, when the normalizer vanishes the normalized block is defined to be zero. Its squared distance from the identity would then equal the full positive dimension.

For each word an isometric inclusion Vu selects the ramified columns, with Vu∗Vu = I. The top rows of the resulting matrix represent the rational arithmetic map after a common invertible row change and a word-dependent invertible column change. At the chosen complex place a single simultaneous conjugation may be necessary. It preserves absolute squares. Invertibility explains how to recognize the arithmetic map.
