Why can we adjoin every group matrix and keep scalar corners?

So far the algebra A is generated by the tangent space. To obtain a representation of Γ from block coefficients, we need an algebra containing ρ(Γ). We use the row identity to enlarge A while retaining the two properties used to construct matrix units.

Take R to be the linear span of all products aρ(g). It contains the identity, A and ρ(Γ). It is closed under multiplication because ρ(g)bρ(g)−1 belongs to A for each b ∈ A. Each generator also preserves every Γ-invariant subspace. To compute its diagonal corner, write aρ(g) = ρ(g)b, with b = ρ(g)−1aρ(g) ∈ A. If the corner is nonzero, the row identity replaces piρ(g) by piw. The corner becomes piwb pi, a scalar multiple of pi by the product calculation. The zero corner is already scalar. Taking linear combinations proves the same assertion on R.

We also need to detect nonzero elements of R. Decompose V into irreducible Γ-subspaces using semisimplicity. If x ∈ R is nonzero, choose a summand W and v ∈ W with xv ≠ 0. Since R preserves W, the vector xv lies in W. Its Γ-translates span a nonzero invariant subspace of W, hence span W. In particular some linear combination b of group matrices sends xv to v. We have b ∈ R and bx fixes the nonzero vector v. No power of bx can be zero. This proves the nilpotence test used to construct the matrix units below.

The identity has coefficient matrix Im. The displayed rule therefore makes r(g) = (cij(ρ(g))) a representation on Km, with inverse r(g−1). Let rC denote the action on the coordinates of class C. Choosing a nonzero vector v ∈ Vb gives one copy of rC inside V. Its coordinate vectors are the independent vectors uiv in the distinct spaces Vi, and the formula for ρ(g) on them is exactly the coefficient matrix. Taking a whole basis of Vb gives a direct sum of dC = dim Vb such copies and spans all the corresponding eigenspaces. Thus

r = ⊕C rC,   ρ ≃ ⊕C rC⊕dC.

Every dC is positive. Taking one copy per class gives r ↪ ρ. With k the largest multiplicity, assign the copies of each class to the first dC of the k available slots to get ρ ↪ r⊕k. Since any subrepresentation of a semisimple representation is semisimple, the first injection also gives semisimplicity of r. Indeed, the intersection with r of an invariant complement in ρ to any subrepresentation of r is a complement in r.

For an example with unequal multiplicities, let Γ = GL₂(ℤ₅) × ℤ₅×. Its element (A, u) acts on a five-dimensional space by diag(A, A, u). The three-dimensional r is diag(A, u). Why must an actual Galois element in every open coset have simple spectrum?

The witness M from the cycle calculation satisfies the polynomial equations of ρ(U). To pass from that algebraic witness to elements of gU, use the structure of the extracted module W of dimension m. For every class C and every copy of rC in V, the projection from r onto that class followed by inclusion of the copy gives an equivariant map from W to V. The copies in the direct sum decomposition span V. The extracted representation also comes with an equivariant inclusion A into V, and a linear left inverse B. Let T range over the equivariant maps just described. Write r for the action on W, and define Φ(Z) = Bρ(g)ZA. For Z = ρ(u′) with u′ ∈ U, this gives Φ(Z) = r(gu′). Each intertwining relation ρ(g)ZT = TΦ(Z) therefore holds on ρ(U). It is a system of linear equations in the entries of Z, so it holds on H, in particular at M.

Let q be the characteristic polynomial of Φ(M). By Cayley–Hamilton, q(Φ(M)) = 0. Moving powers through each T gives q(ρ(g)M)T = 0. Since their images span V, q(ρ(g)M) = 0 on the entire space. Applying this identity to an eigenvector shows that each of the m distinct eigenvalues constructed above is a root of q. Its degree is m, so all its roots are simple. The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.16.1, Cayley–Hamilton[46].

Simple spectrum can be tested by a polynomial in the entries of a matrix L. For example, take the determinant of the m-by-m matrix with entries tr(Li+j), starting the indices at zero. If λ₁, …, λm are the eigenvalues with multiplicity, triangularizing L shows that this matrix equals VλtVλ, where row k of Vλ is (1,λk,…,λkm−1). Two equal roots give identical rows. With distinct roots the matrix Vλ is invertible, because a polynomial of degree less than m vanishing at all those roots is zero. Denote the determinant test by Δ. If every element in gU had repeated roots on W, the polynomial Δ(Φ(Z)) would vanish on ρ(U) and hence at M. This contradicts the simple spectrum just proved. Every open neighborhood in Γ contains a coset of the subgroup fixing some finite Galois extension. Such subgroups are normal of finite index, so the simple-spectrum locus is dense in the Krull topology. It is open as well, since the continuous function h ↦ Δ(r(h)) is nonzero there. 6.11How do the two injections recover the exact data at a prescribed prime?

Consider first a prescribed spherical good prime w away from ℓ. Choose a geometric piece with the annihilation identity at this very prime. For every inverse Frobenius lift there the first injection gives a matrix of size m annihilated by the polynomial with roots R. Its multiset of eigenvalues has m entries, all from R, and its determinant gives the product of the entries. To recover all the multiplicities we use the genericity test imposed at the prescribed prime. For a list α₁, …, αm of its normalized Satake entries it gives

∑ ei = m,   ∏ αiei = ∏ αi   ⇒   e₁ = ⋯ = em = 1.

Indeed, each nonnegative ei is at most m, so there are finitely many exponent lists to test. The genericity polynomial on the unnormalized Satake entries contains a factor given by the difference of these two products for each list other than the all-ones list. A nonzero value excludes every such equality. The common Satake normalization multiplies both products by the same nonzero scalar to the power m. Apply the test to the multiplicities of the eigenvalues to obtain the prescribed characteristic polynomial. For roots {2,3,5}, the determinant 30 forces each prime factor to appear once. With roots {1,2,4}, both diag(1,2,4) and 2I have determinant 8 and are annihilated by (X−1)(X−2)(X−4). Their traces are 7 and 6. This is the collision that the genericity test removes.

At a prescribed spherical w over ℓ outside the two auxiliary real-subfield primes, take a piece that is crystalline there and whose jumps contain the desired m distinct integers. The first injection makes r crystalline at w. Indeed it is a direct summand of the globally semisimple ρ, and each summand of a crystalline representation is crystalline. For the jumps, use the second injection. The space of k copies of r is semisimple as a global representation, so the injection of ρ into it also splits. After restriction to the local group, taking filtered periods preserves these direct sums. Every jump occurring in ρ must therefore occur in r, since the k copies only repeat its jumps. At each inducing embedding the period space of r has dimension m. The m prescribed distinct jumps already use that entire dimension, so each occurs exactly once. Brinon and Conrad, Theorem 5.2.1 and §6.3 on filtered de Rham periods[71].

A further geometric piece can supply the Weil polynomial at the same w. For a Weil element of degree −1, the characteristic polynomial on this piece divides a power of the Satake polynomial. The inclusion of r implies the same divisibility for its Weil polynomial. Thus every root belongs to R. Compatibility of the Weil–Deligne construction with determinants gives the prescribed product, and the same genericity test fixes the multiplicities. Both Weil representations are unramified here, the first by crystallinity and the second by its spherical construction. Each factors through the integer degree map. The eigenvalues at an arbitrary degree are the corresponding powers of those at degree −1, giving equality of the characteristic polynomials at every Weil element.

The geometric input requires the two auxiliary primes to agree on the imaginary quadratic subfield K = ℚ(√(−d)). For the local comparison at w above ℓ choose each auxiliary prime, or its conjugate, to restrict to w|K. There are two primes of K above the split prime ℓ and complex conjugation exchanges them. This choice preserves the underlying primes of E⁺, sphericity, and the cuspidal local type (changing prime identifies the two local unitary groups and transports their compact subgroups). Duality preserves lacunarity of the weight. The preceding uniqueness argument places the comparisons from these choices on one representation attached to U′. The next step needs simultaneous congruences of the eigenvalues to approximate the original system using such representations.

6.12Which evaluations keep a Hecke error small?

At weight zero a Hecke operator is a finite sum of right translations. If all its coefficients have ℓ-adic absolute value at most one, the ultrametric inequality bounds the sum by its largest term. At higher weight, translating the point also changes the vector on which the form is evaluated. We construct a family of test vectors and compute how small each Hecke coefficient must be to compensate for this change.

Let G be the definite unitary group of rank a ≥ 1 attached to the CM field E, viewed over ℚ by restriction of scalars. Fix an identification of the algebraic closure of ℚℓ with ℂ, and use it to read all absolute values ℓ-adically, with |ℓ| = ℓ−1. Realize the weight representation ρ on a finite-dimensional space V of polynomials. Write ‖x‖ for the largest absolute value of a coefficient of x, taking ‖0‖ = 0, and let Λ consist of the polynomials in V with ‖x‖ ≤ 1. A form f(x, g) is linear in x ∈ V and evaluated at an adelic point g.

To transport Λ, record two matrices at each infinite place. The first, c∞(g), reads the archimedean component at the chosen complex embedding. For the second, κ(g), read the finite component at the place above ℓ induced by that embedding and the fixed field identification, then transport its entries back to ℂ. Both constructions respect multiplication. They agree on rational group elements, and κ takes the value 1 on the archimedean subgroup. Put

M(g) = c∞(g)−1κ(g),   eg,x(f) = f(ρ(M(g))x, g),   x ∈ Λ.

Integral evaluation theorem. These evaluations detect every nonzero algebraic form, and each form has a finite bound on all its evaluations. Let λτ,i be the weight entries over all complex embeddings τ of E, with the dual weight at the conjugate embedding. Put D = a ∑τ,i |λτ,i|, using ordinary absolute values of integers in this sum. Consider a Hecke operator with finite support on the finite adelic group and coefficient t(h) at a translation h. For each such h, choose d ≥ 0 so that ℓd clears the denominators of the entries of both h and h−1 at every place over ℓ. If |t(h)| ≤ ℓ−dD for every term, the operator preserves every common bound on the evaluations.

Proof. First we estimate the effect of a matrix on the weight. Suppose every entry of A and A−1 has norm at most B ≥ 1 in every archimedean matrix block, using the transported ℓ-adic norm. Substitution of linear forms into a monomial of degree m gives coefficients of norm at most Bm, by expanding the product. In the block of weight λ₁ ≥ ⋯ ≥ λa, the polynomial part has degree at most ∑i(λi − λa), the sum of its column degrees. The determinant twist contributes at most Ba|λa| by expanding the determinant of A or of its inverse. For each i, (λi − λa) + |λa| ≤ 2∑j|λj|. There is one polynomial block for each conjugate pair of embeddings. The conjugate weight reverses and negates the entries, so the pair contributes 2a∑j|λj| to D, enough for the polynomial degree and the determinant twist together. Adding over the blocks therefore gives ‖ρ(A)x‖ ≤ BD for x ∈ Λ.

For example, take rank two, one infinite place and weight (0, −1). The polynomial part has degree one. The determinant of a two-by-two matrix, or its inverse, costs at most two more powers of B. The two embeddings carry weights (0, −1) and (1, 0), so the uniform formula gives D = 4. Estimating the polynomial and the determinant separately gives B³, within the uniform allowance B⁴.

For detection, take a point g and vector v at which f(v, g) ≠ 0. Multiply ρ(M(g))−1v by a sufficiently high power ℓk to put all its polynomial coefficients in the unit ball. The corresponding evaluation is ℓkf(v, g), which is still nonzero.

For boundedness, take a compact open finite level C fixing f. Borel’s class-number theorem gives finitely many representatives s such that every g has the form γsuk, with γ rational, u archimedean and k ∈ C. Indeed, intersecting the standard finite level with C gives a subgroup of finite index in the standard level, so each standard class splits into finitely many classes. A. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Theorem 5.1.[76]

Left invariance under γ, covariance under u, and invariance under k remove these three factors. In the specified order the matrices satisfy c∞(u)M(γsuk) = M(s)κ(k), which gives eg,x(f) = f(ρ(M(s))ρ(κ(k))x, s). The single exponent d clearing all k ∈ C exists because the denominator conditions form an increasing open cover of the compact group C. Thus ‖ρ(κ(k))x‖ ≤ ℓdD. At each representative s, the functional y ↦ f(ρ(M(s))y, s) is bounded in the coefficient norm. Indeed, coefficient functionals separate points of the finite-dimensional space V, so finitely many form a basis of its dual. Taking the largest bound over the representatives proves the assertion.

Finally take a translation h in the operator. Its archimedean component is the identity, so M(gh) = M(g)κ(h) with the product understood in each block. To evaluate at gh using the vector that was transported to g, apply the inverse change of coordinates and absorb the Hecke coefficient into the vector. This gives

yh = t(h)ρ(κ(h)−1)x,   ‖yh‖ ≤ ℓ−dDℓdD = 1.

By linearity in the test vector, eg,x(Tf) = ∑h egh,yh(f). Every summand is again one of our evaluations. The ultrametric inequality now preserves their common bound, even for a function that is assumed only linear in its weight argument. This allows the same estimate to be applied to every residual in the polynomial approximation.

For an operator supported away from ℓ we can take d = 0. At places over ℓ, any single finite sum can be made integral for this estimate by multiplying it by ℓk. Choose k large enough that ℓ−k|t(h)| ≤ ℓ−dD at each of its finitely many terms. The same multiplier scales its eigenvalue. This accounts for the factors attached separately to the auxiliary Hecke coordinates.

6.13Where do the forms satisfying the local tests come from?

Fix the algebraic weight W of the definite unitary group of rank a ≥ 1, a split auxiliary place w0 above ℓ, and a level K away from w0. The level stays fixed away from w0 throughout the approximation. At w0 we may replace a compact open subgroup by a smaller one. This variation gives the additional forms needed for the approximation.

At each place w of a finite set S, prescribe a nonzero polynomial Φw in the a Satake parameters. Each w is split, lies over a different prime of the real subfield from w0, and has hyperspecial local level. Call a representation admissible here if Φw is nonzero on every ordering of its spherical Satake parameters at every w in S. Write Mgood for the algebraic span of the K-fixed forms of weight W in these representations.

Density theorem at fixed weight and level away from one place. For every K-fixed form f of weight W and every δ > 0, there exist G ∈ Mgood and a scalar function e on the adelic group such that, for every weight vector v and group point g,

f(v, g) − G(v, g) = e(g)f(v, g),   |e(g)|ℓ ≤ δ.

The multiplier is the same for all v at a given g. In particular, every evaluation that vanishes for f also vanishes for G. We derive this statement from two estimates on a finite quotient at w0.

Counting the representations that fail a test. By smoothness choose a compact open subgroup J0 at w0 that fixes f, and a descending congruence tower inside it. The tower construction supplies normal subgroups Jn with finite ℓ-group quotients Hn = J0/Jn. At the full level obtained by adjoining Jn to K, let Bw,n be the span belonging to representations that fail the test at w. The one-place counting estimate asserts that for every η > 0 and every sufficiently large n, this space is finite dimensional with dim Bw,n ≤ η|Hn|. Take η = 1/(2(|S| + 1)) and choose a common depth for the finitely many places. Since each representation failing at least one test belongs to one of these spaces, their sum contains the whole failing span Bn. Hence 2 dim Bn ≤ |Hn|.

One correction. Write H = Hn. The tower provides a label L(g) in H for each adelic point. Right translation by j in J0 changes the label to L(g) times the class of j in H. Multiplying by a function of the label gives a linear map Ψ from functions on H to forms at the refined level,

Ψ(φ)(v, g) = φ(L(g))f(v, g).

Let P be the inverse image under Ψ of the admissible span at this refined level. The automorphic decomposition writes every form there as the sum of admissible and failing contributions. After quotienting by the admissible span, the image of Ψ therefore has dimension at most dim Bn. Its kernel in this quotient is P, so dim P ≥ |H| − dim Bn ≥ |H|/2. Moreover P is stable under right translations of H. Indeed, lift a translation to J0. It fixes f, normalizes the refined level and translates a form inside the same automorphic representation.

Finite-group approximation lemma. A right-translation-invariant subspace of functions on a finite ℓ-group H, of dimension at least |H|/2, contains a function φ satisfying |1 − φ(h)|ℓ ≤ ℓ−1/2 for every h ∈ H. The norm uses the fixed identification of the complex coefficients with the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. Apply this lemma to P. The form Ψ(φ) is admissible by the definition of P. Its error multiplier is 1 − φ(L(g)), so a single correction has a bound strictly smaller than one.

For a two-point example take ℓ = 2 and H = {1, σ}. The sign character spans a translation-invariant line, exactly half the dimension of all functions on H. Taking φ to be that character gives errors 0 at 1 and 2 at σ. The second error has 2-adic absolute value 1/2, smaller than the required 1/√2. Thus a line that contains only functions with values of opposite signs can nevertheless approximate the constant function 1 in this norm.

Iteration. Begin with G0 = 0 and e0 = 1. If the residual is f − Gm = emf, apply one correction to this residual, which still has weight W and level K away from w0. Write B for the resulting admissible form and b(g) for its error multiplier. Set Gm+1 = Gm + B. Then f − Gm+1 = b emf. After m corrections the multiplier has absolute value at most ℓ−m/2 at every point. A finite m achieves any prescribed δ.

By definition of the algebraic span, the resulting G is a finite sum of admissible forms. Group the terms belonging to the same automorphic representation and omit zero sums. When the selected Hecke operators act by scalars on the K-fixed vectors of each representation, each surviving term is a simultaneous eigenform for those operators. With |eg,x(f)|ℓ ≤ R in the integral frame and R ≥ 1, take δ = ε/R. The same list then has residual bounded by ε in every evaluation, as required for the polynomial argument. Simultaneous approximation for all integral polynomials.

The arithmetic input still to be derived in this monograph is the one-place counting estimate along the tower. Its proof uses spherical Hecke operators acting as the identity on the failing representations with arbitrarily small sum of squared complex coefficients. The construction of the tower labels and the proof of the finite-group approximation lemma are also needed for the one-correction argument.

6.14How can one approximation work for every Hecke polynomial?

The Galois construction compares sums and products of Hecke eigenvalues. A finite weighted list of auxiliary systems must work for every polynomial at once. Fix the algebraic weight and the level away from the auxiliary split place above ℓ. At that place the approximants can have deeper level. Write θ for the joint eigenvalues of our form and ηi for those of auxiliary eigenforms. In this passage scalars are read through the fixed identification with the algebraic closure of ℚℓ, and |·| means the ℓ-adic absolute value.

Use the integral family of linear evaluations ex of forms, indexed by a group point and a weight-space test vector. Three properties of this family enter. A nonzero form has a nonzero evaluation, every form in the fixed space has bounded evaluations, and each chosen integral Hecke operator Tj preserves any common bound on the evaluations of a vector. The local denominator bound on each term gives the last property. Normalize the target eigenform f so that e0(f) = 1 at one detecting coordinate. Let R ≥ 1 bound all its evaluations. The density theorem away from the auxiliary place approximates f by a finite sum ∑ifi of allowed eigenforms, with pointwise error given by evaluations of f times a factor bounded by ε/R. Thus the residual has every evaluation bounded by ε.

For any polynomial P with integer coefficients put u(P) = P(θ)f − ∑iP(ηi)fi. For a constant integer this is a multiple of the residual by a scalar of absolute value at most one. Addition preserves the bound ε by the ultrametric inequality. Multiplication by a variable Xj replaces u(P) by Tju(P) because every vector in the sum is an eigenvector for that operator. These three operations construct every integral polynomial. Evaluating at the same coordinate e0 gives

|P(θ) − ∑η cη P(η)| ≤ ε,   cη = ∑i : ηi=η e0(fi).

The finite support and all the coefficients have been chosen before P. The coordinate index set may be infinite because each polynomial uses only finitely many variables. If two forms have the same system, they contribute to the same coefficient. We write θ ∈ 𝒜(S) when for each ε > 0 such a finite weighted list exists in the set S of systems.

6.15How can one remove systems that fail a local test?

Suppose η ∈ 𝒜(T), and let Q be an integral polynomial that is nonzero at η. We want to retain only points x ∈ T with Q(x) ≠ 0. Start with an approximation to η at the finer tolerance ε|Q(η)|. Apply it to PQ and divide by Q(η). The terms with Q(x) = 0 drop out. Each surviving coefficient changes in the same way for every test polynomial:

c′x = cx Q(x)/Q(η),   |P(η) − ∑x c′x P(x)| ≤ ε.

For a finite calculation in ℚ₅ approximate evaluation at 5 by the average of evaluations at 0 and 10. This rule is exact on constants and linear polynomials. On every higher power both the target value and the average are divisible by 25 in ℤ₅. It therefore gives error at most 1/25 on every integral polynomial. Take Q(X) = X. The point 0 disappears and the new coefficient at 10 is (1/2)·10/5 = 1. For P = X the error is now |5−10|₅ = 1/5. It is obtained from the old error on X², namely |25−50|₅ = 1/25, by division by |5|₅. This one finite rule illustrates exactly the precision lost in filtering.

Results in this passage. Filtering and composing simultaneous polynomial approximations

There are two approximation stages in the arithmetic argument. Suppose θ ∈ 𝒜(S) and, for each η ∈ S, η ∈ 𝒜(T) with Q(η) ≠ 0. Choose an outer list at tolerance ε/2 with coefficients aη, and put M = ∑|aη|. For every η on this finite list choose a filtered inner rule with error δ = ε/[2(1+M)]. Sum the rules, giving a shared point x the sum of all products aηc′η,x that reach it. Adding and subtracting the evaluations at η gives

|P(θ) − ∑x c″x P(x)| ≤ ε/2 + Mδ ≤ ε.

The nonvanishing condition holds at the intermediate points where we divide. The outer target θ can lie on the zero set of Q. After filtering we may also forget coordinates. Lift each polynomial in the remaining variables to a polynomial in the original variables, and add the coefficients of all points that project to the same remaining system. The estimate is identical.

6.16Which local conditions survive the approximation?

Keep two split auxiliary places u,v over distinct primes of the real subfield above ℓ. Fix finite sets Z,W of eligible spherical places away from those auxiliary primes, where Z prescribes genericity tests. The power-sum places in W are above ℓ. Both sets consist of split places spherical for the target. In the odd-rank application we test genericity on Z ∪ W. In addition to the original Hecke coordinates indexed by J, introduce one coordinate for every pair (w,n) ∈ W × ℤ, and one detector coordinate for each place z in the finite test set:

θj,   aw,n · power sum at (w,n),   bz · detector at z.

The power-sum operator has the indicated Satake eigenvalue. A spherical Hecke operator at z detects nonvanishing of the chosen genericity polynomial on the Satake parameters. Each nonzero multiplier aw,n or bz puts the corresponding operator within the integral bounds required by the frame. The power-sum multipliers are fixed with Z,W before the family of original Hecke operators is chosen. They may depend on the place and the exponent. The product Q of the detector variables is an integral polynomial because the test set is finite. As each multiplier is nonzero, Q detects simultaneous success at every tested place.

First apply fixed-weight density with generic local systems and the eigenform argument to approximate the extended system by intermediate ones on which Q is nonzero. For each of these, the weight-variation theorem at v and the local type construction at u provide a second approximation, with the required lacunary weight and auxiliary local type. These operators are supported away from both places, so the same extended eigenvalue coordinates can be tested in this second step. Apply the filtering and composition formula to preserve the first condition while imposing the second. Finally forget the detector coordinates. Each retained system still has a representative that passes every local test, and weighted evaluations approximate all integral polynomials in the original Hecke variables and the scaled powers. On weights outside the specified auxiliary primes the construction keeps the original weights. This supplies the simultaneous approximation used in the trace limit, conditional on the stated density, weight-variation, local-type and integral-frame constructions.

6.17Why do all the original Hecke coordinates lie in one finite extension?

The trace limit needs completeness of its coefficient field. Having each eigenvalue in some finite extension of ℚℓ would allow the degrees to grow with the operator. For a family of rational Hecke operators at the chosen weight and level we can bound the degree of every finite list at once.

Choose a nonzero fixed eigenform for the original system. The automorphic rationality input realizes every field conjugate of its eigenvalue system on a nonzero conjugate form, all in one finite-dimensional space M. Rationality of the operators is used here so that applying an automorphism of ℂ carries an eigenvalue to its conjugate for the very same operator. The finite adelic values determine the form, so a nonzero such value still detects each conjugate. Distinct joint systems give linearly independent eigenvectors. Indeed, in a finite relation fix one system χ. For each other system ψ choose a coordinate j at which they differ and apply the factor Tj − ψjI. The product kills every other vector and multiplies the chosen one by a nonzero scalar. Thus χ has zero coefficient in the relation. The full tuple of eigenvalues has at most dim M different conjugates.

Transport the tuple back by ι to the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. For every finite set A of coordinates let LA be the field they generate over ℚℓ. It has [LA : ℚℓ] embeddings into the algebraic closure. One can count them by adjoining the generators in succession: each minimal polynomial in characteristic zero has exactly its degree many distinct roots. Each embedding extends to an automorphism of the algebraic closure, hence, through ι, to a field automorphism of ℂ. Distinct embeddings differ on at least one of the generating coordinates, and therefore yield different full conjugate tuples. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, Proposition 7.4[77].

[LA : ℚℓ] ≤ # conjugate tuples ≤ dim M.

These positive integer degrees have a maximum. Take a finite set attaining it and adjoin any further coordinate. The resulting field contains the previous one and has the same degree, so the coordinate was already there. This gives a single finite extension, complete in its ℓ-adic norm, for all the original rational Hecke coordinates. For instance, in ℚ₅(√2) the infinite sequence 1+n√2, n ≥ 0, has two conjugate tuples. Already the coordinate at n=1 generates degree two, since 2 is a nonsquare modulo 5. The same upper bound of two works for every finite set of indices. A. Sutherland, 18.785, Proposition 10.6, completeness in finite dimension[78].

6.18How does an odd-rank Hecke system give a Galois representation?

Let Ω be an algebraic closure of the CM field E and put Γ = Gal(Ω/E). Fix an odd rank m, an automorphic representation U with its weights, and a coefficient identification ι from an algebraic closure of ℚℓ to ℂ. Choose two split places u and v of E above ℓ whose restrictions to the maximal totally real subfield E⁺ are distinct. Keep this pair fixed as the finite sets of test places vary. The construction gives one representation ru,v for all those sets. The three-place argument will identify the companions from different pairs.

The simultaneous polynomial congruences supply one weighted list for all polynomial tests. The rank extraction from cohomology and the local tests give the geometric representations used here. At a spherical split place w away from ℓ, let Bw be the Satake multiset and multiply each entry by (Nw)(m−1)/2. For an arithmetic Frobenius lift σ and a positive integer b, let xj = σ−b. The spherical Hecke operator indexed by these choices measures the sum of the bth powers of the normalized entries. Transport this number back by ι and denote it by θj. We want these numbers to be traces of one representation.

Two arithmetic inputs enter here. The first constructs representations ρi for auxiliary automorphic systems with prescribed local types and suitably separated weights, using geometric Galois representations. For each auxiliary system i the geometric input gives an open dense subset Vi of Γ and finitely many exceptional places. At an eligible spherical place outside the exceptions, the auxiliary representation is unramified. For each arithmetic Frobenius lift σ there that belongs to Vi, the polynomial at σ−1 agrees with the auxiliary Satake polynomial. The input also gives stronger matches at prescribed test places. The second is a congruence theorem for the Hecke eigenvalues ηi of these systems. With any fixed finite set of test places prescribed, it gives this approximation for each ε > 0. There exist finitely many indices F and coefficients ci such that the same bound holds for every polynomial P with integer coefficients in the Hecke coordinates.

|P(θ) − ∑i ∈ F ci P(ηi)|ℓ ≤ ε.

The theorem also places all θj in one finite extension L of ℚℓ because the chosen operators have rational coefficients. To construct a trace at g ∈ Γ, approach g by indices j at which any prescribed finite list of the auxiliary systems agrees with its Galois traces. Such indices exist in every neighborhood. For a neighborhood H of g, take a nonempty open subset of H−1 and intersect it with the finitely many Vi. The intersection is still nonempty and open. Exclude all exceptional places, the primes over ℓ, and the finite fibres above real-subfield primes excluded by the auxiliary level. The degree-one Frobenius argument still supplies an arithmetic Frobenius σ in the intersection. Taking exponent one gives a test xj = σ−1 in H at which all the selected systems match. Taking P to be the single coordinate j puts θj within ε of the continuous sum ∑ ci tr ρi(xj). Shrink the neighborhood until the sum varies by at most ε. Any two such θj then differ by at most ε in the ultrametric norm. Completeness of L gives a limit T(g). The approximation by the same continuous sums is uniform in g, hence T is continuous.

Any integral polynomial in finitely many values T(g₁), …, T(gk) obeys the same estimate. Fix the approximating list F for ε. For each gh, choose indices subject to two conditions. Their group coordinates must belong to a chosen neighborhood of gh, and they must match every system in a chosen finite list containing F. As the neighborhoods shrink and the lists enlarge, the group coordinates converge to gh and the numbers θj converge to T(gh) by the construction of the limit. Make these choices independently for the finitely many arguments of P. Every chosen coordinate matches every system in F, so the original polynomial estimate holds. Polynomial evaluation and the auxiliary traces are continuous, and the ball of radius ε is closed. The estimate therefore holds at the limiting tuple. In particular, a polynomial identity satisfied by every rank-m matrix trace holds for T, since its absolute value is at most every ε > 0. This gives T(1) = m, T(gh) = T(hg) and the alternating trace identity in m+1 variables. These conditions define a rank-m pseudocharacter. The last identity is the alternating sum over permutations, with one trace of an ordered product for each cycle. For matrices it is zero because the antisymmetrizer on the (m+1)st tensor power of an m-dimensional space is zero.

Realizing the trace. Extend T linearly to the group algebra over the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. In each term of the alternating trace identity, every argument appears exactly once. The expression in the extended trace is therefore multilinear, and its vanishing on all tuples of group basis elements implies its vanishing on the whole algebra. Divide by the ideal of elements A with T(AB) = 0 for every B. The pseudocharacter realization theorem makes this quotient a finite product of matrix algebras. On each block a central linear form is a scalar multiple of trace, as one sees on matrix units. If the scalar is c, substituting the same rank-one idempotent into all m+1 slots of the alternating identity gives c(c−1)⋯(c−m) = 0. Thus c is a nonnegative integer. If it were zero, every matrix A supported in that block would satisfy T(AB) = 0 for every B, since AB stays in the block. The trace pairing has zero radical on the quotient by construction. Every surviving block consequently has positive multiplicity. Take c copies of the defining module of that block. The total dimension is T(1) = m and the resulting semisimple representation r has trace T. For continuity, choose group matrices r(hk) spanning their image algebra. The trace pairing on it is nondegenerate because its restriction to each matrix block is the ordinary trace pairing times its positive multiplicity. Hence every entry of r(g) is a fixed linear combination of the continuous functions T(g hk). Rouquier, Caractérisation des caractères et pseudo-caractères, Lemma 4.1 and §4[79].

A rank-three congruence. For s ≥ 1, the representations of the additive group ℤ₅ given by diag((1+5s)g,1,1) have traces congruent to 3 modulo 5s. Integer powers extend continuously to ℤ₅, since taking fifth powers increases the divisibility of the difference from 1 by at least one power of 5. An integral polynomial in any finite list of these traces is consequently congruent to its value on the constant list of threes. Here one system with coefficient 1 gives accuracy 5−s simultaneously for every polynomial, and the limiting companion is the three-dimensional trivial representation.

6.19How does one recover unramifiedness at a specified place?

Keep the chosen pair and its representation r = ru,v and fix w ∈ Qd away from ℓ where U is spherical. In the construction choose the finite test set {w}. The congruence and geometric inputs then supply a family whose every member is unramified at this w and matches its own Satake parameters there. The trace of the same r is uniformly approximated by finite linear combinations of their traces. Indeed the construction of T passed the estimate for any approximating subfamily to Γ, with the original coefficients. We may now use the subfamily attached to {w}.

Choose s in inertia at a place of Ω above w. Every auxiliary ρi in this subfamily sends s to the identity. Its traces at sg and g therefore agree for every g. Letting the uniform trace error tend to zero gives

tr((r(s) − 1)r(g)) = 0   for every g ∈ Γ.

The tested matrices span the image algebra, and r(s) − 1 belongs to it. Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing gives r(s) = 1. The quantifier over g matters. For instance, in the standard two-dimensional representation of SL₂(ℤℓ) plus a trivial line, let s have diagonal entries 1 and upper off-diagonal entry 1 in its two-dimensional block. Let g be its transpose. Both have trace 3 in dimension three, whereas sg has trace 4. Testing the translate g detects the nonidentity s.

The same subfamily gives the power traces at σ−b for every b ≥ 1 and every Frobenius lift σ at w. Here each approximant matches its own Hecke coordinate at the chosen index, so its two weighted sums coincide. Sending ε to zero in the estimates for θj and for T(xj) gives equality of the two limits. The first m power sums pb recover the characteristic polynomial. Indeed for roots αj put H(z) = ∏(1−αjz). Expanding −zH′/H as ∑b≥1 pbzb and comparing coefficients after multiplication by H determines each coefficient from those preceding it. Division by 1,…,m is valid in characteristic zero. Thus r has exactly the normalized Satake polynomial at w.

For example, a rank-three local multiset {1,1,−1} at norm 5 becomes {5,5,−5} after normalization. Its first three power sums are 5, 75 and 125. The elementary symmetric functions are 5, (5²−75)/2 = −25 and (125−5 · 75−25 · 5)/3 = −125. They give (X−5)²(X+5), retaining the repeated root.

6.20How do three places above ℓ give one companion with the full local data?

The odd-rank approximation first chooses two auxiliary places above ℓ, called u and v. They must lie above different primes of E⁺. For the representation ru,v thus obtained, the unramified matches hold at all the allowed spherical places away from ℓ. Why do the filtration jumps survive a weighted approximation of traces?

Fix a spherical place w above ℓ away from the two auxiliary primes. Write K = Ew for the local field. At each embedding τ of K into the algebraic closure of ℚℓ, every member of the approximating family for {w} has the same multiset of filtration jumps Jτ. A jump h occurs once for each dimension of the graded space Filh/Filh+1 of the de Rham periods at τ. The assertion to prove is that the local restriction of the previously constructed r is crystalline and has precisely those multiplicities. The given convergence concerns linear combinations of global traces. The coefficients can vary with the accuracy, and the representations in a combination can act on different spaces.

From traces to periods. First form the ℤℓ-lattice spanned by the global matrices r(g). Left multiplication by r(g) preserves this lattice, which contains the identity matrix. The lattice comparison theorem uses global semisimplicity and the uniform trace estimates to approximate this action modulo ℓq for each q. Its approximating lattice lies in a finite product of matrix spaces for the auxiliary representations. The lists of representations can be made nested by adjoining the earlier lists and giving the added terms coefficient zero in the current sum. Restrict the resulting actions and comparison maps to the local group at w. On each rationalized approximating lattice, the group acts on the matrix columns by the given auxiliary representations. Thus these columns carry crystalline representations. Taking the maximum of |h| over all Jτ gives a single bound on all their jumps, through every level of approximation.

The bounded-weight Breuil–Kisin comparison for these lattices is the period-theoretic input. It gives integral matrices describing the periods at each level and a frame on the limiting lattice. For every precision a sufficiently deep level agrees with that frame to the required precision under the comparison maps. If the frames on all the levels satisfy the crystalline condition, so does the limiting frame. Its invariant periods span the limiting lattice after extending scalars to the crystalline period ring. To see why this yields periods for r itself, work over a finite coefficient field of definition and view its vector space over ℚℓ. For each vector v, evaluation A ↦ Av on the rational matrix lattice is equivariant and takes the identity to v. After extending scalars to the period ring, this map sends invariant periods to invariant periods. Its image contains 1 ⊗ v, so these invariant periods span the whole target as v varies. This is the period criterion for crystallinity. Brinon and Conrad, Theorem 5.2.1 and Remark 5.2.3 on admissibility over a period ring[80].

Recovering each jump. Fix τ. Choose a local Galois element for which the period construction gives a nonzero ℓ-adic scalar z of infinite multiplicative order. In a period basis adapted to the filtration the associated operator has eigenvalues zh, one for each jump h. Every auxiliary member therefore gives the same nth power trace Sn = ∑h∈Jτ (zh)n, counting repetitions. Write Xn for the corresponding trace on the target representation. Write U for the operator on the auxiliary matrix lattice, whose dimension may exceed the rank of the target. The period comparison bounds its entries and those of the level operators U′ by one constant B ≥ 1. For each precision q it supplies a level and a map Π with ‖UΠ − ΠU′‖ ≤ Bℓ−q, where the norm is the largest absolute value of an entry. The telescoping sum for UnΠ − ΠU′n has terms Ua(UΠ − ΠU′)U′n−1−a. The ultrametric triangle inequality bounds the sum by its largest term. For each fixed power the error thus tends to zero, even if the dimensions of the level lattices grow.

Period operators commute with equivariant evaluation on vectors. If e represents the identity in lattice coordinates, evaluation of Une on each vector therefore gives the nth power of the target operator on that vector. Applying the matrix trace functional to Une recovers Xn. The comparison map preserves that vector and the weighted trace functional to within ℓ−q. Together with the power estimate this gives the following bound with Kn independent of q. The scalar Cq is the sum of the level coefficients in the coefficient embedding used for τ, since every auxiliary member has the very same Sn.

|Xn − CqSn|ℓ ≤ Knℓ−q,   X₀ = S₀ = m.

At power zero this estimate gives |1−Cq|ℓ ≤ K₀ℓ−q/|m|ℓ. Division is valid even when ℓ divides the positive rank. Thus Cq tends to 1. Holding n fixed and letting q increase now gives Xn = Sn. The power-sum recursion recovers the multiset of eigenvalues from its first m positive power sums. Since z has infinite order, zh determines the integer h, including its sign. This recovers the entire multiset Jτ. For an arithmetic check, the lists {0,1,2} and {0,1,4} give identical power sums at z = −1 because 2 and 4 are both even. At z = 2 their first sums are 7 and 19. This is the role of the infinite-order choice.

How does the same companion acquire the local Weil polynomial?

Crystallinity gives the local period space on which Frobenius acts. Its Weil polynomial requires another comparison. For each local Weil element σ, each integer N ≥ 0 and each ε > 0, the congruence theorem supplies a finite set F of these approximants and coefficients cρ in the ℓ-adic coefficient field. How can the chosen place also be one of the original auxiliary places?

Here E contains √(−d), −d is a square in ℚℓ, [E⁺∶ℚ] is even, and E/E⁺ is unramified at finite places. All places above ℓ are split. The remaining field assumption provides three places w₁, w₂, w₃ above ℓ with pairwise distinct underlying primes in E⁺. Fix once and for all the representation from the first two. For an arbitrary spherical target place w above ℓ, at most one of these three lies over the same real-subfield prime as w. Choose the other two for a new auxiliary pair. The corresponding companion now has the strong local conclusion at w. Both companions match the same source polynomial at almost all places of absolute degree one away from ℓ, by the two splitting tests and sphericity. Their characteristic polynomials agree on Γ by continuity and density. Brauer–Nesbitt identifies the semisimple representations. The intertwining isomorphism carries the inertia action, filtered period modules and Weil–Deligne polynomial to those of the companion fixed at the outset. The trace argument for Brauer–Nesbitt.

ru,v ≃ rw₁,w₂   with u, v chosen away from the prime below w.

Why the real-subfield prime matters. Take E⁺ = ℚ(√2,√3), E = E⁺(i), d = 1, and ℓ = 97. The real degree is four. The quadratic extension E/E⁺ is unramified at finite places. Its defining polynomials X²+1 and X²+X+1 have discriminants −4 and −3, respectively. The latter generates the same extension since √3 ∈ E⁺. At every finite place at least one of these discriminants is a unit, so the corresponding quadratic algebra is unramified there. Modulo 97 the numbers 14, 10 and 22 square to 2, 3 and −1, respectively. Their negatives give the other simple roots. Thus the primes of E⁺ above 97 are labeled by sign pairs for (√2,√3), and each splits into two in E. Take the auxiliary real-subfield primes (+,+), (+,−), (−,+). A target over (+,+) uses (+,−) and (−,+), regardless of which root of −1 labels the target itself. This gives the required conclusion for either target on the originally fixed companion. Sutherland, Theorem 12.19 and §12.4 on discriminants of orders[81].

6.21Where do both lifts have the same source parameters?

Fix the two lifts, their common twist κ and the finite lists of auxiliary Hecke characters ψ1,i and ψ2,i. The odd-rank attachment theorem supplies a continuous semisimple representation ρj for each lift. For all but finitely many places in Qd, each ρj already matches the normalized Satake parameters of its lift whenever those parameters exist. This compatibility is an input from the odd-rank construction. We now show that all the hypotheses for applying it to both lifts hold together on a dense set of inverse Frobenius elements.

Each of the finitely many characters is unramified outside a finite set, as is κ. Here is the reason for finiteness. A neighborhood of 1 in the idele group contains every single-place integral unit outside finitely many places, along with every power of that unit. By continuity we can choose the neighborhood so that all its character values lie at distance less than ½ from 1. A complex number with all of its integral powers in this disk must be 1. Its modulus must first be 1 by taking positive and negative powers. For a different point of the unit circle the averages of its first N powers tend to zero by the geometric sum formula, whereas numbers in the disk have real part greater than ½. Thus the character is trivial on the entire local unit group at every remaining place.

Collect in one finite set the places above ℓ, the conductors of all these characters, the exceptions for both odd-rank matches, and the finite exceptional set for sphericity of the source. Outside this union each w ∈ Qd supplies a source Satake multiset Bw. The two lift identities use that very same multiset. Write Bwalg for the result of multiplying each entry by (Nw)(n−1)/2, and Sw for the result of multiplying each entry by κ(w)−1. On applying the fixed coefficient identification, the eigenvalue multiset of ρj at inverse Frobenius is

Sw ⊎ {ψj,1(w), …, ψj,t(w)},   j = 1, 2.

The density result allows this whole finite union to be discarded at once. Adding the other list to each side therefore gives equal polynomials on a dense set. The character-transfer argument extends equality to Γ and isolates the auxiliary lines. The exclusions here serve the density argument. At a particular target place, including one above ℓ, the stronger local conclusion uses the separately prescribed data there and the final untwisting step.

6.22How do good primes identify a character on the entire group?

Fix ℓ and write Γ = Gal(Ω/E), where Ω is an algebraic closure of the CM field E. The two lifts give continuous semisimple representations ρ₁ and ρ₂ of dimension n+t over an algebraic closure k of ℚℓ. Write D(A) for the direct sum of its character lines, and LA(g) for the product of their linear factors X−χ(g).

At a good split place the two Frobenius multisets consist of the same normalized source parameters together with the entries of their respective lists. Add the other list to each side. Now both sides contain the common parameters, every entry of A and every entry of B, with multiplicities. In the local–global application the places belong to the set of good split places just constructed. The argument using finite Galois quotients gives this density for the specified set, and the common local comparison supplies its polynomial identity outside finitely many places. Let Pρ(g) = det(X − ρ(g)). The embedding k ≃ ℂ identifies the polynomials at these Frobenius elements. For any x ∈ k, evaluating both polynomials at x gives continuous k-valued functions of g, since determinants and finite products are continuous. Equality on the dense set extends to every g. Varying x in the infinite field k gives

Pρ₁(g) LB(g) = Pρ₂(g) LA(g)   for every g ∈ Γ.

Brauer–Nesbitt in characteristic zero. Two finite-dimensional semisimple representations of any group over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero are isomorphic if their characteristic polynomials agree on every element. Indeed, their traces agree on the group and therefore on its group algebra by linearity. Take the finitely many distinct irreducible constituents of both representations. By the density theorem for algebras, one group-algebra element can act by a rank-one projection on any chosen constituent and by zero on the others. Its trace counts the copies of that constituent. Characteristic zero recovers these counts as integers. Equal counts for every constituent give an isomorphism of the two direct sums. Etingof et al., Theorem 2.5(ii)[83] and Theorem 2.17(i)[84].

Apply the theorem to the augmented representations. Fix one isomorphism from ρ₂ ⊕ D(A) to ρ₁ ⊕ D(B), and take a basis vector on a line χ in A. Its image is nonzero and transforms by χ under every g. Write its coordinates as (v, (bγ)γ∈B). Projection onto each auxiliary coordinate gives

γ(g) bγ = χ(g) bγ   for every g ∈ Γ.

If bγ were nonzero, γ and χ would agree on all of Γ, contradicting cross-list disjointness. All auxiliary coordinates vanish. Thus v is a nonzero vector in ρ₁ spanning a Γ-invariant line on which the action is exactly χ.

Four group elements. On Γ = (ℤ/2ℤ)² put α(a,b) = (−1)a and β(a,b) = (−1)b. Let ρ₁ = α ⊕ 1 and ρ₂ = β ⊕ 1. Both characters take the value −1 at (1,1), and both take the value 1 at (0,0). At (1,0) their values are −1 and 1. The two original polynomials there are (X+1)(X−1) and (X−1)². Adding β on the first side and α on the second gives (X+1)(X−1)² on each side. For every element the augmented representations have the same three summands, in different order. Removing α from ρ₁ and β from ρ₂ leaves the trivial character in both.

An automorphic form is a function on an arithmetic quotient of a group with specified transformation and regularity properties. A theta lift uses an integral kernel to carry such functions between groups. In the part of the proof examined here, the relevant spaces of forms at fixed level and weight are presented as finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces. Its adjoint T goes from M to V. The row space has designated subspaces Mσ for its types σ. A type here labels a component of the space of forms. The target has subspaces Vπ for target types π.

The required Gram hypothesis says that PT acts by a real scalar λσ on Mσ, strictly positive whenever Mσ is nonzero. For every f in that subspace the adjoint identity gives

Thus a nonzero row vector survives the upward map. Positive semidefiniteness, which is automatic for an operator times its adjoint, would only yield λσ ≥ 0. Which short rows stay independent over the number field?

The height label uses one power of two for each row. To extract those powers we need an invertible rational row matrix Δ for which both the remaining block and its inverse stay bounded. A bound on the entries alone would allow two rows to become almost parallel. The proof brings the volume spanned by the rows into the same estimate. Write D = [E ∶ ℚ], n for the number of rows and r = Dn for the real dimension in the reduction.

Read lengths and volume from one flag. In its real span, let L be the Euclidean lattice generated by the images of an integral basis of the row module. Its jth successive minimum λj is the smallest radius of a closed ball about zero containing j linearly independent lattice vectors. Discreteness gives vectors attaining these radii in a nested sequence of spans. Orthogonalize the resulting real basis. Scale the new orthogonal direction at step j by 1/λj, obtaining a linear map T. If the last nonzero orthogonal coordinate of a lattice vector x is its jth, then x lies outside the previous span. To allow for tied minima, let k be the first index with λk = λj. If x were shorter, it and the first k − 1 vectors would give k independent vectors shorter than λk. Thus ‖x‖ ≥ λj. Every nonzero coordinate of x is scaled by at least 1/λj. Thus ‖Tx‖ ≥ 1.

The inverse image of the open unit ball under T contains no nonzero lattice point. Its volume is vol(ball)·∏λj. By the symmetric convex body bound this is at most 2rcovol(L). To see the volume threshold, shrink the body by one half. If it had more volume than a fundamental cell of L, two of its translates into that cell would overlap. The difference of the two original points would be a nonzero lattice vector in the original body, by convexity and symmetry. The unit ball contains the open cube of side 2/√r, in orthonormal coordinates. For r ≥ 1 these observations give

λ₁ ⋯ λr ≤ rr/2 covol(L).

The covolume is taken in the real span of L. For an integral basis u with image under the row map φ, it is √det Gram(φu).

Take one row from each block of D minima. Suppose we have selected i rows independent over E. Their field span has dimension Di over ℚ. The ball of radius λDi+1 contains Di + 1 real-independent lattice vectors. Lift them through φ to integral combinations of the original rows. A rational relation between the lifts would, after clearing denominators, be an integral relation between the independent images. At least one lift therefore lies outside the previous field span. Choose it as the next row wi+1. Since the minima increase, the first radius in each block, raised to the power D, is bounded by the product of the D radii in that block. Consequently

∏i=1n ‖φwi‖D ≤ ∏k=0n−1 λDk+1D ≤ λ₁ ⋯ λr.

Here φ is only required to be additive and ℤ-linear. It sends a row to its archimedean coordinates after the given change of variables. The dimension argument takes place over E before applying φ.

Why are the inverses of the normalized blocks bounded?

Choose a dyadic scale ai with ‖φwi‖ ≤ ai < 2‖φwi‖. Dividing each row by its scale bounds every entry of the resulting matrix c. Take all D integral-basis multiples of each of the n selected rows. They span a full-rank sublattice of the original row lattice, of index m ≥ 1. Its squared volume is m² det Gram(φu). Each of the D real rows coming from wi carries the same scale ai. With G(c) the Gram determinant of all the rescaled rows, we get

(m covol(L))² = (∏ aiD)² G(c).

The product of the scales is bounded in the form ∏ aiD ≤ 2rrr/2 covol(L). Cancel the covolume. This bounds m² by a constant times G(c). Since m ≥ 1, it also bounds G(c) away from zero. On the bounded closed set of matrix entries this continuous determinant has a finite upper bound. Its positive lower bound keeps c in an invertible compact set, where inversion is bounded. The upper bound gives a uniform bound for the integer m. Taking the factorial of an integer upper bound makes one integer M divisible by every possible m. Multiplication by M therefore puts every original row in the module generated by the selected rows.

Use the same rows at every finite place. Write Ō for the product of the local integer rings at finite places. Given the finite adelic block β, take Λ = {x ∈ En ∣ xβ ∈ Ōn}. An integer clearing the denominators of β shows that Λ contains a multiple of every coordinate row. Clearing the denominators of β−1 bounds Λ inside one fractional free module. As the ring of integers is Noetherian, Λ is finitely generated. Apply the argument at infinity to Λ and call the selected row matrix Δ. The entries of Δβ are integral by construction. For its inverse, choose positive integers d₁,d₂ clearing the denominators of β and Δ−1, respectively. Approximate a row of β−1 by a rational row x so that their difference belongs to d₁d₂Ōn. Multiplying by β shows that xβ is integral. Hence x belongs to Λ, and Mx is an integral combination of the rows of Δ. Multiplication by Δ−1 gives integral entries for MxΔ−1. The original approximation error still has integral entries after multiplication by MΔ−1. This proves that M(Δβ)−1 is integral at every finite place. Together with the compact real block this is the uniform reduction used for the height label.

Why the second row can require the third minimum

Use E = ℚ(i), n = 2, and the ordinary Euclidean norm on ℂ². Let the finite block be diag(1,1/3) above 3 and the identity elsewhere. Its rational row lattice is Λ = ℤ[i]e₁ ⊕ 3ℤ[i]e₂. The first two independent real vectors can be e₁ and ie₁. They span just one line over E. Every row outside that line has length at least 3, attained by 3e₂. The four real minima are 1,1,3,3. The two chosen field rows have squared lengths 1 and 9, whose product equals the covolume 9. The dyadic scales 1 and 4 give the real block diag(1,3/4). Its inverse is diag(1,4/3). With Δ = diag(1,3), the finite block Δβ is the identity above 3 and diag(1,3) elsewhere. Both matrices and their inverses have integral entries at the places where they occur.

Count the centres for a fixed label. At scalar depth k, subtract a rational element from an adele of F to put it in a fixed compact set. Bound its real components in absolute value by a nonnegative integer R. At each real place use the grid 2−kℤ between −R and R. Its integer numerators have exactly 2·2kR + 1 possibilities. Rounding leaves an error of size at most 2−k. The finite component stays in a fixed compact set. Across the d real places the number of scalar centres is bounded by C₀ bk, where b = 2d, C₀ = (2R + 1)d and B = b².

Choose δ in E with conjugate −δ so that (1,δ) is an F-basis. A skew-Hermitian matrix S can be described by n² scalar adelic coordinates tij. Its (i,j) entry is (tij−tji) + δ(tij+tji). On the diagonal this is 2δtii. Off the diagonal the two ordered entries share two scalar coordinates. Cover tij at depth μi+μj. Its error then carries the factor corresponding to the left and right diagonal scalings. Combining the coordinate choices writes S as a rational matrix plus a centre y plus DμωDμ, where Dμ = diag(sμᵢ) and the entries of ω lie in a fixed compact set. The finite set Yμ of centres is the image of the product of the scalar grids. Its size is at most the number of grid tuples.

|Yμ| ≤ ∏i,j C₀ bμᵢ+μⱼ = C₀n² b2n∑μᵢ = C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ.

A rank-two count. Take one real place, a scalar grid with R = 1 and label μ = (1,0). The four ordered depths are 2, 1, 1 and 0. The corresponding lists of integer numerators have 9, 5, 5 and 3 entries. Their product gives 675 tuples. The formula above permits 3⁴·4² = 1,296. These numbers count candidates and bound their image. Counting rational cosets still requires the multiplicity argument.

Why a centre has bounded multiplicity. Subtract the rational unipotent term and put the compact error into a matrix w(q). In the Cayley coordinates the proof obtains a rational invertible matrix Z(q) = z(μ,y)w(q), with w(q) in a fixed compact set. The map q ↦ Z(q) is injective. In fact, equality of two such matrices makes the original rational representatives differ on the left by an element stabilizing the diagonal subspace. They represent the same Siegel coset.

Fix μ and a centre y. For a nonempty finite collection of cosets using them, choose one member q₀. Multiplying by Z(q₀)−1 cancels the common left factor z(μ,y). The relative matrices w(q₀)−1w(q) are rational and belong to a fixed compact set, independent of μ, y and q₀. Each matrix entry belongs to a finite set of rational points, so there are at most N possible relative matrices. Left multiplication preserves injectivity. Each chosen centre can therefore account for at most N cosets. Summing over all available centres gives an upper bound even when some centres are unused and others occur for multiple cosets.

#{q ∈ A with label μ} ≤ N |Yμ| ≤ N C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ   for every finite sample A.

A uniform finite bound on all finite samples also bounds the full fibre, since a larger fibre would contain a finite sample exceeding it. The summability proof uses exactly the finite-sample statement. Multiplication by the height bound raised to the power T gives the geometric decay when T > n.

How do the Fourier coefficients recover the theta mean?

Consider the lower range of the Siegel–Weil formula. Write n for the source rank and m for the dimension of the target Hermitian space V over the quadratic extension E/F. Thus n < m ≤ 2n and n + w < m, where w is the Witt index of V. The evaluation point s₀ = (m − n)/2 can lie on the boundary of absolute convergence or to its left. Take a test function Φ in the global Fock subspace of the Schrödinger model. With this input we can compare one frequency of the two sides at a time. The frequencies are rational Hermitian n × n matrices β. A frequency is nondegenerate when det β ≠ 0.

For an automorphic function F, move g by the upper unipotent matrix u(b) with diagonal blocks 1 and upper right block b. Invariance under rational unipotent translations makes this function of b periodic. Its domain is the Hermitian adelic matrices modulo the rational ones. Use a fundamental region 𝒟 of volume one. Put ⟨β,b⟩ = ½ TrE/F(tr(βb)), with rational entries embedded in the adeles and the field trace extended to the adeles.

Cβ(F)(g) = ∫𝒟 F(u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

On the theta side, a frequency selects a Gram matrix. Write φ = ω(g)Φ for the translated test function. A rational tuple x of n vectors of V contributes φ(h−1x) to the theta kernel. Translating by u(b) multiplies this summand by ψ(⟨Gram(x),b⟩). The target action of h preserves the Gram matrix. After weighting by the inverse β-character, integration gives 1 if Gram(x) = β and 0 otherwise. Absolute theta convergence justifies grouping tuples by Gram matrix, averaging over [U(V)] and integrating the resulting character series. When det β ≠ 0, every tuple in that fibre has rank n, since rank(x∗Gram(V)x) ≤ rank(x). Thus Cβ(I)(g) is the normalized average of the sum over precisely these full-rank tuples, where I is the theta mean.

On the Eisenstein side, the same frequency selects the open cell. For Re z > n/2 the coset sum has a summable bound on a compact set of representatives. This permits integration of the sum by cells. On each other cell, when det β ≠ 0, there is a translation preserving its contribution and multiplying its character by a scalar different from 1. Its integral is therefore zero. The open-cell cosets are indexed by rational Hermitian translations. Their translates of 𝒟 cover the full adelic Hermitian space, giving the integral below. Here w is the Weyl element interchanging the two isotropic coordinate spaces and fz is the flat section.

Cβ(E(·,z))(g) = ∫Hermn(𝔸) fz(w u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

The Weyl action is a Fourier transform. Evaluating it at zero integrates the translated test function against the Gram character. Consequently the section in this integral is the Gram-character integral of φ times the height H(w u(b)g)z−s₀. This identifies the unfolded family on the right half-plane with the Whittaker integral for β. Its holomorphic value at s₀ is the same full-rank fibre average computed on the theta side. The input used here combines finite-place factors, the unramified Gram-density calculation, a real-place computation, global factorization and a low-rank density identity. Finite linear combination treats the compact argument, then the Iwasawa decomposition transports the identity to arbitrary g.

What can be invisible to all the nondegenerate coefficients?

Take the additive group of symmetric 2 × 2 matrices over the field of three elements. This finite example has 27 elements. Set ζ = exp(2πi/3), T = diag(1,0) and F(B) = ζB₁₁. The normalized β-coefficient is the average of ζtr((T−β)B). At β = T all 27 terms are 1. For β ≠ T, at least one of the three matrix coordinates has a nonzero coefficient in this linear form. Its sum is 1 + ζ + ζ² = 0. The off-diagonal entry appears with multiplier 2, which is invertible in this field. Hence every invertible β has coefficient zero, although F(0) = 1. The missing information sits at the rank-one frequency T.

How does the proof rule out such a discrepancy? At a real place selected using the Witt-index inequality, choose a compactly supported test function η whose Fourier transform vanishes on singular Hermitian matrices. Suppose a continuous automorphic function F has zero full-rank coefficients for all g. Integrate its unipotent translates against η. The β-coefficient of this convolution factors into the β-coefficient of F and the transform of η at the associated local frequency. For invertible β the first factor is zero. For singular β the associated local matrix is singular too, so the second factor is zero. All Fourier coefficients of the convolution now vanish, so Fourier uniqueness on the compact Hermitian quotient makes the convolution zero. Density and continuity give the same vanishing with a group translation on either side of the unipotent argument.

Removing a possible pole and computing the value

At this real place, first take the Gaussian Fock vector (the constant polynomial 1). The local signature condition gives a choice of η and of the two translations for which a compact-group average defines an operator T with nonzero scalar c(0) on the theta mean of this vector. On the corresponding regularized Eisenstein family the scalar is c(z−s₀). Meanwhile, the convolution argument shows that T kills every automorphic discrepancy with zero full-rank coefficients. On a discrepancy with eigenvalue c(0), this forces the discrepancy itself to vanish.

To see where holomorphy enters, write the continued Eisenstein family as A(z)/d(z) with holomorphic numerator and polynomial denominator. Factor d(z) = (z−s₀)kd₁(z) with d₁(s₀) ≠ 0. The full-rank coefficient identities ensure that while a power remains in the denominator, the regularized numerator at the point has zero full-rank coefficients. Its eigenvalue forces that value to vanish, so one can divide the numerator by z−s₀ holomorphically and repeat. After k divisions, the difference between the resulting numerator at s₀ and d₁(s₀)I is killed by T and has eigenvalue c(0). It is zero. Division by d₁ now gives the required value.

The standard-model result supplies the lower branch of the doubled formula after the change of model.

Holomorphic value at z = s₀ of E(g,z) = I(g).

What does a full-rank Whittaker factor count at a good finite place?

The open-cell integral compares a Fourier coefficient of the Eisenstein series with the mean of tuples of vectors having Gram matrix T. At a good finite place v, this comparison has a concrete arithmetic content. Count the tuples whose Gram matrix agrees with T modulo increasing powers of a uniformizer. Once the measures are fixed, the normalized count gives the local Whittaker value at z₀ = (M−n)/2, where M is the dimension of the Hermitian space and n is the number of vectors.

Write q for the size of the residue field of Fv. At the places treated here, 2 is a unit, the local quadratic algebra is unramified, the forms J and T are integral with unit determinant, and the scalar character ψv has conductor the valuation ring. The integral lattice is trace-self-dual. Set ε = −1 when the quadratic algebra is the unramified field, and ε = +1 when it splits. The Schwartz function is the characteristic function of the integral M × n matrix lattice. A nonzero rational det T gives this unit condition at almost all places.

Count one Gram fibre. Let Nk be the number of distinct matrices X modulo ϖk satisfying X∗JX ≡ T. Here ∗ is conjugate transpose. There are q2kMn possible input matrices and qkn² Hermitian targets. The density compares the proportion of matrices in this fibre with the proportion one would obtain if every target occurred equally often.

αk(J,T) = Nk · qkn²/q2kMn = ∏j=0n−1 (1 − (ε/q)M−j),   k ≥ 1,   n ≤ M.

At level one a change of basis reduces the unimodular target to the identity. Solutions are orthonormal frames over the residue algebra. Choose one vector of norm one, then choose the next in its orthogonal complement. In dimension r, the norm-one count is q2r−1(1−(ε/q)r). The successive dimensions M, …, M−n+1 give the product above after normalization.

Why does the density stay constant at deeper levels?

Lift a solution modulo ϖk by writing its next representative as X+ϖkY. For k ≥ 1 the quadratic term in Y disappears modulo ϖk+1. The correction must solve the linear equation Y∗JX+X∗JY = H in the residue algebra, with H Hermitian. It is solvable for every H. For instance, since 2 and T are invertible here, take Y = ½XT−1H. The linear map has a domain with q2Mn elements and a codomain with qn² elements. Every fibre has q2Mn−n² elements. Thus Nk+1 gains exactly the factor cancelled by the next density normalization.

  • Every positive level gives the same density

A Gram fibre over nine elements. Take ℚ(i) over ℚ at the inert prime 3, J = I₃ and T = I₂. Then q = 3 and ε = −1. In 𝔽₉ the norm of a+bi is a²+b² in 𝔽₃. There are 252 choices for a norm-one column of length three. For each, its two-dimensional orthogonal complement has 24 norm-one columns. This gives 6,048 frames among 9⁶ matrices at the first level. The normalized density is 6,048/3⁸ = 224/243 = (1+3−3)(1−3−2). Each frame has 3⁸ lifts to level two.

Which integral gives this number? Use the self-dual Haar measure on the matrix space for its Weil pairing and the self-dual Haar measure on the Hermitian matrices for their trace pairing. Write ⟨T,b⟩ for half the quadratic-algebra trace of tr(Tb). The source integrates the following expression in b. Inside it the character has positive Gram phase, and the Fourier projection contributes the negative target phase. The height is h(b) = vol(L+bL)/vol(L) for the standard column lattice L. The auxiliary Haar measure in this ratio cancels.

Wv(z) = ∫ h(b)−(z−z₀) ψv(−⟨T,b⟩) (∫integral X ψv(⟨b,X∗JX⟩) dX) db,   Re z > n².

At a good place the Hermitian integral lattice has volume one. Grouping by its cosets rewrites the integral as a sum. The cosets appear in increasing finite sets indexed by a level k. With t = εMq−(2z+n), their sums of absolute values have a geometric majorant because qn²|t| < 1 in the stated half-plane. Each positive-level sum is the same polynomial in t.

How do congruence counts determine a polynomial?

At each positive level the finite Fourier sum is a polynomial Pk(t) whose terms are weighted by the level character at the negative target, and by a nonnegative lattice-index exponent of t. Evaluate it at t = (ε/q)m for each auxiliary rank m ≥ n. Finite Fourier orthogonality and the Gaussian sums identify that evaluation with the density of T for the identity form in dimension m. The counting formula just proved gives ∏j(1−(ε/q)m−j). This equals the evaluation of ∏j(1−t(εq)j) at the same point. Those points have distinct absolute values, so the two polynomials agree everywhere. The auxiliary rank varies only in this interpolation step.

Wv(z) = ∏j=0n−1 (1−εM+jq−(2z+n−j)),   Wv(z₀) = α₁(J,T).

The product extends to an entire function of z. Substituting 2z₀ = M−n gives exactly the density, since εM+j = εM−j. In the example z₀ = ½, while the integral theorem assumes Re z > 4. The continued value is therefore obtained by evaluating the explicit product.

From places to the global coefficient. The pure adelic datum is standard outside a finite set. The global construction multiplies the real factor, the finitely many exceptional factors and the product of the explicit good factors. The last product is holomorphic on Re z > 0. Agreement on a sufficiently far right half-plane identifies the continuation of the global integral. Since n < M, z₀ lies in this positive half-plane. The remaining identification with the theta coefficient uses the global density theorem equating the product of the real and finite densities at T with the normalized mean of the rational Gram fibre. The comparison then returns through Iwasawa decomposition and the open-cell identity to the coefficient at every group argument.

Apply the strict-rank theorem with the extra range assumption n+2 ≤ M or anisotropy of J, and with an integrability hypothesis on a right half-plane. Its general statement also has an implication imposing a Gaussian vacuum condition if a flag is true. In this branch the flag is false, so that particular implication is automatic. The congruence counts, the Whittaker integral and the density-to-mean identity all enter separately. For the example with M = 3 and n = 2 the positive-definite identity form over ℚ(i) is anisotropic over that field.

What replaces the good-place formula at an exceptional finite place?

The good-place count assumes a particular test function, the indicator of the full matrix lattice. A test supported on just one residue class can change the answer even at an unramified prime. The local argument works at every finite place and gives an entire function of the complex parameter z. Its value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 is the density of the chosen test at the target Gram matrix. The global application has n < M.

Fix the local quadratic algebra Ev = Fv ⊗F E, the local component ψv of the adelic additive character, a nondegenerate Hermitian form J of rank M, and a Hermitian target T of size n whose determinant is invertible in Ev. This allows determinants of nonzero valuation. A test Φ is a locally constant, compactly supported function of the M × n matrix X. Use the self-dual measures μ on the matrix space and ν on the Hermitian space for their respective pairings. For a Haar measure λ on Evn and two compact open additive subgroups L₁, L₂, put r(b) = λ(L₁+bL₂)/λ(L₁). It is at least one. Write ⟨b,S⟩ for half the field-algebra trace of the matrix trace of bS. The opposite signs single out the fibre X∗JX = T.

u(b) = ∫ Φ(X) ψv(⟨b,X∗JX−T⟩) dμ(X),   Wv(z) = ∫ r(b)−(z−s₀) u(b) dν(b)   for Re z sufficiently large.

Why can one compact ball determine an entire function? On a shell R < ‖b‖ ≤ 2R, change variables by b ↦ (1+x)∗b(1+x), with x in a small additive matrix ball of radius C/R. These changes preserve the shell, its Haar measure, the lattice index and the integral containing the positive Gram phase. The negative target phase acquires a term linear in x and a term quadratic in x. The latter has norm bounded by a constant times R(C/R)², so the character is trivial on it for large R. Invertibility of T lets one choose C so that at every b in the shell the linear term gives a nontrivial character of the x-ball. Its Haar integral is zero. Averaging the change of variables therefore kills the shell integral for every z, with one cutoff valid for all z. At a singular target the linear term can lose this oscillation, and the stated density hypothesis covers only the regular set.

Choose a ball B₀ beyond that cutoff and double its radius successively. Adding any of the resulting shells leaves the integral over B₀ unchanged. On B₀ the index and its logarithm are bounded, so one can differentiate the compact integral with respect to z. This gives an entire Wv, with no poles. A separate absolute estimate identifies it with the original integral on a right half-plane. For radii growing by a fixed local dilation, the jth outer shell has r(b) ≥ 2j and volume at most a constant times κj. Thus the integral of the absolute value has a geometric majorant when Re z is large. The statement requires existence of a real threshold depending on the data.

How does the test enter the value? Let g be the supplied continuous density of the pushforward of Φ dμ by X ↦ X∗JX on the open set of invertible targets. At z = s₀ the lattice weight is one. Integrating over a large additive ball Λ in b retains those X whose Gram matrix belongs to T+Λ⊥. Indeed, the average of the phase on Λ is one when the difference annihilates Λ and zero otherwise. The annihilator shrinks into the regular set around T, and self-duality gives ν(Λ)ν(Λ⊥) = 1. The integral is therefore an average of g near T. By continuity it approaches g(T). Every sufficiently large ball already gives Wv(s₀).

∫Λ u(b) dν(b) = (1/ν(Λ⊥)) ∫T+Λ⊥ g(S) dν(S)   ⟶   g(T) = Wv(s₀).

Compute the entire factor for one residue class at 3

Take E = ℚ(i), F = ℚ and the inert prime 3. Let J be the two-dimensional identity, n = 1, T = 1 and L₁ = L₂ = 𝒪Eᵥ. Use a character of conductor ℤ₃. The standard integral lattices have self-dual volume one here. Let Φ be the indicator of X ≡ (1,0) modulo 3. There are four scalar coordinates over ℤ₃, so this class has mass 1/81. Its Gram value N(X₁)+N(X₂) belongs to 1+3ℤ₃. For each lift to the next power of 3, the derivative in the real coordinate of X₁ is 2 modulo 3. For each choice of the other three digits, exactly one digit of this coordinate gives the required next Gram digit. Thus the mass is uniform on 1+3ℤ₃, a set of volume 1/3, and the density there is 1/27.

Integration of the character on this coset, including the negative target phase, gives u(b) = (1/81) · 𝟙3⁻¹ℤ₃(b). On ℤ₃ the lattice index is one. On the shell 3⁻¹ℤ₃ ∖ ℤ₃, of volume two, its value is nine because the residue field of Ev has nine elements. In this example the original integral has compact support and converges at every z.

W₃(z) = (1 + 2 · 9−(z−1/2))/81,   W₃(1/2) = 1/27.

Now keep J = I₂ and T = 1, and restore the full-lattice test. There are 24 norm-one columns modulo 3. At every such column at least one scalar derivative of the norm is nonzero modulo 3, so each residue class contributes the same density 1/27. Summing the 24 contributions gives 24/27 = 8/9, the good-place answer in these same dimensions.

Which domain reaches the global coefficient? The local proof uses no rank inequality to construct the entire function once a density is given. The global theorem supplies these densities from the normalized Gram mean when n < M and either n+2 ≤ M or J is anisotropic. It chooses a finite set S outside which the forms, measures, lattices and test meet the good-place conditions. On Re z > 0 multiply the archimedean function, the finitely many entire factors Wv for v ∈ S, and the convergent good-place product. Farther right this equals the adelic integral for the full-rank Fourier coefficient. The point s₀ lies inside the global half-plane by the strict rank inequality. Substituting the local density values gives the normalized Gram mean there. The resulting global continuation is holomorphic on Re z > 0.
