Why is the archimedean Whittaker factor entire at a nonsingular target?

At infinity the Fourier variable ranges over Hermitian matrices. For a target with nonzero determinant, integration by parts trades oscillation in this variable for extra decay. Repeating this operation reaches every complex parameter. The value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 recovers the density of the test on the target Gram fibre, as in the finite-place calculation.

Start at one real place. A frame identifies the Hermitian form with J = diag(1p,−1q), with p+q = M. The character on ℝ is u ↦ exp(2πiℓu) for a real ℓ ≠ 0. Set t = 2πℓ and c = 2π|ℓ|. In these coordinates the test on a complex M × n matrix X is a polynomial P in the entries of X and their conjugates, multiplied by exp(−c∑|Xᵢⱼ|²). Define A(Y) by integrating this test against the positive phase exp(it tr(YX∗JX)). The Whittaker coefficient uses the negative phase at the target B. Write D(Y) = det(I+Y²) and w = z−s₀. The integration measure here is Lebesgue measure in the n² real coordinates yᵢⱼ = Re Yᵢⱼ + Im Yᵢⱼ.

W(w) = ∫ D(Y)−w A(Y) exp(−it tr(BY)) dY   for Re w sufficiently large.

One determinant derivative moves the convergence line. Put s = sign(ℓ). Gaussian integration gives A as a polynomial in the entries of (I−isY)−1 and (I+isY)−1, multiplied by the determinants of those inverses to powers p and q respectively. Let Δ be the determinant of the matrix of first derivatives in Hermitian coordinates. Integration by parts shows that the negative Fourier transform of Δf is (it)ndet(B) times that of f, whenever the derivatives are integrable. As det(B) ≠ 0, one can divide by this scalar.

For the decay estimate, diagonalize Y with real eigenvalues λj. Cauchy's derivative estimate uses a radius proportional to √((1+|λi|)(1+|λj|)) in matrix entry (i,j). Each determinant term differentiates once in every row and column. The product of the reciprocal radii thus supplies a factor proportional to ∏j(1+|λj|)−1 ≤ D(Y)−1/2. After N determinants, differentiating the weight D−w leaves that weight times a polynomial in w of degree at most nN with coefficient functions of Y. At integer weights 0 through nN one can absorb the weight into the two determinant powers. Polynomial interpolation transfers the same decay bound to the coefficient functions. On compact parameter sets the differentiated amplitude is bounded by a constant times D(Y)−Re w−(M+N)/2.

Where does the determinant come from in two rows?

Write the diagonal entries of the Hermitian integration variable as x,y and its upper-right entry as u+iv. For a Hermitian target with diagonal a,b and upper-right entry c+id, the trace pairing is ax + by + 2cu + 2dv. Its negative Fourier phase is the exponential of this expression times −it. In these unscaled entry coordinates the determinant derivative is ∂x∂y − (∂u² + ∂v²)/4. Applying it to the phase gives (it)²(ab − c² − d²) times the same phase. Integration by parts twice transfers the derivative to the amplitude with positive sign.

For diagonal entries 2 and 3 and upper-right entry 1 + i, the multiplier is −4t², which we may divide out. For the matrix with every entry equal to one it is zero, although the target itself is nonzero. This is why the hypothesis concerns the determinant. In the derivative estimate the two permutations also have the same decay. The mixed diagonal derivative costs one inverse radius for each diagonal entry, while two off-diagonal derivatives each cost the inverse geometric mean of those radii.

Two complex Gaussian variables and one real Fourier variable

Take n = 1, M = 2, signature (1,1), ℓ = 1, and P = 1 in the one-place Lebesgue model. Then s₀ = 1/2. The Gram value is |x₁|²−|x₂|². Since ∫ℂexp(−a|x|²) dx = π/a for Re a > 0, the two rows give factors 1/[2(1−iy)] and 1/[2(1+iy)]. Thus A(y) = 1/[4(1+y²)]. The absolute integral converges exactly for Re w > −1/2.

In radial coordinates u = |x₁|² and v = |x₂|² the measure is π² exp(−2π(u+v)) du dv. Integrating along u−v = B gives g(B) = (π/4) exp(−2π|B|). For B ≠ 0 this equals W(0). Differentiating the scalar Fourier transform of 1/(a²+y²) with respect to a at a = 1 gives W(1) = (π/8)(1+2π|B|)exp(−2π|B|). At w = −1 the weighted amplitude is the constant 1/4. Its second derivative vanishes, and −1 belongs to U₂, so the continued value is zero. At the singular target B = 0, the phase is constant. As real w decreases to −1/2 the positive integral tends to infinity, since its limiting tail is proportional to 1/|y|. This is where the invertibility hypothesis matters.

Why does a product of local Gram densities give a global mean?

At one finite place a density measures how often a tuple has a prescribed Gram matrix. A rational tuple must satisfy the same equations at every place. To bring these two descriptions together the proof averages over all adelic isometries of a single rational Hermitian space. Let E/F be the CM extension, J the nondegenerate Hermitian form on EM, and T a rational nonsingular Hermitian matrix of size n. The theorem assumes n < M, with either n+2 ≤ M or J anisotropic over E. Anisotropic means that a rational vector of norm zero must itself be zero. The test Φ has a Schwartz factor at infinity and locally constant, compactly supported factors at finite places. Almost all finite factors are the characteristic function of the standard lattice. At every place the two Hermitian matrices come from these same rational forms, and each local additive character comes from one global character.

Let H = U(J), and choose a fundamental domain 𝒟 for its rational points in its adelic group. For each h sum Φ(h−1X) over the rational solutions of X∗JX = T. Replacing h by γh for a rational isometry γ permutes these solutions by X ↦ γ−1X. The sum therefore defines a function on the quotient. Integrate it over 𝒟 using Haar measure and divide by vol(𝒟). Equivalently one can first add the measures obtained by moving each rational tuple under h ↦ h−1X, normalizing their sum by the same volume, then integrate Φ. Countability of the rational tuples and integrability justify this equivalence.

vol(𝒟)−1 ∫𝒟 ∑X rational, X∗JX=T Φ(h−1X) dh = g∞(T) ∏v finite gv(T).

Why can grouping the terms change their weights?

A finite group makes the Haar weights visible. Take H to be the six permutations of three letters and put Γ = K = {id,(12)}. A function constant on ΓhK has just two values. The class of the identity contains two permutations. The class of (13) contains the remaining four. Indeed the size of ΓhK is |Γ||K|/|Γ ∩ hKh−1|, and the two intersection sizes are 2 and 1. If the function takes values 2 and 5, the normalized Haar average is (2·2 + 4·5)/6 = 4. Giving both classes weight ½ would give 3½. The same issue arises when a quotient integral is grouped into classes, whose weights come from their volumes. The definition above keeps that weighting by integrating on a fundamental domain.

What fixes the measure on one Gram fibre?

A global product uses the local integral at a specified target T. An identity averaged over T leaves open what happens at an individual target of measure zero. The extra condition that fixes the answer is continuity of the fibre integrals on the nonsingular targets.

Regular Gram-fibre theorem. Work at a completion R of the base field F of the CM extension E/F. Let V be the space of n-tuples of vectors for the scalar extension to R ⊗F E of a nonsingular Hermitian form J on EM. The Gram map G sends a tuple to its matrix of pairings in the space H of Hermitian n × n matrices. Let B be the open set where the determinant is invertible and fix additive Haar measures μ on V and ν on H. There is a unique family of measures mT carried by G−1{T} for T ∈ B, set equal to zero outside B, with the following two properties.

∫G−1(B) φ dμ = ∫B (∫ φ dmT) dν(T)   for every nonnegative measurable φ.

For every real continuous φ compactly supported inside G−1(B), the inner integral is finite and depends continuously on T ∈ B. An empty fibre carries the zero measure. The integration formula concerns the part of the source lying over B.

How one open set of targets acquires its measures

Fix a nonsingular target T₀. The local congruence-section theorem supplies a subgroup L of changes of basis for the tuple such that h ↦ h·T₀ is a homeomorphism onto an open neighborhood of T₀. Here the target action is congruence, and G(h·z) = h·G(z). A tuple above this neighborhood therefore has unique coordinates (h, z) with z in the reference fibre G−1{T₀}. Recover h from the target and act by h−1 on the tuple to recover z.

Write χV(h) and χH(h) for the factors by which pushing forward μ and ν under h multiplies them. Pull μ back to the product coordinates and multiply by the density χV(h). Translating the group coordinate now preserves the result. Applying the same correction χH(h) to the target measure gives a left Haar measure λ on L. The corrected source measure is λ times a measure m₀ on the reference fibre. Indeed, for each relatively compact measurable fibre set A, the masses of rectangles U × A give a locally finite left-invariant measure in U. Haar uniqueness makes it a constant times λ. A fixed compact neighborhood K of the identity gives that constant as the mass of K × A divided by λ(K). This defines m₀, and exhaustion gives the product identity. Undoing the corrections gives mh·T₀ = [χH(h)/χV(h)] h∗m₀. For a compactly supported continuous test, continuity follows by integration on the fixed reference fibre. Near any fixed h, the translated test supports meet the fibre in a common compact set. Sutherland, Theorem 13.3 on Haar measure[27].

How do the entries of a Hermitian matrix give local coordinates?

Let R be a completion of the totally real field F, and K = R ⊗F E for the CM extension E/F. At a real place K = ℂ. At a finite place it is a quadratic local field or the product R × R with the two factors interchanged. Write * for transpose followed by conjugation. Fix an invertible Hermitian matrix S of size n. We seek a continuous choice of q near the identity that solves q*S q = T as T varies near S.

First choose coordinates in which the centre is diagonal. Even an invertible matrix can have a zero first diagonal entry, as does the two-by-two matrix with ones off the diagonal and zeros on it. A nonsingular Hermitian form of positive dimension has a vector of nonzero length. Indeed, if every length vanished, expanding the lengths of v + w and v + αw, with α an invertible scalar whose conjugate is −α, would force both the sum and the difference of a pairing and its conjugate to vanish. Every pairing would be zero. A vector of nonzero length splits off an orthogonal line. To do this, subtract from any vector its projection onto that line, dividing by the length. The orthogonal complement is nonsingular, so repeating gives S = b*D b with b invertible and D = diag(d₁,…,dₙ), each dᵢ in R×. At a finite place this means nonzero in the local field. The length may have positive valuation.

Triangular coordinates near D. Write the first row of a nearby Hermitian matrix as (p, r), and let C be its lower-right block. If p ≠ 0, direct multiplication gives

(prr∗C)=N1∗diag(p,C−r∗r/p)N1,   N1=(1r/p0I).

The next pivot is the first diagonal entry of the smaller matrix C − r*r/p. At D the successive pivots are exactly the nonzero dᵢ. All these computations are continuous where the earlier pivots are nonzero, so every pivot stays nonzero on an open neighborhood of D. If N′ is the triangular matrix for the smaller block, the full triangular matrix is diag(1,N′)N₁, with N₁ the first upper triangular factor in the displayed identity. Recursion uniquely recovers the pivots pᵢ and an upper triangular matrix N with diagonal entries one. The inverse map sends these coordinates to N* diag(p₁,…,pₙ) N. Both directions are continuous. At size zero there is one empty matrix and no pivot to choose.

How does a chart select one change of basis?

Choose an open subgroup U ⊂ R× on which squaring maps homeomorphically onto an open subgroup U². For real R one may use the positive numbers. Restrict the triangular chart to pᵢ ∈ dᵢU². This is open and contains D. Each ratio pᵢ/dᵢ now has a unique square root uᵢ in U, depending continuously on the pivot. With A = diag(u₁,…,uₙ)N, multiplication gives

A*D A = N* diag(d₁u₁²,…,dₙuₙ²) N.

These matrices A form a subgroup L because triangular multiplication multiplies diagonal entries, and inversion inverts them. In the original basis take Q = b−1L b. Then q = b−1A b satisfies q*S q = b* (A*D A) b. Thus q ↦ q*S q is a homeomorphism from Q onto an open neighborhood of S. Its inverse is the required section, with value 1 at S. Congruence here is a right action on forms. In the fibre integration argument one uses the left action in which h sends a tuple X to Xh−1 and its Gram matrix T to (h−1)*T h−1. Inversion in Q relates the two parametrizations.

Which square root does the chart take above 2?

At any finite place the derivative of u ↦ u² at 1 is 2. The local field has characteristic zero, so this derivative is invertible there, also when 2 has positive valuation. The inverse function theorem gives a continuous inverse on a sufficiently small neighborhood. A small closed ball about 1 of radius less than one is open in the ultrametric topology and forms a subgroup. The chart can use such a ball inside the inverse-function neighborhood. Glöckner, generalized implicit function theorem 5.2[87].

One can see the permitted size directly. Normalize the valuation by ord(π) = 1 for a uniformizer π, set e = ord(2), and take an integer k > e. For u = 1 + πkz, its square is 1 + 2πk(z + αz²), with α = πk/2 in the maximal ideal. The difference of z + αz² at z and z′ is (z − z′)(1 + α(z + z′)). The second factor is a unit. The map therefore preserves distances and is injective modulo every πj. Each residue ring is finite, so the map is also surjective there. The unique solutions for successive precisions are compatible, and completeness gives a unique solution in the local integers 𝒪. Thus (1 + πk𝒪)² = 1 + 2πk𝒪.

For R = ℚ₂ and n = 1, centre the chart at S = 1 and take U = 1 + 4ℤ₂. Its square image is 1 + 8ℤ₂. The target 9 has square roots 3 and −3 in ℚ₂. The section takes −3 because −3 ≡ 1 modulo 4. At the centre it takes 1.

Why do two choices agree at every regular target?

Take two such neighborhoods and a nonnegative continuous test supported compactly over their overlap. Write u(T) and v(T) for its two fibre integrals. On every compact target set K inside the overlap, both integrate to the same quantity, the source integral of the test over G−1(K). If u(T) exceeded v(T) at one point, continuity would give a compact neighborhood on which their difference stays bounded below by a positive number. That neighborhood has positive Haar measure. Its two integrals would differ. Thus u = v throughout the overlap. These tests determine a locally finite measure there: compact subsets can be bounded by continuous cutoffs in arbitrarily small open neighborhoods. Fibre support then gives equality of the two measures at each target.

Choose the measure from any chart containing T. To check the integration formula for the resulting family, take a countable subcover B₁, B₂, …, which exists by second countability. Give each target to the first chart containing it. The measurable pieces Bj ∖ ⋃i<j Bi are disjoint, so their integration formulas add without counting overlaps twice. For continuity near a chosen target, multiply the test by a continuous cutoff in the target that equals one near that point and is supported inside one chart. This leaves the nearby fibre integrals unchanged and gives continuity by the local construction.

One exceptional value. For the complex line with G(z) = |z|², use area on ℂ and length ds on ℝ. In polar coordinates area is ½ ds dθ, so each circle s > 0 has fibre mass π. Doubling just the measure at s = 1 would preserve the integration formula because {1} has length zero. Take a continuous test equal to one near the unit circle and supported in a compact annulus. Its fibre integral would jump from π to 2π at 1. This is precisely the ambiguity that continuity removes. The chart for a scalar length at a finite place uses the same uniqueness argument.

One example checks the direction of the transport factor. For G(z) = ‖z‖² on ℂ² and r > 0, dilation z ↦ rz multiplies the length by r². Its pushforward on the four real source coordinates is r−4 times volume, and on the real target it is r−2 times length measure. The mass transported from the fibre at s to the fibre at r²s therefore acquires the ratio r². Directly, the real ball of radius √s has volume proportional to s². Differentiating with respect to s gives a fibre mass proportional to s, as predicted.

What remains after the first vector is fixed?

Suppose the ambient Hermitian space represents the first target length t ∈ F×. Split off a rational vector of that length. In the resulting coordinates the ambient form is ⟨t⟩ ⊕ J, with J a nonsingular form of dimension r. The prescribed Gram matrix is ⟨t⟩ ⊕ T, with T nonsingular of size n. Thus there are n columns still to choose. Work at a completion R of F with K = R ⊗F E. Use coordinate Haar measures throughout, from one additive Haar measure on R and one F-basis of E.

Let e be the first coordinate vector. A first column y with length t can be written hye for a unitary isometry hy. When K is a field, Witt’s extension theorem extends the isometry between the two lines of length t. At a split place a vector is a pair consisting of a vector u and a linear functional ℓ with ℓ(u) = t. Complete u to a basis with the other vectors in ker ℓ. A change between two such bases carries both the vector and, by its inverse dual, the functional. This gives the required isometry there as well. The remaining columns are orthogonal to y. Applying hy−1 puts these columns into the fixed complement. There they have the form (0,Xⱼ), where the smaller tuple X has Gram matrix T for J. Write ι(X) for the tuple with first column e and remaining columns (0,Xⱼ).

The set of tuples is now described, but the conditional measure still needs its normalization. For a nonnegative measurable test φ, let mt1 be the one-column measure in the full space, and mT⊥ the n-column measure in the complement. The local recursion states

∫ φ dm⟨t⟩⊕T = cv(t)n ∫ (∫ φ(hy ι(X)) dmT⊥(X)) dmt1(y).

The inner integral is independent of the isometry because two choices differ on the right by an isometry fixing e. Its restriction is unitary on the complement and preserves mT⊥. The one-vector orbit is the quotient of the locally compact second-countable unitary group by the closed stabilizer of e. The measurable-section theorem for this quotient supplies a measurable choice y ↦ hy and hence a measurable outer integrand.

Where does the factor for each remaining column come from?

Allow the target to move, so that we can use the defining integration formula for the regular fibre measures. Write its upper-left entry as x, its first row after that entry as b, and its lower-right Hermitian block as B. Near x = t the local square-root branch gives x = a²t, with a = 1 at the centre. In the frame carried by hy the first vector is ae, and each remaining vector is (cⱼ,Xⱼ). Computing their inner products gives

b = at c,   GramJ(X) = B − t c*c = B − b*b/x,   det S = x det(B − b*b/x).

Here S is the full moving target and * is conjugate transpose. The determinant identity follows by subtracting the first row times the appropriate multiple from each lower row. Thus, as long as x is invertible, the smaller Gram matrix is nonsingular exactly when S is. For fixed x and b, passing between the two lower-right blocks is a translation, which preserves their additive Haar measure.

The first row changes volume. Normalize |·|v by the rule that multiplication by u scales the volume of a set in R by |u|v. A coordinate of K has two R-coordinates, so pushing its measure forward by z ↦ at z multiplies the measure by |at|v−2. Indeed, the mass assigned to a target set is the volume of its inverse image. There is one such factor for each of the n entries of b. The first-vector measure also varies with a. Under y ↦ ay, source volumes scale by |a|v2(r+1) and its scalar length by |a|v². Hence the measure at x is |a|v2r times the image of the measure at t.

Integrating first over the column coordinates, or first over the entries of the moving target, now gives the same integral. For a continuous compactly supported test the resulting fibre integrals are continuous on this regular neighborhood. In the moving frames the unitary section can be chosen with image in a compact set when y ranges over a compact part of the orbit. For fixed y the smaller regular fibre family gives continuity in the target coordinates under the integral. Compact control of the frames bounds these integrals by a common integrable function of y. Dominated convergence then gives continuity of the outer integral. By pointwise uniqueness, the two measures therefore agree at the specified block target. There a = 1, b = 0, and the complement target is T. The only remaining factor is cv(t)n with cv(t) = |t|v−2. Axler, Theorem 3.31 on dominated convergence[88].

Why is the global normalization one?

Over F = ℚ take E = ℚ(i), the ambient form diag(2,1) and two columns. At the real place fix the first column (1,0) and take the second to be (1 + i,1). Its pairing with the first column is b = 2 + 2i, and its length is 5. Subtracting |b|²/2 = 4 leaves the complement length 1. The full Gram determinant is 2·5 − 8 = 2. Multiplication by 2 in the complex b-coordinate multiplies area by 4, so pushing the original area forward gives the factor ¼. At the place 2, |2|₂ = ½ gives the factor 4. Every other finite place gives one. These two columns in dimension two illustrate the local coordinates and the product of the scalar factors. The global induction below requires at least one extra ambient dimension.

For every rational length t ∈ F×, the product formula gives ∏v|t|v = 1. Hence the product of the local factors cv(t)n is one as well. At almost all finite places the standard lattice test also separates into the standard tests for the first vector and the complement. This latter assertion uses integral isometries at good places. The global induction uses the local recursion in the strict range n + 1 ≤ r, with the full binary space anisotropic when r = 1. The local measure identity itself needs the represented nonzero line and the indicated regular targets. Sutherland, Theorem 13.21 on the product formula[89].

What fixes the constant in the one-vector mass formula?

Fix a nonzero scalar β ∈ F× and consider vectors of Gram value β in a nondegenerate Hermitian space of dimension M ≥ 3 over a CM extension E/F. In the induction on Gram fibres, invariance, support on the fibre and local finiteness identify the normalized theta measure with a scalar c times an Euler product. If a local fibre measure vanishes, both sides are zero even when the product is assigned constant one. Suppose now that all the fibre measures are nonzero. The proof determines c by enlarging just the finite-place test.

An upper bound for the discrepancy. Put d = [F ∶ ℚ]. At infinity choose a strictly positive Gaussian test Φ and denote its integral over the fibre at β by w. It is finite and strictly positive. At a finite place v, take the indicator of a−1Λv for a positive integer a. Let I(a) be the normalized global integral with these tests, and let P(a) be the convergent product of their finite local fibre masses at β, using the reference coordinate measures. The trace form expresses the same global count as a Fourier coefficient of a theta average. Its comparison with the corresponding Eisenstein coefficient yields

|I(a) − w P(a)| ≤ C adM   for every integer a ≥ 1.

Where does the exponent come from? For the indicator of the original lattice the weighted difference between the averaged theta function and the Eisenstein series is bounded after reduction to a Siegel domain. The dilation replaces the real upper-half-plane variable x+i by (x+i)/a². Its imaginary part is a−2 at each of the d real places. The product of the local weights (Im τ)M/2 is therefore a−dM. Removing that weight gives the bound above since integration against the unit-modulus Fourier character costs at most the volume subsequently divided out.

How many nonzero vectors of norm zero enter a shrinking box?

Let E/F be a CM extension, d = [F ∶ ℚ], and J a nondegenerate Hermitian form on EM, with M ≥ 3. Write G for the group of adelic isometries and Γ for the rational isometries. Choose a Haar measure μ on G and a fundamental domain 𝒟 for Γ of finite positive volume V. For a set S of rational vectors stable under Γ, its mean count in an adelic set Ω is

AS(Ω) = (1/V) ∫𝒟 ∑x ∈ S 𝟙Ω(h−1x) dμ(h).

The vector 0 contributes exactly 𝟙Ω(0), since every isometry fixes it. Remove it. Fix an F-basis of E and a positive integer N. The box BN(r) consists of vectors y for which Ny is integral in the finite coordinate lattices and the sum of the absolute real coordinates of y is at most r. We shall bound the mean for S = {x ≠ 0 ∣ ⟨x,x⟩ = 0} by CNr2d(M−1) for every r > 0.

Group the vectors by their rational lines. If the form is anisotropic over E, the count is zero. Otherwise choose a nonzero isotropic vector e. Nondegeneracy supplies z with ⟨e,z⟩ = 1. The vector e′ = z − ½⟨z,z⟩e has norm zero and still pairs to 1 with e. Their span is a hyperbolic plane. Its orthogonal complement has dimension s = M − 2. In these coordinates let Ω denote the image of the fixed unit-radius box. Write τ(x) for multiplication by exp(x) at every real place and by 1 at the finite places. Then the radius-r test is 𝟙Ω(τ(−log r) · ). Choose one vector u on each rational isotropic line. The full contribution of this line at h is Φr(h−1u), where Φr(y) = ∑λ ∈ E× 𝟙Ω(τ(−log r)λy). Replacing the representative permutes the summands.

Compute the volume of a shell. Rational isometries act transitively on isotropic lines. Write P for the adelic stabilizer of Ee. Unfolding the sum over lines gives an integral over (Γ ∩ P) ∖ G. To estimate it, one uses the shell volumes in P and a compact cover transverse to P. The shell estimate uses the finite quotient volume of the isometries of the orthogonal complement. Together they bound the integral by a sum over integer shells j, with a compact family of transverse pairs (u,v) satisfying ⟨v,u⟩ = 1. On shell j the test is evaluated at τ(−j)u. Its integral costs at most a fixed constant times exp(−2d(s+1)j) times the largest test bound on these pairs. To see the exponent, the unipotent coordinates consist of s adelic E-coordinates and one central adelic F-coordinate. Conjugation by a line multiplier a multiplies the former by a and the latter by NE/F(a). For a = τ(j), the real determinant is (ej)2ds(e2j)d. Its reciprocal is the pushforward Haar multiplier in the shell bound.

Count the scalars left in each shell. Put x = j + log r. If τ(−x)λu lies in Ω, pairing it with v gives τ(−x)λ. All these pairings lie in a fixed compact set, since the pairs and Ω range over compact sets. Clearing the finite denominators puts λ in one lattice in E of real dimension 2d. Its archimedean size is at most a fixed multiple of ex. Discreteness excludes every nonzero λ below a threshold x0. At or above that threshold, the box-packing estimate bounds their number by Ce2dx. Combining this with the shell volume leaves

AS(BN(r)) ≤ C r2d ∑j ≥ j0 e−2dsj ≤ C′ r2d(s+1),   j0 = ⌈x0 − log r⌉.

Indeed the series is e−2dsj0 /(1−e−2ds). The first term is at most e−2dsx0r2ds. The condition M ≥ 3 gives s ≥ 1, which makes the denominator positive. The factor 1/V is absorbed in the counting constant.

Which lattice points does an adelic box count?

The sum over isotropic lines leaves a rational scalar to count in each shell. We prove a bound for M coordinates over E and then use it with M = 1. Let E/F be a CM quadratic extension and d = [F∶ℚ]. Choose an F-basis of E. It writes an adelic vector in (𝔸F ⊗F E)M as 2M adelic coordinates over F. At each finite place v require every coordinate to belong to N−1𝒪Fᵥ, where N is a fixed positive integer. At each of the d real places take the absolute values of the 2M coordinates. The box BN(R) consists of vectors satisfying the finite conditions whose real absolute values sum to at most R. This sum is the ℓ¹ norm on ℝν with ν = 2dM.

BN(R) = {‖u‖₁ ≤ R} × ∏v finite (N−1𝒪Fᵥ)2M.

The finite factor is compact and open. Away from the primes dividing N, its factors are the usual integral lattices. Every finite adèle has a denominator at only finitely many places, and powers of the rational primes below them clear those denominators. Thus the open finite factors, as N varies, cover any compact family. Take a finite subcover, use a common multiple of its denominators, and bound the continuous real norm on the same family. Every compact Ω is consequently contained in some BN(r) with r > 0. Sutherland, The ring of adeles, Propositions 25.5–25.6 and Definition 25.7[90].

For a rational vector, each of its 2M coefficients c lies in F. The finite condition says exactly that Nc is integral at every finite place, hence lies in 𝒪F. The allowed rational vectors therefore form the additive subgroup ΛN = (N−1𝒪F)2M in the chosen coordinates. Taking differences preserves every finite condition. The real embeddings identify this subgroup with a lattice, so its intersection with a bounded real ball is finite. Sutherland, §14.2, the integer ring in its real embedding space[91].

How many translates of a small ball cover the rational points?

Let PN(R) count the points of ΛN in the closed real ball of radius R, including zero. For 0 < r₀ ≤ R, choose a maximal collection of these points whose pairwise distances are at least r₀. The open balls of radius r₀/2 about the chosen points are disjoint and fit inside the ball of radius R+r₀/2. Dilation by a positive scalar t multiplies volume in ℝν by tν. The number of centres is therefore at most (1+2R/r₀)ν ≤ (3R/r₀)ν.

Every lattice point in the large ball lies within distance r₀ of a centre, since otherwise it could be added to the collection. Subtracting that centre sends the point into ΛN in the small ball. Each centre therefore accounts for at most PN(r₀) points. Using the coefficient 5 in the subsequent shell estimate gives the comparison

PN(R) ≤ (5R/r₀)ν PN(r₀),   0 < r₀ ≤ R.

When does a dilated compact set contain a nonzero rational point?

Fix Ω ⊂ BN(r) as above. Choose 0 < r₀ ≤ 1 strictly smaller than the real sizes of all nonzero points in BN(1). This is possible because the list is finite, and a nonzero rational coordinate stays nonzero under a real embedding. If the list is empty, take r₀ = 1. Thus PN(r₀) = 1. For an explicit choice take r₀ = min(1, d/(2N)). Indeed, any nonzero coefficient c has |NormF/ℚ(Nc)| ≥ 1 because it is the absolute value of a nonzero integer. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives ∑σ|σ(c)| ≥ d/N.

The dilation τ(x) multiplies real coordinates by exp(x) and fixes finite coordinates. Let AΩ(x) count X ∈ EM with X ≠ 0 and τ(−x)X ∈ Ω. The tested vector then has real size exp(−x)‖X‖₁ ≤ r, so X belongs to the box of radius exp(x)r. Put x₀ = log(r₀/r). Below x₀ the new radius is smaller than r₀ and the count is zero. At and above the threshold apply the two-radius comparison with R = exp(x)r. It bounds even the count including zero, and gives

AΩ(x) = 0   for x < x₀,   AΩ(x) ≤ C exp(νx)   for x ≥ x₀,   C = (5r/r₀)ν.

For example, take F = ℚ, E = ℚ(i), the basis (1,i), M = 1 and Ω = B₂(1). The lattice is ½ℤ[i] with size |a|+|b| on a+bi. Taking r₀ = ¼ gives ν = 2 and x₀ = −log 4. At the threshold the actual nonzero count is still zero, while the displayed upper bound is 25. At x = −log 2 the closed radius reaches ½ and admits exactly the four points ±½, ±i/2.

In the shell integral, pairing a tested vector with its transverse dual recovers a scalar in E. The pair and the tested vector vary in compact sets, so the image of their continuous pairing is one fixed compact Ω. Here the dimension in the count is ν = 2d, one scalar over E, and the variable is x = j + log rtest for shell index j and test radius rtest. Hence the shell sum begins at ⌈x₀−log rtest⌉ and the scalar count contributes at most C rtest2d exp(2dj).

Its coordinates consist of a horizontal vector b ∈ 𝔸Es, a central coordinate z ∈ 𝔸F, an isometry g ∈ U(W)(𝔸F), and the scalar a ∈ 𝔸E× by which the line is multiplied. We need to bound the integral on the region where this last coordinate has logarithmic height near the integer j.

Reduce the four coordinates. The additive quotient 𝔸F/F has compact representatives. Indeed, the Chinese remainder theorem clears the nonintegral finite residues by subtracting a field element, and an algebraic integer then moves the infinite coordinates into a bounded lattice parallelepiped. The same argument works for E and in each of the s horizontal coordinates. Denote the resulting compact sets by Cz and Cb. For the scalar choose a fixed compact set ω of idèles such that every a belongs to E×τ(j)ω for some integer j. To see this, the norm-one idèle classes form a compact group. The idèle modulus of τ(x) is e2dx. Removing the real logarithmic height leaves a norm-one class. Its representatives can be taken in a compact set by lifting a finite cover by relatively compact open neighborhoods. Absorb the fractional part of the height in ω. The four-coordinate factorization makes the changes of variables explicit. Finally put g in a fundamental domain 𝒟W for its rational isometries. After the rational scalar and isometry have been reduced, subtract a rational horizontal vector. This changes the central coordinate by the cross term in the unipotent group law, so subtract a rational central element last. The resulting shells cover modulo rational elements of P. Summing over possible overlaps gives an upper bound. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Theorem 5.8 and its idèle example, p. 22[76]

Why the complementary quotient has finite volume. Borel’s finite-volume theorem applies to a connected linear group over a number field whose characters defined over that field are all trivial. Over E, U(W) becomes GLs. Its algebraic characters are determinant powers. Indeed, on the diagonal torus a character is a monomial whose exponents must be equal by permutation symmetry, and a character is trivial on each elementary unipotent subgroup. Conjugation over F takes the determinant to its inverse. A power descends only when its exponent is zero. Thus 𝒟W has finite volume for any Haar measure on U(W)(𝔸F). The construction by lattice classes below gives an adelic domain with this property. The same argument supplies the finite volume of the complement of dimension M−1 on a nonzero norm fibre. Borel, Theorem 5.6(i), p. 21[76]

For the scalar a, let χ(a) be the multiplier by which conjugation pushes forward the additive measure. The left Haar density contains χ(a) d×a. The calculation of the density fixes the sign of this exponent. On τ(j)ω the character contributes exp(−2d(s+1)j) times its value on ω. This bounds the shell mass by

vol(Cb) vol(Cz) vol(𝒟W) vol×(ω) supω χ · exp(−2d(s+1)j).

Every factor before the exponential is finite and independent of j. The bound grows as j tends to −∞. The compact support of the original indicator and the discreteness of rational scalars supply the lower cutoff in the geometric sum.

Which finite adelic coordinates represent the same lattice?

Removing the hyperbolic plane in the isotropic count leaves a nondegenerate Hermitian space W of dimension s = M − 2 over the CM extension E/F. Its isometries form a group H = U(W,h). Put Γ = H(F), the rational isometries. An adelic isometry has an archimedean coordinate in H∞ and a finite coordinate in Hf. We first show that, up to Γ, only finitely many integral lattice classes occur in the finite coordinate.

Fix coordinates, a reference lattice at the finite places, and its compact open stabilizer K ⊂ Hf. For y ∈ Hf, take the rational vectors in the translated local lattices and multiply them by one fixed nonzero integer to obtain L(y) ⊂ W. This is a finitely generated additive group stable under 𝒪E and spanning W. The finite lattice construction gives two identities

L(γfy) = γL(y),   L(y) = L(y′) ⇔ y−1y′ ∈ K.

The second identity uses recovery of the translated local lattices from their rational vectors by completion. Isometries preserve the pairing, so one integer suffices to make it integral on every translated lattice. The coordinates of the lattices themselves can have arbitrarily large denominators. Clearing denominators in the pairing and its inverse gives one bound D for all y. Explicitly, if L# = {w ∈ W ∣ h(w,L) ⊂ 𝒪E}, then L ⊂ L# and [L# ∶ L] ≤ D. Indeed, one positive integer b sends every such dual into its lattice. A full lattice of additive rank k then satisfies L ⊂ L# ⊂ b−1L and [b−1L ∶ L] = bk.

Finiteness of the lattice classes. In a fixed nondegenerate space, integral lattices with this dual index bound belong to finitely many rational isometry classes. Here is the reduction. Choose a positive Euclidean length that bounds the absolute Hermitian pairings at all archimedean places. When every nonzero lattice vector has length at least 1, lattice reduction with the bounded covolume gives bounded generators. Their Gram entries are algebraic integers bounded at every embedding, a finite set. The Gram entries of spanning generators determine an isometry taking one labelled set to another. If a vector has length less than 1, its Hermitian norm is an algebraic integer of absolute value less than 1 at every embedding. Its field norm forces it to vanish. Split off a hyperbolic plane through the resulting line. Reduction adapted to that line gives finitely many possibilities for the lattices in the two line coordinates and a bounded dual index in the smaller orthogonal complement. Induction gives finitely many models there. For each resulting full split lattice B, the adapted reduction puts the original lattice between B and n−1B for a fixed positive integer n. The finite quotient n−1B/B has only finitely many subgroups.

Choose a representative t for each class attained by L(y). If L(y) = γL(t), the two identities give y ∈ γftK. Thus the double classes Γf ∖ Hf / K are finite. Within the slice tK, exactly the following rational isometries can still identify two points

Γt = {γ ∈ Γ ∣ t−1γft ∈ K} = {γ ∈ Γ ∣ γL(t) = L(t)}.

Γ is countable, since its matrices have entries in a number field, so the union of the translated exceptional sets is still null.

Why the smaller unitary quotient has finite positive volume

It remains to verify the archimedean input. The stabilizer Γt is the integral subgroup of the rational algebraic group obtained from U(h) by restriction of scalars to ℚ, using the underlying integer lattice L(t). The arithmetic finite-volume theorem of Borel and Harish-Chandra says that a connected algebraic group over ℚ with trivial rational character group has an arithmetic quotient of finite invariant volume. Here the character condition can be checked directly. Over ℂ the group becomes a product of general linear groups, one for each real place of F. A character on each factor is an integral power of its determinant. Complex conjugation acts on each determinant by inversion, because the defining isometry equation identifies the conjugate matrix with a conjugate of its inverse transpose. A rational character would have every exponent equal to its negative, hence zero. The theorem gives the required finite archimedean covolume. A. Borel and Harish-Chandra, Arithmetic Subgroups of Algebraic Groups, theorem 9.4, p. 522[93].

One can also see where the volume bound enters reduction by short vectors. For an archimedean isometry g measure vectors with the positive length of g−1x. Where the shortest nonzero vector has length ≥ 1, bounded-basis reduction puts representatives in a compact set. Its finite measure bounds this portion of a fundamental domain. For the same Haar measure μ, any two fundamental domains 𝒟 and 𝒟′ have the same mass. Partition 𝒟′ by its intersections with γ𝒟 and move each piece back by γ−1. Thus replacing μ by cμ multiplies this mass by c. For s = M − 2 the isotropic shell estimate uses the smaller quotient volume as a fixed finite factor. Division by the volume of the ambient quotient takes place in the definition of the mean.

A one-dimensional complement. Take M = 3 over ℚ(i)/ℚ, with a hyperbolic plane and the line of norm zz̄. The smaller group at infinity is the circle. The positive rational number αᾱ generates the unit ideal and must equal 1. Dividing the idele by this rational isometry puts it in K. There is one double class. At a complex component pick a coordinate yᵣ of largest modulus. It is nonzero because the local dot product can equal one. Take a = yᵣ−1 and take z to be the coordinate row with 1 in position r and zeros elsewhere. Every entry of ay has modulus at most one, entry r is exactly one, and z·(ay) = 1. At infinity there are finitely many complex components, and each can choose its own r. Both tuples now belong to a finite product of closed unit discs.

The base valuation ring is compact because its residue classes modulo each uniformizer power form a finite cover by balls of shrinking radius, and it is complete. To see compactness of the norm ball directly in coordinates, write x = u+wθ with θ² = Δ. The norm is u²−Δw², nonzero on the compact sphere max(|u|,|w|) = 1 because Δ is nonsquare. Its absolute value has a positive minimum there. Dividing by a coordinate of maximal absolute value and using homogeneity of degree two bounds max(|u|,|w|) wherever |Norm(x)| ≤ 1. The ball is therefore closed and bounded in the two-dimensional local field coordinates, hence compact. At a split place the algebra is a product of two fields. Choose a maximum separately on each side, giving one invertible pair of scalars and one pair of coordinate rows. The witness may select different positions in the two factors.

For example, over ℚ(i) at the split prime 5, take k ≥ 1. Write a local two-entry column as y = ((5−k,0),(0,5k)). Each single entry has a zero component. The scalar pair (5k,5−k) sends y to ((1,0),(0,1)). The row with these same two entries evaluates to (1,1), the multiplicative identity. The freedom to replace the row already matters at a complex place. For real R ≥ 1 take y = (R,0) and z₀ = (R−1,R²). After rescaling by 1/R, transporting the old row gives (1,R³). Choosing the new row (1,0) bounds both tuples for the whole sequence.

|u²−Δw²|v = max(|u|v,|w|v)².

Both s and 2 are units, so taking their half-sum and their difference divided by 2s recovers integral coordinates from integral components. The fixed change of basis preserves integrality away from its denominator primes. These conditions leave only finitely many exceptional places.

Fix this finite set S independently of y. Use the compact archimedean box from the first step, the local compact sets constructed there at the finite places in S, and Λv everywhere else. Now take an actual witness z₀ for y. Their components both lie in Λv at almost every finite place. Wherever this holds outside S, choose aᵥ = 1 and keep zᵥ = (z₀)v. At the finitely many other places use the local construction to choose aᵥ and zᵥ. Thus aᵥ and aᵥ−1 both equal one at almost all finite places. Equality of adèles can be tested in all components, giving the global identity, with ay,z in the fixed Ω.

One example explains why the input row must itself be adelic. Take a rank-one column over ℚ(i) whose component at each rational prime p is p, and whose complex component is one. The column is integral at all finite places and each local entry is invertible in the local algebra. Yet the only possible dual has component 1/p at every p. It fails the restricted-product integrality condition, so this column has no adelic witness.

For the shell estimate, y is isotropic, and ay remains isotropic. The two compactly bounded inputs ay and z now feed the continuous construction of a hyperbolic partner. Its image on Ω × Ω gives the compact family of pairs to which the adelic Gram-fibre lifting argument is applied. The row normalization by itself requires only the displayed primitivity identity. If M = 0 that identity is impossible, so there is no primitive input in that rank.

How can a compact family of frames be lifted to isometries?

At a real place of the base field, a Hermitian space is a complex vector space V with a nonsingular form h, conjugate-linear in its first variable. For an ordered tuple of columns X = (x₁,…,xₙ), its Gram matrix T has entries h(xᵢ,xⱼ). Suppose det T ≠ 0. Any linear relation on the columns would give a vector in the kernel of T, so the columns are independent. If Y has the same Gram matrix, the map xᵢ ↦ yᵢ is an isometry of the column spans. Witt’s extension theorem gives an isometry of all of V extending that map. The shell estimate needs more. Given any compact set Ω of tuples, one compact set C in the unitary group must supply a lift g with gX = Y for every Y ∈ Ω of Gram matrix T. Sprehn and Wahl, Forms over fields and Witt’s lemma, Theorem 3.4[95].

First diagonalize T by one fixed change of columns in both tuples. Indeed, a nonzero Hermitian form has a vector with nonzero value on the diagonal, by the polarization identity. Split off its line by orthogonal projection and repeat on the nonsingular complement. The new columns are mutually orthogonal with real squared lengths bᵢ ≠ 0, which may have either sign. Undoing the common column change at the end preserves the equation gX = Y.

Move one column and keep the earlier columns fixed. Suppose the next column is currently x and must be sent to y, with h(x,x) = h(y,y) = b ≠ 0. Set t = h(y,x). For at least one choice of λ = ±1 we have |b − λt| ≥ |b|, since the mean of |b−t|² and |b+t|² is b²+|t|². With u = x−λy and δ = b−λt, define

A(z) = z − u h(u,z)/δ,   B(z) = z − (1−λ)y h(y,z)/b.

Here h(u,x) = δ, so A(x) = λy. To check that A is an isometry, expand h(Az,Aw). The coefficient of h(z,u)h(u,w) in the difference from h(z,w) is [h(u,u)−2 Re δ]/|δ|², which vanishes because h(u,u) = 2b−2λ Re t. The second map acts by λ on the line of y and fixes its orthogonal complement. Thus BA is an isometry sending x to y. Each previously matched column is orthogonal to both and stays fixed.

Keep the lifts in a compact set. The subset of Ω on which the Gram matrix equals T is closed in Ω, hence compact. Start there with the identity matrix. At the first column retain both closed subsets where the corresponding sign satisfies |δ| ≥ |b₁|. They cover the compact set, and on each the displayed matrix depends continuously on Y. At the next column use its image under the current matrix as x and repeat within each subset. After n columns there are at most 2n compact subsets. On each, the product of the successive matrices is a continuous function of Y. The union of their compact images is the required C. At a tie either sign supplies a lift.

In the shell argument the two initial vectors e, f are isotropic, with h(e,f) = 1. Their Gram matrix has determinant −1. The column change (e+f, e−f) gives squared lengths 2 and −2, so both steps have a denominator of absolute value at least 2. For instance, the pairs (a e, a−1f) for 1 ≤ a ≤ 2 lift to the compact family diag(a, a−1) on their plane, extended by the identity on its orthogonal complement. The one-vector orbit mean uses the same real-place assertion for a line of nonzero norm. The next argument explains how the integral choices at finite places enter the compact family of adelic representatives.

Theorems used. Witt’s extension theorem for a Hermitian space

Why can the same columns be used at every place?

Fix a CM extension E/F with conjugation and an invertible Hermitian matrix J of size M. Let X be an ordered tuple of n rational columns in EM. When their Gram matrix is nonsingular, the columns are independent and form a frame for their span, which may be smaller than the ambient space. Stack them as a matrix and write T = X∗JX, where ∗ means conjugate transpose. Assume det T ≠ 0. Given an adelic tuple Y with this same matrix of pairings at every place, we seek one adelic isometry carrying X to Y. The first change of basis takes place among the n columns. It can be chosen over E before taking any completions.

Consider the pairing h on the space of column coefficients, with matrix T. For n > 0 there is a vector w of nonzero length h(w,w). To see this, suppose every length vanished. Expanding the length of u+v gives h(u,v)+h(v,u) = 0. Choose a nonzero θ with conjugate −θ by taking the difference of an element of E outside F and its conjugate. Expanding the length of u+θv then gives θ(h(u,v)−h(v,u)) = 0. Together the two identities force every pairing to vanish, contradicting nonsingularity. The nonzero length β is fixed by conjugation and therefore belongs to F. For every z, subtract w h(w,z)/β to obtain a vector orthogonal to w. The orthogonal complement is nonsingular because a vector in its radical would pair to zero with the whole space. Repeating the argument gives an invertible rational matrix S of new columns. The identity serves for the empty tuple. Thus

S∗TS = diag(β₁,…,βₙ),   βⱼ ∈ F×.

For example, over ℚ(i) take two columns e, f of lengths 0 and 2 with h(e,f) = 1+i. The Gram determinant is −2. Choose f first and then e−f(1−i)/2. Their lengths are 2 and −1, and their pairing is zero. The division by 2 is valid in every completion. At places above 2 its inverse lies outside the valuation ring, which matters when we ask whether a local isometry preserves an integral lattice.

The tuples XS and YS have the same diagonal Gram matrix. A unitary map g acts on the left, so g(XS) = YS implies gX = Y on multiplying both sides on the right by S−1. The same rational S and its inverse have integral entries outside finitely many places. We can therefore use this one diagonal model in the local tests that follow.

Which denominator is a unit at a finite place?

Let E/F be a CM quadratic extension, with conjugation z ↦ z̄. Let X be a rational frame of n columns in an M-dimensional nonsingular Hermitian space. Assume its n-by-n Gram matrix has nonzero determinant. The columns are then a basis of their span, with n ≤ M. Suppose an adelic frame Y has the same Gram matrix. We want an isometry carrying X to Y that preserves the coordinate lattice at almost every finite place. Fix a common rational change of columns that makes the Gram matrix diagonal, with nonzero entries β₁,…,βₙ in F. Consider one pair of columns of equal squared length β. The real-place construction divides by δ = β − λ̄t, where t = h(y,x) and λλ̄ = 1. To keep this division integral, we need δ to be a unit.

Here are four possible values of λ, fixed once for the extension. Choose a nonzero θ with θ̄ = −θ by subtracting the conjugate of any element of E outside F. Then d = θ² lies in F× and 1, θ is an F-basis of E. Take s ∈ F× with s² ≠ d. Put P = (s²+d)/(s²−d) and Q = 2s/(s²−d). Expanding the squares gives P²−dQ² = 1, so α = P+Qθ has norm one and Q ≠ 0. Our choices are 1, −1, α and −α.

At a finite place v, write 𝒪v for the integers of Fᵥ and Rᵥ for the ring of integers of E ⊗F Fᵥ, a product of two valuation rings at a split place. For the moment suppose 2, d, Q and β are units of 𝒪v and P is integral. Then θ is an integral unit. Each t ∈ Rᵥ can be written a+bθ with a = (t+t̄)/2 and b = (t−t̄)/(2θ) in 𝒪v. Both quotients are integral and fixed by conjugation. For λ = p+qθ, multiply δ by its conjugate to obtain a scalar in the base ring,

Nλ = δδ̄ = (β−pa+qbd)² − d(qa−pb)².

Suppose all four norms vanish in the residue field. Taking differences gives N−1−N1 = 4βa and N−α−Nα = 4β(Pa−Qbd). The first forces a ≡ 0, and the second then forces b ≡ 0 because Qd is a unit. But now N1 ≡ β² ≠ 0. Thus at least one norm is a unit in 𝒪v. For its phase, δ−1 = δ̄/Nλ belongs to Rᵥ.

Why two signs can fail. At an inert place the residue algebra is a field. If β−t and β+t both vanished there, their sum 2β would vanish. At a split place each sign can fail in a different component. For example, 5 splits in ℚ(i). In the residue algebra 𝔽₅ × 𝔽₅, conjugation swaps the factors and i = (2,−2). Take β = 1 and t = (1,−1). The choices λ = 1 and −1 give δ = (0,2) and (2,0). With θ = i and s = 1, we have α = i. For λ = i both components of δ equal 3 modulo 5, so its norm equals 4 modulo 5 and division is integral.

An integral isometry at almost every finite place

We can now specify a finite set S outside which every step works. Include all places above 2 and all ramified places. Include the places where any diagonal entry βᵢ, d or Q fails to be a unit, or P fails to be integral. Also include any place where the form matrix J, its inverse, the rational frame, or the common change of columns and its inverse have a nonintegral entry. Each fixed number-field entry has finitely many denominator primes, and each nonzero diagonal entry, as well as d and Q, is a unit away from finitely many primes. Finally include the finitely many places where the given adelic frame has a nonintegral entry. For a compact family of frames this last set can be chosen uniformly. The open sets of tuples integral outside a given finite set cover the family, so finitely many suffice, and we take the union of their exceptional sets. Sutherland, The ring of adeles, strong approximation, §25.3, Definition 25.7[90].

Fix v outside S. Write h(z,w) = z*Jw, where * is conjugate transpose. For one pair of integral columns x, y with common squared length β, choose λ by the four-norm test and put u = x−λy. For any column w and scalar c, let Tw,c(z) = z−wc h(w,z). The two maps we need are

A = Tu, 1/δ,   B = Ty, (1−λ̄)/β,   x ⟼ Ax = λy ⟼ BAx = y.

Indeed h(u,x) = δ, and B multiplies y by λ̄. To see that the maps preserve the lattice in both directions, write Lz = w h(w,z). This operator is self-adjoint for h and L² = h(w,w)L. Multiplying (1−c̄L)(1−cL) therefore gives the identity whenever c+c̄ = cc̄ h(w,w). This equality holds for A because h(u,u) = δ+δ̄, and for B because (1−λ̄)(1−λ) = 2−λ−λ̄. Thus each map is unitary with inverse Tw,c̄. Every coefficient of the maps and their inverses is integral since w, J and c are integral.

Start with the identity. If g has matched some columns, use x = gXᵢ and y = Yᵢ for the next pair of diagonalized columns. Every earlier matched column is perpendicular to both x and y, so A and B fix it. Replacing g by BAg matches one more column and preserves the lattice. After the last column, undo the common column change to get gᵥX = Yᵥ for the original frames. At each v outside S, gᵥ belongs to the unitary stabilizer of RᵥM, where M is the ambient dimension. The places above 2 enter S because the norm differences divide by 4. The adelic orbit argument supplies the transformations at the remaining places and assembles the local maps.

Which local inverses form an adelic inverse?

A finite adèle of F is a tuple (aᵥ) in the completions Fᵥ with aᵥ in the valuation ring 𝒪ᵥ outside a finite set. Its inverse is an adèle precisely when every aᵥ is nonzero and almost every aᵥ is a unit of 𝒪ᵥ. Indeed the only possible inverse has components 1/aᵥ. At a place where aᵥ is integral, its inverse is integral exactly when its valuation is zero. At the finitely many archimedean places one just needs a nonzero component. As an example over ℚ, take aₚ = p at every finite prime and a∞ = 1. This is an adèle with every component nonzero. Its componentwise inverse has negative valuation at every prime. In contrast, a fixed nonzero rational number and its inverse have a nonzero valuation at only finitely many primes. Sutherland, The idele group, Definition 26.2[96].

Apply this criterion to a denominator in a unitary change of frame. At a finite place put Aᵥ = Fᵥ ⊗F E. This is a quadratic field or a product of two copies of Fᵥ. In both cases the norm of δ is N(δ) = δδ. A nonzero norm gives the explicit inverse δ/N(δ). In a split algebra the norm tests both components. For example, (0,1) is a nonzero element with zero norm. Each of the four candidate phases gives a scalar norm fⱼ. Why do they generate the unit ideal over the full ring of base adèles? For t = a+bθ, their two differences are 4βa and 4β(Pa−Qbd). The scalars 4β and Qd are nonzero elements of F and therefore have adelic inverses. Hence the ideal generated by the four norms contains a and b. For the phase +1 we have f₁ = (β−a)²−db², so β²−f₁ belongs to the ideal generated by a and b. Adding f₁ shows that the ideal of the four norms contains β². Dividing by β² shows that a linear combination of the norms with adelic coefficients equals one. Evaluating this identity at an exceptional place produces at least one nonzero fⱼ. This suffices in the local field even at a ramified or dyadic place. For instance, over ℚ₂(i) take β = t = 1 and the phases ±1, ±i. Their denominators are 0, 2 and 1±i. None is an integral unit, yet 2 is invertible in the field. Where all the coefficients and norms are integral, at least one fⱼ must be an integral unit, since otherwise the sum would lie in the maximal ideal.

Select an admissible index at each place. Both the numerator δ and the inverse of the selected norm are then integral at almost every finite place. Consequently the entries of the elementary unitary corrections, and of their inverses, are adèles in the chosen coordinates. Different places may use different indices. The four indicator functions of the chosen sets take values in {0,1}, hence are integral everywhere. Multiplying each candidate by its indicator and adding realizes the local choices as a single adelic coefficient. This construction applies at each of the finitely many column steps. Each new correction fixes the already matched columns because they are orthogonal to both vectors used in that correction.

How does a pointwise lift give a single compact family?

Write G for the adelic unitary group preserving J. By the column construction and the rational change of basis, every adelic tuple Y of Gram matrix T equals gX for some g ∈ G. Conversely, an isometry preserves all pairings, so the orbit of X is exactly the fibre Z of the Gram map at T. Without the nonsingularity hypothesis, equality of Gram matrices can leave several orbits. In a hyperbolic plane the zero vector and a nonzero isotropic vector both have Gram matrix (0). Every invertible linear map fixes zero.

For the shell bound we need one compact family of such g as Y varies in a given compact set Ω. We first check the topology needed to pass from points to compact sets. In any basis of E over F, an adelic coefficient is a pair of base adèles. Conjugation is linear in these coordinates and multiplication is polynomial. The tuple space is therefore locally compact and Hausdorff, and the entries of the Gram matrix are continuous. The fibre Z is closed. Give an invertible matrix the topology of the pair (g,g−1). In the product of the two matrix spaces, the equations gh = hg = I and g∗Jg = J define a closed set. This gives G local compactness, the Hausdorff property and a countable basis, inherited from the finite powers of the adèle ring. The action is continuous by matrix multiplication.

Why the adelic orbit map is open. Given any neighborhood W of the identity in G, choose a compact neighborhood K with K−1K ⊂ W. The translates of the interior of K cover G, and second countability gives a countable subcover. Transitivity then covers Z by countably many translates of the compact, hence closed, set KX. By the Baire category theorem at least one of these closed translates has nonempty interior in Z. Translating back, choose kX in the interior of KX with k ∈ K. Then k−1 int(KX) is a neighborhood of X inside K−1KX ⊂ WX. Translating this inclusion to each group element proves that g ↦ gX is open onto Z. The Stacks Project, Lemma 5.13.3, Baire category theorem[97].

Take a relatively compact open neighborhood of each group element. Their images under this open map cover Z, so finitely many images cover Ω ∩ Z. The union of the closures of those finitely many neighborhoods is a compact family of adelic isometries giving all the required lifts.

This compactness controls all places together. To see its force, consider the open sets of matrices for which both the matrix and its inverse have integral coordinates outside a prescribed finite set of places. They cover G as the finite set varies. A compact set of representatives meets the requirement for one common finite set, by taking the union from a finite subcover. In coordinates one can enlarge that set to include the finitely many primes in the multiplication table of the chosen rational basis. Applied to the hyperbolic pair, the compact family transports the fixed pair to each of the pairs used in the shell comparison.

Why does a compact set have finite mean on a nonzero norm fibre?

Fix t ∈ F× and a compact adelic set Ω. An unrepresented norm contributes zero. If ⟨e,e⟩ = t for a rational e, the line Ee is nondegenerate. Its orthogonal complement has dimension M−1. The stabilizer G1 of the vector e is the adelic unitary group of this complement. Witt’s extension theorem identifies every rational vector of norm t with γ−1e for some γ ∈ Γ. Two choices give the same vector precisely when they differ by left multiplication by an element of Γ1 = Γ ∩ G1. Thus the classes are Γ1γ in Γ1 ∖ Γ. Unfolding replaces the sum integrated over Γ ∖ G by the integral of f(h) = 𝟙Ω(h−1e) over Γ1 ∖ G, before division by V.

The compact representative theorem supplies a compact set C of isometries such that every norm-t vector in Ω has the form ce with c ∈ C. It uses adelic Witt extension and compact lifting on the closed orbit. Consequently, whenever f(h) = 1, we have h−1e = ce and hc fixes e. Thus the support lies in G1C−1. The compact-cover integral bound for a function ≤ 1 bounds its unfolded integral by a fixed constant times the volume of Γ1 ∖ G1. Finite arithmetic quotient volume in the smaller dimension proves integrability on this fibre.

Finally, the continuous norm maps Ω into a compact adelic set, which meets the closed discrete diagonal copy of F in finitely many points. Add the finite means for those nonzero norms. Enclose Ω in one box and apply the isotropic bound to its nonzero vectors of norm zero. This gives the finite reference mean used in the large-radius packing estimate. Including the origin in that reference box adds exactly one.

Use the height to choose the radius. After reduction write yw = Im τw and Y = minw yw. There are fixed t, κ > 0 such that Y ≥ t and every yw ≤ Y/κ. The finite test φ is locally constant and compactly supported, so it is bounded and its support has a common denominator N. Positive definiteness of the Gaussian majorant bounds the absolute weight of a vector of maximum coordinate size s by a constant times exp(−cYs²) for some c > 0. For √Y s ≤ 1 use the ball of radius 1/√Y. For 2j−1 < √Y s ≤ 2j use the ball of radius 2j/√Y and weight exp(−c4j−1). The ball bound costs at most a constant times 4jkY−k/2, since Y ≥ t. The exponential makes the sum over shells finite. Multiplying by the modular weight ∏w ywM/2 ≤ (Y/κ)k/2 cancels this power, even as Y tends to infinity.

Subtract the common term. The zero vector contributes φ(0) to the theta average. The Eisenstein expansion begins with the same term. Its remaining summands, indexed by b ∈ F, have absolute value at most a constant times den(b)−M ∏w |τw + w(b)|−M. Here den(b) is the norm of the ideal of integers clearing its denominator. Group b by its class modulo 𝒪F. Summing the real factors over integral translates costs at most a constant times ∏w yw1−M. For each denominator ideal 𝔞 there are at most N(𝔞) classes, since they lie in 𝔞−1/𝒪F. Their total is bounded using ∑𝔞≠0 N(𝔞)1−M, which converges for M ≥ 3. After multiplication by the modular weight the remaining height factor is ∏w yw1−M/2, bounded for yw ≥ t.

For each τ, the cusp row construction gives an integral matrix followed by one of finitely many rational matrices. Balancing by a unit gives the height inequalities on this region. Although the integral matrix can vary, each resulting test is a linear combination of the indicators of a fixed finite set of cosets of one compact open subgroup, with uniformly bounded coefficients. Applying the reduced estimate to those finitely many tests after the finitely many cusp representatives gives a bound for every τ. Apply it to the undilated lattice at τw = (xw+i)/a². The weight is a−k. The Fourier character for β ≠ 0 has modulus one, so the normalized coefficient integral preserves the resulting bound C ak. This proves the one-vector discrepancy estimate.

Take F = ℚ, E = ℚ(i), M = 3 and a single height Y = 4. The innermost ball has radius 1/2. Its two powers in the count are (1/2)³ and (1/2)⁶. Where do the finitely many cusp matrices come from?

Let F be totally real of degree d, with ring of integers 𝒪. A point of the Hilbert upper half-space has one coordinate τw = xw + iyw, with yw > 0, at each real embedding w. For a matrix in SL₂(F) with bottom row (c,b), direct multiplication by the conjugate denominator gives Im(gτ)w = yw/|w(c)τw+w(b)|². We need one row whose denominator is small at every embedding.

Embed 𝒪² in ℝ2d using all its real embeddings. At each place, apply to a pair (a,b) of real coordinates the determinant-one map (a,b) ↦ (√y · a, (xa+b)/√y). The product map preserves the covolume of the lattice for every τ. Choose a cube [−R,R]2d of volume greater than 22d times this covolume. Minkowski’s convex body theorem supplies a nonzero lattice point in it. Adding the squares of the two coordinates at each place gives a pair (c,b) ∈ 𝒪², independent of the place, with

|w(c)τw + w(b)|² ≤ 2R²yw   at every w.

Complete that row. Its two entries generate a nonzero integral ideal I. The class group is finite, so fix an integral ideal J in each class. For the class of I there is a scalar λ with λI = J. Hence |N(λ)| = N(J)/N(I) ≤ N(J), uniformly bounded by a constant B over the fixed finite list. Put (p,q) = λ(c,b). From pJ−1 + qJ−1 = 𝒪 choose a,b′ ∈ J−1 with aq−b′p = 1. This gives a determinant-one matrix g with top row in J−1 and bottom row in J. Choose one such matrix r for each class that occurs. Every entry of r−1g is a difference of two products in J J−1 = 𝒪. Thus g = rk with k ∈ SL₂(𝒪) and r in a fixed finite set. Multiplying (p,q) by a unit preserves the ideal, so the same construction works for every unit multiple. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 4.19 (Minkowski)[98] · Theorems 4.3–4.4 (ideal classes)[99]

Why does each imaginary part have a positive lower bound?

Write y′w for the heights obtained with bottom row λ(c,b). Put A ≥ max(1,2R²) and enlarge B to at least 1. The small-denominator inequality gives y′w ≥ 1/(A|w(λ)|²). Multiplying over the embeddings yields ∏wy′w ≥ P = 1/(AdB²). A product lower bound alone still permits one height to tend to zero.

To balance them, take the numbers ½ log y′w and subtract their mean. Dirichlet’s unit theorem says that the vectors (log |w(u)|)w of units u form a full lattice in the hyperplane of coordinate sum zero. Add a lattice vector to move the centered numbers into a fixed bounded parallelepiped. If each resulting coordinate has absolute value at most L, the differences of the logarithms of the new heights have absolute value at most 4L. The required new bottom row is u−1λ(c,b). Its height zw = |w(u)|²y′w gains the square of the unit, and its product is unchanged since |N(u)| = 1. Set κ = e−4L. The largest zw is at least P1/d, and the smallest is at least κ times the largest. In particular the following constants work for every τ. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 5.9[100]

t = κ min(1,P) > 0,   t ≤ Im(rkτ)v,   κ Im(rkτ)w ≤ Im(rkτ)v   for all v,w.

The rightmost matrix k acts first. These inequalities suffice for the theta and Eisenstein estimates at unbounded heights. The finite list is the list of matrices r. The integral matrix k can vary with τ.

Check the local power at the inert prime 3

For E = ℚ(i), F = ℚ, J = I₃ and β = 1, normalize the standard coordinate lattices to volume one. Modulo 3 each of three complex coordinates contributes a sum of two squares. How is the scalar fixed in an anisotropic plane?

One vector in an anisotropic binary space needs a different normalization argument. The proof combines local mass and compactness estimates with a representation principle and invariance under similitudes. Why can two spheres of different lengths have the same mass coefficient?

Fix a CM extension E/F with conjugation, and an anisotropic Hermitian plane with nonsingular matrix J. Write Q(x) = x*Jx, where * means conjugate transpose. For β ∈ F×, the rational sphere consists of x ∈ E² with Q(x) = β. Average its rational points over the adelic unitary quotient to obtain a measure Θβ. The first mass formula for this length supplies a nonnegative number κ such that, on product tests, Θβ integrates as κ times the product of the local Gram-fibre integrals. A separate choice of κ for each β would leave an unknown weight inside the sum over lengths. A rational change of variables makes the same κ work throughout that sum.

Build the change of variables from two points. Suppose Q(x) = β and Q(x′) = β′, both nonzero. If x*J = (r₀,r₁), put y = (−r₁,r₀)t and take the two columns of Pₓ to be x and y. Then x*Jy = 0 and det Pₓ = r₀x₀ + r₁x₁ = β. Taking determinants in its diagonal Gram matrix gives βQ(y) = β² det J. Thus the two frames give the same diagonal form up to their respective lengths.

Pₓ*JPₓ = β diag(1, det J),   γ = Pₓ′Pₓ−1,   γ*Jγ = λJ,   λ = β′/β.

In particular γx = x′. Its entries belong to E and its multiplier λ belongs to F. This one matrix bijects all rational points of the first sphere with those of the second. On the group used in the average, put h′ = γhγ−1. It is unitary and γ(h−1x) = (h′)−1γx. Pull back the Haar measure and the fundamental domain together under this conjugation. The volume dividing the average is preserved. Reindexing the sum and changing variables gives γ∗Θβ = Θβ′ because the normalized theta measure is independent of these auxiliary choices.

Compute what happens on a fibre. At a place v, write dX for ambient additive Haar measure and db for Haar measure on the scalar length coordinate. The Gram-fibre measures mᵥ(b) recover the ambient integral by integrating over b on the regular locus. Define the positive factors aᵥ and bᵥ by γ∗dX = aᵥ dX and (multiplication by λ)∗db = bᵥ db. Since Q(γX) = λQ(X), the changed family must reconstruct aᵥ dX using bᵥ db. Uniqueness of the normalized fibre measures fixes the quotient, including its direction. Combine all infinite places in F∞.

γ∗mᵥ(β) = (aᵥ/bᵥ) mᵥ(β′),   (a∞/b∞) ∏v finite (aᵥ/bᵥ) = 1.

For the first product formula the proof expresses γ as a linear map in F-coordinates. For the second, scalar congruence on a one-by-one Hermitian matrix acts by λ². Its Haar factor is the square of the positive factor for multiplication by λ, so taking square roots gives the required product formula on lengths. Outside finitely many places the factors are one and γ and its inverse preserve the standard lattice. On a product test enlarge its finite set of places to include these exceptions. All local changes of measure then cancel in the product, leaving exactly the original κ in the formula for Θβ′.

Follow the factor at infinity and at 2 for a sphere of length two

Over ℚ(i)/ℚ take J = I₂, x = (1,0)t and x′ = (1,i)t. Their lengths are 1 and 2. The frame gives γ with rows (1,i), (i,1). Multiplication gives γ*γ = 2I₂ and detℚ(i)γ = 2. In the four rational coordinates its determinant is the norm of 2, hence 4. A pushforward measures the inverse image of a set. At infinity its factor on vectors is therefore 1/4, and on lengths it is 1/2. The fibre factor is (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2. At 2 the absolute values are |4|₂ = 1/4 and |2|₂ = 1/2, giving pushforward factors 4 and 2 and fibre factor 2. At every odd prime the factors are one. Thus the product of the fibre factors is (1/2)·2 = 1, although the real fibre measure alone changes. This computes the transport of a mass formula without evaluating either sphere’s individual mass.

Which lengths reach the counting theorem? Start with the coefficient supplied for a fixed β ≠ 0. If the infinite fibre measure or any finite fibre measure is zero, its factorization forces Θβ = 0. The local finiteness and summability already supplied let one write the zero factorization with coefficient 1 directly. Otherwise the binary representation theorem gives a rational vector of length β from the nonzero infinite fibre measure. Now consider every β′ ≠ 0. A represented β′ receives the same κ by the preceding argument. For an unrepresented β′ the rational sum is empty, and the contrapositive of that representation theorem gives zero infinite fibre measure. Apply the individual mass formula for β′ to obtain its finiteness and summability conditions. Its zero factorization now holds with the chosen κ as well. For example, length −1 is empty over the reals in the positive definite plane above. The degree-one Gram matrix at β = 0 is singular, and anisotropy leaves only the zero rational vector there. The counting theorem uses precisely the nonzero lengths. Having a common κ on all of them permits the positive-volume comparison that gives κ = 1.

Why does the infinite fibre detect a rational point in this plane?

For a proposed nonzero length t, compare J with diag(t, t det J). Their determinants differ by t², the norm of t from E to F. At an indefinite real place both planes have one positive and one negative direction. At a definite place representing the sign of t makes their signatures agree there too. With all signatures equal, Landherr’s classification gives a rational isometry of the two Hermitian forms. The image of the first basis vector then has length t. Consequently a missing rational length has the wrong sign at some definite real place. The infinite fibre is empty there and its supported measure vanishes. The archive obtains the classification result used here from a quadratic Hasse norm theorem.

How much mass does one length carry at a good prime?

A Hermitian vector in a plane has two coordinates over E. Each has two coordinates over F. At a finite place v, fixing its length therefore imposes one quadratic equation on four coordinates over Fv. Fix the basis and lattice used in the product formula. Write 𝒪 for the local integers, π for a uniformizer, and q for the number of elements of the residue field. Normalize scalar Haar measure by vol(𝒪) = 1 and use its fourth power on the source. Let gv(s) be the mass on the length-s fibre of the standard lattice.

Good-place mass estimate. Remove the finitely many places where 2 or the determinant of the trace form fails to be a unit, or an entry of its matrix fails to be integral. At each remaining place, for s ≠ 0 one has

gv(s) = 0 for s ∉ 𝒪,   |gv(s) − 1| ≤ 3/q for s ∈ 𝒪,   |gv(s) − 1| ≤ 1/q² for s ∈ 𝒪×.

In the chosen coordinates the length is Q(x) = ½xtBx, where B is the symmetric matrix of the trace of the Hermitian pairing. The factor ½ occurs because the field trace doubles a scalar from the base field. The local Gram-fibre integration formula identifies gv on nonzero lengths with the continuous density of the pushforward of volume on 𝒪⁴ by Q. In particular, if the ratio of the inverse-image volume to target volume is constant on all sufficiently small target balls about s, it equals the fibre mass there. Integrality of B and ½ confines the support to 𝒪. The zero-length vectors also have source volume zero. Choose a vector on which Q is nonzero and take it as the first vector of a basis over the local field. For each choice of the other three coordinates the equation Q = 0 has at most two roots in the first. Singletons have Haar measure zero, so Fubini gives zero volume. An invertible linear change of basis preserves null sets. Thus integrating the regular density gives the entire volume vol(𝒪⁴) = 1.

How is a measure on a single length defined?

Even when a vector of length s exists, the set of all vectors of that length has zero four-dimensional volume. We can still assign it a three-dimensional measure. At a good finite place, choose a primitive residue class C = a + π𝒪⁴. Since B is invertible modulo π, some coordinate of B a is a unit. Keep the other three coordinates y as parameters and use the length in place of that coordinate. For any s in I = Q(a) + π𝒪 and any compatible y, there is exactly one remaining coordinate in its residue class. Indeed, given a solution modulo πk, changing its next digit changes the next length digit by multiplication by that unit. Every required digit has a unique lift, and completeness gives the coordinate. Call this vector x(s,y).

For each fixed y this correspondence preserves one-dimensional Haar measure. It gives a bijection of the residue balls at every precision, and corresponding balls have the same volume. Integration in the length and the three free coordinates now gives, for a locally constant test function φ on C,

∫C φ(x) dx = ∫I (∫y ≡ afree mod π φ(x(s,y)) dy) ds.

The inner integral defines the contribution of this class to the length-s fibre. For φ = 1 it equals q−3 throughout I. For example, over ℚ₃ take the sum of four squares and the class (1,0,0,0) modulo 3. Each of the last three coordinates ranges over 3ℤ₃. The contribution is 1/27 at every length congruent to 1. Integrated over that target ball it gives (1/27)(1/3) = 1/81, precisely the volume of the source class.

Every nonzero integral vector has a unique expression πjz with j ≥ 0 and z primitive. On this shell four-dimensional volume scales by q−4j and length by π2j, so the fibre measure scales by q−2j. At a fixed nonzero integral s only 2j ≤ ord(s) can occur. The shell sum for φ = 1 thus defines a locally constant density near s. It agrees pointwise with the continuous regular Gram-fibre mass used in the product formula by uniqueness on regular fibres. Both integrate to the same volume on every sufficiently small target ball, and every such ball has positive measure.
