Which central directions still need averaging?

The form ω realizing the cocycle already has two symmetries. It is invariant under Γ = GLN(𝒪L′) and under a common positive scaling at all infinite places. The next estimate uses independent scalar changes at every place. Write c(t) for the central matrix whose component at w is exp(tw)I. A complex scalar zw acts on a positive Hermitian matrix by Hw ↦ |zw|−2Hw, since the action uses the inverse matrix on the right and its adjoint on the left. Thus only the real logarithms tw = log |zw| matter.

Let r be the number of complex places of the totally complex field L′. The line of constant vectors in ℝr acts trivially on ω by pullback. A unit u gives another symmetry because uI ∈ Γ. Its logarithm vector ℓ(u) = (log |w(u)|)w lies in V = {t ∈ ℝr ∣ ∑w tw = 0} by the product formula. Dirichlet’s unit theorem gives a lattice Λ of rank r − 1 in V, generated by the logarithms of fundamental units. Subtracting the coordinate mean from any t leaves a vector in V. Consequently the central parameters still to be averaged form the compact torus V/Λ. For r = 1 the initial symmetries already suffice.

The proof integrates one unit direction v = ℓ(u) at a time. For the pullback of the form, including its tangent arguments, it takes

Avω = ∫₀¹ c(τv)∗ω dτ.

Unit invariance makes the integrand 1-periodic in τ. Translating the interval of integration therefore preserves the average, so every real multiple of v fixes Avω. Central scalars commute, which preserves the directions already treated. Iterating uses ordinary Lebesgue measure of mass one on each unit interval. In the coordinates of the fundamental units their product induces Haar probability on V/Λ. The output ω′ is invariant under every scalar tuple.

Why does the average have exactly the original periods? Fix a finite bar cycle z based at the identity matrix I. For fixed τ, centrality moves the basepoint of every simplex from I to c(τv)·I, keeping the same group labels. Join the old and new vertices by the simplices of a prism. Its side faces cancel on the cycle because ∂z = 0. The remaining two evaluations agree because ω integrates to a cocycle on simplices. Thus for every τ the sum over the cycle already equals its original value. Interchanging the finite sum, simplex integrals and the unit-interval integral preserves that value. The averaged form still integrates to a cocycle by the same interchange on a boundary. Its moving-frame bound retains the exponent am for a form of degree m, since the path τ ↦ c(τv) is compact and right translation there changes the height by a bounded factor.

Check the factor of two and a period

In L′ = ℚ(i,√2), label the two complex places by the sign of √2. For u = 1 + √2 and a = log(1 + √2), the absolute values of u at these places are exp(a) and exp(−a). Take N = 1 and work with the cyclic subgroup generated by u. On the pair of positive numbers (H₁,H₂) set s = (log H₂ − log H₁)/(4a). Under c(τℓ(u)) log H₁ decreases by 2aτ and log H₂ increases by 2aτ, so s goes to s + τ. Averaging (2 + cos(2πs)) ds gives 2 ds. The cycle [u] moves s from 0 to 1 at the identity basepoint. The two primitives 2s + sin(2πs)/(2π) and 2s both increase by 2 along that cycle. On an open arc from 0 to 1/4 their increments differ by 1/(2π).

How large must the matrix be to integrate the coefficients?

Even a finite-volume quotient can have an unbounded function whose square has infinite integral. Here the possible growth occurs at the cusps, where a lattice or its dual has a short vector. For the tuple of Hermitian forms h = x·I, let λ(h) be the infimum of the sum of its values over the complex places on a nonzero integral vector. The height is 1/[λ(h)λ(h∨)], where h∨ = (h⁻¹)T at each place. For every totally complex number field L′ and every integer A ≥ 0, the proof chooses a finite-volume Haar fundamental domain for SLN(𝒪L′) in ∏wSLN(ℂ) on which heightA is integrable whenever N ≥ A + 2.

For a form of degree m, the bound on the norm of its coefficients in the moving frame is K heightam. The partition of unity supplies a for the field before the matrix size is chosen. Squaring calls for A = 2am. The comparison therefore chooses N large enough for this moment, for the separate Hecke stability threshold, for the requested starting size, and for N ≥ 3. This one size works for every cocycle of the specified degree m < r₂(L′). The zeroth moment gives finite volume, so the inequality u ≤ u² + 1 for the coefficient norm also gives integrability of the coefficients themselves. Their mean is now defined.

Why do finitely many regions suffice for the cusp integral?

Let L be totally complex and set Γ = SLN(𝒪L). In the product of SLN(ℂ) over the complex places, a single matrix can travel arbitrarily far out a cusp. What becomes finite is the choice of arithmetic coordinate system. For fixed L and N ≥ 1, there are finitely many matrices cj and one region S such that for every x, some γ ∈ Γ and some j satisfy cj−1γx ∈ S. Inside S the diagonal parameters can still grow. This is the cover used in the height moment.

How does a shortest row control the cusp diagonal?

Take a number field L of degree d over ℚ and an adelic invertible matrix g of size N ≥ 1. For a nonzero row x over L, form xg at every place. Its height Hg(x) is the product of the Euclidean lengths at the infinite places, squared at complex places, and the maximum entry norms at the finite places. The product formula makes this height invariant under scaling x by L×. Below any fixed height there are only finitely many rational lines. Place a minimizing row last in a rational basis and factor the resulting matrix as an upper triangular matrix times a maximal compact element. The right compact factor preserves all the row lengths. Reduce the upper left block by induction, keeping the last row in place.

For N ≥ 2 the only new adjacent pair is the bottom block [[α, u], [0, β]]. Write A = |α|𝔸, B = |β|𝔸 for the products of their normalized local absolute values. The last row has height B. Two-dimensional approximation produces a nonzero rational row whose image under this block has height at most C√(AB), with C depending only on L. Putting the two coordinates in the last two slots gives a competitor for the minimum, since the triangular matrix has zeros to their left. Hence

B ≤ C√(AB)  ⟹  B ≤ C²A.

Induction gives this inequality for every pair of consecutive diagonal entries, with the same constant.

Where the square root comes from

If A ≥ B, the row (0, 1) already works. Otherwise put s = (A/B)1/(2d). Divide the block by β. After multiplying its first row by a scalar in L×, the upper left entry is a positive idèle of archimedean size s² times an element of a fixed compact set. Call the adjusted upper right entry a. In an integral basis, (H + 1)d candidate multiples of a fall into Hd boxes after rational translation to clear finite denominators and reduction modulo the integer lattice at infinity. Two lie in one box. Their difference gives a nonzero integer ℓ of L of archimedean size O(H + 1) and c ∈ L such that ℓa + c is integral at all finite places and O(1/H) at infinity. For H = ⌈1/s⌉ both coordinates of the resulting row have size O(s) at infinity. Its finite norm product is bounded by compactness. Restoring β bounds the height by a field constant times B sd = √(AB).

To obtain the real cusp parameters, take rᵢ = |bᵢᵢ|𝔸1/d. The idèle with value rᵢ at every infinite place and 1 at every finite place has norm rᵢd. Dividing it out leaves a norm-one idèle. Rational diagonal scalings bring these remainders into compact representatives of the norm-one idèle classes. Rational upper triangular row additions bring the entries of the upper unitriangular factor into compact additive representatives. The resulting factorization has the fixed compact triangular set, positive diagonal and maximal compact subgroup used in the cusp cover, with t ri+1 ≤ rᵢ for t = C−2/d. At finite places the positive diagonal is the identity, so for g = (x, 1) the rational change of basis has finite component in a fixed compact set.

Check the complex-place exponent over ℚ(i)

Take g∞ = [[1, 2], [0, 3]] and identity at every finite place. Every rational line has a primitive Gaussian integer representative (u, v), whose finite height factors are 1. Its height is |u|² + |2u + 3v|². Height 1 would require a unit u with 3 dividing 2u, since u = 0 gives height 9 for a primitive row. The row (1, −1) attains height 2. Use it as the last row of γ = [[0, −1], [1, −1]]. Multiplying γg∞ on the right by the unitary matrix [[1, 1], [1, −1]]/√2 gives [[−3/√2, 3/√2], [0, √2]]. At finite places γ is integral and invertible, so the triangular factor there can be the identity. The last diagonal idèle has norm 2, and its real parameter is √2. The first has norm 9/2 and real parameter 3/√2.

First choose finitely many rational matrices. Append the identity at the finite places to an archimedean point x. The shortest-row construction supplies a rational matrix η such that ηx has a bounded upper triangular factor, a positive diagonal and a compact factor. The positive diagonal equals the identity at the finite places. Thus the finite part of η belongs to one compact set C, the finite projection of the product of the compact triangular set and the maximal compact subgroup. The subgroup U of matrices integral and invertible at every finite place is open. Its left cosets cover C, and finitely many suffice. In each of these cosets that occurs for a rational η, choose one rational representative a. Then a−1η and its inverse are integral at every finite place. Each entry therefore lies in 𝒪L. Writing δ = a−1η, we have δ ∈ GLN(𝒪L) and δx equals a−1 times the reduced factors. The finite list for this GL cover consists of the inverses g = a−1.

Correct the determinant. The unit det δ can be written vNu₀. Here v is a unit and u₀ comes from a finite list. Indeed, express a unit as a root of unity times powers of the fundamental units and reduce each exponent modulo N. The list has at most |μ(L)|Nrank 𝒪L× entries. Put D(u) = diag(u,1,…,1). This gives an integral change of coordinates of determinant one.

γ = v−1D(u₀−1)δ,   det γ = v−Nu₀−1 det δ = 1.

The chart now depends only on (g, u₀). Set G = D(u₀−1)g. At each complex place w choose a scalar zw with zwN det w(G) = 1 and take cj,w = zww(G). This is the precise rationality used for the height bound. The underlying matrix G is defined over L, while the scalar can depend on the place.

A determinant correction over the Gaussian integers

Test the correction with N = 2, L = ℚ(i), x = g = I and δ = [[i,1],[0,1]]. Here v = 1 and u₀ = i work. Then γ = [[1,−i],[0,1]]. Choose z = exp(πi/4), so z² = i and c = z diag(−i,1) has determinant one. In this chart c−1γ = z−1δ = [[1,1],[0,1]] diag(i/z,1/z). The last factor is unitary of determinant one. This tests the correction on one admissible triangular factorization. The full list of charts may contain other representatives.

How are the chart bounds shared across places?

Before the determinant correction, write the positive diagonal entries as rᵢ, with t ri+1 ≤ rᵢ for fixed t > 0. Compactness bounds the entries of each triangular factor Bw by M and bounds its diagonal moduli below by M−1. After the correction the local scalar is αw = w(v−1)/zw. Use the same diagonal coordinates at every place by setting

sᵢ = log rᵢ + meanw(log |αw| + log |Bw,ii|).

The local determinant-one equations give ∑isᵢ = 0. Subtracting two places’ determinant equations also gives |log |αw| − log |αw′|| ≤ 2 log M. After removing exp(sᵢ) and moving the diagonal phases into the unitary factor, every triangular entry has modulus at most M⁴ and each diagonal modulus is at least M−4. In each diagonal position their product over the places is one, by the definition of the mean. The common region uses si+1 ≤ sᵢ + 4 log M − log t. These bounds hold across all charts for this field and matrix size.

Integrate over the cover. Write F for a Haar fundamental domain, and let f be a nonnegative Γ-invariant integrand. Moving pieces of F by Γ gives an upper bound by the integral over the union of the charts. Subadditivity and left invariance of Haar measure then give

∫F f dμ ≤ ∑j ∫S f(cjy) dμ(y).

Overlaps are allowed. Each chart has its own finite height constant, and there are only finitely many summands. For f = heightA the remaining integral on each chart is finite when N ≥ A + 2. This last convergence comes from the decay in the unbounded diagonal variables.

Why the cusp integral converges

Reduction theory covers the quotient by finitely many charts. After a fixed translate, each point has a bounded triangular factor, a diagonal factor with entries exp(sᵢ) shared across the complex places, and a unitary factor. The determinant gives ∑sᵢ = 0, and the adjacent entries satisfy si+1 ≤ sᵢ + T for a fixed T. Clearing denominators in a chart gives lower bounds proportional to exp(−2 max sᵢ) and exp(2 min sᵢ) for the primal and dual minima. Set W = ∑i<N|sᵢ − si+1|, using indices 1,…,N. Then max sᵢ − min sᵢ ≤ W, so heightA ≤ C exp(2AW).

Write Φ = ∑i<j(sᵢ − sⱼ). A unit box in the logarithms has Haar measure at most C′ exp(−2Φ) for every admissible s in it. Indeed, the packing argument fits at least exp(2Φ) translates of the box in a translate of a fixed compact set, with uniformly bounded overlap. When the coordinates decrease, the gap sⱼ − sj+1 occurs j(N − j) times in Φ, at least N − 1 times. For the allowed upward errors of size T, the cone estimate gives the following quantitative version.

2AW − 2Φ ≤ C″ − δ ∑i|sᵢ|,   δ = 2(N − 1 − A)/N > 0.

Index the boxes by the integer parts of their coordinates. The integral over a box with index u is bounded by a constant times exp(−δ ∑|uᵢ|). Summing over all boxes gives a product of convergent geometric series. For instance, along (3t, −t, −t, −t) with t ≥ 0, W = 4t and Φ = 12t. At A = 2 the combined exponential is exp(−8t). At A = 3 it equals 1 along the ray. This explains the strict inequality A < N − 1 in the estimate and leaves the endpoint moment undecided.

How a finite incidence count bounds an angle

Let π be the prime element used in the Hecke average, 𝒪 the ring of integers of the field, and k = 𝒪/(π), of order q ≥ 25. Take N ≥ 3. In SLN(L′) consider three conjugates of SLN(𝒪). The group Kᵣ is Dᵣ−1SLN(𝒪)Dᵣ, where the diagonal matrix Dᵣ has π in its first r positions and 1 elsewhere, for r = 0,1,2. Put Eᵢⱼ = Kᵢ ∩ Kⱼ and B = K₀ ∩ K₁ ∩ K₂. At each vertex Kᵣ, the two incident subgroups stabilize a pair of nested subspaces after reduction modulo π. Such a pair is a flag.

Use coordinates 0,…,N − 1 after conjugating by Dᵣ. The following pairs are in the order used by the angle bound. The first subgroup in each pair is called E and the second E′.

  • In K₀, E₀₁ fixes the line spanned by e₀ and E₀₂ fixes the plane spanned by e₀,e₁.
  • In K₁, E₁₂ fixes the line spanned by e₁ and E₀₁ fixes the hyperplane x₀ = 0.
  • In K₂, E₁₂ fixes the hyperplane x₁ = 0 and E₀₂ fixes its subspace x₀ = x₁ = 0.

Here “fixes” means preserves the subspace as a set. The bipartite graph has a vertex for each subspace of the first or second type, and one edge for each incident pair. Equivalently, take the translates of the two coordinate subspaces under Kᵣ. The stabilizer of their common edge is B. In the first two cases a matrix outside E moves the distinguished line to a different line. Row additions preserving the first line can take that new line to a fixed second coordinate line. Thus all such matrices form one double coset of E. Transposing gives the same result for the distinguished hyperplane in the third case.

Count the flag choices in a finite group

At any one vertex, the proof passes to the finite group G = Kᵣ/core(B), where core(B) is the intersection of all Kᵣ-conjugates of B. Use the same letters for subgroup images. A real function f constant on the cosets Ek has a value at each vertex of the first type. Suppose its mean is zero. Use the uniform measure on G and form its correlation c(s) = meank f(sk)f(k). It equals ‖f‖² on E. Elsewhere it is constant because it depends only on the double coset. Its mean over s is zero, so its value outside E is nonpositive.

Average f over left multiplication by E′, writing P′f for the result. Expanding its squared norm and reindexing gives the mean of c(s) over s ∈ E′. Only the elements of E′ ∩ E = B can give a positive contribution. Their proportion is 1/[E′:B]. For a function g constant on the cosets E′k, averaging preserves the pairing with g. Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|⟨f,g⟩| = |⟨P′f,g⟩| ≤ ‖f‖‖g‖ / √[E′:B].

At vertex 0, the matrices I + t e₁₀ in E₀₂ move the line to span(e₀ + t e₁) inside the same plane. Distinct t modulo π give distinct flags, so [E₀₂:B] ≥ q. Likewise I + t e₂₁ in E₀₁ sends e₁ to e₁ + t e₂ while fixing e₀. This supplies [E₀₁:B] ≥ q, the other needed index. Thus every pairing has coefficient at most 1/√q ≤ 1/5. On the arithmetic quotient the first vector is orthogonal to all Kᵣ-invariant functions. Subtracting its local Kᵣ-average gives a representative with zero mean on each finite fiber. Integrating the finite estimate gives the three angles used in the Hecke norm calculation.

A calculation at the threshold. In size N = 3 over 𝔽₂₅, the graph at vertex 0 joins points to lines in the projective plane. There are (25³ − 1)/(25 − 1) = 651 points and as many lines. Each line contains 26 points. Give one point value +1, a second point value −1, and all other points zero. Averaging on each line gives +1/26 on the 25 lines through just the first point, −1/26 on the 25 through just the second, and zero elsewhere. The common line cancels. The ratio of output norm to input norm is √(50/26²)/√2 = 5/26. In fact this is the norm on the entire mean-zero subspace. If A is the line-by-point incidence matrix, ATA has diagonal entries 26 and off-diagonal entries 1, since two points determine one line. It acts by 25 on vectors with zero sum. The averaging matrix is A/26. Here the general bound 1/√26 and its uniform relaxation 1/5 both exceed the exact value 5/26.

Why are the common invariant functions constant?

The Hecke angle estimate applies after the common invariant component has been removed. Work on the common finite cover for the three groups in the flag calculation. Put Eᵢⱼ = Kᵢ ∩ Kⱼ and B = K₀ ∩ K₁ ∩ K₂. A real L² class fixed by all three edge groups Eᵢⱼ is represented almost everywhere by a constant. Since the cover has positive finite volume, a constant with integral zero is zero. In the proof the Hecke average v has integral zero. Its inner product with every such constant vanishes, which places v in the orthogonal complement needed for the angle estimate.

Which arithmetic group is dense? Write Γ = SLN(𝒪L), where L is totally complex and N ≥ 3. For a prime element π let Dᵣ have its first r diagonal entries equal to π and the rest equal to 1. Then Kᵣ = Dᵣ−1ΓDᵣ inside SLN(L). It is the group generated by K₀ and K₁ whose simultaneous archimedean image is dense in ∏w SLN(ℂ). The norm threshold |𝒪L/(π)| ≥ 25 enters the flag estimate; the density theorem requires only that π be prime.

For distinct indices let Tᵢⱼ(a) = I + a eᵢⱼ, with eᵢⱼ the matrix unit. K₀ supplies these transvections for every integral a. Conjugating supplies T0j(1/π) in K₁. With three distinct indices, ordinary matrix multiplication gives

[Tᵢₖ(a), Tₖⱼ(b)] = Tᵢⱼ(ab),   [A,B] = ABA−1B−1.

This multiplies denominators. In the induction from πm to πm+1, use coordinate 0 as the intermediate index for two nonzero endpoints. For a starting index 0, use a third index and the new 1/π on the first factor. For an ending index 0, append an integral transvection to a pair of nonzero endpoints already obtained at the new level. This produces all Tᵢⱼ(a/πm) with integral a.

These parameters are dense simultaneously in ∏wℂ. The integer lattice has a finite covering radius R in this product. Given ε > 0, put ε′ = ε/(1 + R). Minkowski’s theorem supplies a nonzero q = y/πm with all |w(q)| < ε/(1 + R). Indeed the volume of the body |w(y)| < ε′|w(π)|m grows in proportion to |Norm π|m, and |Norm π| ≥ 2. Round the tuple (zw/w(q)) to the embeddings of a single algebraic integer a ∈ 𝒪L within distance R. Then aq approximates the whole tuple within ε. By continuity the group closure contains a complex transvection at any one place with identity at the others. Transvections generate SLN(ℂ), giving every factor of the finite product.

Two commutators that give a denominator of 49

Take L = ℚ(i), N = 3 and π = 7. The residue field has 49 elements. The first commutator [T₁₀(a), T₀₂(1/7)] gives T₁₂(a/7). The second, [T₀₁(1/7), T₁₂(a/7)], gives T₀₂(a/49). Choose a = 69 + 85i by rounding the coordinates of 49(√2 + i√3). The resulting parameter is within √2/98 of √2 + i√3. This is the one-place version of the simultaneous approximation.

How does density act on an L² class? Choose a measurable, B-invariant representative F of a common class. For each edge group E the finite coset average of F is pointwise E-invariant. Its difference from F has squared norm zero on the cover, so the two agree almost everywhere there. Both are B-invariant, hence the exceptional set is Haar-null in the whole group by the fundamental-domain formula. Left translation preserves null sets. It follows for each γ ∈ E that F(γx) = F(x) for almost every x. The set of γ satisfying this condition is a subgroup, since a translated null set is null.

Why does this subgroup contain both full vertex groups? In K₀ the stabilizer E₀₁ has only one double coset outside itself, by two-transitivity. The index [E₀₂ : B] ≥ 25 supplies an element of E₀₂ outside E₀₁. The subgroup therefore contains that whole double coset and all of K₀. In K₁ use E₁₂ and an element of E₀₁ outside B in the same way. Thus F is invariant almost everywhere under each element of the dense subgroup above.

Why does invariance extend to every translation?

Fix a Borel set U of real values and let T = F−1(U). The translations preserving T up to a null set form a closed set. To see this, take gₙ → g. On a compact test region C, the images gₙC and gC eventually lie in one compact set L₀. The set T ∩ L₀ has finite measure. The measure of the symmetric difference between its two translation preimages tends to zero. If each gₙ preserves T almost everywhere, then g does so on C. A countable compact cover gives the assertion everywhere up to Haar measure zero. Density now gives invariance for every fixed g.

Such a set has measure zero or has null complement. Indeed, if T has positive measure, Fubini gives a point a ∈ T such that ba ∈ T for almost every b. Right multiplication by a preserves the Haar null sets, so the complement of T is null. Applying this argument to inverse images of a countable family separating real values shows that F is constant almost everywhere. The argument allows the exceptional set to depend on the translation throughout.

How the three local bounds of 1/5 give a gap of 3/5

Work in the real Hilbert space of square-integrable coefficients on the common cover. Let P₁, P₂ and P₃ be the orthogonal projections onto the spaces of functions invariant under E₀₁, E₀₂ and E₁₂, respectively. Write Qᵢ = I − Pᵢ for the part lost in this projection. Start with a pair of spaces, and remove from x its projection onto their common subspace. Call the result z. This removal leaves both Qᵢx and Qⱼx unchanged. Write a = Pᵢz, b = Pⱼz and S = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖². The flag estimate gives 2⟨a,b⟩ ≤ S/5. Since S = ⟨z,a + b⟩, Cauchy–Schwarz gives S² ≤ ‖z‖² · (6/5)S. Thus the sum of the two squared losses, T = 2‖z‖² − S, is at least (4/5)‖z‖².

Set rᵢ = Qᵢx. For the pair, ⟨rᵢ + rⱼ,z⟩ = T. A second application of Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖rᵢ + rⱼ‖² ≥ (4/5)T, including the zero case. Sum over all three pairs. Every individual ‖rᵢ‖² occurs twice on the right. On the left the sum of pair squares is ‖∑rᵢ‖² + ∑‖rᵢ‖². Subtraction leaves the factor 2 · (4/5) − 1 = 3/5. In operator notation, for D = ∑Qᵢ, we have ‖Dx‖² ≥ (3/5)⟨Dx,x⟩.

To put the bound on the original coefficient, write E(x) = ⟨Dx,x⟩ = ∑‖Qᵢx‖². Cauchy–Schwarz for the positive form ⟨D·,·⟩ gives ‖Dx‖⁴ ≤ E(x)E(Dx). The preceding estimate now implies E(y) ≥ (3/5)‖y‖² for every y in the range of D. The kernel of D consists of the vectors fixed by all three projections. The common-invariance argument identifies these vectors with the constants. Since D is self-adjoint, its range is dense in their orthogonal complement. Continuity gives the same inequality for every mean-zero coefficient on the cover.

Where the Hecke factor 3/5 enters

For a prime element whose ideal has norm at least 25 and N ≥ 3, take a continuous, arithmetic- and scalar-invariant real coefficient of mean zero in L². To estimate its Hecke average, lift its translate w and the coset average v of that translate to a common finite cover. Averaging there gives ⟨v,w⟩ = ‖v‖². The angle bound for the invariant subspaces gives |⟨v,w⟩| ≤ (2/5)‖v‖‖w‖. Cancelling ‖v‖ when positive gives a norm bound of 2/5. Both squared norms acquire the same positive covering index, so it cancels on returning to the quotient. The proof weakens 2/5 to 3/5 and preserves mean zero at each step, giving the norm factor (3/5)j after j averages. This is the upper estimate compared with (4/5)j for the stabilized periods.

The average v is orthogonal to the constants. Subtracting the mean of w therefore preserves ⟨v,w⟩, preserves the edge-group invariance of w, and can only decrease its norm. We can now estimate the angle using mean-zero vectors on both sides. The preceding Hilbert-space estimate gives ∑‖(I − Pᵢ)y‖² ≥ (3/5)‖y‖² for every mean-zero y. Take mean-zero unit vectors u fixed by P₁ and P₂, and z fixed by P₁ and P₃, choosing the sign so t = ⟨u,z⟩ ≥ 0. For y = u + z the first error is zero. Since ⟨u,P₂z⟩ = t, the second error has square 1 − ‖P₂z‖² ≤ 1 − t². The third has the same bound. Thus (3/5)·2(1 + t) ≤ 2(1 − t²). Cancelling 2(1 + t) gives t ≤ 2/5.

How can the mean of the coefficients define a form at every point?

The previous average over central scalars produced a form ω′ with the original periods. Now we want a form invariant under every archimedean matrix. Let G = ∏w GLN(ℂ), let S = ∏w SLN(ℂ), and write Agh = (g−1)*h g−1 for their action on Hermitian matrices. The tangent spaces of the positive cone are copies of the same real vector space. At y ∈ S pull the form at AyI back to the identity. This gives an alternating multilinear form F(y) = ω′(AyI) ∘ Ay, with Ay applied to each tangent argument. It is left invariant under the arithmetic subgroup Λ = SLN(𝒪L′) in its archimedean embedding. Let D be a fundamental domain for Λ in S of positive finite Haar volume. The height moment makes F square-integrable there, hence integrable. We can now take an ordinary vector-valued mean in a fixed space.

M = (vol D)−1 ∫D F(y) dy,   ω̄(AgI) = M ∘ Ag−1.

Why do two matrices taking the identity to the same point give the same answer?

The ambiguity at the identity is a tuple of unitary matrices u. At each place choose a unit-modulus Nth root of det u and divide by it. The resulting k belongs to S and acts exactly like u on Hermitian matrices. Hence F(y) ∘ Au = F(yk). Right translation by k preserves Haar measure on S. It also carries a fundamental domain to another one, since it commutes with left multiplication by Λ. Integrating a Λ-invariant integrable function over either domain gives the same integral. This proves M ∘ Au = M. Every positive Hermitian tuple can be written AgI by factoring each matrix in the tuple as B*B and choosing g = B−1. Two choices differ on the right by a stabilizer of I. The displayed transport rule therefore gives a single value at every point. The group law then makes ω̄ invariant under all of G, with constant moving-frame coefficients M.

How does a bound in L² control the period of one cycle?

A low-dimensional simplex can have zero volume in the surrounding space. An L² estimate on the ambient quotient therefore gives no direct estimate for restriction to that simplex. What makes the argument work here is that a closed cycle has the same period after its vertices are averaged. The resulting integral can be estimated using ambient volume.

Fix a finite bar cycle z of degree m ≥ 1 in GLN(𝒪L′). Write F(y₀,…,ym) for the integral of the form ω on the affine simplex with those vertices in the cone of positive Hermitian matrices. The proof assumes that F is invariant under the arithmetic group and that its alternating sum over the faces of every (m + 1)-simplex vanishes. For a bar symbol [g₁|…|gm], set h₀ = 1 and hj = g₁⋯gj. Choose independent points Y₀,…,Ym with normalized volume on a closed ball about the identity matrix I, small enough to lie inside the cone. Then

⟨ω,z⟩ = ∑g z(g) · 𝔼[F(h₀·Y₀,…,hm·Ym)].

To see why, allow each vertex to carry one of two marks, “fixed at I” or “averaged.” Removing a vertex leaves the same product probability law on the others. The alternating face sum of the marked cochain is therefore the expectation of a face sum of F, hence zero. The prism between the two choices of basepoint has coboundary equal to the difference between all-averaged and all-fixed evaluations. On z this difference is zero because ∂z = 0.

A one-dimensional check. Let ℤ act on ℝ by translations, put P(x) = x + sin(2πx), and take F(x,y) = P(y) − P(x). Integer translation leaves F unchanged and its three face terms telescope. The bar cycle [2] has period F(0,2) = 2. Take independent Y₀,Y₁ uniform on {0,1/4}. The four values of F(Y₀,2 + Y₁) are 2, 13/4, 3/4 and 2. Their mean is 2. This discrete example checks the averaging identity. The volume estimate uses the ball with its continuous distribution.

For that estimate, fix a bar symbol. Let Aj be the invertible real linear action of hj on the ambient Hermitian space of real dimension d. A point of the random simplex is ∑j τjAjYj, with nonnegative barycentric coordinates summing to one. Some τi ≥ 1/(m + 1). Hold all the other vertices fixed. Changing variables in Yi gives a density bounded by (m + 1)d/(vol(B) |det Ai|), where B is the ball. The edge lengths are uniformly bounded and the possible simplex points fill a compact set K inside the cone. Integrating in the simplex parameters now bounds the expected absolute simplex integral by a constant times ∫K ‖ω‖.

Central-scalar invariance lets the proof unfold this last integral into a bound by the integral of the moving-frame norm ‖fr ω‖ on a compact set K′ inside ∏w SLN(ℂ). Write Λ for the image of SLN(𝒪L′) and D for its fundamental domain. If λ₀x and λx both belong to K′, then λλ₀⁻¹ lies in the finite set Λ ∩ K′(K′)⁻¹. Its cardinality bounds the number of visits from any one orbit. Arithmetic invariance therefore bounds the integral on K′ by this cardinality times ∫D ‖fr ω‖. Cauchy–Schwarz supplies the last factor vol(D)1/2 ‖fr ω‖2. Summing over the finite support of z with weights |z(g)| gives a constant Cz independent of the form.

Apply this bound to ωj = Hjω₀. The Hecke contraction acts on each scalar coefficient in a fixed basis at the identity. Finite-dimensional norm comparison bounds the squared norm of the whole form by Kbasis times the sum of its squared coefficients. If S₀ is the sum of their initial L² norms squared, then for every j ≥ 0,

|⟨Hjω₀,z⟩| ≤ Cz √(KbasisS₀) (3/5)j.

The local estimate holds for each fixed cycle and every admissible square-integrable form. Mean zero, N ≥ 3 and a prime element of norm at least 25 enter when applying the contraction. The second estimate on the stabilized cycles recovers the period before iteration.

Finding bounded frames for a compact set of forms

The simplex estimate ends with an integral over a compact set K of positive Hermitian forms. The period bound needs an integral on a matrix group. A positive matrix has a frame that carries the identity to it, but that frame can have any nonzero determinant. We first separate its scalar part and bound what remains.

At each infinite place of the number field use the real vector space of complex Hermitian N × N matrices, with N ≥ 1. Write V for their product and P for its positive definite cone. The action is Ag(H) = (g−1)∗Hg−1 at each place. Fix a compact subset of P. Continuity of inversion on invertible matrices and continuity of the determinant give bounds R2 on the moduli of all entries of Q−1 and R3 on det Q for all its local components Q. There are only finitely many places here.

Take Y = Q−1/2 by the spectral theorem. Then AY(I) = Q and YY∗ = Q−1. The squared Euclidean length of row i of Y is (Q−1)ii. Each entry of Y is therefore bounded in modulus by a = max(1,R2). Choose an Nth root c of det Y and set T = c−1Y. Taking determinants gives

det T = 1,   |c|2N det Q = 1.

With D = max(1,R3) we have |c| ≥ D−1/(2N) ≥ D−1. Dividing an entry of Y by c thus costs at most D. The single radius R = aD bounds the entries of both Y and T throughout the compact set. For example Q = diag(16,1) gives Y = diag(1/4,1), c = 1/2 and T = diag(1/2,2). More generally, for Q = diag(u²,1) with u ≥ 1, the entries of its inverse stay bounded by one while the second diagonal entry of T grows as √u. S. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, chapter 7, spectral theorem and positive square roots[102].

Which determinant changes the volume?

Write S = ∏w SLN(ℂ) and take the compact neighbourhood W of its identity defined by |(sw − I)ij| ≤ 1/2 for every entry. It lies in a bounded closed set of matrices with determinant one and contains an open neighbourhood of the identity. In particular 0 < ν(W) < ∞ for the chosen left- and right-invariant Haar measure ν on S. Enlarge the original compact set to K1 = {As⁻¹p ∣ s ∈ W, p ∈ K}. This is a compact subset of P and K ⊆ AsK1 for every s ∈ W.

Let μ be additive Haar measure on V. For a nonnegative measurable function f on P, the linear change of variables gives

∫K₁ f(Asp) dμ(p) = |detℝ As|−1 ∫AsK₁ f dμ ≥ |detℝ As|−1 ∫K f dμ.

Thus an upper bound D0 ≥ 1 on |detℝ As| gives the lower multiplier 1/D0 needed on the right. Continuity on W gives such a bound. Here one can even compute it. For a single matrix g with singular values σ1, …, σN, the unitary factors act isometrically on Hermitian matrices in the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product. The diagonal factor in the action scales real coordinate Hii by σi−2. It scales both real coordinates of every complex entry Hij, i < j, by (σiσj)−1. Multiplying these factors gives |detℝ Ag| = |detℂ g|−2N. The Jacobians multiply across places, hence D0 = 1 works on S. For s = diag(4/3,3/4) in W, the two diagonal coordinates scale by 9/16 and 16/9, while the complex off-diagonal coordinate stays fixed. J. Hunter, Measure Theory, §2.8, linear changes of Lebesgue measure[103] · Axler, chapter 7, singular value decomposition[102].

Moving the integral onto the special linear group

Let ω be a continuous differential form of degree q on P, invariant under pullback by the independent scalar matrices at all places. Write fr ω(g) for its value at AgI pulled back to the tangent space at I by Ag. We use the maximum absolute matrix entry over all places as norm on V, with its induced operator norm on forms. Fix p in K1 and choose its frame Y = cT by the first result, using the radius R for K1. For s in W, each entry of s has modulus at most 3/2. The products sY and sT both have entries bounded by R′ = 3NR/2. Thus W T lies in the fixed compact set K′ of determinant-one matrices at all places with entries bounded by R′.

Set X = sY = csT. To recover ω at Asp = AXI from fr ω(X), apply the inverse tangent action H ↦ X∗HX to each of the q tangent arguments. Each matrix entry in that expression is a sum of N² terms of modulus at most (R′)²‖H‖. The cost for a form is therefore B = (N²(R′)²)q. Scalar invariance gives fr ω(csT) = fr ω(sT). Consequently ‖ω(Asp)‖ ≤ B ‖fr ω(sT)‖. Right invariance of ν and WT ⊆ K′ bound its integral over s ∈ W by B ∫K′ ‖fr ω‖ dν. This estimate holds for each fixed p and needs only the existence of its frame.

Integrate the real-Jacobian inequality first over W, with f = ‖ω‖. Tonelli’s theorem allows us to integrate over s first on the other side, since the joint integrand is continuous on W × K1 and nonnegative. The preceding pointwise estimate then gives

∫K ‖ω‖ dμ ≤ C2 ∫K′ ‖fr ω‖ dν,   C2 = D0 B μ(K1)/ν(W).

The sets, the measures and the degree fix this finite constant before ω is chosen. The cycle-period estimate now counts visits of the arithmetic group to K′ and applies Cauchy–Schwarz on its fundamental domain. T. Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory, §1.7, Tonelli’s theorem[104].

Choose a prime element π whose ideal has norm at least 25. The normalized Hecke operator H averages over the finite cosets in Γ diag(π,1,…,1) Γ. On each mean-zero coefficient its L² norm contracts by a factor at most 3/5. The estimate for an averaged cycle then gives |⟨Hjω₀,z⟩| ≤ Cz(3/5)j for each fixed cycle. Letting j tend to infinity forces x₀ = 0. Homological stability makes the chosen cycles span also in size N, so ⟨ω̄,z⟩ = ⟨c,z⟩ for every cycle. This equality lets one test a nonzero filtered homology class by an invariant form. On the filtered cycles every such test is a linear combination of the r₂ one-place traces. This gives the upper bound on the rank of their homology image.

Where the lower factor 4/5 comes from

Let In and IN be the numbers of cosets in the respective Hecke averages and put α = In/IN. The cosets inherited from size n contribute α times a smaller-size Hecke period vector yj. For the other cosets, transfer from their stabilizers gives the original periods after summing. Thus xj+1 = (1 − α)xj + αyj. The smaller-size operator acts linearly on a finite-dimensional space of period vectors, so ‖yj‖ ≤ K‖xj‖ with K independent of N and j. Since IN ≥ N, we can arrange α(1 + K) ≤ 1/5. The reverse triangle inequality now gives ‖xj+1‖ ≥ (1 − α(1 + K))‖xj‖ ≥ (4/5)‖xj‖. For example, if ‖x₀‖ were 1 and the upper constant were 2, three iterations would require 64/125 ≤ ‖x₃‖ ≤ 54/125. The limit argument works for every finite constant.

Which cosets carry the original period into the next Hecke average?

Fix the smaller size n while enlarging to N = n + r. To obtain the lower bound on a period, we need the share of the Hecke sum that acts as the original period on a stabilized cycle. That share has a concrete description in the residue field.

Write ΓN = GLN(𝒪L′), q = diag(π,1,…,1) and k = 𝒪L′/(π). A matrix γ lies in the subgroup SN that labels the Hecke cosets precisely when qγq−1 is integral and invertible over the integers. Conjugation divides the first column below its top entry by π and multiplies the rest of the first row by π. The determinant stays a unit. Thus membership is equivalent to preserving the line ke₁ modulo π. For a right coset SNc, take the residue line of c−1e₁. Two representatives determine the same line exactly when they determine the same coset. There are finitely many such lines, and swapping the first coordinate with each coordinate realizes N distinct lines. In particular the index IN is at least N.

A coset inherited from Γn has all its last r coordinates zero on this line. Conversely, if those coordinates vanish, some coordinate in the first block is nonzero. Swap it into first position. Over k, subtract multiples of the first row to clear the other entries. These row additions lift to invertible integral operations in size n. The resulting line is ke₁, so the original coset came from the smaller group. Stabilization identifies its cosets bijectively with this part of the larger sum. Their normalized total is the smaller Hecke average times In/IN.

Why summing the other cosets recovers an unshifted period

The smaller group permutes the complementary set X of cosets by right multiplication. For each x take the difference Φx between the cocycle translated by its Hecke representative and the original stabilized cocycle. On cycles of the stabilizer of x, this difference has zero period. Here the nonzero coordinate in the last block matters. It permits a change of basis in which the translated stabilizer acts by integral matrices with diagonal blocks h and 1 and only one possible off-diagonal block above them. The arithmetic affine-block homology comparison identifies the image of a stabilizer cycle under this action with its block-diagonal image. Basepoint independence on cycles then gives the claimed zero.

To pass from a stabilizer to the whole group, choose one representative x₀ per orbit. The cochain criterion for a zero class supplies a primitive Ψ on tuples from the whole smaller group, invariant under the stabilizer, with δΨ = Φx₀. Transport it to each x in that orbit by an element carrying x₀ to x. Two such choices differ on the left by a stabilizer element, so give the same translate. The sum of these translates is invariant under the smaller group, which permutes the terms. Its coboundary is ∑x∈X Φx. Evaluated on a cycle z, this is the primitive evaluated on ∂z = 0. The sum over X therefore contributes |X| copies of the original period before normalization.

Why can the upper-right block be erased on a stabilizer cycle?

Fix the totally complex field L′ used in the Hecke transfer, with r₂ pairs of complex embeddings. Write Γn = GLn(𝒪L′) and let 1 ≤ m < r₂ be the homology degree. Suppose a group H acts through integral block matrices f(h) with upper-left block f₀(h) ∈ Γn, upper-right block B(h) of size n × r, and bottom row of blocks (0, Ir). Let D(g) = diag(g,Ir). For every real m-cycle z in H, the following difference bounds a real (m + 1)-chain in Γn+r.

f∗z − (D ∘ f₀)∗z = ∂y.

Both chains live in that same matrix size over the same field. The separate stable-range condition n ≥ 2m + 4 is used when comparing homology across sizes. Here one can take any block sizes. In the Hecke application n, r ≥ 1 and H is a stabilizer. Once its two images agree in homology, changing the base point in the period leaves their evaluations equal.

Find a unit that detects every translation degree. Put A = Matn×r(𝒪L′) with addition. The block group P consists of pairs (B,g) with product (B + gB′,gg′). Projection p forgets B and its section s inserts zero. Choose a unit v so that every product ∏w |v|waw with 1 ≤ ∑w aw ≤ m differs from one. Here aw are nonnegative integers and |·|w is the usual complex modulus at a place. For any one choice of exponents, some aw is zero because m < r₂. Dirichlet’s unit theorem supplies a unit with negative logarithm at every other place. The corresponding sum of logarithms weighted by the aw is strictly negative. Its kernel thus has infinite index in the unit group. To see why one unit works for all the exponents, pass to the free abelian group of units modulo roots of unity. Each kernel there has smaller rank, so its rational span is a proper subspace. Finitely many proper subspaces cannot cover a vector space over ℚ. Clear the denominators of a point outside their union to obtain an integer exponent vector, hence a unit outside every kernel. At total degree r₂, the all-ones choice would instead give one for every unit by the product formula.

Set u = v−1In. It is central in Γn. Inside P, conjugation x ↦ s(u)−1x s(u) multiplies the translation block by v. The group A is free abelian of finite rank. Its real cohomology in degree j is spanned by cup products of j additive coordinate functionals. After extending the coefficients to ℂ, the embeddings of each matrix entry give coordinates in which multiplication by v scales such a product by Λ = σ₁(v)⋯σj(v). For 1 ≤ j ≤ m its modulus differs from one by the choice of unit. To return to real coefficients, pair each eigenvalue with its conjugate. The real polynomial (X−Λ)(X−Λ) kills this component and takes the value |1−Λ|² at 1. Multiplying these factors gives a polynomial Fj that kills degree j in the translation cohomology and satisfies Fj(1) ≠ 0.

Which cochains detect the translations in the upper-right block?

A translation in the affine block is a matrix in the additive group A = Matn×r(𝒪L′). Its entries lie in a free abelian group of finite rank. We first work with any such A and trivial real coefficients. A homogeneous cochain of degree j is a function on Aj+1 unchanged when the same element is added to all its vertices. The coboundary δ sums the values obtained by omitting vertex i, with sign (−1)i starting at i = 0. Tuples can have repeated vertices. For an additive character α ∶ A → ℝ, the edge value α(y₁ − y₀) is closed because the two edge increments along a triangle add to the third.

Choose j characters α₁, …, αj. Read the ordered edges of a simplex in succession. Their product is the following closed j-cochain.

Cα(y₀, …, yj) = ∏i=1j αi(yi − yi−1).

In every degree j ≥ 1, any invariant closed c has an equality of cochains c = ∑ν aνCαν + δe, with finitely many real coefficients and an invariant (j − 1)-cochain e. The proof writes j = q + 1, so c takes q + 2 vertices and e takes q + 1. The formula uses coefficient one on each ordered cup before the linear combination. It asserts generation and allows different choices of characters and primitive.

Proof by splitting off one integer coordinate

Choose an integral basis. At rank zero every cochain is constant. In odd positive degree, closedness forces the constant to be zero. In even positive degree the constant of the same value one degree lower is its primitive. This follows by counting the alternating face signs. For the induction write P = ℤ × G, let ι(g) = (0,g), let ρ discard the first coordinate, and let ℓ read it as a real number. The known result on G supplies words for the part U = ρ∗ι∗c seen on the slice of height zero.

The missing information is a cocycle one degree lower. Put ψ(h,g) = (−1,g). The prism Kψ on an ordered tuple sums over i the evaluations on (y₀, …, yi, ψyi, …, ψyj−1) with sign (−1)i. Its identity δKψ + Kψδ = ψ∗ − 1 makes b = ι∗Kψ(U − c) closed. Indeed, on the slice, ψ translates every vertex by (−1,0), which preserves both cochains. In ℓ ∪ ρ∗b, the first edge supplies the height difference, and the remaining vertices supply b. On the slice the prism of this cup evaluates to −b. Only the first prism simplex has a first edge of height −1. All the later first edges have height zero.

[c] = [U] + [ℓ ∪ ρ∗b].

To see exactness in the invariant complex, set R = c − U − ℓ ∪ ρ∗b. Both its restriction and its restricted ψ-prism are zero. Put x = KιρR. Then δx = −R, and x is invariant under G. Let Δ be pullback by translation by (1,0) minus the identity. For j ≥ 2 the two vanishings give (Δx)|G = 0, so w = −KιρΔx satisfies δw = Δx. A finite signed sum of translates of w, from height zero to the height of the first vertex, gives a G-invariant W with ΔW = w. Thus −x + δW is invariant under the new generator as well, and its coboundary is R. In degree one Δx is already a constant of value zero.

Apply induction to ι∗c and to b. Prepending ℓ to an ordered cup gives the next word, and δ(ℓ ∪ e) = −ℓ ∪ δe absorbs the coboundary with its sign. When j = 1, b is an invariant function of one vertex, hence a scalar. Transporting the resulting decomposition along the chosen basis proves it for A.

A unit square distinguishes the two orders

Take the coordinate characters x, y on ℤ², with unit vectors u, v in that order. The bar simplex [a|b] has vertices 0, a, a + b. Its boundary is [b] − [a + b] + [a]. Thus z = [u|v] − [v|u] is a cycle. On its two triangles x ∪ y has successive values 1 and 0, so it evaluates to 1 on z. Reversing the characters gives 0 and 1, hence −1 on z. Every coboundary evaluates to zero on this cycle, so the first cup represents a nonzero class.

In the affine argument a separate eigenvalue calculation supplies a polynomial Fj that kills each cup word under pullback by multiplication by a chosen unit v. Applying it to c leaves δ(Fj(v∗)e), because pullback commutes with δ and preserves invariance. This is where generation gives the annihilator on every class. Generation holds in all positive degrees. The split extension A → P → Γn gives cochains with a horizontal differential in the quotient variables and a vertical differential in the group variables. A prism between translation and conjugation shows that Fj(R) of the cochain is vertically exact, by the polynomial calculation on the kernel. A horizontal prism shows that R − 1 is horizontally exact on this cochain. Since Fj(X) − Fj(1) is divisible by X − 1, the scalar multiple Fj(1) times the cochain is a sum of horizontal and vertical coboundaries. Division by that scalar removes this contribution. In the first column the horizontal translation fixes the cochain and the vertical coboundary alone suffices. Repeating through the positive vertical degrees expresses any degree-m cocycle c of P as p∗b + δe for a quotient cocycle b.

Write S = s ∘ p. Subtracting the pullback by S gives c − S∗c = δ(e − S∗e), since pS = p. Thus every real cocycle evaluates to zero on w − S∗w for a cycle w of P. Why does one trace per complex place suffice on the filtered cycles?

The transported mean gives a form ω invariant under every archimedean change of basis. To integrate it on a homology class, we first need its integral to vanish on boundaries. Write M = ω(I) for its value at the identity tuple and Y₁,…,Ym for Hermitian tangent vectors. All matrix operations below are taken place by place. For a positive Hermitian tuple x, the matrix g = x−1 takes I to x², and sends Y to xYx. Invariance therefore gives ω(x²)(xY₁x,…,xYmx) = M(Y₁,…,Ym). Near I the squaring map has a smooth inverse because its derivative is twice the identity. Solving this formula for ω by undoing each tangent map gives smoothness near I.

DωI[X](Y₁,…,Ym) = −½ ∑j=1m M(Y₁,…,XYj + YjX,…,Ym).

To obtain the derivative, put x = I + tX in the preceding identity. The base point moves with velocity 2X and the jth argument with velocity XYj + YjX. The right side is constant. To obtain the exterior derivative, alternate the left side of the displayed formula in its m + 1 inputs. Swapping X and the selected Yj preserves their sum of products and reverses the sign. Every term cancels. Invariance carries dω = 0 from I to every positive tuple. Stokes’ theorem now makes the integral of ω over the boundary of every affine simplex zero. Its periods therefore descend to homology. The two Hecke estimates then show that the transported mean has the periods of the original detecting cocycle.

Count the independent block labels. At I, M is invariant under unitary conjugation at each place. The tensor invariant theorem expresses it as a real linear combination of alternating real or imaginary parts of products of traces. Each product is indexed by a permutation of the m inputs. A cycle (i₁ … iℓ) contributes tr(Yi₁,w ⋯ Yiℓ,w) at a single place w. This trace sums over matrix indices around a closed loop. Replace each matrix by d identical diagonal blocks. A nonzero matrix entry must stay within one block, so the entire loop chooses a single block in d ways. With j permutation cycles there are dj choices. This is the weight j of the period under block repetition.

In odd degree m, a single cycle orders all the matrices at one place. Relabeling the inputs of its alternating trace changes only the sign. Reversing their order conjugates the trace because each matrix is Hermitian. Reversal has sign (−1)m(m−1)/2, so the alternating trace is real for m ≡ 1 modulo 4 and purely imaginary for m ≡ 3 modulo 4. This leaves at most one real functional per place. The filter on the selected cycles kills every weight from 2 to m. Any surviving invariant period is thus a linear combination of these r₂ one-place evaluations. A nonzero filtered homology class has a detecting period, which gives the rank bound.

Why do these trace products span all invariant tensors?

After allowing complex scalars, the tensor at the identity is represented by a matrix T acting on a tensor power. Unitary invariance says that T commutes with every tensor power of a placewise unitary matrix. Consider the operators that permute the tensor slots and select a place in each slot. The first finite-dimensional matrix result says that every operator commuting with all of them is a linear combination of those unitary tensor powers. Thus T commutes with all such operators. The second matrix result says that this puts T itself in the span of the slot permutations with place selections. In one such term, a matrix entry links index ai to aπ(i). Summing around each cycle gives its trace. If the place changes across a link, the entry vanishes. Taking real parts and alternating recovers the real tensor M.

Why do permutations account for every invariant tensor?

Let W be a finite set of places and V = ⊕w∈W ℂN. A separate unitary matrix uw acts on each summand. On V⊗q the resulting operator is D⊗q, where D = diag(uw). To recover the invariant forms, we need the matrices T that commute with every such operator. The proof works for all finite block sizes N and tensor degrees q, including N < q. It gives a spanning family whose members can coincide in small dimension.

A basis index I is a word of q pairs (place, coordinate). For a place pattern w = (w₁,…,wq) and a permutation σ, define Pσ,w by its rows and columns.

(Pσ,w)I,J = 1 if place(Ii) = wi for every i and J = I ∘ σ, and 0 otherwise.

These matrices commute with every D⊗q. Indeed, a block unitary preserves the place pattern and the same D acts in every slot. Let 𝒜 be their complex span and 𝒰 the span of the unitary tensor powers. Write 𝒮′ for the matrices commuting with all of 𝒮. The archive proves 𝒜′ ⊆ 𝒰 by interpolation and 𝒜″ ⊆ 𝒜 by orthogonal projection. Thus 𝒰′ = 𝒜.

How commuting with the permutations forces a tensor expansion

If Z commutes with the projections Pid,w, its entry ZI,J can be nonzero only if the places of I and J agree slot by slot. Commuting with all the other Pσ,w gives ZI∘σ,J∘σ = ZI,J. If EI,J denotes a matrix unit, expand Z in these units and sum over slot permutations. The resulting identity counts each permutation, including those fixing an index pair.

q! Z = ∑I,J ZI,J ∑σ EI∘σ,J∘σ.

Suppose a complex linear functional φ vanishes on 𝒰. For any block diagonal D, we claim φ(D⊗q) = 0. Start with Hermitian blocks and fix their unitary eigenbases. As the diagonal eigenvalues vary, the expression is polynomial of degree at most q in each variable. It vanishes on the grid where every diagonal entry is a (q + 1)st root of unity, because every resulting block is unitary. Interpolating in one variable at a time gives vanishing at the actual eigenvalues. Now write arbitrary blocks as H + iK with H, K Hermitian. The same argument on the grid {0,…,q}² for aH + bK gives vanishing at (a,b) = (1,i).

For a pair I,J of matching places, put D(t) = ∑i tiEIᵢ,Jᵢ on V. Each matrix unit stays in one block. The coefficient of t₁⋯tq in D(t)⊗q is exactly the inner permutation sum above, because each variable must be chosen once. The polynomial vanishes after applying φ, hence so does this coefficient. It follows that q! φ(Z) = 0. In finite dimension, if Z lay outside 𝒰 some functional vanishing on 𝒰 would be nonzero at Z. This proves 𝒜′ ⊆ 𝒰.

For a ∈ 𝒜, both 𝒜 and its orthogonal complement are stable under left multiplication by a, the latter because a∗ ∈ 𝒜. Hence Π(aY) = aΠ(Y).

View a matrix Y as a list of columns. Each block of Π taking one input column to one output column now commutes with a for every a ∈ 𝒜. Any T ∈ 𝒜″ commutes with every such block, so Π(TY) = TΠ(Y). Substituting the identity for Y gives Π(T) = T. Thus T belongs to 𝒜.

Why does a filtered cycle stay detectable in a larger matrix group?

Write Γn(R) = GLn(R) and use integral group homology with trivial coefficients. Stabilization sends g to diag(g,1). The proof establishes two one-step bounds in homological degree m. The stable-range parameter s belongs to the ring. A unimodular row of length n + 1 can be shortened whenever n ≥ s, by adding multiples of the last entry to its first n entries while keeping them generators of the unit ideal. Compute the stabilization map from an alternating face map

Fix an ambient size b and put G = Γb(R). An ordered split sequence of length p is a list of vectors and covectors (v₁,λ₁), …, (vp,λp) with λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on these sequences. The group acts on the vectors by g and on the covectors by precomposition with g−1. The differential dp from Cp+1 to Cp deletes one pair with alternating signs. The empty sequence gives C₀ = ℤ.

When p + s ≤ b, the action is transitive. The stabilizer of the last p standard vector–covector pairs is diag(Γb−p,Ip). Fixing both the vectors and the covectors forces the two off-diagonal blocks to vanish. Shapiro’s lemma for this permutation module therefore identifies Hq(G,Cp) with Hq(Γb−p,ℤ). When p + 1 + s ≤ b, both consecutive identifications are isomorphisms. In these coordinates each deletion gives the same stabilization map. A permutation of the final coordinates arranges the remaining pairs in standard order and commutes with Γb−p−1. The sum of p + 1 alternating signs is one for even p and zero for odd p.

Hq(Γb−2)   ⟶0   Hq(Γb−1)   ⟶stab   Hq(Γb).

Set b = n + 1. The integral filling argument shows that cycles on split sequences of length p bound when 2p + s + 1 ≤ b. It gives the exactness of the required part of the sequence of coefficient modules. Group homology need not preserve exactness in each row. For this reason the proof uses induction on the target degree m. In degrees q < m each relevant pair of adjacent maps is a stabilization next to a zero map. Exactness there asks for injectivity of the outgoing stabilization or surjectivity of the incoming one, already known in the corresponding smaller degree and matrix size.

To reach degree m, factor each dp+1 through the kernel of dp. The long exact group homology sequences for these kernels transfer the lower-degree row exactness to surjectivity of Hm(d₀). With one further step of module exactness they give ker Hm(d₀) = im Hm(d₁). The displayed row shows that the latter image is zero. For m ≥ 1, the lower-degree map at p = 2 and q = m − 1 starts at rank n − 2. Surjectivity there requires n − 2 ≥ 2(m − 1) + s + 1, while injectivity requires the right side plus one. The two induction steps check the remaining positions in their respective ranges. Composing the resulting one-step isomorphisms over 𝒪L carries degree-m integral homology unchanged from size n to every size N ≥ n once n ≥ 2m + 4.

When does every cycle of ordered split pairs bound?

A split pair in Rn is a vector v with a specified linear functional λ satisfying λ(v) = 1. An ordered list of pairs is split if λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on such lists of length p. Its boundary deletes one pair at a time, starting with sign +. Thus a vertex has boundary the empty list, and an edge has boundary its last vertex minus its first. The stability argument needs to know when these signed lists can fill a cycle.

2p + s + 1 ≤ n   ⟹   for every c ∈ Cp with ∂c = 0, some B ∈ Cp+1 satisfies ∂B = c.

This holds for every commutative ring with identity and all nonnegative integers n, p, s satisfying the ring’s stable-range hypothesis at s. That hypothesis says that whenever d ≥ s and the entries of (r₁,…,rd,t) generate the unit ideal, one can find a₁,…,ad so that the entries ri + ait still generate it. Length zero gives surjectivity onto the augmentation group ℤ. For p ≥ 1 the conclusion is vanishing of reduced integral homology in degree p − 1. In particular, length one controls differences of vertices.

A plain unimodular list admits covectors making it split, but leaves the choice open. Introduce chains Da,b on a split list of length a and a plain list of length b. Each covector in the first list must kill every vector in the second. Deleting from the first list defines h and deleting from the second defines v. The deletions commute because their signs count positions in separate lists. Each operator squares to zero.

Fix the split list on the diagonal a + b = p. When a + s ≤ n, a matrix g carries it to the last a standard pairs. Acting by g on vectors and by precomposition with g−1 on covectors preserves all pairings. The proof straightens one pair, then straightens the remaining pairs in its coordinate complement. The auxiliary vectors must now have their last a entries zero. Restricting their witnessing covectors, or extending such covectors by zero, identifies this column with ordinary unimodular lists in Rn−a.

The ordinary-list theorem fills every cycle of length b when b + s ≤ n − a, as required on this diagonal. For s ≥ 1 its proof uses exactness of links in coordinate subspaces and their unions with affine translates. At s = 0, shortening the row (1) forces the zero ring, where prepending zero fills every cycle.

What the detecting cycles can miss

The cycle bound controls the image of a twisted norm. Here is how much of the arithmetic count that image can miss. Keep the enlarged field L′ fixed, with r₂ complex places. At depth ν the cyclic layer F/L′ has generator γ and degree n = ℓν−c. Write q = ℓν, a = (1 + ℓc)e and f = vℓ(e) for the positive twist e. Write 𝓧 for the group of equivariant characters at this depth. Each element assigns a value φ(P) in ℤ/q to each prime ideal, vanishes on principal divisors when extended additively, and satisfies φ(γ−1P) = aφ(P). Define C by quotienting the ideal class group of F by the image of γ−1 − a. Each φ descends to C and is recovered from its values on primes. Its target is an ℓ-group, so there are at most |C|ℓ such characters, where |·|ℓ means the ℓ-part of a finite group order.

Where the matching power of q comes from. Write E for the integral units 𝒪F× modulo roots of unity and the image of γ−1 − a, using additive notation. The finite group W in the norm construction satisfies |W| = |E| |C|. Indeed, its map to the class group has unit kernel E and image the kernel of γ−1 − a on that group. A finite group endomorphism has kernel and cokernel of equal order. To compute |E|, take logarithms of units at the infinite places and add one constant coordinate direction to complete the unit lattice. Above each complex place of L′ the action permutes n places in a cycle. On this block the absolute determinant of the permutation minus a times the identity is an − 1. The extra constant direction contributes a − 1. Thus |E|(a − 1) = (an − 1)r₂.

The valuation formula vℓ((1 + ℓc)h − 1) = c + vℓ(h) holds for positive h, with c ≥ 1 and c ≥ 2 when ℓ = 2. Apply it with h = e and h = en. The unit identity gives |E|ℓ ℓc+f = ℓ(ν+f)r₂ ≥ qr₂. The second valuation also shows that the exact valuation of (an − 1)/q is f. For example, at ℓ = 3, c = 2, e = 3 and ν = 3 we have a = 1000 and n = 3. The number 1000³ − 1 has 3-adic valuation 4. Dividing by 27 leaves valuation 1. Increasing ν by one also increases the numerator’s valuation by one.

Why the kernel cost stays bounded. Write N for the twisted norm, additively, and δ = γ−1 − a. Expanding the geometric sum gives δN = Nδ = (1 − an)γ−1. If ℓbN(y) is a q-multiple modulo roots of unity, applying δ and dividing by q in the torsion-free quotient shows that ℓb(an − 1)/q kills the class of y in W. On its ℓ-primary part the prime-to-ℓ factor is invertible. The kernel there is killed by ℓb+f. Each multiplication by ℓ on W[ℓj] has image in W[ℓj−1] and kernel of size at most |W[ℓ]|. It remains to count just the elements killed by ℓ.

Those elements inject into invariant classes represented by α with all valuations divisible by ℓ. If ρ generates the roots of unity in F, their invariance gives γα/α = vℓρt, 0 ≤ t < ℓ. For each t the field norm of v has at most ℓ possible values, since its ℓth power is Norm(ρ)−t. Equal pairs (t, Norm(v)) give a norm-one ratio of the two v’s. Hilbert’s Theorem 90 then lets the ratio of the two α’s descend to the base field modulo ℓth powers. Its valuations away from ℓ remain divisible by ℓ because the layer is unramified there. The base-field classes with this property have at most ℓ2D+⌊log₂ h⌋ elements, where D = [L′:ℚ] and h is its class number. The three contributions come from units modulo ℓth powers, ℓ-torsion ideal classes, and the valuations modulo ℓ at primes over ℓ. The ≤ ℓ² choices of the pair thus give |W[ℓ]| ≤ ℓg for g = 2D + ⌊log₂ h⌋ + 2.

|𝓧| qr₂ ≤ B ℓX,   X = (b + f)g + c + f.

Here B bounds the image seen by the detecting cycles. The kernel costs ℓ(b+f)g and the unit comparison costs ℓc+f. In the application B = qr₂T2e+1T2e, so cancelling the positive common factor leaves |𝓧| ≤ T2e+1T2eℓX. The base field, twist, and b were fixed before ν. This bound therefore applies at every allowed depth ν ≥ c.

Where the exponent 150 comes from

The torsion proof uses an exact complex with bounds on the numbers of orbits and on stabilizers. In degree j ≤ 2e + 1 and rank ≤ 4e + 6 it proves log Tj ≤ K24(e,n′,Δ′). Set u = 2en′ and Y = log(2Δ′). The class-number estimate and the bounds on b, c and f give X log ℓ ≤ u⁹Y. Taking logs in the character bound gives two contributions at most exp(u24Y) and the polynomial term. For u ≥ 2 and Y ≥ ½ the numerical comparison bounds their sum by exp(u26Y). Now put x = 2en. The layer estimates give u ≤ x⁵ and Y ≤ x¹¹ log(2Δ). Hence s(L) log ℓ ≤ K141(e,n,Δ), since 5 · 26 + 11 = 141.

How an integral boundary matrix bounds torsion

The character count above uses the orders of the torsion subgroups of two integral homology groups. A torsion class is killed by a nonzero integer. An infinite free summand in homology can therefore coexist with the finite quantity we need to bound. Start with a free lattice E = ℤr, with r ≤ A, and any set of integral relation vectors. Write Λ for their integer span. Suppose each relation has sum of absolute coordinates at most b, where b ≥ 1. The bound used in the proof is

|tors(E/Λ)| ≤ bA.

If we have r independent relation vectors, put them in a square matrix V. The sublattice they generate has index |det V|. Expanding the determinant as a signed sum over permutations and taking absolute values gives a sum of products. Allowing every choice of one column for each row only increases this sum, and the enlarged sum factors as ∏i ∑j |Vij|. This proves the bound br. Additional relations give a quotient of this finite group.

Suppose instead that the relation vectors span only a proper rational subspace. Choose a maximal independent subset and complete it to a rational basis using standard unit vectors. Let K be the integer span of that completed list. Its determinant still has absolute value at most br, since every added vector has length one. To compare torsion, choose a lift in E for each torsion class in E/Λ and reduce its lift modulo K. If two images coincide, the difference x of their lifts lies in K. Their difference class is torsion, so some nonzero multiple of x belongs to Λ. Consequently x lies in the rational span of the original relations. In the completed basis every coefficient of an added vector must then vanish. Because x belongs to K, the remaining coefficients are integers. Thus x is an integer combination of selected relations and the two classes were equal. This injects the set of torsion classes into the finite set E/K.

For example, impose the three relations (2,0,0), (0,2,0), (1,1,0) in ℤ³. The third coordinate stays free. In the first two coordinates a vector is a relation exactly when the coordinates have the same parity. Hence the torsion subgroup has order two. Choosing the first two relations and the third unit vector gives det V = 4. The general bound gives 2³ = 8. The three numbers measure respectively the actual torsion, the index for this completed list, and the estimate using the common row bound.

The extra cost in positive homological degree

Let a group G permute the simplex basis in each degree and commute with each face map. Suppose the augmented complex is exact through degree m. An orbit identifies simplices related by the action. A stabilizer fixes a specified simplex. Suppose there are at most A orbits per degree up to m and every corresponding stabilizer has order at most s ≥ 1. A boundary in degree m + 1 is an alternating sum of m + 2 faces. After identifying generators in the same orbit, coordinates add and the sum of their absolute values can only decrease. In degree zero the coefficient module at the end of the induction is generally a kernel. Identifying g x with x presents the coinvariants of that module. It gives the determinant factor (m + 2)A.

For positive degree, take the short exact sequence given by the first permutation module, its augmentation and its kernel. The connecting map in the long exact sequence compares the desired torsion with the torsion one degree lower for that kernel and the finite homology of the permutation module. For a single orbit the latter is the homology of the stabilizer by Shapiro’s lemma. A group of order h has hj bar generators in degree j > 0, and the two equivariant coefficient maps show that multiplication by h kills its positive-degree homology. The cycles form a subgroup of a free abelian group with that many generators, hence the homology has order at most hhʲ. Combining the orbits costs at most sA sʲ. Repeating the exact-sequence comparison for j = m, …, 1 gives

|tors Hm(G,ℤ)| ≤ (m + 2)A sm A sᵐ.

The last exponent uses ∑j=1m sj ≤ m sm. This part needs the orbit and stabilizer estimates, exactness of the complex, the long exact sequence, Shapiro’s lemma and annihilation of finite-group homology. Each supplies a distinct input.

For G = GLN(𝒪L) with L totally complex of degree n, the complex of ordered faces is exact, with an orbit bound A and the stabilizer bound s = 3nN². With N ≤ 4e + 6, 1 ≤ N and m ≤ 2e + 1 for e ≥ 1, substitution into the logarithm of the displayed bound gives the witness 24 in K24. The later character count and the change of field turn this into 5(max(24,9) + 2) + 11 = 141. In the character count the torsion estimate is applied over the enlarged field L′. The last numerical step expresses its degree and discriminant in terms of those of the original L.

Why the order of a stabilizer kills positive-degree homology

Suppose a group G acts transitively on a nonempty set X of faces. Choose a face x and write S for its stabilizer. The module ℤ[X] consists of finite integral sums of faces, with G permuting their labels. To compute its group homology we can keep just x and the group that fixes it.

Shapiro’s lemma for homology. For a subgroup S of G, a left ℤ[S]-module M, and any degree j ≥ 0, there is a natural isomorphism

Hj(G, ℤ[G] ⊗ℤ[S] M) ≅ Hj(S, M).

One proof starts with a free resolution of the trivial right ℤ[G]-module ℤ. On restriction to S it is still a free resolution, since the elements of each coset gS give a copy of the regular right module ℤ[S] in ℤ[G]. Tensoring that resolution over ℤ[G] with the induced module on the left of the formula gives, by associativity of tensor product, the same chain complex as tensoring it over ℤ[S] with M. For trivial M = ℤ, the induced module identifies with ℤ[X] by g ⊗ 1 ↦ [gx]. Indeed gx = g′x exactly when gS = g′S. C. Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, lemma 6.3.2 and corollary 6.3.3[105].

Now suppose S is finite of order h. Give ℤ the trivial S-action and ℤ[S] the left regular action. Define two coefficient maps

ℤ → ℤ[S] → ℤ,   1 ↦ ∑t∈S[t],   [t] ↦ 1.

Left multiplication permutes the summands of the first image, and the second map sums coefficients. Both maps therefore respect the action. Their composite multiplies by h. Applying homology in degree j gives maps in the same order. On a representative chain their composite multiplies each coefficient by h, so it also multiplies the homology class by h. But the middle group is Hj(S, ℤ[S]) ≅ Hj({1}, ℤ) by Shapiro applied to the regular orbit. For j > 0 this group vanishes, since ℤ itself is a free resolution of length zero over the trivial group. Thus h kills every class in Hj(S, ℤ). In degree zero the middle group is ℤ. All basis elements [t] become equal in the coinvariants, so the first map multiplies by h and the second sends their common class to 1. The composite on H0(S, ℤ) = ℤ is still multiplication by h.

How many classes can one orbit contribute?

In positive degree j, the integral bar chain group with trivial coefficients has one generator for each ordered j-tuple of elements of S, including tuples with identity entries. Its rank is hj. The cycles form a subgroup of this free abelian group, hence are free of some rank r ≤ hj. One can see the rank bound by projecting onto the first coordinate. The image is cyclic, and the kernel lies in a free abelian group with one fewer coordinate. A lift of a generator of a nonzero image extends a basis of that kernel. The images of the r basis cycles generate homology. Since h kills each image, every class can be written with all coefficients between 0 and h − 1. This gives

|Hj(S, ℤ)| ≤ hr ≤ hhj.

Suppose now X has at most A orbits and every stabilizer is finite of order at most s, with s ≥ 1. Splitting a sum of faces by orbit splits ℤ[X] as a finite direct sum of permutation modules. The bar differential preserves these summands, so their homology groups also form a direct sum. Shapiro and the one-orbit bound give each summand order at most ssj. Multiplying these orders gives |Hj(G, ℤ[X])| ≤ sA sj. For X empty the group is zero and its order is one. This is the factor used once at each positive degree of the homology bound for the face complex. Weibel, §§6.5.1–6.5.4, the bar resolution[106].

A stabilizer of order two. Let S = {1, t} with t² = 1. Its free resolution has one copy of ℤ[S] in each degree. The differential is multiplication by t − 1 in odd degrees and by 1 + t in positive even degrees. To check exactness, write an element as a + bt. The first multiplier kills exactly the multiples of 1 + t, and the second kills exactly the multiples of t − 1. The augmentation also has kernel generated by t − 1. Tensor with the trivial module ℤ. The two differentials become 0 and 2, giving H1 ≅ ℤ/2 and H2 = 0. The actual orders are 2 and 1, within the respective one-orbit bounds 4 and 16. Weibel, calculation 6.2.1 and theorem 6.2.2[107].

How a stabilizer bound enters the next homological degree

Let ⋯ → C1 → C0 → M → 0 be a complex of integral G-modules, where Cp = ℤ[Xp] and G permutes the basis of faces. Fix j ≥ 1. Assume the complex is exact at M and at C0, …, Cj. Suppose each Xp up to degree j has at most A orbits and stabilizers of order at most s ≥ 1. Put K = ker(C0 → M). Exactness identifies K with the image of C1 → C0. Thus 0 → K → C0 → M → 0 is short exact. The tail ⋯ → C2 → C1 → K → 0 gives the complex for the next step. Its last map is the same boundary with its target restricted to its image, so its kernel is still the image of C2.

The connecting map. Apply the long exact homology sequence to the short exact sequence of coefficients. Indeed the bar resolution is free in each degree, so tensoring it with the three modules preserves exactness degree by degree. The resulting homology sequence has the following segment, exact at its middle term.

Hj(G, C0) → Hj(G, M) →δ Hj−1(G, K).

To see the degree drop, lift a cycle with coefficients in M to a chain with coefficients in C0. Its boundary maps to zero in the chains with coefficients in M, hence has coefficients in K. The class of this boundary is δ of the original class. Changing the lift adds a boundary with coefficients in K. If the original cycle changes by a boundary, lift a chain that produces that boundary and add its boundary to the old lift. Taking the boundary again gives zero for the added term. If δ vanishes, subtract a chain with coefficients in K whose boundary is that of the lift. The corrected lift is a cycle, which explains exactness at the middle term. Weibel, theorem 1.3.1, the long exact homology sequence[108].

In an exact segment U → V → W of abelian groups, suppose U is finite and the torsion subgroup of W is finite. The homomorphism tors V → tors W has kernel contained in the image of U, and its image lies in tors W. Counting a kernel and its cosets gives |tors V| ≤ |U| · |tors W|. The distinction matters even for the familiar exact sequence 0 → ℤ →×n ℤ → ℤ/n → 0, with n > 1. Its last three terms are ℤ → ℤ/n → 0. Both outer torsion subgroups have order one, yet the middle torsion subgroup has order n.

The permutation-module estimate bounds the whole group on the left of the homology sequence, so the comparison becomes

|tors Hj(G, M)| ≤ sA sj · |tors Hj−1(G, K)|.

If each basis boundary Cj+1 → Cj has sum of absolute coefficients at most b ≥ 1, this same boundary remains at the top of every shortened complex. At degree zero the integral presentation of the coinvariants therefore contributes at most bA. Unwinding the inequality supplies one power of s for each positive degree, with total exponent A(s + ⋯ + sj). Since each of the j summands is at most sj, the product is at most bA sj A sj. For the face complex take M = ℤ with trivial action, and b = j + 2 because a basis element in degree j + 1 has that many face terms. This recovers the stated torsion bound.
