An exact complex for the arithmetic group

The degree shift requires an augmented complex that is exact over the integers. For the group of invertible integral matrices we will build it from Hermitian forms on the embedded lattice. Two questions govern the construction. Which ordered tuples share a supporting functional, and how can a cycle of such tuples be filled?

Why do the lattice inequalities force positive definiteness?

In the count of frames on a common face, the only initial constraint on the Hermitian forms is a lower bound on lattice vectors. Let L be the totally complex number field, let N ≥ 1, and put d = [L∶ℚ]N. Choose one embedding σw in each complex conjugate pair. For a family of Hermitian matrices hw indexed by these places, set qh(y) = ∑w σw(y)*hwσw(y), where * denotes conjugate transpose. Every summand is real. Suppose qh(y) ≥ 1 for all nonzero y ∈ 𝒪LN. An integral basis of 𝒪L in each coordinate identifies these vectors with ℤd. Denote by G the real symmetric matrix of their quadratic form in this basis. We claim

G is positive definite,   1 ≤ (4d)d det G.

First, nonnegativity on all integer points implies nonnegativity on rational points by clearing denominators and using homogeneity of degree two. Density and continuity give nonnegativity on ℝd. Strict positivity on rational points alone could leave an irrational null direction. The uniform lower bound of one rules this out, as the following volume calculation shows.

For ε > 0, put Gε = G+εI. It is positive definite and still takes value at least one on each nonzero integral vector. Write Gε = BtB using its positive square root. The lattice Bℤd has covolume |det B|. Set t = |det B|1/d. The symmetric cube [−2t,2t]d has volume 4d|det B|, strictly greater than the Minkowski threshold 2d|det B|. It therefore contains some Bc with 0 ≠ c ∈ ℤd. Its squared Euclidean length is at most 4dt² and at least one. Raising to the power d gives 1 ≤ (4d)d det Gε. The determinant is a polynomial in ε, so the same inequality holds at ε = 0. The nonnegative eigenvalues of G have positive product and hence are all positive. Sutherland, Theorem 14.13, Minkowski’s lattice point theorem[56].

This also gives positivity at each individual place. The real coordinates in the integral basis parameterize the entire product ∏w ℂN as a real vector space. Indeed the matrix of all embeddings of the basis is invertible by its nonzero discriminant. Solving for a tuple whose entries at conjugate embeddings are conjugate gives real coefficients, by uniqueness of the solution. In particular any nonzero z at one chosen place, with zeros elsewhere, comes from a nonzero real coordinate vector. Its value for G is z*hwz > 0. Every hw is therefore positive definite. Sutherland, Proposition 12.6, the embedding matrix and the discriminant[109].

Where does the discriminant enter the frame bound?

Write D = |disc L|, m = [L∶ℚ] and P = ∏w det hw. The factors of P are positive by the real Gram estimate. To compute their product from G, take an integral basis b₁,…,bₘ and form T = (σ(bⱼ))σ,j using all embeddings. The matrix of traces TrL/ℚ(bᵢbⱼ) is TtT, so its determinant gives (det T)² = disc L, and |det T|² = D.

Apply T separately to each of the N coordinates, and group the output by embedding. Call the resulting square matrix U. Reordering the coordinates leaves |det U|² = DN. In this output space form a block diagonal matrix H with hw at the chosen embedding and its conjugate, equivalently its transpose, at the conjugate embedding. An entry of U*HU is a sum over all embeddings. The two summands for a conjugate pair add to twice the real part of the chosen summand, precisely that pair’s contribution to 2G. Thus U*HU = 2G. The two blocks in each conjugate pair have the same real determinant, so det H = P². Taking determinants now gives

2d det G = DN P²,   1 ≤ DN dd P.

For the inequality, substitute the identity in 1 ≤ (4d)ddet G. The right side becomes (2d)dDNP². Because d ≥ 2 and D ≥ 1, this is at most (ddDNP)². Taking the positive square root proves the assertion. Now let the columns of an integral matrix A be independent common minimal vectors. Their values for qh are one. Hence each diagonal entry of each pulled-back form σw(A)*hwσw(A) is at most one. Hadamard’s determinant inequality bounds its determinant by their product, hence by one. Multiplying over the places gives |NormL/ℚ(det A)|P ≤ 1. The preceding lower bound for P therefore bounds the index |NormL/ℚ(det A)| by DNdd in the count of common frames. Writing J = DNdd, the same calculation gives a lower bound at each place. The product of the pulled-back determinants is at least P ≥ 1/J, since the nonzero integral determinant has absolute norm at least one. Every factor is at most one, so each individual determinant is at least 1/J. This is the bound used in the coordinate estimate. Hadamard’s inequality here follows by writing the positive matrix as a Gram matrix and orthogonalizing the vectors that it represents. Each projected length is at most the original vector length.

For a check with a nonreal matrix entry, take L = ℚ(i), N = 2 and h with diagonal entries 1 and upper-right entry i/2. Its eigenvalues are ½ and 3/2. On a Gaussian integer vector (a+bi,c+ei) it takes the integer value a²+b²+c²+e²−ae+bc, so every nonzero vector satisfies the bound of one. With the integral basis (1,i), the real Gram matrix separates into the (a,e) and (b,c) blocks, both of determinant ¾. Thus det G = 9/16. Here d = 4, D = 4 and P = ¾, giving 2⁴ · 9/16 = 9 = 4² · (¾)².

Which Hermitian forms can a positive functional see?

The torsion estimate uses a complex of ordered vertices. Its boundary deletes one vertex at a time. To use the complex we must prove that every integral cycle in it bounds. We start by finding the geometric object that records which tuples are allowed.

Let F be totally complex and take one complex embedding from each conjugate pair. A point h in our real vector space is a tuple of Hermitian matrices of size N ≥ 1. Each nonzero vector y in 𝒪FN gives a real linear functional on that space, namely the sum qy(h) of its Hermitian values over the chosen embeddings. Write P for the closed convex set on which all these functionals are at least one. A form is a vertex when the equalities qy(h) = 1 determine it uniquely. Equivalently, the only variation annihilated by every active functional is zero.

The embedded integer vectors form a full real lattice. A sufficiently large multiple of the identity form therefore belongs to P. The real Gram bound makes every member positive definite at each place. In a neighborhood of any such form the least eigenvalues stay above a common positive constant c. An equality qy = 1 there forces the squared Euclidean norm of the embedded vector to be at most 1/c. Only finitely many lattice vectors occur in that ball. All other inequalities stay strict throughout the neighborhood.

Let T be the closed cone of tuples of positive semidefinite matrices and let X consist of all linear functionals strictly positive on its nonzero elements. The sum of the traces belongs to X since a nonzero positive semidefinite matrix has a positive eigenvalue. For a vertex v the normal cone collects the functionals minimized at that vertex.

Aᵥ = {ℓ : ℓ(v) ≤ ℓ(h) for every h ∈ P}.

Each cone is closed and convex because it is an intersection of closed half-spaces. To see that the cones cover X, fix ℓ ∈ X. On the unit vectors of T, compactness gives ℓ a strictly positive minimum. Thus bounded upper levels of ℓ on P are compact. The minimum on P is attained, and its minimizers form a compact convex set. Choose a minimizer of maximal squared Euclidean norm in that set. Strict convexity of the squared norm prevents this point from being the midpoint of two distinct minimizers. If some nonzero direction killed all its active functionals, small displacements in both directions would be feasible. Indeed only the finite list above can become active nearby. The two displaced values of ℓ average to the minimum and so both attain it. This contradicts the midpoint property. The chosen minimizer is a vertex.

Only finitely many cones can meet the convex hull of a finite set of functionals ℓ₁,…,ℓs in X. Fix any h₀ ∈ P. If a convex combination of the ℓᵢ is minimized at v, at least one ℓᵢ satisfies ℓᵢ(v) ≤ ℓᵢ(h₀). Those finitely many compact sublevels contain only finitely many vertices. A finite neighborhood cover gives a finite pool of possible active inequalities, and their active subset determines each vertex uniquely.

For a two-dimensional example, impose h₁ ≥ 1, h₂ ≥ 1 and h₁+h₂ ≥ 3. A positive functional with equal coefficients is minimized along the segment from (1,2) to (2,1). Both endpoints belong to its minimizing face. A slight increase in the coefficient of h₁ selects (1,2) alone. How does cutting a convex set help fill a cycle?

Given closed convex sets Aᵢ covering a nonempty convex set X, keep an ordered tuple of labels whenever the corresponding sets share a point of X. This collection is the nerve of the cover. Deleting a label keeps the same witness. A chain of degree p is a finite integer sum of such tuples of length p+1. Labels can repeat. The boundary of a tuple is the alternating sum over deletions. Deleting two different positions in the two possible orders produces opposite signs, so the boundary applied twice is zero. In degree zero, summing the coefficients defines the augmentation to ℤ.

Consider first a nonempty compact convex portion K that meets finitely many cover sets. Suppose that all the sets meeting K contain one common point in K. Choose one of their labels a. Prepending a to each tuple defines an integral operator s. Deleting its newly prepended entry returns the original tuple, and every other deletion has the opposite sign from the corresponding term in s∂. Hence ∂s+s∂ is the identity, including the augmentation if s sends the empty tuple to [a]. A cycle z is filled by sz.

In the general compact case, count the unordered subsets of active labels that have a common witness in K, including the empty subset. This finite count controls an induction even though tuples may have repeated entries and arbitrarily large length. Choose a realized subset Σ of largest cardinality. Unless all active labels have a common witness, some active label i is outside Σ. There is no point witnessing Σ together with i. The witnesses of Σ form a nonempty compact convex set, disjoint from the nonempty compact convex set K ∩ Aᵢ. Separate them by a hyperplane, with i strictly on the left and Σ strictly on the right. In Euclidean coordinates the midpoint hyperplane perpendicular to a shortest segment between the two compact sets works. Varying either endpoint toward another point of its set cannot shorten the segment, which puts the entire set on its own side. Boyd and Vandenberghe, §2.5.1, pp. 46–47[110].

Each closed half of K and the slice on the hyperplane has fewer realized subsets. The left half loses Σ, the right half loses {i}, and the slice loses both. Each is nonempty since K contains the segment joining the opposite witnesses. The nerve on K is the union of the two half nerves. Their intersection is the nerve of the slice. Indeed a tuple witnessed on both sides is witnessed on the joining segment, at the point where it crosses the hyperplane, since every set named by the tuple is convex.

To join the fillings, split an integral cycle as z = u+v with chains in the two halves. The boundary b = ∂u = −∂v belongs to their intersection. Exactness there gives a chain e with ∂e = b. Now u−e and v+e are cycles in the two halves, so the induction fills them. Their fillings add to a filling of z. For zero-dimensional cycles b is an integer and multiplying a slice vertex by b gives a chain of augmentation b. This proves

∂(U+V) = (u−e) + (v+e) = z.

Why does the arithmetic face complex give an exact sequence?

On [0,4] take the closed intervals A = [0,1], B = [1,3], C = [3,4]. There is no common point of all three, and no edge [A,C]. Cut at 2. Only B meets the slice. The cycle [C]−[A] splits into −[A] on the left and [C] on the right. The two augmentations are −1 and 1. Use −[B] on the slice to correct them. The corrected cycles [B]−[A] and [C]−[B] are the boundaries of [A,B] and [B,C]. Their sum cancels the artificial vertex in the boundary. At the contacts 1 and 3 the cut still gives the union and intersection identities. One half then keeps all the faces. Every cut strictly between 1 and 3 separates the chosen witness sets, reducing the face count on both sides.

Return to the normal cones of the Hermitian vertices. The parameter space X of positive functionals can be unbounded. A cycle has finite support, so choose one witness in X for each tuple that occurs and include one fixed point of X. Their convex hull K lies in X and is compact, being the image of a finite-dimensional closed simplex under the convex-combination map. By the finite-cone property only finitely many normal cones meet K. They cover it. Every tuple in the cycle already occurs in its nerve, and the compact filling argument supplies a finite integral chain with that boundary. Its witnesses in K are also witnesses in X.

⋯ → ℤ[ordered triples] → ℤ[ordered pairs] → ℤ[vertices] → ℤ → 0.

Here ℤ[ ] means finite integer combinations of the allowed tuples. The augmentation from ℤ[vertices] to ℤ sends each vertex to 1 and is onto because the cover contains a vertex. In every preceding degree the alternating deletion rule puts every boundary in the kernel. The filling puts every kernel element in the image. An integral change of lattice basis permutes the vertices and carries a common supporting functional to its pullback. This commutes with deletion at each position. We have therefore constructed the exact complex of permutation modules needed in the group homology bound. The face orbits and stabilizers are counted separately. Exactness here is asserted before identifying equivalent faces under the group action.

How many faces can an arithmetic group have up to symmetry?

In the homology inequality, A bounds the number of face orbits and s bounds the order of the subgroup fixing any one face. A face in this chain model is an ordered tuple of vertices, with repetitions allowed. Two such tuples represent one orbit if the same group element moves every entry of the first tuple to the corresponding entry of the second. Here the group is G = GLN(𝒪F), with F a totally complex number field, n = [F : ℚ], D = |disc F|, N ≥ 1 and d = nN. Thus d is the integer rank of the vector lattice 𝒪FN. We will count orbits in each face degree p ≥ 0.

Find a frame shared by the whole face

For each infinite place of F take a Hermitian form on ℂN. Their values on the images of a lattice vector y add to a real number qh(y). Impose qh(y) ≥ 1 for every nonzero y. A vector is minimal for h when equality holds. A vertex is a feasible family h uniquely determined by its equalities. A degree-p face in the complex is an ordered list of p + 1 such vertices at which one supporting linear functional attains its minimum. That functional is strictly positive on nonzero positive semidefinite families. The definition allows repeated vertices.

The common minimal vectors of a face span FN. To see why, average the vertices. At the average a lattice inequality is tight exactly when it is tight at every vertex. If the common minimal vectors missed a direction, a nonzero F-linear functional λ would vanish on their span. The family of rank-one forms obtained from |λ|² at all embeddings is positive semidefinite and nonzero. A sufficiently small subtraction of this family from the average preserves the tight constraints. Local finiteness of the inequalities keeps the others feasible. The supporting functional would strictly decrease below its minimum. Thus we can choose N independent common minimal columns and place them in a matrix A. They form a basis over F. Its integral determinant can be a nonunit. The determinant estimate gives

r = |NormF/ℚ(det A)| ≤ J,   J = DNdd.

For this last inequality pull back each local form by A. The pulled-back determinants have product at most one by the diagonal bounds and Hadamard’s inequality. Their product is r times the product of the original determinants, for which the geometric lower bound is 1/J.

One congruence count for the frame

Fix its positive integer r. Over F put B = rA−1. Why does this have integral entries? The principal ideal (det A) has norm r and contains the integer r. Hence r/det A lies in 𝒪F, and multiplying the integral adjugate of A by that element gives B. Reduce its entries modulo r𝒪F. Suppose a second frame A′ has the same norm and its matrix B′ has the same residue list. Write B − B′ = rX with X integral. Over the field this gives

A′A−1 = 1 + A′X,   AA′−1 = 1 − AX.

Both matrices are integral and they are inverses. The first therefore belongs to G and takes A to A′ by left multiplication. An integral basis identifies 𝒪F/r𝒪F as an additive group with (ℤ/rℤ)n. The list of N² entries has at most rnN² = rdN values. Choosing one frame for each attained list covers every orbit. Summing the bound for r = 1,…,J costs at most J1+dN.

Example. In ℤ[i] take the one-column matrices A = 1 + i and A′ = 1 − i. Both norms are 2. The scaled inverses are B = 1 − i and B′ = 1 + i, so X = −i. The formula gives g = −i, and multiplication by this Gaussian unit sends 1 + i to 1 − i. This tests the congruence argument for frames of bounded determinant norm.

How many vertices can share a chosen frame?

Fix a representative A. A nearby vector is one that can be minimal for some feasible form making every column of A minimal. The coordinate estimate gives |σ((By)j)| ≤ R = NNJ² at every embedding. Since AB = r·1, the vector By determines y. Each of its coordinates has at most (2R + 1)n possibilities. Indeed, if two such algebraic integers differ by (2R + 1)x, every conjugate of x has absolute value at most 2R/(2R + 1) < 1. A nonzero algebraic integer has nonzero integer norm, ruling this out. The residue count thus bounds the number of nearby vectors by M = (2R + 1)d. The coordinate estimate on the scaled inverse, separation by conjugate size, counting all coordinates. The column replacement argument below derives the coordinate bound at each embedding.

The equations qh(y) = 1 are linear in the unknown coefficients of h. At a vertex, at most dN independent equations suffice to determine it. Their vectors lie in the nearby set. A set of at most dN vectors drawn from M choices can be recorded as a list of length dN by sorting it and padding with a blank. Hence this frame admits at most (M + 1)dN vertices. Each entry of an ordered tuple can use any of these in an upper bound. Together with the frame count this gives the orbit bound

Ap = J1+dN(M + 1)dN(p+1) ≤ (2Dd)12(p+1)d³N.

This count allows lists that fail the common-support condition, which only enlarges the bound. Formally choose a frame and a translated tuple for each orbit. Equal choices of frame and entries give the same tuple, hence the same orbit.

How a determinant bounds one coordinate

A vector can have small energy and large coordinates if the form measuring its energy is nearly singular. The determinant measures the loss we must allow here. Let G be a positive semidefinite Hermitian N × N matrix with every diagonal entry at most 1. If a complex column c has energy c*Gc ≤ 1, then for each coordinate a,

|det G| · |ca| ≤ N! ≤ NN.

Write ⟨x,y⟩ = x*Gy. Positivity gives |⟨x,y⟩|² ≤ ⟨x,x⟩⟨y,y⟩. Indeed, subtracting ⟨x,y⟩x/⟨x,x⟩ from y leaves a vector of nonnegative energy. If x has zero energy, the energy of y + tx can stay nonnegative for all complex t only if ⟨x,y⟩ = 0. Apply the inequality first to two coordinate vectors and then to a coordinate vector and c. It gives |Gij| ≤ 1 and |(Gc)i| ≤ 1.

Replace column a of G by Gc. This new column is the sum of the original columns weighted by the coordinates of c. Expand the determinant in that column. Every term except the ath has a repeated column, so the determinant equals ca det G. Each entry of the new matrix has absolute value at most 1. Its determinant is a signed sum of N! products, each of absolute value at most 1. This proves the bound even when G is singular. To bound |ca| itself we now need a positive lower bound for the determinant. Gilbert Strang, MIT 18.06, Lecture 20, Cramer’s rule[111].

Why the integral coordinates lie in one box

Fix a nonsingular integral frame A over the totally complex field F. A vector y is nearby if one feasible family of forms h makes both y and every column of A minimal. Each y may have its own family. Set r = |NormF/ℚ(det A)| and use the integral matrix B = rA−1. For n = [F : ℚ], d = nN, D = |disc F| and J = DNdd, every such y satisfies

|σw((By)a)| ≤ R,   R = NNJ²,

for every coordinate a and one embedding σw in each complex conjugate pair. Its conjugate gives the same absolute value. To see the bound, let Hw be the local matrix of the chosen family and put Aw = σw(A), Gw = Aw*HwAw. The diagonal entries of Gw are nonnegative. For each column their sum over the places is the energy of that column, exactly 1. Thus each diagonal entry is at most 1. The frame estimate, using the discriminant bound, gives both 1 ≤ r ≤ J and det Gw ≥ 1/J at every place.

Let cw = σw(By)/r. Since AB = rI, multiplying cw by Aw recovers σw(y). The resulting local energies cw*Gwcw are nonnegative and sum to the energy of y, exactly 1. Apply the preceding coordinate estimate at each place. Dividing by det Gw costs at most one factor J. Multiplying by r to recover the integral coordinate costs at most another. This gives the stated R. The map y ↦ By is injective, because multiplying its output by A recovers ry. The count of nearby vectors can therefore count integral columns in this fixed box.

A minimal Gaussian vector with a denominator in frame coordinates

Over ℤ[i] take the form q(u,v) = |u + (1 + i)v/2|² + |v|²/2. Every nonzero integral pair has energy at least 1. If v = 0 this follows from |u| ≥ 1. If |v|² ≥ 2 the second term suffices. For a Gaussian unit v, the real and imaginary parts of (1 + i)v/2 are both half-integers, so the first term is at least 1/2.

Take frame columns (1,0) and (−i,1 + i). They are orthogonal for this form and each has energy 1, so their Gram matrix is the identity. Their determinant is 1 + i and r = 2. The vector y = (0,1) also has energy 1. Solving Ac = y gives c = ((1 + i)/2,(1 − i)/2), of squared length 1. Multiplication by r gives the integral column By = (1 + i,1 − i). Multiplying that column by A gives (0,2), as required.

Why reduction modulo three counts stabilizers

An element fixing an ordered tuple fixes its first vertex. The first vertex has finitely many minimal vectors, and these include N independent ones. The images of those basis vectors under an element fixing the vertex are again minimal and determine the element. Thus the stabilizer is finite. Now view it as a subgroup of the units of the matrix ring T = MN(𝒪F). Distinct elements have distinct residues in T/3T. Otherwise their quotient would be a finite-order unit congruent to 1 modulo 3.

Here is the divisibility argument behind this separation. If such a unit were nontrivial, one of its powers would have prime order l and still be congruent to 1. Write that power as 1 + 3kY with k ≥ 1 maximal and Y nonzero modulo 3. Maximality follows by looking at any nonzero integer coordinate in the free abelian group T. For l ≠ 3 its lth power differs from 1 by l3kY modulo 3k+1, which is nonzero. For l = 3 the leading term is 3k+1Y modulo 3k+2. The other two terms in the cube are divisible by 32k+1 and 33k, both at least the required power. This contradicts prime order in both cases. Induction on the order gives the same separation.

The additive rank of T is nN² = dN, so the stabilizer bound is s = 3dN, uniform in the face degree. In rank one over ℤ[i] the units 1, −1, i, −i already have four distinct residues among the nine available. In homology degree m, Am bounds every face degree p ≤ m. Substituting it and s into the homological torsion inequality gives the estimate used in degree two. The discriminant lower bound for the form determinants, the Cramer estimate for nearby coordinates and exactness of the face complex are inputs to this calculation.

What survives when a localization map is reduced modulo ℓ?

Let L be a number field, ℓ a prime and S the finite places over ℓ. Choose a prolongation of each place and write Dv for its decomposition group. On the global Galois group GS unramified outside S, take T = ℤℓ(e + 1) and A = (ℚℓ/ℤℓ)(−e). The shift comes from the cyclotomic factor in the Tate dual. The dual of T/ℓrT with this factor identifies with A[ℓr]. The arithmetic application has e ≥ 1 and L totally complex. The finite-level global duality used here requires ℓ odd or no real places of L.

Write X = H²(GS, T) and Y = ∏v∈S H²(Dv, T). Localization λ sends a class to its restrictions. Its kernel K is the locally trivial integral degree-two group. Its cokernel C measures which tuples of local classes come from global ones. At depth r ≥ 1, reduction identifies the degree-two groups for the finite coefficients T/ℓrT with X/ℓrX and Y/ℓrY. This uses vanishing of degree three modulo ℓ to lift cocycles. A class reducing to zero is an ℓr multiple. Restriction commutes with reduction on cocycles, so the finite localization is the resulting map λr.

Which reduced classes lift? Put t = ℓr and B = λ(X). Both C/tC and coker λr are quotients of Y by B + tY. For a kernel class, choose a representative x in X. Its reduction belongs to ker λr precisely when λ(x) belongs to tY. To obtain an integral kernel representative, subtract tx′ from x. This works precisely when λ(x) = tλ(x′). The following criterion spells out the distinction.

K/(K ∩ tX) ↪ ker λr   is onto exactly when   B ∩ tY = tB.

For e ≠ 0, every Dv contains an element g with χ(g)−e ≠ 1. The nonzero ℓ-adic integer χ(g)−e − 1 annihilates the invariants ADᵥ. The finite set S gives a common exponent c such that ℓc kills all these invariants. Finite local Tate duality, local finiteness and passage through the torsion levels give each local H² the length of its finite invariant group. Thus Y has finite length and ℓmY = 0 for some m. At every depth r ≥ m the criterion holds.

How the finite dualities give a length. The last arrow of the finite Poitou–Tate sequence identifies the order of coker λr with the order of the global invariants in A[ℓr]. These invariants increase to H⁰(GS, A). The quotients C/ℓrC separate points because C is finitely generated over ℤℓ. Comparing their orders gives length(C) = length H⁰(GS, A).

The finite kernel ker λr is paired with the locally trivial H¹ for A[ℓr]. To pass to A, filter its locally trivial H¹ by the classes represented by a cocycle whose values and local coboundary witnesses are all killed by ℓr. Every class occurs because a continuous cocycle from a compact group to discrete A has finite image and only finitely many local witnesses are needed. There is one more lifting issue. If a finite-level cocycle becomes the global coboundary of a in A, choose a local witness b killed by ℓr at any place over ℓ. Then a − b is locally invariant, so ℓc(a − b) = 0. For r ≥ c, a itself is an allowed witness. At sufficiently large depths the filtration terms therefore have the orders of K/(K ∩ ℓrX). This decreasing filtration on K has zero intersection. If the common orders stay bounded, they attain a maximum. Beyond that level the inclusions and quotient maps are bijections. Exhaustion then gives the whole degree-one group, and separation makes the remaining integral kernel of reduction zero. If the orders grow without bound, both groups have infinite length. Hence length(K) = length Ш¹(GS, A), where Ш¹ denotes the kernel of all restrictions at S. The source treats e = 0 separately using the trivial action.

Finally, X/K ≃ B and Y/B = C. Additivity of length in the two short exact sequences gives length(X) + length(C) = length(K) + length(Y). Substituting the three duality comparisons gives the balance below. Lengths take values in ℕ ∪ {∞}, so this additive form also applies before finiteness is known.

length H²(GS, T) + length H⁰(GS, A) = length Ш¹(GS, A) + ∑v∈S length H⁰(Dv, A).

The nonnegative global H⁰ term gives the upper bound used in the degree-two estimate. Why does ψ survive both steps defining ψ′ in the second row? On the two auxiliary prime factors the characters have order dividing two, and the group of units modulo the power of two also has power-of-two order. The odd part of the order of ψ therefore divides the order of χ. For ℓ outside Bχ it is prime to ℓ. Moreover ℓ−1 ∣ 2e gives ℓ ≤ 2e+1 < q,d. Since ℓ is odd and ℓ ∤ Q, it does not divide the modulus N. Thus taking the prime-to-ℓ part and removing the component at ℓ both preserve ψ.

8.16Why the exterior sum is uniform in the number of primes

Take any finite set of odd primes outside Bχ. Bounding every prime by a constant and then counting the whole set would lose uniformity. In case I the source instead groups pairs (ℓ,ψ) by the kernel K of ψ on G = (ℤ/Nℤ)×. The image of a character is cyclic. A cyclic quotient of order m has φ(m) faithful complex characters, one for every primitive mth root. Their pullbacks have precisely kernel K. Distinct kernels give disjoint lists, and G has |G| complex characters. Therefore the sum of φ([G : K]) over kernels that occur is at most |G| ≤ N. For example, in a cyclic group of order six, the quotients of orders 1, 2, 3, 6 contribute 1+1+2+2=6.

The rank-three unitary estimate supplies the sum over primes for each kernel, with its totient weight. Its two test primes r1, r2 and its constants are chosen for χ before the host and the twist. Both host primes q and d must exceed each of r₁ and r₂. If A is its power exponent, the preceding count leaves a bound of the form C₀N[N(e+1)]A. Choose k with C₀ ≤ 16k. Since 16 ≤ N and e+1 ≤ t, this is at most Mk+1+A. Write CI for this exponent.

Outside case I, ℓ−1 divides 2e, so ℓ ≤ 2e+1 ≤ 2t. There are at most 2t such primes and at most N characters per prime. Let K0 be the maximum exponent from Z, II and III. Their individual bounds already include log ℓ. The inequality ℓNe ≤ M³ gives at most 2M·M3K₀ at each twist. The Z branch is especially simple. The parity of the trivial character forces e even, hence e ≥ 2. The excluded set contains 3, so ℓ ≥ 5. The vanishing theorem at such divisible even twists bounds the restricted length by zero. Cases II and III receive their estimates from the joint rank-four symplectic construction.

t (MCI + 2M1+3K₀) ≤ MCI+3K₀+4.

Here t ≤ M and M ≥ 2. This bound holds for every finite exterior prime set, however many case-I primes it contains.

8.17Where the auxiliary layer enters the interior sum

Fix ℓ ∈ Bχ and a layer index j. Characters in branch IV have conductor dividing Q. All of them become trivial on the absolute Galois group of the same field L1. This is a degree-ℓj cyclotomic layer over a field realizing the full cyclotomic datum of modulus ℓQ. Its degree over ℚ is at most D=ℓQℓj. Restriction to that field bounds each character length by the locally trivial length there plus a local invariants error. After coefficient normalization this error is bounded by D·2Ne. Summing this term for 1 ≤ e < t costs at most MD+3. If the layer supplies a total bound B, each such character thus contributes at most B+MD+3 across the whole twist range.

Let Oℓ be the union over the relevant twists of the selected characters with ψ′ of odd order. Its members have conductor dividing Q, so |Oℓ| ≤ Q. This is why the coefficient of B is independent of t. For the other characters the estimate is pointwise. At e=1 the source compares R₁=16 ord(χ)(ℓQ)²4n₀ with 2c₂, where c₂ is the conductor exponent of the 2-component and n₀ is the 2-adic valuation of ℓf₀−1 for the character-dependent order f₀ specified in the source. When R₁ ≤ 2c₂, apply the rank-three estimate in case V. In the other branch the proof bounds the character order, chooses a field of degree bounded in terms of χ, and applies duality and the independent degree-two theorem there.

One finite-sum inequality explains the bookkeeping. If every entry outside Oℓ has weight at most K, each twist has at most N entries, and each distinguished character has total unweighted contribution at most S, then

(log ℓ) ∑e ∑ψ ∈ Xe ve(ψ) ≤ (log ℓ) |Oℓ| S + tNK.

In the first sum on the right, interchange characters and twists, enlarging to all twists by nonnegativity. In the other sum count the entries twist by twist. The integral reduction error contributes a further polynomial in M. The source obtains MCℓ+CℓB for this prime. It can absorb the coefficient (log ℓ)Q since ℓ and Q were fixed before the window.

8.18How a trace congruence bounds one character

Fix the primitive character χ. The level N may vary among the hosts built from χ. Given a cutoff t satisfying the host condition, an odd prime ℓ, a coefficient ring O and an integer e with 0 < e < t, take a character ψ trivial on the host subgroup and satisfying ψ(−1) = (−1)e. Let L be the O-module length of its cohomological obstruction and eO the ramification index of O over ℤℓ. Each case considered here proves that L is finite and (L/eO) log ℓ ≤ (ℓNe)C. The exponent is chosen before the host, ℓ, O, t, e and ψ. How can a finite list of Galois representations measure this length?

In cases II and III the matrices have size four and preserve a symplectic form up to a scalar. At a prime p of good reduction, choose a Frobenius element σ. For each representation r let a(r) = tr r(σ) − tr r0(σ), where r0 is the reference representation. Two integral traces whose difference has valuation d agree to ℓ-adic precision d. With |ℓ|ℓ = ℓ−1, that difference contributes −log |a(r)|ℓ = d log ℓ.

The deformation algebra records the allowed lifts of the reference data. A first-order variation of a point r has matrices r(g) + εB(g), where ε² = 0. Multiplication makes B(g)r(g)−1 a cocycle for conjugation. The rigidity proof places its projection, after a twist over a CM field, in an adjoint Selmer group with prescribed local conditions. The supplied vanishing makes the class a coboundary. Projecting back gives B(g) = Y r(g) − r(g)Y for one symplectic Lie algebra element Y. This is exactly the variation obtained by conjugating with 1 + εY.

Coordinates in the deformation algebra have integer weights for a rescaling action. With rigidity, finiteness of the degree-zero part and exclusion of the specified endoscopic points, the algebraic lemma M produces a finite set meeting the rescaling orbits of points having nonzero coordinates of both signs. It bounds the length of the weight −1 cotangent quotient at the reference point by twice the sum of the valuations of the trace differences. This quotient keeps the linear terms in the defining equations. Lemma M′ bounds the obstruction length through its injection into the solutions of those linear equations modulo a coefficient ideal. Choosing a minimal orbit cover gives a finite family Ξ with one representative for each orbit in the cover. Conjugate matrices give the same orbit, so no conjugate representation is counted twice. Transferring the cotangent bound to the original obstruction gives

(L/eO) log ℓ ≤ 2 ∑r∈Ξ −log |a(r)|ℓ.

8.19One integer pays for all the congruences

At the auxiliary automorphic level M, the counting theorem supplies a finite indexed list of Frobenius eigenvalue multisets. Different indices may carry identical multisets. For each index with trace s, form the difference between s and pe+1z₁ + pez₂ + p z₃ + 1, including all simultaneous conjugates of the chosen kth roots of unity z₁, z₂, z₃. For p ≥ 5, e ≥ 2 and y = pe, the purity estimate on the eigenvalues gives |s| ≤ 7y/2. The first summand has size py > 7y/2 + y + p + 1, so every difference is nonzero. The factors are algebraic integers. All field automorphisms permute them. Their product is therefore a nonzero rational integer m. Bounding each factor by p2(e+1) and counting all the factors gives log |m| ≤ cφ(k)[M(e+1)]A log p, with φ Euler’s totient.

Each member of Ξ selects a different index in the product. Equal values at different indices retain their multiplicity. The unused factors have ℓ-adic norm at most one, whence |m|ℓ ≤ ∏r∈Ξ|a(r)|ℓ. Taking negative logarithms bounds the sum by vℓ(m) log ℓ ≤ log |m|. For example, the integer 45 allows at most two powers of 3 across selected integral factors, since 45 = 3² · 5. This elementary divisibility step turns the complex size estimate into the required ℓ-adic inequality.

The auxiliary level grows with the data. Write Q for the conductor of χ, o for its order and X = ℓNe. The construction takes M = ℓ 2n′NP, k = (ℓ−1)2n′(2o). Here P = 1 in case II and is a fixed auxiliary prime determined by χ in case III. In case II, if c₂ is the dyadic conductor exponent of ψ and n₀ = v₂(ℓf₀ − 1), with f₀ the multiplicative order of ℓ modulo lcm(4, ord θ₁) for the auxiliary character θ₁, the integer n′ is the ceiling of the base-two logarithm of max(ℓN4n₀, 2c₂+6oℓ³Q²). The host bounds give 2c₂ ≤ N and 2n₀ < ℓφ(4o). Rounding up to a power of two costs at most a factor two. Together these bounds give 2n′ ≤ X2φ(4o)+10. Case III uses max(ℓQP4n₀, 8ℓ²) and gives the exponent 11 + Q + P + 2φ(4o). The comparison prime satisfies p ≤ 2ℓNP + 10. Thus every factor in 2ck[M(e+1)]A log p is bounded by a power of X whose exponent is fixed once χ is fixed.

The proof may enlarge O to contain enough roots of unity. Independence of normalized length brings the estimate back to the original ring.

8.20The rank-three estimate in case V

Here ℓ belongs to the finite exceptional set for χ, e = 1 and the case-V count applies when 16o(ℓQ)²4n₀ ≤ 2c₂, the conductor threshold denoted by R₁ ≤ 2c₂.

Indeed rescaling that coordinate by (1 + εb)j gives precisely this derivative. For each nonzero d ∈ O the finite-coefficient obstruction embeds into vectors over O/(d) supported in weight −1 and killed by the linearized relations. The resulting bound is uniform in d. Taking d = ℓn bounds the length of the full torsion obstruction because every element is killed by some power of ℓ.

Choose an inert prime p ≡ 3 modulo 4 with 7 ≤ p ≤ 12ℓN and p ∤ ℓN. The Frobenius over this prime has residue norm p². The trace test uses its inverse. Representatives are distinguished up to isomorphism after restriction to the Gaussian subgroup. Group them by the two embeddings of ℚ(i) into the chosen algebraic closure. The unitary counting theorem includes all φ(N)th roots of unity in its integral product. Applying it in each embedding group gives

∑r vℓ(a(r)) log ℓ ≤ 2a φ(N)[N(e+1)]b log p ≤ X2a+1+b+3.

The constants a,b here come from the counting theorem for the fixed field. The inequalities φ(N) ≤ X, N(e + 1) ≤ X and log p ≤ p ≤ X³ explain the exponent. The cotangent estimate introduces a final factor two, absorbed into one more power of X. 8.21One field for all three estimates

The exterior exponent Cout and auxiliary test primes depend on χ. The interior exponents also depend on the layer choices j(ℓ). Bound each by their sum D over Bχ, and put k = |Bχ|. Splitting any finite set of odd primes into its two parts now gives at most k(MD+DB)+MCout. With M ≥ 2, one can take C=Cout+D+k+kD. In particular, 1+k ≤ Mk absorbs the number of polynomial terms and kD ≤ C absorbs the multiple of B. The window chooses j(ℓ)=⌊logℓ Rℓ⌋+3 and B=exp(x4ε/5) before applying this result to any field at x.

Why is M equal to t times the field conductor, as the next theorem requires? Let E be any realization of the four fixing conditions. It embeds into the cyclotomic field of modulus N. If it also embeds at modulus M′ with a smaller exponent at a prime p dividing N, there is a unit c modulo N congruent to 1 modulo N/p outside the fixing subgroup. At the auxiliary primes one can use −1 in the corresponding component, since these primes are 3 modulo 4. At a prime whose exponent comes from χ, primitivity supplies a unit detected at the last power of that prime. In the remaining 2-primary case, 1+2n+1 is 1 at the preceding level and is neither sign at modulus 2n+2. The Chinese remainder theorem puts the chosen component together with the required trivial components.

Pass to lcm(M′,N). The witness lifts to a unit reducing to c modulo N and to 1 modulo M′. Its automorphism would both move and fix the same field. Hence N divides every admissible modulus and the conductor is exactly N. The field is also CM. In the ambient cyclotomic field a quadratic Gauss sum has square −q and transforms by the quadratic character at q. The defining subgroup fixes it, so E contains a square root of −q. An abelian extension of ℚ containing this element is totally imaginary and hence CM. Thus conjugation, the plus estimate, and the minus estimate all refer to this same field. The large-prime hypotheses make q,d coprime to Q and allow the same pair throughout the chosen window.

Which representation results supply these inequalities?

The final call obtains I from the unitary rank-three orbit estimate, II and III jointly from symplectic rank four, and V from a reduced unitary lift with cohomological finiteness, local duality and Euler characteristics. IV is the restriction argument on the bounded-degree layer above. The Z branch uses a trivial-character vanishing theorem. The separate estimate for large R₁ at twist one uses degree two. These distinct calls make clear which proof inputs one would have to strengthen to improve the plus bound.

Since 2 is invertible in ℤℓ, the two sign lengths add to the whole kernel length.

How one Bernoulli value bounds a module length

Fix a primitive character ψ of conductor f, an odd prime ℓ prime to its order, and a twist e ≥ 1 with ψ(−1) = (−1)e+1. Write O for the coefficient ring, a discrete valuation ring finite as a module over ℤℓ, v for its additive valuation with v(π) = 1 at a uniformizer π, and A for the cleared Bernoulli value at the conductor. The goal is lengthO ≤ v(A) for this character component. An integer can kill a whole module without controlling its length. For example, 3 kills (ℤ/3)d for every d. The proof needs local tests that measure how much length remains after each one.

Let χ be the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character and ψG the Galois character attached to ψ. The scalar action on the cocycles in the count is α = (χeψG)−1. First consider the case where α(g) − χ(g) is a unit for some g. Choose a nonzero cutoff a₀ ∈ O. Work with cocycles c in the torsion coefficient module O ⊗ℤℓ (ℚℓ/ℤℓ) whose values are killed by a₀. At one auxiliary cyclotomic level, choose δ inducing −1 on the exponents of its roots of unity. Parity gives α(δ) ≡ −1 modulo the maximal ideal. Since ℓ is odd, α(δ) − 1 is a unit. The same δ works for every cutoff. Normalize the cocycles to have c(δ) = 0. Subtracting the coboundary of c(δ)/(α(δ) − 1) achieves this.

Outside the level the scalar action is trivial on inertia, so the local coboundary condition forces the normalized cocycle to vanish there. At a conductor prime p ≠ ℓ the initial condition supplies a witness w on inertia I. Primitivity in this prime-to-ℓ character case supplies t ∈ I with α(t) − 1 a unit. For any d in the decomposition group, d−1td lies in I. Evaluate the cocycle identity on td = d(d−1td). It gives (α(t) − 1)[c(d) − (α(d) − 1)w] = 0. Cancellation extends the same witness to the entire decomposition group. At ℓ a decomposition-group witness is already part of the original condition. Choose a single cutoff killing that witness and the finite image of the continuous cocycle on its compact source. It then kills the witnesses at conductor primes by the same unit cancellation, and conjugation covers the other places over ℓ.

As a₀ runs through powers of π, the images of these spaces cover the locally trivial classes. A bound uniform in the cutoff will therefore bound the entire length.

Choose m after a₀ and put F = fℓ′ℓm, where fℓ′ is the prime-to-ℓ part of the conductor. Outside the primes dividing fℓ this introduces no new ramification. Here F denotes an integer level. Write [t] for the least nonnegative representative of t modulo F. For a suitable b < F and lifts σt acting on Fth roots of unity by the power t, the scalar used in the count is

z = ∑t∈(ℤ/Fℤ)× (⌊[t]b/F⌋ − ⌊[−t]b/F⌋) α(σt)−1.

The evaluation theorem arranges a₀z ∣ ℓm and z ∣ A. Here is the valuation principle behind the second divisibility. The unit-difference hypothesis gives a residue b for which ψ(b)be+1 − 1 is an ℓ-adic unit. The congruence for the floor sum compares it, after explicit scaling, with the nonzero Bernoulli value divided by e + 1. The source takes m large enough that the approximation error is strictly smaller than the norm of the comparison term after scaling. In a nonarchimedean norm, |x−y| < |y| forces |x| = |y|. The resulting norm of z is |Be+1,ψ/(e+1)|. Multiplying by integral factors to get the cleared value A can only increase its valuation.

How multiplication modulo the level produces a Bernoulli value

The length argument needs an integer-like scalar whose ℓ-adic valuation is exactly that of a special value. The floor in its definition records the carry when an integer product is reduced modulo the level. This permits a direct comparison of the two quantities, one residue at a time. Keep the level F = fℓ′ℓm chosen above, put k = e + 1 ≥ 2, and let χ denote the Dirichlet character induced by ψ at level F throughout this calculation. The cyclotomic character will enter again when the sum is compared with the Galois lifts.

For a unit residue, write u for its representative in 1,…,F−1. Choose b prime to F and divide bu by F, obtaining a quotient j and a remainder y between 1 and F−1. The opposite residue is represented by F−u. Its product with b is (b−j−1)F + (F−y). Subtracting the two quotients gives the signed carry θ(u) = 2j − (b−1). Define S = ∑u θ(u)ueχ(u), summed over the unit representatives. The use of ue in place of a lifted cyclotomic character changes the scalar by a multiple of ℓm.

Write C(u) = Fk−1Bk(u/F)/k, where Bk(x) is the Bernoulli polynomial. Let P be the product of the primes at most k + 1 and set D = 2kP. The first two coefficients of the polynomial give

C(u) = uk/(kF) − uk−1/2 + (2F/D)nu,   nu ∈ ℤ.

Indeed the term of Bernoulli index h ≥ 2 has a factor Fh−1. The denominator bound for the Bernoulli number Bh says that PBh is an integer for h ≤ k. Thus the terms after the first two are all multiples of F/(kP).

Compare C(y) and bkC(u) with y = bu − Fj. In the leading power, the first-order change divided by kF is −j(bu)e. In the second power, the surviving term is (b−1)(bu)e/2. Their sum is −θ(u)(bu)e/2. To keep track of the remainder, expand yk modulo F² and ye modulo F. Multiplication by D clears every denominator in the remainder, with one factor F left. In particular the following quantity is an integer multiple of F.

D[beθ(u)ue + 2(C(y) − bkC(u))] ∈ Fℤ.

Multiply by χ(bu) and sum over u. Multiplication by b permutes the units, so ∑χ(bu)C(y) = ∑χ(u)C(u) = TF, the generalized Bernoulli value at level F divided by k. The other terms use χ(bu) = χ(b)χ(u). Every summand on the remainder side is divisible by ℓm in the coefficient ring. This gives the congruence used by the count.

D[χ(b)beS − 2(χ(b)bk − 1)TF] ≡ 0   (mod ℓm).

What a Frobenius test measures

Choose a base prime r ≡ 1 modulo F. Let L be a list of distinct auxiliary primes q ≡ 1 modulo F, different from r, at which the multiplicative order of r is prime to ℓ. Call the space at this cutoff, before imposing the base-prime condition, Sbefore. Write SL for its cocycles vanishing on the entire decomposition groups over r and the primes in L. Even S∅ imposes vanishing over r. With each list comes a second function νL in the dual character χα−1. On the subgroup fixing the Fth roots of unity its values are additive and killed by ℓm. Their annihilator is a principal ideal, with generator aL. Put jL = v(aL) and J = v(ℓm). Thus jL ≤ J. The induction uses lists for which the cutoff a₀ divides aL. The initial list has this property, and each new test preserves it.

If SL contains a nonzero c, the prime selection theorem chooses a new q with two properties at once. Evaluation on a Frobenius element φ at q detects c, meaning c(φ) ≠ 0. Every value of νL on the subgroup fixing the roots of unity is an O-multiple of νL(φ). For the longer list L′ there is then an inertia element τ at q for which νL′(τ) equals νL(φ) times a unit. The two values have identical annihilators. Since the entire next system contains this inertia value, aL divides aL′. Denote their quotient by d.

Reciprocity controls the image of the linear evaluation map c ↦ c(φ). In the finite coefficient quotient the characters of the two cocycles multiply to χ. Their cup product is a global degree-two class. At the other primes in the finite ramification set the local coboundary condition makes its restriction trivial. The global sum of local invariants thus leaves zero at q. Local unramified orthogonality, with c zero on inertia there, makes the product of the inertia coefficient of the dual class and the value c(φ) vanish. This conclusion holds in the finite coefficient quotient. The proof first tests it with linear functionals which separate its elements.

Concretely, choose a generator w of the cyclic coefficient subgroup killed by aL′ and write νL′(τ) = y w. Its annihilator is (aL). If the inertia value is nonzero, its order in a cyclic module over a discrete valuation ring gives v(y) = v(d). Thus the reciprocity relation y c(φ) = 0 implies d c(φ) = 0. If the inertia value is zero, its annihilator is the unit ideal and the cutoff dividing aL forces the cutoff space to vanish. The chosen nonzero evaluation therefore forces v(d) > 0. The image of evaluation, lying in cyclic d-torsion, has length at most v(d). An element in its kernel vanishes at the whole decomposition group over q. On the roots-of-unity subgroup it is additive, and the quotient of the decomposition group by inertia is topologically generated by Frobenius. Conjugation transports vanishing to the other places over q. Thus the kernel lies in SL′.

length SL + jL ≤ length SL′ + jL′,   jL′ = jL + v(d) ≤ J.

Check one length loss over ℤ₃

In ℚ₃/ℤ₃ take w = 1/27 modulo ℤ₃. Its annihilator is (27), and the annihilator of 3w is (9). Their quotient is 3. As an example of the evaluation map, send (ℤ/9) ⊕ (ℤ/3) onto the order-three subgroup generated by 1/3 via the second coordinate. The source has length three, the kernel has length two, and the image has length one. Adding this loss to the old annihilator valuation changes 2 to 3. This finite calculation checks the direction and size of one step. Choosing a Frobenius with these properties is the arithmetic assertion above.

Whenever SL is nonzero, the next integer jL′ is strictly larger. It cannot exceed J. In the complementary case α agrees with χ modulo the maximal ideal at every group element. Primitivity and the prime-to-ℓ order imply that α is unramified away from ℓ. At ℓ, an inertia element acting by −1 on ℓth roots of unity gives a unit α(δ) − 1 since ℓ is odd. For a normalized cocycle killed by π, the local coboundary witness over ℓ must be zero. Evaluating its defining equation at δ multiplies the witness by the unit α(δ) − 1 and gives zero. Away from ℓ the cocycle already vanishes on inertia.

To see what these local conditions force globally, apply an additive functional from the π-torsion to the field of ℓ elements. The resulting scalar cocycle s has cyclotomic action. Kummer theory realizes it by a radical β with βℓ = a ∈ ℚ× and gβ/β = ζs(g) for a primitive ℓth root ζ. Vanishing on inertia makes every prime exponent of a divisible by ℓ. Unique factorization in ℚ and oddness of ℓ now give a = uℓ for a rational u, including its sign. For example, −8/125 has exponents 3 and −3 and cube root −2/5. Thus β = uζi, so s(g) = i(χ̄(g) − 1), where χ̄ is the action modulo ℓ. At δ the left side is zero and χ̄(δ) − 1 is nonzero. Hence i = 0. All the scalar tests vanish, and linear functionals separate the π-torsion points. Finally, if πk+1c = 0, apply this first step to πkc and descend on k. The original length here is zero.

The construction of the auxiliary functions gives the unit relating the two local values. The carry congruence gives the valuation against which the length is bounded. Prime selection uses Chebotarev, and the test of each new restriction uses duality and orthogonality.

Which character takes values in the cyclotomic integers?

The Jacobi identity multiplies two algebraic integers. A sum computed only modulo p would lose the ideal it is supposed to measure. Let K = ℚ(ζ), where ζ has order M ≥ 1, and choose a prime ideal of norm p with p ∤ M. Its quotient has p elements. Identify it with 𝔽p and call the resulting reduction π. The algebraic integer ζ satisfies the cyclotomic polynomial ΦM. Its reduction satisfies the same polynomial modulo p. As p ∤ M, the roots of XM − 1 are simple, and the cyclotomic factors for the divisors of M have disjoint roots. A root of ΦM therefore has exact order M. In particular πζ has that order and M divides p − 1.

Put h = (p − 1)/M. For each nonzero x in 𝔽p, the element xh is an Mth root of unity. The M powers of πζ are distinct and list every such root. Find the exponent 0 ≤ a < M with xh = (πζ)a and set χ(x) = ζa. Set χ(0) = 0. Multiplying two residues adds their exponents modulo M, so χ is multiplicative. Its order is exactly M. Indeed, if χk = 1, a generator g of 𝔽p× satisfies ghk = 1 after reduction. Hence Mh divides hk, so M divides k. Conversely all nonzero values have Mth power one. This explains why the nontriviality checks on the Jacobi characters reduce to exponent checks.

Take M = 5 and p = 11, with πζ = 3. The powers of 3 starting at exponent zero are 1, 3, 9, 5, 4 and then 1. Since h = 2, square the input 2 to obtain 4. The required lift is χ(2) = ζ⁴. Squaring this value gives χ(4) = ζ³. Checking the other way, 4² ≡ 5 ≡ 3³ modulo 11. For the other reduction π′ζ = 9, the input 2 still gives 2² = 4. Since 9² ≡ 4 modulo 11, its lift is now χ′(2) = ζ². The prime ideal is part of the construction.

Why every prime above p occurs only once

For each invertible residue t modulo M let σt(ζ) = ζt and put Pt = ker(π ∘ σt). This inverse-image convention is what sets the indices in the signed divisor. Every reduction is onto, since ordinary integers already give all of 𝔽p. Its kernel is therefore a maximal ideal of norm p. If two kernels agreed, subtract from any algebraic integer the ordinary integer representing its first reduction. The difference would also belong to the second kernel, forcing both reductions to agree on that element. Applying this to ζ gives (πζ)s = (πζ)t, hence s = t.

These φ(M) distinct maximal ideals are pairwise coprime, and each divides (p). Their product divides (p) and already has norm pφ(M). This equals the norm of (p), because [K : ℚ] = φ(M). The leftover integral ideal has norm one and is the unit ideal. Thus (p) = ∏tPt. For a Jacobi sum J dividing p, this gives ordPₜ(J) ∈ {0,1}. Testing π(σtJ) = 0 tells exactly which exponent is one. In the example at 11 the four reductions send ζ to 3, 9, 5 and 4. A repeated prime would exhaust too much of the norm.

To tell which primes occur, reduce σt(Jj) modulo P. The result is ∑ xA(1 − x)B with A = h[t]N and B = h[jt]N. Both exponents lie strictly between 0 and p − 1. Expand the binomial. In degree A + k the sum of powers over the field vanishes unless p − 1 divides the degree. Since all degrees are positive and below 2(p − 1), only k = p − 1 − A can contribute. When this index is in the expansion its binomial coefficient is nonzero modulo p, since B < p. Thus the residue is zero exactly when A + B < p − 1, or [t]N + [jt]N < N. Each addition without a carry contributes one factor of Pt to (J).

Let e(t) count these additions. For b ≥ 1 there are b − 1 steps. The number of carries is ⌊b[t]N/N⌋, since each new addition increases the integer quotient by one precisely when a carry occurs. Hence e(t) = b − 1 − ⌊b[t]N/N⌋. Conjugation exchanges Pt and P−t, so the exponent in (c(J)/J) is e(−t) − e(t) = θN(t). The product with its complex conjugate is 1 by cancellation. At b = 0 the Jacobi product is empty and XP = 1, as all the floor weights vanish.

Compute a denominator at level 5

Take N = 5, b = 3 and p = 11, so h = 2. At t = 1 the Jacobi factors for j = 1,2 give exponents (A,B) = (2,2),(2,4). Both sums vanish modulo 11 because their degrees stay below 10. At t = 4 the pairs are (8,8),(8,6). Both reach degree 10. The surviving terms give −28 ≡ 5 and −15 ≡ 7 modulo 11. Thus e(1) = 2 and e(4) = 0. The quotient c(J)/J has exponent −2 at P1, +2 at P4, and 0 at the other two primes. This agrees with θ5(1) = ⌊3/5⌋ − ⌊12/5⌋ = −2.

Why each Jacobi sum divides the split prime

The cyclotomic construction determines a signed ideal by testing a product of Jacobi sums at the primes above p. A zero residue proves that one such prime divides a factor. How can we tell that its square does not? Each factor has an explicit partner whose product with it is p. At a split unramified prime, the order of p is one, so the nonnegative orders of the two partners sum to one. This turns the residue test into an exact exponent.

In the product Gψ(χ)Gψ(φ), group pairs (x,y) by t = x+y. At t = 0 their total is φ(−1)∑x(χφ)(x) = 0. At t ≠ 0 put x = tu. The two characters contribute (χφ)(t)χ(u)φ(1−u). Summing yields Gψ(χφ)J(χ,φ).

A second orthogonality identity says Gψ(ρ)Gψ−1(ρ−1) = p for nontrivial ρ. To see why, expand the two sums and put x = uy for y ≠ 0. At each y the summand becomes ρ(u)ψ(y(u−1)). We can include y = 0 because its total is ∑uρ(u) = 0. Summing over all y now leaves only u = 1, contributing p. Apply the first identity twice, once with ψ and once with its inverse and the inverse multiplicative characters. Multiplication and the second identity give pJ(χ,φ)J(χ−1,φ−1) = p². Cancelling p and using injectivity of the two field embeddings gives the claimed identity in R.

Take the level M = 3, b = 2 and p = 7. In ℤ[ω], with ω²+ω+1 = 0, choose the cubic character determined by χ(3) = ω, since 3 generates 𝔽₇×. At the prime where ω reduces to 2 it satisfies the required reduction χ(x) ≡ x². Here the Jacobi product has one factor, J(χ,χ). The inputs 0 and 1 contribute zero. For x = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 the five contributions are ω², 1, ω², 1, ω². The sum and its inverse-character partner are 2+3ω² and 2+3ω. Their product is 4+6(ω+ω²)+9 = 7. At ω ≡ 2 modulo 7 the first is zero and the second is one. At ω ≡ 4 their roles reverse. Each factor has order exactly one at the prime where it vanishes.

How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class

The Jacobi sum uses a prime ideal P whose residue field has a prime number of elements. To apply that calculation to an arbitrary nonzero integral ideal 𝔞, the same P must make 𝔞P principal. For a prime of a number field K above a rational prime p, its absolute norm NP is the residue field size pf. Thus absolute residue degree one means NP = p. We can require this degree, prescribe the ideal class [P] = c and exclude any finite set of prime ideals of K.

Let H be the Hilbert class field of K. Its Artin isomorphism sends [P] to the arithmetic Frobenius at a prime above P, acting on residues by x ↦ xNP. Apply the degree-one prime theorem to H/K with target automorphism Art(c). The Frobenius supplied by the theorem restricts to this precise automorphism. Two Frobenius lifts at the same place agree modulo inertia, and inertia in H/K is trivial. Applying Art−1 gives [P] = c. In the cyclotomic application take c = [𝔞]−1 and exclude the primes dividing N𝒪K, where N is the cyclotomic level. This set is finite because N ≠ 0. Then p ∤ N, reduction preserves the order of ζN, and N divides p − 1 as the character construction requires. The inverse on [𝔞] comes from [𝔞][P] = 1.

How can the proof still impose absolute degree one?

Write L/K for the finite Galois extension and g for the requested automorphism. The proof chooses an auxiliary prime ℓ with [L : K] dividing ℓ − 1 and Φℓ irreducible over L. In L(ζℓ) choose an automorphism h restricting to g on L and raising ζℓ to a generator τ of (ℤ/ℓℤ)×. Irreducibility permits this choice by adjusting a lift of g with an automorphism fixing L. Take the fixed field Z of ⟨h⟩ inside this compositum. The powers of h realize every exponent on ζℓ, so Φℓ is still irreducible over Z.

Above the finite exclusions and the ramified primes of L/K there are only finitely many primes of Z. Away from these, seek a prime w with Nw ≡ τ modulo ℓ. A prime-distribution result gives divergence of the sum of reciprocal prime-ideal norms in this residue class. Primes of absolute degree at least two contribute at most [Z : ℚ]∑p primep−2, since at most [Z : ℚ] primes of Z lie above each p. The finite exclusions also contribute a finite amount. Hence a remaining w has prime norm p. For P below w, the equality Nw = (NP)f(w/P) forces NP = p.

A Frobenius lift at w fixes Z and acts on the ℓth roots by the pth power, since p ≠ ℓ and those roots remain distinct after reduction. Its action in the compositum is therefore hj with τj = τ. Thus j ≡ 1 modulo ℓ − 1. The order of g divides [L : K], which divides ℓ − 1, so gj = g. The equality of norms lets the same lift serve as an arithmetic Frobenius at P.

Its ideal has the required factors for (y), and pairing t with −t gives Z(y)c(Z(y)) = 1 by antisymmetry. Divide this element by XP. How much does the choice of generator matter? If X and X′ solve the same problem, their quotient w generates the unit ideal. It is an algebraic unit, and wc(w) = 1. Both conditions on the generator enter this argument. For example, (3 + 4i)/5 in ℚ(i) has complex absolute value one, but its trace 6/5 rules out integrality.

What happens to the exponents under the norm?

Let q be a prime with q ∤ N, and let u be its residue modulo N. For b < q, sum the weights of the units upstairs lying over a fixed t downstairs. Among the q possible lifts [t]N + iN, exactly one is divisible by q, namely q[u−1t]N. Its missing floor is ⌊b[u−1t]N/N⌋. Summing before removing that lift gives ⌊b[t]N/N⌋ plus a constant independent of t. For 0 < b < q, this follows because the residues ib run once through all residues modulo q. Taking the difference at t and −t cancels the constant. At b = 0 both sides vanish.

∑t′ ↦ t θqN(t′) = θN(t) − θN(u−1t).

Take a nonzero ideal 𝔞′ upstairs and elements X′ and X satisfying the two defining conditions for 𝔞′ and its relative norm downstairs. The field norm of X′ multiplies its conjugates over KN. Grouping the factors of their ideals by the fibres t′ ↦ t gives the sum on the left. On the right the first weight is the exponent for X and the second gives the exponent for σu−1(X). The principal fractional ideals of the field norm and of X/σu−1(X) therefore coincide. Both generators have product one with their complex conjugates, so their quotient is a root ξn in the smaller field with ξn2N = 1.

Which degree counts the conjugates, and which degree counts the ideal?

Put N = Fd and enlarge the level to qN by a fresh prime q coprime to N. The construction chooses its two cyclotomic fields inside one algebraic closure. Even if the two embeddings were initially chosen separately, every Nth root of unity is a power of a primitive root of order qN. This puts the smaller field inside the larger one in precisely one way compatible with the chosen embeddings. Restricting the same place above the rational prime r then gives primes 𝔭′ above 𝔭.

The field norm counts conjugates. A relative automorphism fixes the roots of order N and can act by any nonzero residue on a primitive qth root. Indeed, for a generator g modulo q, the Chinese remainder theorem gives an exponent equal to 1 modulo N and to g modulo q. The resulting power map on roots gives an automorphism τ of KqN over KN. Its first q − 1 powers are distinct on the primitive qth root. They exhaust the relative Galois group since the degree is φ(qN)/φ(N) = q − 1, where φ counts invertible residues. Hence the product of τi(Xqd) for 0 ≤ i < q − 1 is its field norm.

The ideal norm counts residue-field degree. For r ∤ qN, write ordn(r) for the least positive k with rk ≡ 1 modulo n. At either level the prime is unramified, and Frobenius acts on the roots by the rth power. Its order is the absolute residue degree. Write κ(𝔭) for the residue field at 𝔭. Degrees multiply in the tower of residue fields, giving

s = [κ(𝔭′) : κ(𝔭)] = ordqN(r) / ordN(r),   Norm(𝔭′) = 𝔭s.

Thus Xds satisfies the two generator conditions for Norm(𝔭′). Raising to the power s multiplies each ideal exponent by s and preserves the identity with complex conjugation. This explains its exponent in both the norm formula and the congruence. The denominator in the norm formula uses the inverse of the qth-power action on the lower roots. The admissible auxiliary primes have orders of r prime to ℓ, and r ≡ 1 modulo F. By the Chinese remainder theorem their least common multiple is ordqN(r), so ℓ ∤ s.

8.24Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

To combine several primes in the minus estimate, the proof discards some character factors from an ℓ-adic product. This step is safe when each discarded factor has nonnegative valuation. Where does that integrality come from? At twist j put k = j + 1 ≥ 2. If χ has level N, conductor f and primitive character χ*, its denominator-cleared Bernoulli value is α = NPkBk,χ*, where Pk is the product of the primes at most k + 1. The two integer multipliers pay for different denominators.

Expand the Bernoulli polynomial in ordinary Bernoulli numbers Bh. The rational coefficient attached to one residue a is

fk−1Bk(a/f) = ∑h=0k binom(k,h) Bh fh−1ak−h.

At h = 0 the factor f−1 can introduce a conductor denominator. Multiplying the entire sum by f changes every exponent to the nonnegative integer h. For a positive even h, the von Staudt–Clausen formula expresses Bh as an integer minus a sum of 1/p over primes with p−1 dividing h. Each such p is at most h+1 ≤ k+1, so it divides Pk. The remaining indices give B₀ = 1, B₁ = −½ and Bh = 0 for odd h > 1. Thus PkBh is integral throughout, and fPk times the displayed coefficient is an integer, residue by residue.

Multiplying these integers by χ*(a) and summing keeps the result in the ring generated by the character values. A unit value is a root of unity, hence an algebraic integer, and a nonunit contributes zero. Each unit modulo f lifts to a unit modulo N, so the values of χ* belong to the ring generated by the original χ. Finally f divides N. Multiplying by the integer N/f proves the required integrality of α in that ring.

The same scaling also allows a single archimedean bound. For k ≥ 2 the Fourier expansion on [0,1] pairs the positive and negative frequencies. Each pair of unit complex phases has absolute value at most 2. Its reciprocal-power sum is bounded by 2∑m≥11/m² = π²/3 < 4. Consequently |Bk(x)| ≤ 4k!/(2π)k. There are f terms in the primitive sum, each carrying fk−1 and a character value of absolute value at most 1. Using f ≤ N, Pk ≤ 4k+1 and 4/(2π) ≤ 1 gives |α| ≤ 16Nk+1k!. The denominator bound uses von Staudt–Clausen and the primorial estimate. The absolute-value bound uses the Fourier series and the sum of reciprocal squares.

For a localization-kernel class x, choose a power ℓs killing x. At a sufficiently high cyclotomic level the congruence for z holds modulo ℓs and the restriction of the approximating element vanishes on x. The error acts by zero on x. Descent gives z(φ(H)x) = 0. On the sign component c acts by (−1)k, so the determinant of multiplication by z on the quotient imposing this sign also kills φ(H)x. This last deduction uses the adjugate identity in the quotient.

A denominator-cleared nonzero integer multiple of this determinant has absolute value at most the determinant bound raised to ⌊n/2⌋. Its ℓ-adic valuation bounds an exponent r₀ for the determinant. With r₁ = vℓ(φ(H)), the power ℓr, r = r₀ + r₁, annihilates the minus summand. Bounding the logarithm of the determinant bound together with log(Nℓ) gives

r log ℓ ≤ 30n(j+1) log(jℓN).

For the other factor in the length estimate, pass to the first cyclotomic layer of degree m over ℚ, with m ≤ ℓn. The ℓ-torsion of the ambient cohomology injects into a finite Selmer quotient of size at most ℓ2m times that layer’s class number. The class-number estimate gives a torsion length g ≤ 8ℓn log(ℓN). For the minus submodule M killed by ℓr, multiplication by ℓa−1 embeds each layer M[ℓa]/M[ℓa−1] into M[ℓ]. The bottom layer is finite by the Selmer count. Induction through at most r layers proves that M is finite and its length is at most rg. For ℤ/9 ⊕ ℤ/3, the subgroup killed by 3 has order 9, and the next quotient has order 3. Its length is 2+1=3, within the allowance 2·2. The annihilating determinant bounds the number of layers and the Selmer count bounds the size of each. Combining these inequalities gives mℓ,j log ℓ ≤ 240ℓn²(j+1) log²(jℓN). The constant in the public theorem is existential. The factors 30 and 8 exhibit one witness.

Each automorphism of the ambient cyclotomic field, raised to 2e+1o, fixes E. This follows from the 2-power congruence, the kernel condition defining the base field, and the two quadratic character conditions, which are killed by squaring. The Galois quotient has order n. If an odd prime ℓ divides n, Cauchy’s theorem gives a quotient element of order ℓ, hence ℓ divides o. Summing the preceding estimate over 1 ≤ j < t bounds the contribution of each such prime by 240ℓn²t² log²(tℓN). All terms are nonnegative, so the sum can be enlarged to the fixed odd prime divisors of o. In particular, for o a power of two the first term alone suffices.

Counting the generators before bounding the length

Fix an odd prime ℓ dividing the degree of the field E. The determinant calculation above tells us how many powers of ℓ annihilate the minus group. One also needs to bound how many independent classes can survive a single multiplication by ℓ. Write X for the ambient twisted first cohomology group and X[ℓ] for its subgroup killed by ℓ. The argument counts this subgroup even though it only needs a bound for the minus classes.

Let F = E(μℓ) and put m = [F:ℚ], n = [E:ℚ]. Choose, for each class in X[ℓ], a cocycle taking values in the order-ℓ subgroup of ℚℓ/ℤℓ. Indeed, if ℓ times a representative is the coboundary of a coefficient b, choose b′ with ℓb′ = b in the divisible group ℚℓ/ℤℓ. Subtract the coboundary of b′. The new representative is killed by ℓ pointwise. Over F the cyclotomic character is 1 modulo ℓ. Restricted to this subgroup of values, the twisted cocycle rule becomes ordinary addition. One obtains an additive character of the absolute Galois group of F, unramified outside the primes over ℓ because the original cocycle factors through the Galois group with that ramification condition. If two chosen cocycles give the same character, their difference restricts to zero. The index [F:E] divides ℓ − 1, so averaging over the cosets is allowed in ℤℓ. The coboundary lemma then identifies their classes over E. This gives an injection of sets. If E embeds in the cyclotomic field of level N, then F embeds at level ℓN.

Choose a primitive ℓth root ζ in F. Kummer theory attaches to such a character φ a nonzero radical β with gβ = ζφ(g)β and βℓ = a in F×. Unramifiedness makes the valuation of a divisible by ℓ at each prime outside S, where S is the set over ℓ. Changing a by an ℓth power in F leaves the character determined by the radical unchanged. Indeed the two resulting radicals, after scaling, differ by a root of unity fixed by every g. The characters therefore inject into the multiplicative group of allowed a modulo ℓth powers.

To count this quotient, remove the primes in S from the fractional ideal of a and divide the remaining prime exponents by ℓ. Its class in the ideal class group with these primes inverted belongs to ClS(F)[ℓ]. Every such class occurs because its ℓth power is principal away from S, and a generator gives an admissible a. The kernel consists of S-units modulo powers. These are the elements with valuation zero outside S. For a concrete count, take ℚ, S = {3} and cubes. After removing a rational cube every allowed number is represented by exactly one of 1, 3 and 9. The sign is already a cube. This illustrates the quotient being counted. The earlier injection uses a field containing μℓ.

Over F, the S-unit factor has order ℓr₁+r₂−1+|S| |μℓ(F)|, where r₁ counts real embeddings and r₂ counts conjugate pairs. The root-of-unity factor is at most ℓ, both r₁+r₂ and |S| are at most m, and the order of ClS(F)[ℓ] is at most the ordinary class number hF. If g is the dimension of X[ℓ] over the field with ℓ elements, the count gives the following inequality.

ℓg ≤ ℓ2mhF.

The cyclotomic comparison gives log hF ≤ 3m log(ℓN). Taking logarithms, using m ≤ ℓn and log ℓ ≥ log 2 > 5/8, gives g ≤ 8ℓn log(ℓN). Finally, if ℓr kills the group being bounded, its length is at most rg. For successive kernels of ℓi on X, multiplication by ℓi injects the next quotient into X[ℓ]. There are r quotients. This explains the product of the constant 8 from the dimension estimate and the constant 30 from the determinant estimate. 8.26Absorbing the bound into the window

Set u = Nt and suppose 1 ≤ N,t, n ≤ N, and log u ≤ 2W. Then nt ≤ u, t ≤ u, and log(ℓu) ≤ ℓu. The first term is at most 3u³ ≤ 3u⁴. Each term inside the exceptional sum is at most ℓ³u⁴. Consequently

B− ≤ Ku⁴ ≤ K exp(8W),   K = 3 + |C| ∑ℓ∣o, ℓ odd prime ℓ³.

Here K depends only on the bound’s constant and the fixed base degree. The count theorem converts the free-parameter estimate into its admissible-window version at height exponent 401. For 0 < ε < 1/52 the Page-layer condition, conductor estimate and prime-pair bound give log(Nt) ≤ 2xε/4 for sufficiently large x in the selected interval. With W = xε/4, the odd-minus term joins the prime-2 and odd-plus terms under the common ceiling √exp(xε). The argument here uses the specified duality and orthogonality inputs, the primitive reciprocity count, the integral Stickelberger congruence, and the Kummer radical and class-number theorems used to count generators.

8.27Finding two primes that work for every required twist

The host construction applies the following prime-pair theorem to a fixed primitive character’s window. For a fixed primitive ψ, take M equal to its conductor and A equal to the cohomological window exponent J. Fix 0 < ε < 1/52 and A ≥ 1. For every sufficiently large Y one pair of primes q,d has to work at every y between Y and YA, for every required character. A zero-free box of height H means that L(s,χ) never vanishes for Re s > 1 − 1/400 and |Im s| ≤ H.

Put z = Yε/5 and z′ = z(log Y)². Take q ≡ 3 modulo 8 with z/2 < log q ≤ z. For this q, let B be q times the product of the odd primes at most z. The second prime must satisfy d ≡ 7 modulo 16 and d ≡ −1 modulo B, with z′/2 < log d ≤ z′. The Chinese remainder theorem makes these two conditions one reduced residue class modulo 16B. For a small illustration, z = 3 and q = 11 give B = 33. The prime 263 is 7 modulo 16 and 263 + 1 = 8 · 33. This checks the congruences alone. The analytic selection still has to take place inside that progression.

8.28How many primes can a failed twist eliminate?

In either selection step write U for the upper bound on the candidate prime p. The candidates form a set P in one reduced progression with √U < p ≤ U. The modulus m must be positive and divisible by 8, with a residue class coprime to m. The size conditions are (log Y)² log m/4 ≤ log U and Yε/6 ≤ log U ≤ Yε/5(log Y)². For the mean-square estimate each prime divisor of m must either be at most Yε/5 or exceed (YA)400. On this range the prime-count theorem supplies |P| ≥ U9/10. Let Ξ be a set of at most R primitive base characters, with conductor ≤ F ≤ √U. For ξ ∈ Ξ, twisting by the quadratic symbol (·/p) gives a primitive character of conductor fp, where f is the conductor of ξ. The inequality p > F ensures coprimality. Set H = FU.

Why the progression still contains enough primes

The selection argument spends a fraction of the primes in one residue class. It needs a positive lower bound for the denominator even when the modulus grows with the first chosen prime. As in both stages, 8 divides m and a is coprime to m. Put L = log U, let π(U;m,a) count all primes up to U congruent to a modulo m, and write li(u) = ∫₂ᵘ dt/log t. The progression theorem supplies a main term B. Without an exceptional zero it is li(U)/φ(m). With an exceptional pair (χ, β) it is

B = [li(U) − Re χ(a) li(Uβ)] / φ(m).

Here χ is a nontrivial quadratic character modulo m with a real zero β between 1 − 1/(8 log m) and 1. Keeping this term matters for a progression on which χ(a) = 1, because it subtracts almost the whole main term if β is close to one. The relative prime-number estimate bounds the error by B times a constant times [exp(−c₃L/log m) + exp(−√(c₃L))]. Uniformly over the admitted data this multiplier is at most ½ for sufficiently large Y. Indeed L/log m ≥ (log Y)²/4 and L ≥ Yε/6. The lower and upper admitted bounds on L also give log m ≤ 4Yε/5, which puts L in the theorem’s range C₀ log m · log(log m + 2) ≤ L.
