How can the error shrink with the exceptional main term?

Write d = log m, L = log U, and φ = φ(m). When an exceptional pair exists, set η = min{1, (1−β)d} and s = χ(a) ∈ {−1,1}. In its absence take η = 1, s = 0 and β = 1. The difficulty occurs at s = 1. As β approaches one, both the expected number of primes and the permissible error in this class shrink. We need the same factor η in two estimates.

Lower bound for the corrected main term. Suppose U ≥ 16 and L ≥ d. Then B ≥ P, where

P = Uη/(2φL).

Indeed β ≥ ½ and Uβ ≥ 2. If s ≤ 0, integrating 1/log t from U/2 to U already gives φB ≥ U/(2L). If s = 1, integrate from Uβ to U. Throughout this interval 1/log t ≥ 1/L. Its length is U[1−exp(−(1−β)L)] ≥ Uη/2. Here (1−β)L ≥ η and 1−exp(−η) ≥ η/2 for 0 ≤ η ≤ 1, by concavity and the endpoint values. This gives the bound for both signs.

The corresponding saving in the error. Let Ψ(t) sum log p for each prime power pk ≤ t congruent to a modulo m. Its model is F(t) = (t − s tβ/β)/φ. The analytic input, obtained by summing the errors for Dirichlet characters and applying their orthogonality, gives constants A, c > 0 such that

|Ψ(t) − F(t)| ≤ A tη[exp(−c log t/d) + exp(−c√(log t))]/φ.

This holds for 8 ∣ m, gcd(a,m) = 1 and log t ≥ C d log(d+2) with an absolute C large enough. To see where η enters for large moduli, recall that the contribution from a zero ρ, after dividing the weighted explicit formula by t, contains tRe ρ−1. A very close exceptional zero forces the remaining zeros farther to the left by the Deuring–Heilbronn theorem. The density estimate at this modulus counts zeros separated in height for each character. A local count restores their multiplicities. Once the weighted bound is available, partial summation converts it to a prime count. After the exceptional zero has been set aside, these two inputs bound the relevant weighted zero sum by a constant times η dN exp(−c′ log t/d) for fixed N and c′ > 0. The remaining power of d can be paid for explicitly. Once log t ≥ (2N/c′)d log(d+2), we have dN exp(−c′ log t/(2d)) ≤ 1. Half the exponential decay and the whole factor η survive. When d is at most a fixed small multiple of √(log t), the small-modulus argument recovers η while summing the character errors. The explicit formula, zero-density and repulsion estimates are the deeper analytic inputs to this step. A published zero-density theorem incorporating repulsion is given by Thorner and Zaman, Refinements to the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions, Theorem 2.1[112].

How does the square-root exponential arise for one character?

Write d = log m, s = √(log y), and ψχ(y) = ∑n≤y Λ(n)χ(n). In the small-modulus range, d is at most a fixed small multiple of s. Take cZ to be the smaller of 1/20 and a positive constant provided by the ordinary zero-free-region theorem. Its region is Re z ≥ 1 − cZ/log(m(|Im z| + 2)), with 0 < cZ ≤ 1/20. Let Bχ consist of the zeros of L(·,χ) in this region. Across the characters of this modulus there is at most one such zero. If present, it is simple, real, and belongs to a nonprincipal quadratic character. The product over all characters is what makes uniqueness simultaneous. See Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Theorem 12.3[113]. There are constants c, C > 0 such that for y ≥ 2 and d ≤ cs,

|ψχ(y) − 𝟙χ principaly + ∑β∈Bχ yβ/β| ≤ Cy exp(−cs).

For a nonprincipal χ, smooth by weighting Λ(n)χ(n) with y/n − 1 for n ≤ y. Denote this sum by S(y). The contour formula for it has a linear term D(1)y, where D = −L′/L, and a term −yβ/[β(β − 1)] for each β in the region. To see the rate of decay of the remainder, take height T = exp(cZs/2) and put J = log(m(T + 2)). For d ≤ cZs/4 we have J ≤ 3cZs/4 + 2. The shifted line can be chosen with real part σ ≤ 1 − cZ/(4J). Truncation and the shifted line together cost at most a constant times (s + 2)³(y/T + Tyσ). For sufficiently large s, J ≤ s/4, so Tyσ ≤ y exp(−cZs/2). Absorbing the cubic factor and increasing the constant on bounded s gives a remainder of order y exp(−cZs/4).

To undo the smoothing take u = y(1 + h). The expression [yS(u) − uS(y)]/(u − y) gives weight one to n ≤ y, and a weight between zero and one to the at most yh + 1 integers in (y,u]. This costs at most (yh + 1)log u. The linear term cancels. The difference of the β term is −yβ/β with error at most 2yh, uniformly up to β = 1 from below. Indeed the difference quotient for S(x)/x averages xβ−2 over [y,u], with a factor −yu/β. The relative factor multiplying −yβ/β lies between (1 + h)β−1 and 1 + h, hence within h of 1 since ½ ≤ β < 1. The two contour remainders, after differencing, are of order y exp(−cZs/4)/h. These competing errors explain why the width of the averaging interval matters.

For the principal character, the unrestricted smoothed zeta sum has main term x log x − (1 + γ)x, where γ is Euler’s constant, and error of order x exp(−cζ√(log x)). This zeta estimate also follows from the ordinary prime number theorem. If ψ(t) = t + E(t), partial summation gives S(x) = x ∫1x ψ(t)dt/t². The bound |E(t)| ≪ t exp(−b√(log t)) makes ∫x∞ |E(t)|dt/t² exponentially small in √(log x), after decreasing b. Its constant ∫1∞ E(t)dt/t² equals −1 − γ. Indeed −ζ′(w)/[wζ(w)] − 1/(w − 1) is the integral of E(t)t−w−1 for real w > 1. Taking w down to 1 in the integral and the Laurent expansion gives the constant. See Koukoulopoulos, proof of Theorem 8.1[113] and DLMF (25.2.4)[114].

The difference of the principal main term gives y(1 + h)log(1 + h)/h, between y and y(1 + h). Remove the powers of primes dividing m. At each exponent their weights sum to at most log m, and there are at most log y/log 2 exponents. Now put c₀ = min(1, cζ, cZ/4) and h = exp(−c₀s/2). Both h and exp(−c₀s)/h equal exp(−c₀s/2). The logarithms in the short interval and the deleted prime powers fit within Cy exp(−c₀s/4) when d ≤ c₀s/4. This proves the displayed estimate with c = c₀/4. The large-modulus formula below uses the same elementary weights with a different contour and a longer list of zeros.

For a single character let Mχ(y) be y if χ is principal and zero otherwise, with yβ/β subtracted if χ = χ₁. Put η = min(1,(1 − β)d) if a pair was chosen and η = 1 otherwise.

Set cA = min(c/4,cZ) and assume d ≤ cAs. If a selected β lies in the region, the character bound already contains its contribution. If the selected β lies outside, the regional list for χ₁ is empty. The additional term in Mχ₁ has modulus at most 2y exp(−s/2). Indeed β ≥ ½, and 1 − β > cZ/log(2m) ≥ cZ/(2d) ≥ 1/(2s). Since log y = s², this is precisely the loss in the exponent of yβ. This is the exponent-one case of Siegel’s lower bound. For a real primitive character of conductor f and a real zero β near 1 one has 1 − β ≥ bεf−ε. A character modulo m is induced from conductor f ≤ m, and its additional Euler factors have no zeros of positive real part. The factor d in η is at least log 8. Thus introducing η costs at most one further factor m/b. But m² ≤ exp(2cAs), with 2cA ≤ c/2 and 2cA ≤ 1/10. Both exponentials survive. ∑χ mod m |ψχ(y) − Mχ(y)| ≤ [(C + 2)/b] yη exp(−c′s),   c′ = min(c/2, 2/5).

For a reduced class a, multiply each error by the conjugate of χ(a), whose modulus is one, and divide the sum by φ(m). Character orthogonality gives the small-modulus contribution to the weighted progression estimate. The error still falls with η in a class where the exceptional term subtracts from the main term. The right side moves with y but stays to the right of 1. All enclosed zeros therefore stay in the same list at both arguments of the difference. How much of a logarithmic derivative comes from nearby zeros?

A zero of order a gives a term a/(s−ρ) in f′/f. To move a contour near many zeros, we need to bound both their total multiplicity and the part of the derivative left after removing them. Both follow from the same comparison of the size of f at the centre of a disk with its size on the boundary.

Local zero expansion. Let f be analytic on a neighbourhood of the closed disk of centre z₀ and radius r > 0. Suppose f(z₀) ≠ 0 and |f(z)| ≤ B|f(z₀)| throughout the disk, with B ≥ 1. Let Z consist of all zeros at distance at most r/3 from the centre. Write aρ for the order at ρ and N for the sum of these orders. At every s within r/6 of the centre where f(s) ≠ 0,

N ≤ log B / log 2,   |f′(s)/f(s) − ∑ρ∈Z aρ/(s−ρ)| ≤ 72 log B / r.

The zeros in the smaller closed disk are finite, since an accumulation point there would force f to vanish identically. Divide f by the polynomial P(z) = ∏(z−ρ)aρ. At each zero its Taylor expansion shows that the quotient g extends holomorphically with a nonzero value. At the centre, |P(z₀)| ≤ (r/3)N. On the outer circle each zero is at least 2r/3 away. There |P| ≥ (2r/3)N, hence |g| ≤ B 2−N|g(z₀)|. The maximum-modulus principle carries this inequality back to the centre. Cancelling |g(z₀)| gives 2N ≤ B. Maximum-modulus principle, DLMF §1.10(v)[119].

On the disk of radius r/3 the quotient is zero-free. Choose the analytic logarithm H of g/g(z₀) with H(z₀) = 0. Its real part is at most log B by the preceding bound. The Borel–Carathéodory inequality gives |H| ≤ 6 log B on the disk of radius r/4, since 2(r/4)/(r/3−r/4) = 6. For |s−z₀| ≤ r/6, the circle of radius r/12 about s stays in that disk. Cauchy’s estimate bounds |H′(s)| by 72 log B/r. Since f′/f = P′/P + H′, this is exactly the remainder in the displayed formula. Siu, the Borel–Carathéodory theorem[120] · Cauchy’s integral formula for derivatives, DLMF §1.9(iii)[121].

For example, take f(z) = exp(z)(z−1/9)² on the unit disk about zero. At the centre f′/f = −17. The zero contributes 2/(0−1/9) = −18, and the remaining 1 is the logarithmic derivative of the exponential. Counting the zero once would leave an extra pole in the remainder.

Choose 0 < δ ≤ ½, put u = (1 + δ)y and b = yu/(u − y) = y(1 + δ)/δ. Multiply the difference Sχ(u)/u − Sχ(y)/y by b. For every n ≤ y, the two weights differ by 1/y − 1/u = 1/b. Thus these terms contribute exactly ψχ(y). An integer in (y,u] contributes with weight b(1/n − 1/u) between zero and one. Their total in absolute value is at most (δy + 1)log(2y).

Check the weights at 4, 5 and 6

Take the principal character modulo 3, y = 4 and u = 6. Then b = 12. Every integer up to 4 has weight one in the scaled difference. Only 2 and 4 contribute, giving 2 log 2. At 5 the weight is 12(1/5 − 1/6) = 2/5. At 6 it is zero. The difference equals 2 log 2 + (2/5)log 5, so its entire discrepancy from ψχ(4) comes from the short interval.

Two distinct zeros of the same character in this list must have ordinates at least one apart. The strip argument explains how to put the multiplicities back afterwards. The problem here is to bound the number of these separated pairs.

Take q = ⌈mT⌉, V = q³, J = 8(⌊log₂ q⌋ + 1), and N = 2J. Thus q⁸ ≤ N ≤ 256q⁸. For a character χ let PN(s) = ∑n≤N χ(n)n−s. Multiply it by MV(s) = ∑d≤V μ(d)χ(d)d−s. Here μ is the Möbius function. It is zero on integers divisible by a prime square and equals (−1)k on a product of k distinct primes.

In the product the coefficient of χ(n)n−s is bN(n) = ∑dk=n, d≤V, k≤N μ(d). This equals 1 at n = 1. For 1 < n ≤ V every divisor occurs, and their Möbius sum is ∏p∣n(1 − 1) = 0. The product is consequently 1 + DN, where the remainder runs over V < n ≤ VN. Partition it into J sums on doubling intervals. With U = V2j their common form is

BN,U(χ,ρ) = ∑U<n≤2U bN(n)χ(n)n−ρ.

Nonprincipal detector. At a zero of a nonprincipal character, |PN(ρ)| ≤ 8qN−Re ρ. Indeed, complete periods of χ sum to zero, so partial sums on every interval are bounded by 2(m + 1). Partial summation of the tail of the L-series bounds it by 2(m + 1)(1 + |ρ|/Re ρ)N−Re ρ, and 1 + |ρ|/Re ρ ≤ 3T. These bounded partial sums give locally uniform convergence on Re s > 0, so the series there agrees with the continued L-function. Since L(ρ,χ) vanishes, the finite sum equals the negative of the tail. Also |MV(ρ)| ≤ V. Thus |1 + DN| ≤ 8q · q−6 · q³ = 8/q² ≤ ½. The remainder must have absolute value at least ½. At least one of its J blocks therefore has absolute value ≥ 1/(2J).

Check the cancellation before grouping the blocks

Use small cutoffs V = 3 and N = 4 just to check the coefficients. At n = 2 and 3 they are 1 − 1 = 0. At n = 6 the admissible pairs (d,k) are (2,3) and (3,2). Each contributes −1, so the coefficient is −2. The cutoff has removed the pairs (1,6) and (6,1) that would complete the divisor sum. These surviving coefficients are exactly what the detector measures.

The Dirichlet convolution formula gives this identity and the multiplicativity of r. See DLMF (27.5.1)[123].

For n = ph, r(n) = 1 + χ₁(p) + ⋯ + χ₁(p)h. It equals h + 1 when χ₁(p) = 1. When χ₁(p) = −1 it alternates between zero for odd h and one for even h. Subtract this identity at N₀ = ⌊y⌋ and N₁ = ⌊x⌋. The constant γ cancels. Which prime powers survive for the quadratic character modulo 3?

The character has χ₁(2) = −1 and χ₁(7) = 1. At 2 and 4 the divisor sums are 0 and 1, and the prime coefficients are 0 and 2 log 2. At 7 the divisor sum is 2 and the prime coefficient is 2 log 7. At 3 the divisor sum is 1 but the prime coefficient is zero. Thus the divisor sum can count more mass while still detecting the cancellation at 2.

Keep the n indices with |ua| ≥ ε, where r = 16e² and ε = 1/r. The index with value ½ survives and nε² ≤ S. At order j ≥ 2 the discarded terms have total absolute value at most εj−2S. Divide the retained values by their largest modulus, which is at least ½, to obtain n numbers za of modulus at most one with maximum modulus one.

For instance, (1 + i)/2 and (1 − i)/2 both satisfy the disk inequality for u. Their squares sum to zero and their fourth powers sum to −½. Removing failed twists

First remove primes for which some such character has a zero in the box of height H. Choose one offending character for each removed prime. Its conductor determines the prime uniquely. Indeed if fp = f′p′, primality forces p to divide f′ or p′. The first possibility contradicts 0 < f′ ≤ F < p, so p = p′. The zero-density theorem bounds the number of offending primitive characters by C H1/4. Dividing by the number of candidates makes the loss tend to zero.

#primes removed / |P| ≤ C(FU)1/4/U9/10 ≤ C U−21/40.

Thus the same exclusion works for every member of Ξ. The fixed exponent 1/4 counts characters admitting a zero in this particular rectangle.

How can one count characters whose L-function has a zero?

Write Q for the height H of the box in the preceding prime selection. Consider all primitive characters of conductor at most Q that have at least one zero ρ with Re ρ > 399/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. The number of these characters is at most CQ1/4 for every real Q ≥ 3 and a single absolute constant C. One zero, chosen separately for each character, suffices. The argument turns it into a large finite sum on one interval, then bounds how many characters can give large sums on the same interval.

Detecting one zero. For large Q take X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋ + 1) and N = 2J. Here Y is the length of an auxiliary sum within this proof. Multiply the first N terms of L(s,χ), denoted P(s), by M(s) = ∑d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−s, summing over positive integers. The Möbius function μ is zero on multiples of squares of primes. On a product of k distinct primes it is (−1)k, including μ(1) = 1. In the product the coefficient multiplying χ(n)n−s is

a(n) = ∑db=n, 1≤d≤Y, 1≤b≤N μ(d).

For 2 ≤ n ≤ Y every divisor occurs, since Y ≤ N. The sum is zero by expanding (1−1)k over the distinct prime divisors. At n = 1 it is one. Thus PM = 1 + D, where D uses only Y < n ≤ YN. For a short calculation set Y = 3 and N = 4. At 6 only (2,3) and (3,2) qualify, so a(6) = −2. At 4 only (1,4) and (2,2) occur, and their contributions cancel. Truncating the product can leave either outcome beyond the initial range.

How many characters can select the same block?

Write σ₀ = 399/400. Suppose T characters selected one block (U, 2U]. Place their values in rows vχ(n) = χ(n)n−(ρχ−σ₀), and put b(n) = a(n)n−σ₀. Multiplying each row by this same column gives its selected large block. The squared norm of a row is at most U. For two different rows the character χψ̄ at their common product modulus is nonprincipal: equality of the induced characters would identify their conductors and then the original primitive characters. Complete periods of this product sum to zero, so its partial sums have modulus at most the product of the conductors, at most Q². Partial summation against the complex power gives the bound 2Q²(1+|w|) for the inner product, with w = ρχ−σ₀ + conj(ρψ−σ₀). Each of these nonprincipal zeros has real part below 1, and the two imaginary parts have absolute values at most Q. Thus the inner product has modulus at most 8Q³.

The number of divisors of n bounds |a(n)| and is at most a constant times n1/400. Squaring after multiplying by n−σ₀ and summing the U terms gives ∑|b(n)|² ≤ C U−99/100 ≤ C U−197/200. Applying the bound to the rectangular matrix and the column b gives

T/(4J²) ≤ ∑χ |∑n b(n)vχ(n)|² ≤ (U + 8TQ³)C U−197/200.

Since U ≥ Q⁴, the coefficient of T on the right is at most 8CQ−47/50. Above a single threshold independent of the characters, this is at most 1/(8J²), so we can subtract it and obtain T ≤ 8CJ²U3/200. For bounded Q, the finite number of characters below the fixed threshold can be absorbed into the same absolute constant. How accurately does a finite character sum approximate the value at a zero?

Let χ be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo q. Write A(n) = ∑1≤k≤n χ(k) and PN(s) = ∑1≤n≤N χ(n)n−s. A complete period of χ sums to zero. Deleting whole periods bounds |A(n)| uniformly, and we may take B = q+1. For any complex s with σ = Re s > 0, put f(x) = x−s on the positive real axis. The point of using the partial sums A(n) is that the differences of f are absolutely summable throughout this half-plane.

Indeed, integrate f′(x) = −s x−s−1 from n to n+1, and take absolute values inside the integral. This gives |f(n)−f(n+1)| ≤ (|s|/σ)(n−σ−(n+1)−σ). Moreover, on any compact subset with σ ≥ σ₁ > 0 and |s| ≤ K, the difference is at most K n−σ₁−1. Thus G(s) = ∑n≥1 A(n)(f(n)−f(n+1)) converges locally uniformly and defines a holomorphic function there. For finite N, replacing χ(n) by A(n)−A(n−1) gives

PN(s) = ∑1≤n≤N A(n)(f(n)−f(n+1)) + A(N)f(N+1).

The last term tends to zero. For σ > 1, the limit on the left is the absolutely convergent Dirichlet series for L(s,χ). By uniqueness of analytic continuation G therefore gives L throughout σ > 0. Subtracting the displayed identity from G leaves the sum of differences beginning at N+1, followed by minus A(N)f(N+1). In the bound for the sum, the consecutive differences of n−σ telescope to (N+1)−σ. The boundary term costs B(N+1)−σ. Hence for all integers N ≥ 1,

|L(s,χ)−PN(s)| ≤ B(1+|s|/σ)(N+1)−σ ≤ 2B(1+|s|/σ)N−σ.

The second, deliberately weaker bound is the one used in the detector. It applies at a zero even on the left of the line of absolute convergence. One can see the boundary term already with the quadratic character modulo 4, s = 1 and N = 2. Here A(1) = A(2) = 1, so the first two differences give (1−1/2)+(1/2−1/3) = 2/3. The boundary term is +1/3 in the finite identity, giving P₂(1) = 1. Kiran Kedlaya, Notes on analytic number theory, Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.5 and equation (3.2.3)[125].

Why are there exactly J possible blocks?

Fix Q ≥ 20 and a primitive character of conductor 1 < q ≤ Q. It is nonprincipal because the principal character is induced from conductor one. Take a zero ρ with σ = Re ρ > 399/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. For this step the lower bound on σ suffices. Put X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋+1) and N = 2J. The number 2⌊log₂ X⌋+1 is strictly larger than X, including when X is a power of two. Its eighth power is N, so N ≥ X⁸ ≥ Y.

At ρ the remainder bounds |PN(ρ)|. Since |ρ| ≤ σ+Q and σ > 1/2, we have 1+|ρ|/σ ≤ 2+2Q ≤ 3X. Also q+1 ≤ 2X. The weaker inequality σ ≥ 15/16 already gives Nσ ≥ X15/2 = X⁷√X ≥ 4X⁷. The other factor in the detector is MY(ρ) = ∑1≤d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−ρ. Each summand has modulus at most one, so |MY(ρ)| ≤ Y. All four estimates hold simultaneously for every allowed character and zero. Multiplying them gives

|PN(ρ)MY(ρ)| ≤ 2(2X)(3X) X⁴/(4X⁷) = 3/X ≤ 1/2.

By the finite Möbius product identity, the same product is 1+D, where D sums the coefficients a(n)χ(n)n−ρ over Y < n ≤ YN. The reverse triangle inequality gives |D| ≥ 1/2. Partition these integers with endpoints Y, 2Y, 4Y, …, Y2J = YN. There are J+1 endpoints and exactly J intervals. For index j = 0,…,J−1, write Bⱼ(ρ) for the sum on (Y2j, Y2j+1]. The first integer included is Y+1. Each internal endpoint belongs to the earlier interval, and the last interval includes YN. Thus

1/2 ≤ |D| ≤ ∑j=0J−1|Bⱼ(ρ)| ≤ J max0≤j<J|Bⱼ(ρ)|.

For the small product example Y = 3, N = 4 = 2², the two intervals are (3,6] and (6,12]. The coefficient a(6) = −2 belongs entirely to the first block, and a(12) = −1 belongs to the second. In the zero count, each character supplies at least one block of modulus ≥ 1/(2J), with equality allowed. Choosing one such index per character produces the families in the block mean-square estimate. That estimate also needs Re ρ < 1. The Euler product excludes zeros with Re ρ > 1, and the classical nonvanishing theorem excludes the whole line Re ρ = 1 for a nonprincipal character, including the real point ρ = 1. Every chosen zero of conductor greater than one therefore lies strictly to the left of that line. Kedlaya, equation (3.2.1) and Theorems 3.8, 3.10 and 3.11[125].

For the mean square itself the points may be anywhere in that strip, even at the same height. Fix a positive integer U and use the same U integers U < n ≤ 2U for every row. Set vχ(n) = χ(n)n−(ρχ−σ₀). ∑χ∈S |∑U<n≤2U b(n)vχ(n)|² ≤ (U + 8|S|Q³) ∑U<n≤2U|b(n)|².

Write Gχψ = ∑ vχ(n) conj(vψ(n)). The diagonal is at most U since each term is at most one. For χ ≠ ψ let m be the product of their conductors. The sequence ξ(n) = χ(n) conj(ψ(n)) is a character modulo m. On units it is the quotient of the two induced characters. On a nonunit at least one factor vanishes. If ξ were principal, the two induced characters would agree on every unit. Uniqueness of the primitive character inducing a given character would force χ = ψ. A complete period of ξ therefore sums to zero. Multiplication of the unit classes by some a with ξ(a) ≠ 1 leaves the sum unchanged and multiplies it by ξ(a). Deleting complete periods gives |A(r)| ≤ m for A(r) = ∑0≤n<r ξ(n). Andrew Sutherland, Theorem 18.13 and Corollary 18.15[126].

The complex weights vary across the block. Put w = ρχ−σ₀ + conj(ρψ−σ₀), so 0 < Re w < 1 and |Im w| ≤ 2Q. For f(x) = x−w, the derivative has modulus |w|x−Re w−1 ≤ |w|/U throughout the block. Substituting ξ(n) = A(n+1)−A(n) and shifting the second sum leaves endpoint terms f(2U)A(2U+1)−f(U+1)A(U+1), followed by −∑U<n<2U (f(n+1)−f(n))A(n+1). Each endpoint costs at most m and the full difference sum costs at most m|w|. Hence |Gχψ| ≤ 2m(1+|w|) ≤ 8Q³, using m ≤ Q² and |w| ≤ 1+2Q.

It remains to pass from pairwise comparisons to the sum of squares. Write V for the row matrix and Δ = U + 8|S|Q³. Every absolute row sum of G = VV∗ is ≤ Δ, and the same holds for columns by Hermitian symmetry. For any vector z, bound each term in z∗Gz by |Gχψ| (|zχ|²+|zψ|²)/2. Summing gives ‖V∗z‖² ≤ Δ‖z‖². Take z = Vb. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖z‖² = |⟨V∗z,b⟩| ≤ √Δ ‖z‖ ‖b‖. For z ≠ 0 division and squaring give the stated inequality. For z = 0 it already holds.

For a small check of that matrix argument, use the unweighted quadratic characters modulo 3 and 4 on the integers 5, 6, 7, 8. Their rows are (−1,0,1,−1) and (1,0,−1,0). The off-diagonal entry equals −2 even though the complete product period of length 12 sums to zero. The diagonal entries are 3 and 2, so one may take Δ = 5. Against b = (1,0,−1,0) the row outputs are −2 and 2. Their squared sum 8 is bounded by 5‖b‖² = 10. This example checks the finite matrix inequality for arbitrary coefficients.

Here is a uniform constant for that coefficient bound. For ε = 1/400 let K = ⌈21/ε⌉, A = max(1,1/(ε log 2)) and D = AK. If p ≥ K, a prime power pk has k+1 ≤ 2k ≤ pεk divisors. Why averaging the square over primes saves a power of the height

Choose 0 < ε ≤ 1, K ≥ 1 and a sufficiently large Y. Set Z = (YK)400. Fix one height y ∈ [Y,YK] and one complex sequence |κ(n)| ≤ 1 for the entire progression P of primes √U < q ≤ U, q ≡ a mod m. We can take the absolute value of each such sum after summing over q. This order retains cancellation among primes.

For a product nn′, let s be the product of primes outside m whose exponent in nn′ is odd. For an admitted progression and sufficiently large Y, its lower cutoff √U is at least N² and hence every q exceeds N², so a square factor has symbol +1. The primes dividing m contribute a fixed sign on the progression. Indeed, 8 divides m, which fixes the symbol of 2 and the sign in quadratic reciprocity. For odd primes dividing m it also fixes the residue of q modulo that prime. Hence for a sign σ depending on the pair and the progression,

(n/q)(n′/q) = σ(q/s),   σ ∈ {−1,+1}.

For example, 53 and 101 are both 5 modulo 24. The pair (4,3) has s = 1 even though 12 is not a square. Its symbol is −1 at both primes. For (3,5) the symbol is −(q/5), giving +1 at 53 and −1 at 101. These two terms cancel exactly. The example illustrates the correlation on two primes.

Why should ∑q∈P(q/s) be small for s > 1? Split the progression into reduced classes b mod ms above a. Their ordinary prime-counting main terms cancel because the nontrivial character (b/s) sums to zero. A real zero β of a quadratic character χ can add a term proportional to ∑b(b/s)χ(b). Multiplying every class by a unit u ≡ 1 mod m permutes the sum. If χ(u) differs from (u/s), this multiplies it by −1, forcing it to vanish. If the characters agree on these units, the logarithmic integral li(Uβ) is small enough unless β > 1 − c₀/log(mY800K). The near-one uniqueness theorem makes any two such near-one characters agree on common units. Distinct squarefree s would give different symbols on one of those units. The Chinese remainder theorem lets us choose a nonresidue at one prime dividing just one of them and 1 at every other prime involved, as well as modulo m. Thus at most one integer s★ escapes the bound |∑(q/s)| ≤ η|P|, η = Y−(K+1). It is chosen for the progression before y and κ.

To place the output interval beyond a prescribed lower bound, choose X so large that X1/J exceeds that lower bound, the prime-pair threshold, b³ and b400. Choose the primes at X1/J, then take the cohomological window [W, W²] with W ≥ X1/J and W² ≤ X.

Set Z = bW. Since W ≥ b³, Z3/2 ≤ W². For every x ∈ [Z, Z3/2] set x′ = x/b. Both x′ and x are in [W, W²]. Evaluating the page rule at x′ gives xr ≤ c2e(x′) ≤ 2xr. Evaluating the cohomological bound at that same x′ supplies its field at exactly that same tower level. Since x′ ≥ b400, we have

x400 = b400(x′)400 ≤ (x′)401,   exp((x′)ε/2) ≤ exp(xε/2).

All summands in the cohomological sum are nonnegative. Shortening the twist range and increasing the allowed upper bound therefore gives the cohomological bound at the rescaled window. The loss of one power from 401 to 400 pays for rescaling. Within a chosen window the primes can stay fixed, while the tower index depends on the point of evaluation.

8.31From finite subsets of primes to a series

The arithmetic comparison eventually needs a summable sequence of nonnegative terms. Choose the algebraic closure and local data attached to the arithmetic datum. Finiteness of each module length ensures conversion from extended natural numbers to integers recovers its value. For each prime the arithmetic contribution is bounded by its logarithm times the sum of these lengths in the specified range. All finite subsums are bounded by the same B. Their supremum is therefore finite, and equals the sum of the full nonnegative series. This is the use of the universal quantifier over finite sets of primes. The conclusion also includes the finiteness assertion on the relevant twists.

Why is an exponential bound small enough for a final estimate near √x? At the same scale x the weight in a single arithmetic measurement is b = exp(xε). The cohomological series has sum at most exp(xε/2) = √b. Since b ≥ 1, it fits within the allowance b in the finite-place lattice estimate. This is a bound on one input to the measurement. Only after the arithmetic comparisons are added does the proof divide the error by the total weight to bound the centered prime sum.

Turning this bound into the final divisible-lattice estimate also requires rank equalities, the local-to-global normalization and common family parameters. The preceding sections explain how the tower bounds, degree-two estimate and signed character counts apply to the same pair and field. The two-stage prime selection supplies the smoothed-sum and zero-free conditions for the same pair. The remaining interfaces there are the underlying progression, zero-density, mean-square and contour estimates.

9The one-sided window theorem

Suppose the arithmetic argument repeatedly finds a stretch of scales on which a centered prime sum stays below a small power of the scale. A zero of an associated L-function would force a pole of its transform. How can a bound on scattered stretches rule out even one pole? High derivatives let us choose where the integral sees the function.

9.1The hypothesis in logarithmic coordinates

Fix 0 < θ < 1 and δ > 0. Write g(u) = GF(exp u) for a real weighted sum from a finite character family F. The abstract theorem below allows any real measurable g with |g(u)| ≤ C0 exp(2u) for u ≥ 0. Its transform Φ(s) agrees with ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−su) du for Re s > 2. Assume it extends holomorphically in the right half-plane outside a set Z of simple poles, every one of which has positive real part. Every point of the half-plane must have a punctured neighborhood free of Z, including points outside Z. At each pole the residue is nonzero, and at each real pole it is real and strictly positive.

Put U = log Y. Then [Y, Y1+δ] becomes I = [U, (1 + δ)U]. For every η > 0 and every lower limit U0, suppose there exist U ≥ U0 and a majorant R on I with R ≥ max(g, 0), such that R(u) exp(−θu) is integrable there and

∫I R(u) exp(−θu) du ≤ exp(ηU).

Theorem. Every ρ ∈ Z satisfies Re ρ ≤ θ. The window and its majorant may depend on η and U0. Between windows the growth estimate still holds. An arithmetic upper bound GF(y) ≤ C yθ on arbitrarily distant windows suffices. Take R(u) = |C| exp(θu). Its weighted integral equals |C|δU, which is at most exp(ηU) once U is large.

Test the hypothesis on a single pole. Take θ = ½, δ = ½ and g(u) = exp(¾u). Its Laplace transform is 1/(s − ¾). On [U,3U/2] even the smallest admissible majorant has weighted integral 4(exp(3U/8) − exp(U/4)). For η = ⅛ this eventually exceeds exp(ηU) on every window. Change the sign of g and R = 0 works on every window, although the transform still has a pole at ¾. Its residue is now −1. This example explains the sign hypothesis at real poles and why the arithmetic only needs an upper bound.

9.2Choosing a derivative that sees the window

For Re z = σ > 2, define Ak(z) = (−1)kΦ(k)(z)/k!. In a small neighborhood with Re z ≥ 2 + α, α > 0, the differentiated integrand is bounded by C0uk exp(−αu), an integrable function. Repeated differentiation under the integral therefore gives

Ak(σ + iγ) = ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−iγu) Kk,σ(u) du,   Kk,a(u) = ukexp(−au)/k!.

This nonnegative kernel has its maximum at u = k/a for k > 0. Its integral is a−k−1, by substitution and integration by parts. The term g itself may change sign. Adding Re Ak(σ) to the triangle inequality for |Ak(σ + iγ)| replaces |g| by |g| + g = 2 max(g, 0). On I, use this majorant and the inequality vk/k! ≤ exp(v) at v = (σ − θ)u. Off I, use the growth bound. The result is

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ 2 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k + 2C0 ∫(0,∞) ∖ I Kk,σ−2(u) du.

The real derivative acts as a correction for sign. Write g = g+ − g−, both parts nonnegative. The triangle inequality at σ + iγ counts both with a plus sign. At the real center, Ak(σ) = ∫(g+ − g−)K. Adding cancels the entire negative part and leaves at most 2∫g+K. The same derivative order must therefore work at both centers.

The integrand in this tail contains σ − 2 because |g| can grow as exp(2u). Estimating the tails of Kk,σ alone would lose that factor.

9.3A uniform estimate for the tails

For s > λ ≥ 0 and V = (1 + δ)U, multiply the integrand on u > V by exp(λ(u − V)), and on u < U by exp(λ(U − u)). Both multipliers are at least one in their respective regions. Extending the resulting integrals over the positive half-line gives

∫(0,∞) ∖ I Kk,s ≤ exp(−λV)/(s − λ)k+1 + exp(λU)/(s + λ)k+1.

Fix the center of the transform in terms of δ, then choose the derivative order for the window. Take λ = 2 + 6/δ, M = λ(1 + δ), σ = M(2 + λ), s = σ − 2, and k = ⌈(1 + δ/2)σU⌉. For U ≥ 1 we have k ≥ U and s > λ. To bound the first term after multiplication by σk, set a = s − λ. The inequality log(σ/a) ≤ (σ − a)/a = 1/(M − 1), together with (1 + δ/2)σ = M(M − 1), gives −λV + k log(σ/a) ≤ 1. Its contribution is at most exp(1)/a.

For the second term set b = s + λ. Then log(σ/b) ≤ −(λ − 2)/b. Since (1 + δ/2)(λ − 2) = λ + 1 and λ(σ − 2 + λ) ≤ (λ + 1)σ, the lower bound on k gives λU − k(λ − 2)/b ≤ 0. Therefore this contribution is at most 1/b. Both bounds are independent of the chosen window. Combining with the preceding inequality gives a constant C1 such that, for every η > 0 and arbitrarily large U, some integer k ≥ U satisfies simultaneously for every real γ

Locate one of the kernels numerically

Take δ = 1 and U = 10. These choices give λ = 8, M = 16, σ = 160 and k = 2400. The known interval is [10,20], and K2400,160 peaks at 15. Even the kernel after the growth correction peaks at 2400/158 ≈ 15.19. For fixed δ and growing U, how wide is a kernel compared with the interval? Normalizing Kk,a to have integral one gives mean (k + 1)/a and variance (k + 1)/a². Both follow by taking its first two moments with the integral formula above. Thus its standard deviation grows like √U, while the window’s width grows like U. The exponential tail inequalities give the stronger rate needed for the pole argument.

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ C1 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k.

The order k can change each time the arithmetic supplies a new window.

9.4Isolating the pole seen by the derivatives

Suppose a pole has real part greater than θ. All poles lie to the left of σ because the Laplace integral is holomorphic on Re s > 2. Write E = σ − θ. The closed disk of radius E about σ lies in Re s ≥ θ > 0, so it contains finitely many poles by compactness and the punctured-neighborhood assumption. If it contains no poles, take D = E. The hypothesized pole then has horizontal distance strictly less than D and gives the first case below. Otherwise let D be the distance from σ to a nearest pole in the disk. In both cases the open disk of radius D is pole-free.

If a pole ρ1 has σ − Re ρ1 < D, then a disk of radius D centered at σ + i Im ρ1 contains it. Move that center by a sufficiently small vertical amount. Only finitely many poles in a slightly enlarged disk matter, and two distinct poles equally far from the moving center can tie at at most one height. Indeed their squared distances have a difference affine in the height. For equal imaginary parts the equality would also require equal real parts, since both poles lie to the left of σ. Avoiding the finitely many ties gives a center z = σ + iγ with a unique nearest pole ρ at distance d < D. This nearest pole can differ from the one that led us to shift the center. Its real part is at least σ − d > σ − D ≥ θ, so proving a contradiction for it suffices. Choose a radius r with d < r ≤ D isolating this pole.

In the other case all horizontal distances σ − Re ρ are at least D. There must be a nearest pole in the disk because the hypothesized pole has horizontal distance less than E. For any nearest pole the Euclidean distance D is at least its horizontal distance, now at least D. Equality forces the imaginary part to vanish. This identifies one real pole β = σ − D > θ. Every other pole in the finite disk is strictly farther away. Choose r with D < r ≤ E isolating β.

9.5Two incompatible derivative rates

In the first case subtract c/(s − ρ), where c is the nonzero residue. Its subtraction leaves a holomorphic function on the disk after filling the removable value at ρ. For R = (d + r)/2, Cauchy's estimate on the circle of radius R gives

|Ak(z) − c/(z − ρ)k+1| ≤ M1/Rk.

The real center also has a pole-free disk of radius D > R, so |Ak(σ)| ≤ M2/Rk. Substituting these estimates into the upper bound for the derivatives yields

(|c|/d) d−k ≤ (M1 + M2) R−k + C1 exp(ηU) E−k.

For a numerical reading of the last step, suppose d = 2, R = 3 and E = 4. With η = ½ log(3/2), multiplying by 2k leaves a first error proportional to (2/3)k. Since U ≤ k, the window error is at most a constant times (√(3/2)/2)k. Both tend to zero, however sparsely the integers k occur, while the residue contributes |c|/2 every time. The inequalities below apply the same comparison to the actual radii.

Choose 0 < η < log(R/d). Multiply the inequality by dk. Because U ≤ k and E ≥ R > d, the right side tends to zero along the chosen windows. The left side is a fixed positive number.

In the real-pole case take d = σ − β. At the real center the pole contributes c/dk+1 to Ak(σ) with real c > 0. Cauchy's estimate bounds the remainder by M1/Rk for R = (d + r)/2. The nonnegative absolute-value term in the derivative bound can be dropped. The same rate contradiction follows. A negative real residue would reverse the critical sign, which explains the positive-residue hypothesis.

9.6Choosing the exponent after choosing the alleged zero

Let β > 1/2 be the real part being tested. Pick h = ½ min(β − 1/2, 1/2) and θ = 1/2 + h. This ensures θ < min(β,1). Fix a level containing a retained character with the alleged zero. The associated Dirichlet characters, their weights and the function tested for poles are now fixed. The arithmetic construction supplies eD, eL and ε1 > 0 before ε is chosen. Set C = eD + eL + 7 and take ε = min(ε1/2, h/(|C| + 1)). Then Cε ≤ h. Choose the auxiliary arithmetic data for this ε and their large-scale threshold, then choose windows beyond that threshold and beyond 1. These data supply a bound for the weighted sum at the level already fixed. On those windows, the arithmetic exponent can be increased to θ. The theorem excludes a family pole with real part β. For the concrete analytic family, the proof also invokes known nonvanishing at Re s ≥ 1 and uses its pole construction for the remaining open strip.

10Reflection and the final statement

Once every Dirichlet character has a zero-free right half-plane, the passage to classical RH is short. Two small points do most of the work. A change of modulus introduces finite Euler factors, and reflection changes the character.

10.1Removing an imprimitive level

The conductor f of χ modulo N is the least divisor through which its character on units factors. Write ψ for the primitive character at that conductor. Changing to modulus N suppresses Euler factors at primes dividing N. On the common domain of the change-of-level identity, this gives

L(s,χ) = L(s,ψ) ∏p∣N (1 − ψ(p) p−s).

For a prime dividing f, ψ(p) = 0 and the displayed factor equals one. For every other prime its absolute value before subtraction satisfies |ψ(p) p−s| ≤ p−Re s < 1 whenever Re s > 0. Each factor is therefore nonzero. The formula initially follows from Euler products and extends where the continued identity applies. The formal change-of-level lemma asks that ψ be nonprincipal or s ≠ 1. If χ is nonprincipal then ψ must be nonprincipal too, since inducing a principal character would give χ principal. Thus the exception χ = 1 and s = 1 is accounted for.

A change of modulus you can calculate. Let ψ be the character modulo 3 that takes −1 at 2. Induce it to χ modulo 6. On the odd integers the two agree, and the change removes the even terms. Thus L(s,χ) = (1 + 2−s)L(s,ψ). The factor at 3 is one because ψ(3) = 0. When Re s > 0, the added term 2−s has absolute value strictly below one. At the boundary point s = πi/log 2 it equals −1 and the finite factor vanishes. This locates precisely where the zero-transfer argument uses strict positivity of the real part.

10.2The strip theorem for characters

Assume 0 < Re s < 1 and L(s,χ) = 0. The finite factors transfer the zero to ψ. Its completed function is obtained by multiplying by the real gamma factor appropriate to the parity of ψ. The gamma arguments have positive real part in this strip, so the factors are finite and nonzero. In particular the completed function vanishes too. The functional equation for ψ−1, evaluated at s, gives a zero of the completed function for ψ−1 at 1 − s. On units the inverse character is its complex conjugate. The arguments s and 1 − s avoid 0 and 1. Returning to the uncompleted function gives L(1 − s, ψ−1) = 0.

If Re s < ½, then Re(1 − s) > ½, contradicting right-half-plane nonvanishing for the inverse primitive character. If Re s > ½, nonvanishing for χ already contradicts the original zero. This leaves Re s = ½. It proves the strip statement for arbitrary moduli.

Follow a hypothetical zero of a complex character

Modulo 5, the residue 2 generates the unit group. The rule ψ(2) = i therefore fixes a primitive character and ψ−1(2) = −i. If L(¼ + 2i,ψ) vanished, the completed functional equation would give a zero for ψ−1 at ¾ − 2i. The modulus is still 5. The character has changed, so the right-half-plane theorem must cover the inverse as well. Conjugating this latter zero would give a zero for ψ at ¾ + 2i. This last operation explains why the same-character symmetry in a plot is a reflection across a vertical line, even though the functional equation uses 1 − s.

10.3Why classical RH excludes the negative even integers

The public zeta theorem follows a slightly different route. Specialize right-half-plane nonvanishing to the unique character of modulus one. Suppose ζ(s) = 0 with s ≠ 1 and s outside the negative even integers. The right-hand case is impossible immediately. For Re s < ½, put w = 1 − s. Since ζ(0) = −½, s ≠ 0 and w ≠ 1. We have Re w > ½, so ζ(w) ≠ 0, and w avoids all nonpositive integers. In the normalization used by this source the functional equation reads

ζ(1−w) = 2(2π)−w Γ(w) cos(πw/2) ζ(w).

The power of 2π is nonzero and Γ has no zero for Re w > 0. If the cosine vanished, w would be an odd integer, so s would be even. Positive even integers contradict Re s < ½, zero has already been excluded, and negative even integers are exactly the excluded trivial zeros. Every factor on the right is therefore nonzero, contradicting ζ(s) = 0. This proves the implication from the nonvanishing input to the exact classical target.

Why can the same argument accommodate ζ(−2) and ζ(0)?

For s = −2 one has w = 3. The gamma and zeta factors on the right are finite and nonzero, but cos(3π/2) = 0. The equation gives ζ(−2) = 0. For s = 0 one has w = 1. Now the cosine vanishes while ζ(w) has a pole, so value-by-value multiplication at w = 1 is unavailable. Writing w = 1 + h, cos(πw/2) = −πh/2 + O(h³) and ζ(w) = 1/h + O(1). Their product tends to −π/2. The remaining multiplier tends to 2(2π)−1Γ(1) = 1/π. This recovers ζ(0) = −½.

Contents · Chapter references

Notation and references

Adeles
A compatible list of local entries, one in each completion of a number field, integral at all but finitely many finite places. The diagonal embedding sends one field element to its value in every completion. Read in context
Almost everywhere
A property holds almost everywhere if the set where it fails has measure zero. Two functions in L² can differ on such a set and still represent the same vector. Read in context
Analytic continuation
An extension agreeing with a given analytic function on its original domain. Agreement on an open subset determines the continuation on a connected domain. Read in context
Annihilator
The characters of a finite abelian group that are identically one on a specified subgroup. Subgroup averaging selects exactly these characters. Read in context
Augmentation of the face complex
The homomorphism from integer combinations of vertices to the integers that sends each vertex to one. Its kernel consists of the zero-dimensional cycles that the edges must fill. Read in context
Automorphic function
A function on an adelic group that descends under its rational subgroup and satisfies the prescribed regularity and other conditions. Square-integrability on the quotient matters for the lifts here. Read in context
Bar chain
A finite linear combination of ordered words in a group. Its boundary takes alternating faces obtained by omitting an end entry or multiplying neighboring entries. Read in context
Bernoulli value of a character
A weighted finite sum of Bernoulli polynomial values at fractions of the conductor. The minus estimate clears its denominators and uses the same algebraic integer at every coefficient prime. Read in context
Bockstein map
In the coefficient sequence for reduction modulo q, lift a cycle to an integral chain. Its boundary is a multiple of q. Dividing that boundary by q gives a class one degree lower, killed by q. This map distinguishes the two torsion orders in the cycle count. Read in context
Character / χ
A homomorphism from a finite group to nonzero complex numbers. A Dirichlet character extends by zero off the units modulo N. Read in context
Class group / Cl(K)
Fractional ideals of the number field K modulo principal fractional ideals. The quotient Cl(K)/ℓCl(K) measures the number of independent characters of order ℓ. Read in context
CM field
A number field that is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field. Complex conjugation interchanges the two embeddings over any real place of the base. Read in context
Cocycle
A function c satisfying c(gh)=c(g)+g·c(h). Its class in degree one identifies functions differing by g↦g·a−a. Local conditions impose restrictions on these classes. Read in context
Cocycle test on a prism
A linear functional that vanishes on boundaries. For the residue test, consecutive pairs contribute carries and the last entry contributes an additive index. Read in context
Coinvariants
Given an operator g on a module M, the quotient M/(g−1)M identifies each element with its translate under g. The quotient by gᵈ−1 maps onto it because gᵈ−1 is divisible by g−1. Read in context
Conductor / f
The least divisor of the modulus from which a Dirichlet character is induced. A primitive character has conductor equal to its modulus. Read in context
Covolume
The volume of a fundamental parallelepiped of a lattice in its real span with the chosen metric. Read in context
Covolume of a lattice
The volume of one fundamental parallelepiped, measured in the chosen ambient coordinates. In the complex plane the lattice generated by α and iα has covolume |α|². Read in context
Critical strip / σ
The region 0 < Re s < 1. Here s = σ+it; σ = ½ is the critical line. Read in context
Cyclotomic layer
A stage in a tower formed by adjoining roots of unity. In the ℓ-adic tower here, layer m has relative degree ℓᵐ over the chosen base field. Read in context
Discrete valuation ring
A ring in which each nonzero element has the form uπⁿ for a unit u, a fixed uniformizer π and a nonnegative integer n. This exponent measures divisibility. For ℤℓ one can take π=ℓ. Read in context
Double coset
For subgroups Γ and K of a group, the double coset of h consists of the products γhk with γ in Γ and k in K. Grouping an integral by these classes preserves the measure of each class. Read in context
Doubling integral
An integral obtained by placing two copies of a unitary group in a larger group and pairing a section there with matrix coefficients on the original copies. Its local factors determine the partial L-function in the theta norm. Read in context
Elementary divisors
A pair of full local lattices can be put into diagonal form by integral changes of bases. The integer exponents of a uniformizer classify their relative position. Their sum gives the determinant valuation and the sum of their absolute values gives the degree in the split-place series. Read in context
Euler’s constant / γ
The limit of 1+1/2+⋯+1/n − log n; it is the constant Laurent coefficient of ζ at 1. Read in context
Field norm and ideal norm
In a Galois extension the field norm multiplies all conjugates of an element. The ideal norm sends a prime above a base prime to the power of the base prime given by the relative residue degree. For a principal ideal these two constructions agree. Read in context
Formal degree
The positive constant in Schur orthogonality for a discrete series and a chosen Haar measure. For a unit vector v it satisfies ∫|⟨v,σ(g)v⟩|² dg = 1/dσ. Read in context
Formal group and formal logarithm
A group law in power series at the identity and a change of coordinate taking that law to addition. Read in context
Frame of a regular Gram fibre
An ordered list of independent vectors whose matrix of mutual Hermitian pairings is nonsingular. Its length can be smaller than the ambient dimension. Read in context
Frobenius and inertia
Inertia is the subgroup of a local Galois group acting trivially on the residue field. A Frobenius class acts there by raising to the residue-field size. Read in context
Genus mass
For a positive definite lattice, sum 1/|Aut(L)| over one representative of each isometry class in its genus. A weighted average of a count divides the corresponding weighted sum by this mass. Read in context
Genus of a Hermitian lattice
The full lattices in a fixed rational Hermitian space that are isometric to a given lattice at every finite place. A genus may contain several global isometry classes. Read in context
Gram matrix
The matrix of pairwise inner products of a list of vectors. Its diagonal records squared lengths. If the vectors are columns of M in orthonormal coordinates, the Gram matrix is M* M. Read in context
Haar measure
A translation-invariant measure on a locally compact group. Its normalization matters when comparing the two sides of the Petersson identity. Read in context
Hecke operator
An operator formed by summing translates indexed by the cosets in a double coset. The operator in the invariant-period comparison divides by the number of cosets, so it fixes constants. Read in context
Homology and cohomology
A cycle is a chain with zero boundary, and its homology class records it up to addition of boundaries. A cohomology class tests cycles by a cocycle, which vanishes on boundaries. Torsion counts and bounds on the dimension over the reals give different information. Read in context
Idèle modulus
The product of the normalized local absolute values of an invertible adèle. The product formula makes it one on each nonzero field element. Read in context
Isotropic flag
A nested sequence of subspaces on which every two vectors have Hermitian pairing zero. Its successive increases in dimension are its rank jumps. Read in context
Jacobi sum
For two multiplicative characters of a finite field, extended by zero at zero, sum χ(x)φ(1−x) over the field. In the nondegenerate cyclotomic case the product with the inverse-character sum is the size of the field. Read in context
Matrix coefficient
The scalar formed by translating one vector by a group element and pairing it with a second vector. When the vectors coincide, its value at the identity is their squared norm. Read in context
Mellin transform
Here the integral from 1 to infinity against x^(−s−1) dx. Under x=eᵘ it becomes a Laplace transform. Read in context
Module length
Number of simple quotients in a composition series. For a finite ℤℓ-module of order ℓᵈ the length is d. Its minimum number of generators can be smaller. Read in context
Mollifier for an L-function
A short Dirichlet polynomial chosen to cancel the early coefficients of a product with the L-series. Here its weights are μ(d)χ(d), where μ is the Möbius function. A zero forces the product of the two truncated sums to be small. Read in context
Moving frame
An identification of tangent spaces used to compare a form at different points. In the cone of positive Hermitian matrices, the action carrying the identity to a point pulls the form back to a tensor at the identity. Read in context
Multiplicity / m
At an isolated zero ρ, the integer m≥1 such that L(s)=(s−ρ)ᵐh(s) with h holomorphic and h(ρ)≠0. The balance chapter also uses m for a chain length. Read in context
Nerve of a cover
An ordered tuple of cover labels is allowed when their sets share a witness. Deleting a label gives a face. Alternating deletion gives the boundary on integer combinations of tuples. Read in context
Partition of unity
A collection of smooth nonnegative weights that add to one, with only finitely many nonzero in a neighborhood of each point. Here the weights index translates by the arithmetic group. Read in context
Period of an automorphic form
An integral of an automorphic function over a specified quotient, often after restricting the function to a subgroup or pairing it with a second function. The bottom period here restricts a core function to the row group and integrates their product. Read in context
Petersson pairing
The integral of the product of an automorphic function and the complex conjugate of another on the automorphic quotient, with the chosen measure. On the diagonal it gives a squared norm. Read in context
Poincaré series
A sum of translates of a test function over a discrete group or a coset space. The sum used to separate a row has an identity contribution large enough to dominate the sum of the other contributions after unfolding its period. Read in context
Pole and residue
The residue is the coefficient of (s−ρ)⁻¹ in a Laurent expansion. A simple pole has a nonzero residue and no higher-order singular terms. Read in context
Positive part / u₊
The number max(u,0). In a ramp it cuts off the sum; in the window estimate it keeps the side controlled by the hypothesis. Read in context
Ramification index
The multiplicity of a prime in the extended prime ideal. It enters the weighting of the finite-place contributions to divisibility. Read in context
Regulator
The volume spanned by logarithms of a basis of free units after deleting one place coordinate. The complex coordinates use log |z|². In a field with unit rank zero this volume is one. Read in context
Residue degree
The degree of an extension of residue fields. In an unramified quadratic extension, a split base prime has two primes of residue degree one. An inert prime has one of degree two. Read in context
Restricted product
A family of local coordinates integral at all but finitely many finite places. For the multiplicative group, both a coordinate and its inverse must be integral there. Read in context
Satake parameters
The unramified eigenvalue data that encode the action of the spherical Hecke operators at one place. The normalization used here specifies their powers of the residue-field size in the local Euler factors. Read in context
Saturation of a lattice
The saturation of Λ in E is the set of x in E such that kx lies in Λ for some nonzero integer k. Modulo Λ it gives exactly the torsion subgroup of E/Λ. Read in context
Schwartz function
A smooth function on a real vector space whose derivatives of every order decay faster than every inverse power of the norm. A Gaussian is an example. Read in context
Self-dual Hermitian lattice
A full lattice L consisting exactly of the vectors whose Hermitian pairings with L are integral. This condition makes integral adjoints available in the construction of a frame. Read in context
Semisimple representation
A direct sum of irreducible representations. One can compare multiplicities constituent by constituent once an isomorphism of the global representations has been established. Read in context
Sha-type local kernel
The subgroup of degree-one Galois cohomology classes whose restrictions at the specified places vanish. Its module length enters the cohomological window bound. Read in context
Shapiro’s isomorphism
Homology with an induced coefficient module can be computed in the subgroup. Here the module of functions on a finite cyclic quotient turns a homology calculation for G into one for the kernel. Read in context
Siegel parabolic
The subgroup preserving a maximal isotropic subspace in the doubled Hermitian space. Its rational cosets index the Eisenstein series used to identify the normalized theta mean. Read in context
Signature of a real unit
The signs of a unit at all real embeddings. Recording a negative value as one and a positive value as zero turns multiplication of units into addition of bit vectors. Read in context
Similitude
An invertible linear map that multiplies a Hermitian form by a single nonzero scalar. It sends the sphere of one length to the sphere of the scaled length. Read in context
Slope
For a Euclidean lattice of positive rank, its Arakelov slope is the negative log of its covolume divided by its rank. Extremal slopes measure sublattices and quotients. Read in context
Spherical data
At a good finite place the vectors are fixed by the specified maximal compact subgroup. This invariance permits the local integral to be evaluated by Hecke eigenvalues. Read in context
Split sequence
An ordered list of vectors vᵢ with specified linear functionals λᵢ satisfying λᵢ(vⱼ)=1 when i=j and 0 otherwise. Deleting one pair gives a shorter sequence. Read in context
Stabilizer
The subgroup of symmetries that take an object to itself. In the arithmetic face count a finite stabilizer acts faithfully on a finite set of shortest vectors. Its order contributes to the bound for integral homology. Read in context
Stickelberger element
An element of a group ring acting on ideal classes in cyclotomic arithmetic. Its annihilation property supplies a relation on a quotient of the class group in the tower argument. Read in context
Successive minima
For a lattice in a Euclidean space, the jth successive minimum is the least radius of a ball about zero containing j real-linearly independent lattice vectors. In the number-field row argument, independence over the field requires taking the radii in blocks. Read in context
Target slice
For a kernel K(x,y) and a fixed source point x, the function y ↦ K(x,y) on the target. Its square-integral as x varies controls the change of integration order in the theta pairing. Read in context
Tate twist
A change in a Galois action by a power of the cyclotomic character, which records the action on roots of unity. Its exponent matters in a local restriction kernel. Read in context
Theta lift
An integral operator with a theta kernel carrying an automorphic function between spaces for two groups. Read in context
Thick part
The region of positive Hermitian forms where both the primal and dual lattice minima are at least a fixed positive constant. A compact set meets every arithmetic orbit in this region. Read in context
Trace-dual basis
For a finite separable extension, bases (uᵢ) and (vⱼ) are trace-dual when Tr(uᵢvⱼ) is 1 for i=j and 0 otherwise. Then x=∑ᵢ Tr(xuᵢ)vᵢ. Clearing both bases at once produces the split residue calculation. Read in context
Valuation / vₚ
The exponent of p in a nonzero rational number, extended by vₚ(0)=+∞. The normalized p-adic absolute value is p to the power −vₚ. Read in context
Von Mangoldt function / Λ
Λ(pʲ)=log p for a prime p and integer j≥1; its value at every other positive integer is zero. Read in context
Whittaker coefficient
A Fourier coefficient obtained by integrating along a unipotent matrix variable against an additive character. In the Siegel–Weil calculation, a nonsingular Hermitian matrix specifies the character. At the special parameter the coefficient reads the density of tuples with that Gram matrix. Read in context
Window / Y, U, δ
An interval [Y,Y¹⁺ᵟ] with δ>0; in logarithmic coordinates its endpoints are U=log Y and (1+δ)U. Read in context
Witt index
Largest dimension of a subspace on which the entire Hermitian pairing vanishes. It determines which convergence hypothesis is required for the doubled theta integral. Read in context

Theorems used in the book

  1. The pole of the zeta function

    The series for ζ(s) on Re s > 1 extends meromorphically to the plane. At its only pole the expansion begins ζ(s) = 1/(s−1) + γ + O(s−1), where γ is Euler’s constant.

    Taking the logarithmic derivative of this expansion specifies the two centering terms in the smoothed prime sum.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.2(i) and (ii), especially (25.2.4).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2

    Used in From a series to a function · Why the correction terms have these signs · How is the principal character detected?

  2. Euler product for a Dirichlet character

    If χ is a Dirichlet character and Re s > 1, then L(s,χ) is the absolutely convergent product over primes p of (1−χ(p)p⁻ˢ)⁻¹. A prime dividing the modulus contributes the factor 1.

    Taking the logarithmic derivative turns each Euler factor into a sum over powers of its prime. That sum supplies the weights in the Mellin transform.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (25.15.2).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15.E2

    Used in From one ramp to a logarithmic derivative · Which disk controls a Dirichlet character at height t? · Why are there exactly J possible blocks?

  3. Dirichlet nonvanishing at one

    For every nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ the continuation of L(s,χ) is holomorphic at 1 and L(1,χ) is nonzero.

    This makes L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ) a finite centering constant. The principal character requires the separate pole calculation.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.15(i) and (25.15.9).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15

    Used in Why the correction terms have these signs · Reflect from zero to one. · Why are there exactly J possible blocks?

  4. Removing Euler factors at a larger modulus

    If χ modulo q is induced by χ₀ of conductor d, then L(s,χ) equals L(s,χ₀) times the product of 1−χ₀(p)p⁻ˢ for p dividing q. The identity holds meromorphically.

    At Re s > 0 every added factor is nonzero, so changing level preserves zeros there.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (25.15.4).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15.E4

    Used in Removing an imprimitive level

  5. Reflection for a primitive Dirichlet character

    For primitive χ of conductor q, put a=0 or 1 according as χ(−1)=1 or −1. The completed function Λ(s,χ)=(q/π)^((s+a)/2)Γ((s+a)/2)L(s,χ) satisfies Λ(s,χ)=εχΛ(1−s,χ̄), where |εχ|=1.

    In the open critical strip the gamma factors are finite and nonzero. A zero on the left therefore gives a zero for the conjugate character on the right.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.15(i), primitive functional equation (25.15.5)–(25.15.6).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15.i

    Used in The strip theorem for characters · Reflect from zero to one.

  6. The boundary of the critical strip

    The only zeros of ζ outside 0 < Re s < 1 are the negative even integers. In particular there are no zeros on Re s = 1.

    Once both open halves of the strip have been handled, this identifies the exceptions in the classical statement about all zeros.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §25.10(i).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.10.i

    Used in Which zeros? · Why classical RH excludes the negative even integers

  7. Changing the order of integration

    On two σ-finite measure spaces a nonnegative measurable function has the same integral in either order, possibly infinite. For a complex measurable function, finiteness of the integral of its absolute value makes both iterated integrals exist almost everywhere and gives the same value. One may take the completed measures.

    In the Mellin identity one variable has counting measure. In the theta integral a majorant must first control two noncompact variables.

    Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory, §1.7, Theorem 1.7.18 and Corollary 1.7.23.https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/gsm-126-tao5-measure-book.pdf#page=222

    Used in From one ramp to a logarithmic derivative · Change the order. · How much does one flag type contribute? · What is the probability of one ordered rank type? · How is a measure on a single length defined? · How much mass does one length carry at a good prime? · What fixes the measure on one Gram fibre? · Why does the probability lose the residual volume? · Where does the factor for each remaining column come from? · How does a general Schwartz test reach every regular fibre? · Why does a unit slab determine the whole determinant measure? · Why does an ideal of norm N receive weight N−j? · How can a shell estimate on the stabilizer bound an integral on the whole group? · What measure and weight does a single rational class contribute? · How does a bound on one column locate a translate of bounded matrix norm? · Moving the integral onto the special linear group · Which density makes this product of measures left invariant? · What changes when the shell moves one step?

  8. Cauchy’s estimate for derivatives

    Suppose g is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk of radius R about σ, with |g| ≤ M on the circle. For each k ≥ 0, |g⁽ᵏ⁾(σ)|/k! ≤ M/Rᵏ. This follows by bounding the integrand in Cauchy’s derivative formula and multiplying by the circumference.

    Subtracting the principal part of an isolated pole gives such a g. The estimate quantifies the advantage of the pole when its distance from σ is smaller than R.

    NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §1.9, Cauchy’s integral formula for derivatives, (1.9.31).https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.9.E31

    Used in Two incompatible derivative rates · How does a real zero push other zeros away from 1? · How much of a logarithmic derivative comes from nearby zeros? · Why do three different terms appear in the prime moment?

  9. Uniqueness of analytic continuation

    Two holomorphic functions on a connected open set agree throughout it if they agree on a set having a limit point there. For meromorphic functions the same conclusion follows by removing their poles locally.

    This carries an equality from the half-plane where an integral converges into the region where the continued coefficients are evaluated.

    NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §1.10(ii), Analytic Continuation.https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.10.ii

    Used in One determinant derivative moves the convergence line. · Removing an imprimitive level

  10. Legendre’s formula for a factorial

    For a prime p and integer n ≥ 0, the exponent of p in n! is ∑ⱼ≥₁ ⌊n/pʲ⌋. Each integer from 1 to n contributes once for each power of p that divides it.

    This is the valuation gained when one passes from a Taylor coefficient to a derivative.

    Gennady Eremin, Legendre’s formula and p-adic analysis, §1, formula (1).https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.11902

    Used in Proving the one-variable estimate · Why is the von Mangoldt sum at most three times the cutoff?

  11. Orthogonality of finite characters

    On a finite abelian group the average of a character is 1 for the trivial character and 0 otherwise. Indeed, translating the sum by a group element multiplies it by the value of the character at that element.

    Applying the identity to a subgroup retains exactly the characters trivial on that subgroup in the arithmetic balance. On a four-dimensional residue space the same identity turns the fibre equation into an additive-character sum.

    Keith Conrad, Characters of Finite Abelian Groups, Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2.https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/grouptheory/charthy.pdf

    Used in Which characters survive? · Why is the error smaller at a unit length? · How can the error shrink with the exceptional main term? · How does the difference recover the sharp prime count? · Where does the exceptional factor come from at small modulus? · How do two different characters interact in the same detector block? · How accurately does a finite character sum approximate the value at a zero?

  12. Orbit–stabilizer counting

    When a finite group G acts on a set, the orbit of x is in bijection with the cosets of its stabilizer. In particular the orbit size divided by |G| equals 1/|Stab(x)|.

    The same pairs can be counted by first fixing a lattice or by first fixing a marked subspace. The reciprocal stabilizer order is the weight in the second count.

    Keith Conrad, Group Actions, Theorem 3.16.https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/grouptheory/gpaction.pdf

    Used in Why average over a genus? · Proof for two factors of rank at least two. · Why mark a maximal lattice before counting smaller ones?

  13. Product formula in a number field

    For nonzero a in a number field, multiply |a|ᵥ over all places, using the normalized absolute values, with the complex modulus squared at a complex place. The product equals 1.

    The scalar and determinant in a rational similitude contribute cancelling local Jacobians over all places.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 7.15.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=114

    Used in Compute what happens on a fibre. · Why is the global normalization one? · Why a near term has exactly the traces of the identity

  14. Local classification determines a global Hermitian space

    Let E/F be quadratic over number fields. Two nondegenerate Hermitian spaces over E of the same rank are isometric if their localizations are isometric everywhere. At nonsplit finite places the determinant modulo local norms distinguishes the two classes of a given positive rank. At real places becoming complex one uses the whole signature. For a global space the product of the local determinant signs is +1.

    To represent a given nonzero length in a plane, compare it with a diagonal plane whose first vector has the prescribed length. An isometry carries that vector into the given plane. For a definite subspace this classification identifies the rational space after adjoining one determinant line. The product condition also rules out a single nontrivial inert determinant sign.

    Benedict H. Gross, Incoherent definite spaces and Shimura varieties, §3, especially Theorem 3.1.https://abel.math.harvard.edu/~gross/preprints/incoherent.pdf

    Used in Which lengths reach the counting theorem? · From the local lattices to a marked class · Which ideal records the isometry class of a rational subspace? · How many rational subspace orbits can one discriminant order require?

  15. Hasse’s norm theorem

    Let L/K be a cyclic extension of number fields. An element of K× that is a norm at every completion is the norm of an element of L×.

    In the dyadic argument the extension is quadratic. A choice of real signs supplies the norm condition at infinity and the ideal calculation supplies it at the finite places.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter VIII, Theorem 3.1.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=243

    Used in How many sign patterns can a dyadic class miss? · Which lengths reach the counting theorem? · From the local lattices to a marked class

  16. Kronecker’s criterion for a root of unity

    A nonzero algebraic integer whose conjugates all have absolute value at most 1 is a root of unity. Its powers have bounded degree and bounded coefficients in their monic minimal polynomials, so two powers coincide.

    A quotient of conjugate generators is a unit. Checking its complex absolute values now restricts the ambiguity to roots of unity.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Proposition 5.5 and Corollary 5.6.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=89

    Used in How many sign patterns can a dyadic class miss? · Which ideal does the cyclotomic element generate? · Where does the extra factor ℓ come from?

  17. The logarithmic lattice of units

    In a number field with r real places and s complex places, the logarithms of the units form a full lattice of rank r+s−1 in the product-formula hyperplane. The kernel is the finite group of roots of unity.

    The lattice gives a compact torus when integrating along the center. Its rank also determines how many independent unit directions a determinant can measure.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 5.9 and the preceding description of the logarithmic map.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=90

    Used in Which central directions still need averaging? · Why can the upper-right block be erased on a stabilizer cycle? · What the detecting cycles can miss · Where does the extra factor ℓ come from? · How much do all coefficient lines contribute? · Why does each imaginary part have a positive lower bound? · How can small ideals bound a regulator?

  18. The S-unit theorem

    Let S be a finite set of places of a number field containing all its infinite places. The elements with valuation zero outside S form a finitely generated group. Modulo roots of unity it is free abelian of rank |S|−1.

    Allowing denominators at primes above ℓ adds one free direction for each such prime in the generator estimate.

    Paul Fili and Zachary Miner, A generalization of Dirichlet’s S-unit theorem, §1, statement of the S-unit theorem.https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/zminer/dirichlet-thm.pdf

    Used in Counting the generators before bounding the length

  19. Hilbert’s Theorem 90

    In a cyclic field extension F/K generated by γ, an element v of norm one has the form z/γ(z) for some z in F×.

    After two twisted-norm classes yield the same finite data, their ratio has norm one. Writing that ratio as a coboundary gives the descent used in the kernel count.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter II, Corollary 1.23.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=76

    Used in What the detecting cycles can miss · How does the minus class count control the plus classes?

  20. Artin reciprocity and the existence of class fields

    Fix a modulus 𝔪. Let I be the fractional ideals prime to 𝔪, and P the principal ideals whose generators satisfy its congruences and real sign conditions. For every subgroup H with P ⊆ H ⊆ I there is a class field L/K whose Artin map induces I/H ≃ Gal(L/K). A prime outside 𝔪 maps to arithmetic Frobenius.

    For the ordinary ideal class group this gives the Hilbert class field. Prime-ideal classes can therefore be prescribed by choosing Frobenius elements.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter V, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=167

    Used in Which ideal-class characters survive the local conditions? · How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class · Why does a carry give a principal ideal? · How does the minus class count control the plus classes?

  21. Chebotarev’s density theorem

    For a finite Galois extension L/K and a conjugacy class C in its group G, the unramified primes of K with Frobenius in C have density |C|/|G|. Excluding finitely many primes preserves this density.

    The argument chooses auxiliary primes with a prescribed action. Its extra conditions on residue degree are treated in the cited passages.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 8.31.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=149

    Used in How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class · Which Frobenius fixes the invariant, and which exchanges the CM roots? · Turning a determinant into a cycle evaluation · Why does a carry give a principal ideal? · How do good primes identify a character on the entire group? · Can these places realize any finite Galois test? · How can a cohomological piece of unknown dimension determine rank m?

  22. The Chinese remainder theorem

    For pairwise comaximal ideals I₁,…,Iₙ in a commutative ring R, reduction identifies R/(I₁⋯Iₙ) with the product of the R/Iⱼ. Thus each compatible list of independent residues is attained.

    Coprime moduli let the prime selection impose several congruences at once. They also let an exponent act independently on different primary parts.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.15.4, tag 00DT.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DT

    Used in Finding two primes that work for every required twist · Where the auxiliary layer enters the interior sum · Which degree counts the conjugates, and which degree counts the ideal? · How many common witnesses can two flags have? · What do vectors divisible by the prime contribute? · Why can a rational correction put the finite component in the level? · From integral matrices to unitary matrices on one layer · Which arithmetic volumes enter an isotropic-line shell? · Why does the gluing count cost only twice the perpendicular rank plus one?

  23. Local Tate duality with finite coefficients

    For a finite extension K of ℚₚ, a finite continuous Galois module A and its dual Aᴰ=Hom(A,μ∞), cup product and the local invariant give perfect pairings between Hⁱ(K,A) and H²⁻ⁱ(K,Aᴰ), for 0 ≤ i ≤ 2.

    In degree two the local group order becomes the order of a dual invariant group. This is one of the factors in the localization calculation.

    J. S. Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, second edition, Part I, §2, Corollary 2.3.https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/ADTnot.pdf#page=36

    Used in How the finite dualities give a length. · The inverse action and the Tate twist

  24. Poitou–Tate duality for localization

    Let A be a finite Galois module over a number field, unramified outside a finite set S containing the archimedean places and the places dividing |A|. Localization in degree two has cokernel dual to H⁰(K,Aᴰ). At real places the sequence uses modified local cohomology. Write Shaⁱ(A) for the kernel of localization in degree i. There is also a perfect pairing of Sha²(A) with Sha¹(Aᴰ).

    For odd ℓ the archimedean corrections vanish for ℓ-primary coefficients. The cokernel gives the global invariant factor in the localization count. The kernel pairing gives equality of the orders of the two finite locally trivial groups in descent.

    J. S. Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, second edition, Part I, Theorem 4.10.https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/ADTnot.pdf#page=65

    Used in How the finite dualities give a length. · The inverse action and the Tate twist

  25. The Chowla–Selberg product over imaginary quadratic ideal classes

    For an imaginary quadratic field of fundamental discriminant D<0, put F(z)=√Im(z) |η(z)|², h=|Cl(K)|, and w=|μ(K)|, the number of roots of unity. Write χᴰ for the quadratic character of D. The product of F over the CM points of the ideal classes equals (4π√|D|)^(−h/2) times the product of Γ(a/|D|)^(wχᴰ(a)/4) for 1 ≤ a ≤ |D|.

    Taking logarithms turns the product into a class mean. The period calculation specifies the additional scaling for lattices whose discriminant has been normalized to one.

    A. Barquero-Sanchez et al., Faltings heights of CM elliptic curves and special Gamma values, §3, (3.2), and Theorem 5.1 at conductor one.https://doi.org/10.1007/s40993-017-0077-7

    Used in Why the root discriminant appears · Take the logarithm of the class product.

  26. Cauchy–Binet for a Gram determinant

    Let X be a complex m by r matrix, m ≥ r. The determinant of X*X is the sum of |det Xᵢ|² over all r-element sets of rows i, where Xᵢ is the corresponding square submatrix. This follows by applying the product formula for determinants of rectangular matrices to X* and X.
