    For a basis of a Gaussian plane in four dimensions the six two-row minors therefore measure its determinant. The first two values can be counted exactly. A second use expands a compressed Hermitian exponential as a probability-weighted sum over its eigenvalue subsets.

    Andrew Putman, The Cauchy–Binet formula, Theorem 0.1.https://www3.nd.edu/~andyp/notes/CauchyBinet.pdf

    Used in Count the first two determinants in a four-dimensional Gaussian lattice · How does a gap between two weights make a matrix coefficient small?

  27. Siegel–Weil in the convergent unitary range

    In the unitary dual pair over a quadratic extension of number fields, let the Hermitian target have dimension b and Witt index w, and let the doubled source have split rank a. When b−w>a, the theta integral of the standard Schwartz test converges absolutely. For the associated section of the Siegel induced representation the Eisenstein series is regular at (b−a)/2 and its value equals that integral with the measures of the formula.

    Here a<b, so a target of Witt index zero also lies in this range. Expressing the target integral with probability measure produces the explicit inverse volume in the chapter.

    Shunsuke Yamana, The Siegel–Weil formula for unitary groups, Pacific J. Math. 264 (2013), pp. 236–237, convergence criterion and Theorem 2 in the case m−r>n.https://msp.org/pjm/2013/264-1/pjm-v264-n1-p11-p.pdf#page=4

    Used in When does the theta mean equal an Eisenstein value? · Where the quotient volume comes from

  28. The Rallis inner product formula at first occurrence

    In the unitary case of the cited theorem let n<m≤2n, and let the target have Witt index r≤n. Suppose π is irreducible cuspidal and its theta lifts to the smaller indices in this tower vanish. The pairing of two theta lifts is [E:F] times the value at s=(m−n)/2 of the product L(s+1/2,π×χ)Z*(s), with χ the splitting character attached to the target space V and Z* the normalized doubling integral for the chosen vectors.

    The factorization identifies the global L-value and the normalized local factors. The chapter supplies the formula for its own ranks and follows the measure and vector normalizations at each step of the chain.

    W. T. Gan, Y. Qiu and S. Takeda, The regularized Siegel–Weil formula (the second term identity) and the Rallis inner product formula, §11.6, (11.3), and Theorem 11.4(i).https://arxiv.org/pdf/1207.4709v3#page=54

    Used in Where the quotient volume comes from

  29. Norms in an unramified local extension

    If L/K is a finite unramified extension of nonarchimedean local fields, every unit of K is the norm of a unit of L. The valuation of a norm is a multiple of [L:K]. These two facts characterize the nonzero norms.

    At an inert place of the unramified quadratic extension, even valuation therefore suffices. At a split place the norm sends (x,y) to xy, which attains every nonzero scalar.

    J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter III, Proposition 1.2, with the norm of a uniformizer.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf#page=107

    Used in How many sign patterns can a dyadic class miss? · Why are the residual lattices equivalent at a finite place? · Which ideal records the isometry class of a rational subspace?

  30. Lagrange inversion for formal power series

    Over a characteristic-zero field let T(u) have constant coefficient zero and invertible linear coefficient. Write u(T) for its inverse. For any power series H and n≥1, n[Tⁿ]H(u(T))=[uⁿ⁻¹]H′(u)(u/T(u))ⁿ.

    Taking H to be the formal integral of the invariant differential gives λ₂₅=99/1280 on the curve at 5.

    I. M. Gessel, Lagrange Inversion, Theorem 2.1.1, formula (2.1.1).https://people.brandeis.edu/~gessel/homepage/papers/Lagrange.pdf

    Used in The first denominator on a good curve at 5

  31. The von Staudt–Clausen denominator theorem

    For even h≥2, adding 1/p to the Bernoulli number Bₕ for each prime p with p−1 dividing h gives an integer. Each such p occurs just once in the denominator.

    For h≤k, all these primes are at most k+1. A single product of primes therefore clears the denominators in the character sum.

    K. Dilcher, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §24.10(i), (24.10.1).https://dlmf.nist.gov/24.10.i

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

  32. Fourier series of the Bernoulli polynomials

    For integer k≥2 and real x in [0,1], the Fourier coefficient of Bₖ at nonzero integer m is −k!/(2πim)ᵏ. The constant coefficient vanishes and the series converges absolutely.

    Pairing the positive and negative frequencies bounds |Bₖ(x)| by 2k!ζ(k)/(2π)ᵏ at once for all x.

    K. Dilcher, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (24.8.3).https://dlmf.nist.gov/24.8.E3

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

  33. Euler’s evaluation of ζ(2)

    The series of reciprocal squares of the positive integers has sum π²/6.

    For k≥2 the sum of reciprocal kth powers is at most ζ(2). Both signs of the frequencies in the Bernoulli series therefore cost at most π²/3<4.

    T. M. Apostol, NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, (25.6.1).https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.6.E1

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

  34. An elementary upper bound for the product of small primes

    For each integer N≥1 the product of the primes p≤N is at most 4ᴺ. For n≥2 the product over n<p≤2n divides the binomial coefficient (2n−1 choose n), which bounds the cost of doubling the cutoff.

    At N=k+1 this bounds the size of the same integer that clears the Bernoulli denominators.

    A. Granville, The distribution of primes, Appendix E, Lemma E1.1 and Proposition E1.2.https://www.math.mcgill.ca/darmon/courses/10-11/nt/Granville-appendices.pdf

    Used in Why the Bernoulli factor is integral · A single integer controls the primes away from the field degree

  35. Hensel lifting of a simple root

    For a complete discrete valuation ring R, a simple root of a monic polynomial modulo the maximal ideal lifts uniquely to a root in R with that residue.

    At the inert prime p, the derivative 2δ is a unit. The two residue roots of X²+d lift distinctly, which identifies the sign of Frobenius on δ.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.153.9 and the simple-root criterion in §10.153.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04GM

    Used in Which Frobenius fixes the invariant, and which exchanges the CM roots? · How is a measure on a single length defined? · Which primes can test the two lifts?

  36. Nakayama’s lemma

    If a finitely generated module M over a local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪 satisfies 𝔪M=M, then M is zero. In particular generators modulo 𝔪 lift to generators of M.

    Apply this with 𝔪=(ℓ) to the finite-module quotient in the cokernel comparison. This gives the asserted bound for one additional cyclotomic layer.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.20.1, tag 00DV.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DV

    Used in The cost of one more cyclotomic layer

  37. Minkowski’s bound for an ideal class

    For a number field of degree n and discriminant Δ with r₂ pairs of complex embeddings, every ideal class contains an integral ideal of norm at most (4/π)^(r₂)(n!/nⁿ)√|Δ|. Here the exponent r₂ counts conjugate pairs.

    For ℚ(√−5) only norms one and two need checking. For ℚ(ζ₉) the bound is less than 4.47 and gives a second short list of ideals.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 4.3.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT301.pdf

    Used in Which ideal-class characters survive the local conditions? · Fixed classes and coinvariants in two dimensions · Where do the finitely many cusp matrices come from? · What does one zeta residue cost per flag block?

  38. Minkowski’s convex body theorem

    Let Λ be a full lattice in ℝⁿ with covolume V. A convex body symmetric about the origin of volume greater than 2ⁿV contains a nonzero point of Λ.

    The simultaneous bounds at the infinite places describe such a body in the real embedding space. Its volume grows with the denominator exponent, giving a nonzero field element small at every required embedding.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 4.19.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT301.pdf

    Used in Why are the common invariant functions constant? · Where do the finitely many cusp matrices come from? · How can small ideals bound a regulator? · Why do the lattice inequalities force positive definiteness? · How short a vector does every integral line contain?

  39. Shapiro’s lemma for group homology

    For a subgroup H of G and a left ℤH-module M, Hⱼ(G, ℤG⊗ℤH M) is naturally isomorphic to Hⱼ(H,M) in every degree j≥0. The tensor product here is over the group ring of H.

    An orbit of chains gives an induced coefficient module. The lemma replaces its group homology by homology of the stabilizer, where the arithmetic estimates apply.

    C. A. Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, Lemma 6.3.2.https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/weibel/06-group_homology_and_cohomology.pdf

    Used in The extra cost in positive homological degree · Why one coefficient is a unit · Compute the stabilization map from an alternating face map · Why the order of a stabilizer kills positive-degree homology

  40. The Ferrero–Washington theorem

    For every prime ℓ and abelian number field K, the cyclotomic ℤℓ-extension of K has Iwasawa μ-invariant zero.

    The monograph needs a uniform upper bound on the number of generators of the ℓ-class groups of its finite layers. The tower argument reconstructs the class-group consequence used here.

    B. Ferrero and L. C. Washington, The Iwasawa invariant μₚ vanishes for abelian number fields, Annals of Mathematics 109 (1979), 377–395.https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1979/190-2/p05

    Used in What Ferrero–Washington supplies in this proof · Putting the three estimates on one interval

  41. Weyl’s dimension formula

    For integral highest weight λ₁≥⋯≥λₙ, the dimension of the irreducible complex representation of U(n) is ∏_{i<j}(λᵢ−λⱼ+j−i)/(j−i). A common determinant twist leaves every difference unchanged.

    At the real places the product of weight differences can be compared term by term with the Vandermonde factors in the formal degree.

    P. Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory, §5.22, Theorem 5.22.1 and its dimension formula.https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/representationtheorybook.pdf

    Used in How an integral fixes the missing constant · What survives in the quotient of dimensions? · An upper bound for the scale of every word

  42. Schur–Weyl duality on tensor powers

    For a finite-dimensional complex vector space V, every endomorphism of V⊗ᵐ commuting with all g⊗ᵐ for g∈GL(V) is a linear combination of permutations of its m tensor factors.

    The permutations give the trace contractions of the invariant tensors. Their cycles determine the powers acquired under block repetition.

    P. Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory, §§5.18–5.19, the double centralizer and Schur–Weyl duality.https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/representationtheorybook.pdf

    Used in Why do permutations account for every invariant tensor?

  43. Hadamard’s determinant inequality

    The absolute determinant of a complex square matrix is at most the product of the Euclidean lengths of its columns. Applying this after taking a positive definite square root gives the corresponding Gram determinant bound.

    Multiplying the local determinant bounds over the complex embeddings controls the ideal index of a set of short vectors.

    K. Lange, Hadamard’s Determinant Inequality, American Mathematical Monthly 121 (2014), 258–259.https://doi.org/10.4169/amer.math.monthly.121.03.258

    Used in Bound the absolute norm of the determinant. · Find a frame shared by the whole face · How a compact part of the cone supplies a partition everywhere · Where does the discriminant enter the frame bound?

  44. Stokes’ theorem on a simplex

    On an oriented smooth p-simplex σ, the integral of a smooth (p−1)-form over the alternating boundary of σ equals the integral of its exterior derivative over σ.

    A closed form thus vanishes on boundaries when integrated over chains. Its period depends only on the homology class.

    D. Calegari, Notes on Differential Forms, Theorem 2.1.https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/courses/differential_topology_2016/differential_forms_notes.pdf

    Used in How does a group cocycle become a differential form? · Why does one trace per complex place suffice on the filtered cycles?

  45. Cauchy’s theorem for a finite group

    For a prime ℓ dividing the order of a finite group, the group has an element of order ℓ.

    The exponent bound on the Galois quotient then forces every odd prime dividing its order to divide the fixed level order.

    J. S. Milne, Group Theory, Theorem 4.13.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GTe6.pdf

    Used in When an odd prime divides the field degree

  46. Howe duality for local unitary pairs

    Over a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic different from two, the small theta lift of an irreducible smooth representation for a unitary dual pair is either zero or irreducible. Distinct representations with nonzero lifts have distinct partners.

    This gives the local uniqueness underlying the pairing condition. The row argument separately uses its global pairing hypothesis, positivity of the Gram operator and spanning of the target by orthogonal components.

    W. T. Gan and S. Takeda, A proof of the Howe duality conjecture, Theorem 1.2.https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.1995

    Used in Locating one target type

  47. Sinnott’s separation principle

    Suppose Y₁,…,Yₘ are pairwise multiplicatively independent nontrivial Laurent monomials in independent variables over a field k. If ∑rⱼ(Yⱼ)=0 for rational functions rⱼ over k, every rⱼ is constant.

    This is the independence principle behind the separation argument. The finite group-algebra proof in the chapter supplies the required congruence depth and isolates an individual coefficient.

    W. Sinnott, On a theorem of L. Washington, Astérisque 147–148 (1987), appendix restating Proposition 3.1 of his 1984 paper.https://www.numdam.org/article/AST_1987__147-148__209_0.pdf

    Used in Sinnott’s separation argument.

  48. Siegel’s lower bound on a real exceptional zero

    For every ε>0 there is c(ε)>0 such that a real zero β of a real nonprincipal Dirichlet character of modulus m satisfies 1−β≥c(ε)m⁻ᵋ. The constant is ineffective.

    The progression estimate needs a positive lower bound for the distance of the possible exceptional zero from one. Taking ε=1 gives the coarser scale c/m.

    D. Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Theorem 12.10.https://dms.umontreal.ca/~koukoulo/documents/publications/primes.pdf

    Used in Why only one quadratic twist can keep a near-one zero · Why the progression still contains enough primes · Why must one of the power sums be large? · Where does the exceptional factor come from at small modulus?

  49. Perron inversion for the ramp

    For c>1 and t>0, the inverse Mellin integral of tˢ/[s(s−1)] along Re s=c, with measure ds/(2πi), is max(t−1,0). The two simple poles at 1 and 0 give the term t−1 for t>1.

    On a line where the Dirichlet series converges absolutely, take t=u/n and sum with coefficients Λ(n)χ(n). This gives the contour representation used to compare two endpoints.

    D. Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Chapters 5 and 7 on Perron inversion. The stated ramp kernel follows by integrating the step kernel.https://dms.umontreal.ca/~koukoulo/documents/publications/primes.pdf

    Used in How the finite prime sum controls the centered ramp · Why does a smoothed prime sum produce this list of zeros?

  50. Digamma values at one and one half

    For ψ=Γ′/Γ, one has ψ(1)=−γ and ψ(1/2)=−γ−2 log 2, where γ is Euler’s constant.

    The logarithmic derivative of the completed odd quadratic L-function contains these two values when reflected between zero and one. Their mean determines the constant in the CM period identity.

    NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §5.4(ii), (5.4.12) and (5.4.13).https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.4.ii

    Used in Reflect from zero to one.

  51. The geometric series and its tail

    If 0 ≤ q < 1 and H is a nonnegative integer, the sum of qʰ for h ≥ H is qᴴ/(1−q). Multiplication of a finite sum by 1−q cancels consecutive terms, and the remaining endpoint tends to zero.

    The count at one complex place grows by at most a square of the radius for each minor. The cubic weight leaves a decaying geometric series in each place index.

    Gilbert Strang, Calculus, §10.1, equations (1)–(2).https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/res-18-001-calculus-fall-2023/mitres_18_001_f17_full_book.pdf

    Used in Why the remaining power pays for every list · Why does the decay beat the number of distant terms? · From one flag to the volume lost in the trace · How far to the left must a remaining zero lie? · How many nonzero vectors of norm zero enter a shrinking box? · Why does a translated coefficient become small away from the stabilizer? · What changes when the shell moves one step?

  52. An orthonormal eigenbasis for the Gram operator

    On a finite-dimensional complex inner product space every self-adjoint operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis. The eigenvalues of A*A are nonnegative because its quadratic form is the squared norm of Ax. Its zero eigenspace is the kernel of A.

    The positive eigenvalues count image dimensions and their first and second power sums give the two traces in the rank estimate. In the unitary period the same diagonalization describes principal determinants and the polar factor. In the cohomological integral it gives a bounded frame and identifies the real Jacobian.

    Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th edition, §7B, theorem 7.31, and §7C on positive operators.https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf#page=260

    Used in How close are the period operators to a common orthonormal frame? · What happens when all the words share the same rows? · Why do the lattice inequalities force positive definiteness? · Which Hermitian forms can a positive functional see? · How does a gap between two weights make a matrix coefficient small? · Why does the compact average preserve that decay? · Finding bounded frames for a compact set of forms · Which determinant changes the volume?

  53. Cauchy–Schwarz for the nonzero eigenvalues

    For k real numbers λᵢ, (Σ λᵢ)² ≤ k Σ λᵢ². This follows by taking the inner product of the vector of entries with the vector of k ones.

    When the entries are the positive eigenvalues of the frame operator, the quotient of the squared trace by the trace of its square is a lower bound for its rank. In the unitary period, at most twice the real rank many eigenvalues enter each partial sum.

    Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th edition, §6A, inequality 6.14 and example 6.16(a).https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf#page=203

    Used in How close are the period operators to a common orthonormal frame? · What happens when all the words share the same rows? · How much survives the ramification conditions? · How does a gap between two weights make a matrix coefficient small?

  54. The field norm as a product of conjugates

    In a number field E the determinant of multiplication by x is the product of τ(x) over the embeddings into ℂ. If x is a nonzero algebraic integer, this determinant is a nonzero rational integer. In a CM field the complex embeddings pair up, giving the squared absolute value at each pair.

    Apply the norm to the difference of two distinct integral minors. Their images cannot occupy the same half-unit cell at every complex place.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Chapter 2, Proposition 2.19 and its proof.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=33

    Used in How many lists of minors have a given size? · When does a dilated compact set contain a nonzero rational point? · Where does the discriminant enter the frame bound? · How short a vector does every integral line contain? · How does one short representative bound the number of lines?

  55. Rank and nullity

    For a linear map on a finite-dimensional domain, the dimension of the kernel plus the dimension of the image equals the domain dimension. Extend a basis of the kernel to one of the whole domain. The images of the added basis vectors form a basis of the image.

    An upper bound for the dimension lost to the kernel gives the number of independent images of one word.

    Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th edition, §3B, theorem 3.21.https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf#page=76

    Used in How many independent directions do the period maps detect?

  56. Cycling rectangular factors under the trace

    If A has m rows and n columns and B has n rows and m columns, then tr(AB) = tr(BA). Both traces sum the same products of matrix entries over all row and column indices.

    Moving the period matrix past its adjoint turns the two traces on the common row space into sums of squared inner products between columns.

    Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th edition, §8D, theorem 8.49.https://linear.axler.net/LADR4e.pdf#page=340

    Used in What happens when all the words share the same rows?

  57. Stickelberger annihilation in a cyclotomic field

    Let L = ℚ(ζₘ), G = Gal(L/ℚ), and Θ = (1/m) Σₜ [t]ₘ σₜ⁻¹, summing over unit classes and using their least nonnegative representatives. For β in ℤ[G] such that βΘ has integral coefficients, βΘ acts as zero on the ideal class group of L.

    An explicit β gives the integral relation on the image of 1−J, including when ℓ is two. The text reconstructs the relation by carries and Jacobi sums.

    C. S. Yogananda, “Stickelberger Revisited”, p. 151, opening theorem, in Cyclotomic Fields and Related Topics.https://people.math.rochester.edu/faculty/dthakur2/BPCyclotomic.pdf

    Used in Which integral element kills the ideal classes?

  58. Abel’s partial summation formula

    Let A(t) be the sum of aₙ over positive integers n ≤ t and let f be continuously differentiable on [y,z]. Then the sum of aₙ f(n) over y < n ≤ z equals A(z)f(z) − A(y)f(y) − ∫ᵧᶻ A(t)f′(t) dt.

    Weighting the logarithmic prime sum by the reciprocal logarithm transfers its error to a bound for counting primes in a residue class.

    Dimitris Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, §1, formula (1.8) and Example 1.8.https://dms.umontreal.ca/~koukoulo/documents/publications/primes.pdf

    Used in How does a weighted error give a relative error for the number of primes? · What does a zero force a finite sum to do? · How does a real zero control the mass of prime powers? · Why do three different terms appear in the prime moment? · How accurately does a finite character sum approximate the value at a zero? · How do two different characters interact in the same detector block?

  59. Euclidean transference for the covering radius

    For a full lattice of positive dimension D in a Euclidean space, the covering radius times the length of the shortest nonzero vector in the Euclidean dual lattice is at most D/2.

    A lower bound on a trace-dual matrix gives an integral matrix close to any family of real-place targets after accounting for the factor two in the field trace.

    W. Banaszczyk, “New bounds in some transference theorems in the geometry of numbers”, Mathematische Annalen 296 (1993), 625–635.https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01445125

    Used in Why do both radii involve a ratio of lattice sizes?

  60. A finite torsion-free module over a Dedekind domain is projective

    Over a Dedekind domain, every finitely generated torsion-free module is finite locally free and hence projective. A surjection onto such a module has a linear section.

    Splitting off the quotient by the orthogonal sublattice provides the integral projection used to lift a rounded matrix on the middle layer.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 15.22.11(2) and the finite projective criteria of Lemma 10.78.2.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AUW

    Used in How do we round a map on the middle quotient? · Why is the central error quadratic in the size of the short lattice? · What must an adapted frame remember? · Which ideal does a marked vector remember? · Why mark a maximal lattice before counting smaller ones? · Why a near term has exactly the traces of the identity · What do the two projections of an integral lattice remember? · Why does the gluing count cost only twice the perpendicular rank plus one? · Which sublattices of a line survive a discriminant cutoff?

  61. The norm of the different ideal

    For a number field E the inverse different consists of the elements pairing integrally with the ring of integers under the field trace. Its inverse ideal, the different, has absolute norm |disc(E)|.

    Multiplication by the different clears the denominator of a trace-dual map. Its effect on a normalized lattice size is the root discriminant.

    Keith Conrad, The Different Ideal, §4, in particular Theorem 4.8.https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/gradnumthy/different.pdf

    Used in Why do both radii involve a ratio of lattice sizes?

  62. Turán’s second main theorem on power sums

    If n ≥ 1 complex numbers are ordered by decreasing modulus with the largest modulus one, then for every integer h ≥ 0 one of the next n powers has a sum of modulus at least 2[n/(8e(h+n))]ⁿ when all coefficients are one.

    The minimum of the initial coefficient sums is one. Weakening 8e to 1600 gives the bound used to detect the distinguished zero among the other zero distances.

    H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory III, Appendix K, §K.2, Theorem K.3, p. 350.https://personal.science.psu.edu/rcv4/Vol3/Vol3.pdf

    Used in Why must one of the power sums be large?

  63. The lowest compact type of a discrete series

    For U(p,q) with a regular Harish-Chandra parameter λ and a compatible choice of positive roots, the lowest compact type has highest weight λ plus the half-sum of the positive noncompact roots minus the half-sum of the positive compact roots. Its multiplicity is one.

    This identifies the compact type at derivative order zero. The other reachable types are controlled by roots acting on this space.

    D. Vogan, Understanding restriction to K, slide 8, theorem of Schmid and Hecht–Schmid. For U(p,q) the formula is also (2.24) of Harris, Kobayashi and Speh.https://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/conferences/schmid_2013/docs/vogan.pdf#page=8

    Used in How large can an archimedean derivative be? · Which derivatives determine the lowest-type coefficient? · An integral formula for the compressed operator · Which compact types can occur in one derivative? · How large is one derivative after the vector has already been differentiated? · How does the chosen translate affect the period derivative? · Which shifted weights give actual spaces of vectors? · Why do the two compact types have matching coefficients on the whole group? · Why opposite-sign lowering must stop

  64. The scalar of the quadratic matrix Casimir

    For the trace pairing on gl(n), the sum of EᵢⱼEⱼᵢ acts by ∥λ∥² − ∥ρ∥² at infinitesimal character λ, where ρ is the half sum of positive roots. On a highest-weight module of highest weight μ, λ = μ + ρ.

    Apply the same identity to the two compact blocks and subtract the full Casimir to compute the sum of squared derivative norms.

    Zhuoke Yang, New approaches to the gl(N) weight system, Izvestiya Mathematics 87 (2023), §5, Example 5.4, p. 1265.https://doi.org/10.4213/im9379e

    Used in How does a bound on weights control every vector? · The Casimir on one noncompact direction · How much of the weight gap survives? · How large is one derivative after the vector has already been differentiated? · Why does one map per regular shift suffice? · How can a distant ambient representation predict a smaller weight? · How can a compact-finite trial vector retain the same error? · Which compact component inherits the trial bound?

  65. Witt’s extension theorem for a Hermitian space

    Over a field, a linear isometry between two subspaces of a finite-dimensional nondegenerate Hermitian space extends to an isometry of the whole space.

    Apply extension to the lines generated by two vectors of the same nonzero length. A direct basis argument covers the split quadratic algebra.

    D. Sprehn and N. Wahl, Forms over fields and Witt’s lemma, Theorem 3.4.https://web.math.ku.dk/~wahl/Forms.pdf

    Used in What remains after the first vector is fixed? · How many nonzero vectors of norm zero enter a shrinking box? · How can a compact family of frames be lifted to isometries? · How does an isometry of two subspaces move them inside the ambient space?

  66. A locally bounded measurable section of a homogeneous space

    For a second-countable locally compact group G and closed subgroup H, the map G → G/H has a Borel section taking compact sets into relatively compact sets.

    Select an isometry for each first vector measurably. On a compact family of first vectors the choices stay in a compact part of the group after taking closure.

    E. T. Kehlet, Cross sections for quotient maps of locally compact groups. See D. P. Williams, Crossed Products of C*-Algebras, Theorem 4.33 and the preceding note on second countability.https://math.dartmouth.edu/~dana/cpcsa/draft-31Jan06.pdf

    Used in What remains after the first vector is fixed? · Where does the factor for each remaining column come from? · How do different residual stabilizers fit inside one volume?

  67. The trace pairing of a separable field extension

    For a finite separable extension L/K, the bilinear pairing (a,b) ↦ Tr(ab) is nondegenerate.

    A nonsingular Hermitian space over a quadratic finite-field extension has a vector of nonzero Hermitian value, including in residue characteristic two.

    The Stacks Project, Fields, Lemma 9.20.7.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BIL

    Used in Why are the residual lattices equivalent at a finite place? · Where can a maximal integral lattice fail to be self-dual? · How does the isometry return to the original space?

  68. Weak approximation at finitely many places

    For a field with finitely many pairwise inequivalent nontrivial absolute values, the diagonal field is dense in the product of its completions.

    Approximate the entries of a skew-adjoint matrix at the one or two primes over a finite base place. Continuity of the Cayley transform then yields a rational isometry in the desired open coset.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 7.20 and its consequence for completions.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf#page=116

    Used in Why are the residual lattices equivalent at a finite place?

  69. Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem

    If measurable functions converge almost everywhere and their absolute values are bounded by a common integrable function, the integrals converge to the integral of the limit.

    An integrable inverse power of the radius on one regular Gram fibre controls the translates of a Schwartz test on nearby fibres.

    Sheldon Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis, Theorem 3.31.https://measure.axler.net/MIRA.pdf

    Used in How does a general Schwartz test reach every regular fibre?

  70. The analytic class number formula

    For a totally complex field of degree 2f the Dedekind zeta function has residue (2π)ᶠhR/(w√|disc E|) at one, where h is the class number, R the regulator in the doubled complex logarithms, and w the number of roots of unity.

    The archimedean mass of all rank-one coefficient classes gives the initial value in the induction on block rank.

    A. V. Sutherland, Number Theory I (Fall 2021), Lecture 19, Theorem 19.12.https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes19.pdf#page=9

    Used in How much do all coefficient lines contribute? · Where do the class sums enter the flag probability? · What does one zeta residue cost per flag block?

  71. Poisson summation on a Euclidean lattice

    For a full lattice L and a Schwartz function f, the sum of f over L is the sum of its Fourier transform over the dual lattice divided by the covolume of L, with Fourier kernel exp(−2πi⟨x,y⟩). The Gaussian exp(−π‖x‖²) is its own Fourier transform.

    The zero vector on each side supplies the unmarked term when integrating the Gaussian identity across the space of coefficient lattices.

    O. Regev, Lattices in Computer Science, Fourier Transform, Poisson Summation Formula and Example 5.https://cims.nyu.edu/~regev/teaching/lattices_fall_2004/ln/FourierTransform.pdf

    Used in How can a count with a marked vector determine an unmarked volume?

  72. Finite volume of the adelic quotient

    For a connected linear algebraic group over a number field, the quotient of its adelic group by its rational points has finite invariant volume if it has no nontrivial rational character defined over the base field.

    The determinant changes to its inverse under the quadratic involution. The resulting unitary group has no nontrivial base-field character, so the transverse isometry group contributes finite volume.

    A. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Publ. Math. IHÉS 16 (1963), Theorem 5.6(i), p. 21.https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1963__16__5_0.pdf

    Used in Which arithmetic volumes enter an isotropic-line shell? · Why the smaller unitary quotient has finite positive volume

  73. Compactness of the norm-one idèle classes

    The idèles of modulus one in a number field, modulo the embedded nonzero field elements, form a compact topological group.

    After removing the common real height, finitely many relatively compact sets lift a cover of this quotient. They control the multiplicative coordinate in each logarithmic shell.

    A. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Publ. Math. IHÉS 16 (1963), Theorem 5.8, special case following the theorem, p. 22.https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1963__16__5_0.pdf

    Used in Which arithmetic volumes enter an isotropic-line shell?

  74. Baire category for a locally compact orbit

    If a nonempty locally compact Hausdorff space is a countable union of closed subsets, some member has nonempty interior.

    A countable family of translates covers the closed orbit. One has interior, which gives a neighbourhood in the image of a prescribed neighbourhood of the identity under the orbit map.

    The Stacks Project, Topology, Lemma 5.13.3, tag 0CQN.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CQN

    Used in How does a pointwise lift give a single compact family?

  75. When an adèle is invertible

    An adèle of a number field is a unit precisely when every component is nonzero and its valuation is zero at almost every finite place.

    The inverse norm of a selected column denominator has integral components away from a finite set. This allows division simultaneously over the adelic coefficient algebra.

    Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Fall 2019, Lecture 26, Definition 26.2 and its derivation.https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2019fa/LectureNotes26.pdf#page=2

    Used in Which local inverses form an adelic inverse? · Why do the local scalings form a single idèle?

  76. Uniqueness of the primitive inducing character

    Every Dirichlet character comes from a unique primitive character of conductor dividing its modulus. Two primitive characters inducing the same character at a common multiple therefore coincide, including their conductors.

    For distinct primitive characters, the product of one with the conjugate of the other is nonprincipal after passage to a common modulus. Its sum over a complete period vanishes.

    Andrew V. Sutherland, 18.785 Number Theory I, Fall 2021, Theorem 18.13 and Corollary 18.15.https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes18.pdf#page=5

    Used in How do two different characters interact in the same detector block?

  77. The radial gamma integral and sphere area

    For real a and b positive, the integral of exp(−rᵃ) rᵇ⁻¹ over the positive reals equals Γ(b/a)/a. At positive integers Γ(m+1) equals m!.

    Equating radial and Cartesian evaluations of the complex Gaussian integral gives the sphere factors left after taking the quotient of compact volumes.

    NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, equations 5.9.1 and 5.4.1.https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.9.E1

    Used in Why does removing a few directions cost so much volume?

  78. Nonvanishing on the line of real part one away from its real point

    For a Dirichlet character χ and any nonzero real t, L(1+it,χ) is nonzero.

    Together with nonvanishing at one for a nonprincipal character and the absolutely convergent Euler product to the right, this places the selected zeros strictly to the left of one.

    K. S. Kedlaya, Notes on analytic number theory, Theorem 3.8.https://kskedlaya.org/ant/chap-lfunc.html

    Used in Why are there exactly J possible blocks?

  79. Strict separation of disjoint compact convex sets

    Two nonempty disjoint compact convex sets in a finite-dimensional real vector space lie in opposite open half-spaces of an affine hyperplane.

    The two sets contain the witnesses of an incompatible label and a maximal face. Cutting between them decreases the finite number of realized faces on both sides and on their section.

    S. Boyd and L. Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, §2.5.1, pp. 46–47, shortest-segment proof.https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf

    Used in How does cutting a convex set help fill a cycle?

  80. Uniqueness of Haar measure up to a positive constant

    On a locally compact Hausdorff group two nonzero left Haar measures differ by a positive scalar. Transport by a topological group isomorphism gives another Haar measure.

    At one real place and then on the product, a scalar compares two normalizations. It multiplies the coefficient integral and the diagonal quantity used to normalize it.

    A. V. Sutherland, Number Theory I, Fall 2016, Lecture 13, Theorem 13.3.https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2016fa/LectureNotes13.pdf

    Used in How is the size of the identity term used as the unit of comparison? · What measure and weight does a single rational class contribute? · Which determinant changes the volume? · Gluing the finite slices into a fundamental domain · Why the smaller unitary quotient has finite positive volume · Which density makes this product of measures left invariant?

  81. The determinant after replacing a column

    If c is a column vector, replacing column j of a square matrix G by Gc gives determinant cⱼ det G. This follows by multilinearity and also holds for singular matrices.

    Replacing one column relates a single coordinate of a vector to a determinant with bounded entries. This is the step that turns a bound for the whole form into a bound for every coordinate.

    G. Strang, MIT 18.06, Spring 2010, Lecture 20, Cramer’s rule, inverse matrix, and volume. The column identity is proved in the linked passage.https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06-linear-algebra-spring-2010/resources/lecture-20-cramers-rule-inverse-matrix-and-volume/

    Used in How a determinant bounds one coordinate

  82. The long exact homology sequence

    A short exact sequence of chain complexes gives a long exact sequence of homology groups. Its connecting map takes a cycle in the quotient, lifts it to the middle complex, and takes the class of the lifted boundary in the subcomplex.

    For a permutation module mapping onto the coefficient module this compares torsion in the target homology with the finite homology of the permutation module and torsion one degree lower in the kernel.

    C. A. Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, Theorem 1.3.1, p. 10.https://math.mit.edu/~hrm/palestine/weibel/01-chain_complexes.pdf#page=10

    Used in How a stabilizer bound enters the next homological degree

  83. Schur orthogonality for a square-integrable unitary representation

    For an irreducible square-integrable unitary representation of a unimodular group with fixed Haar measure, the integral of |⟨u,π(g)v⟩|² is ‖u‖²‖v‖²/dπ. Polarization gives orthogonality for mixed coefficients. The positive constant dπ is its formal degree for this measure.

    The total mass of the mixed coefficient and its mass on each stabilizer fibre refer to two distinct formal degrees. Orthogonality also turns the entries of the period operator into coefficients of an orthogonal family in L².

    M. Duflo and C. C. Moore, On the regular representation of a nonunimodular locally compact group, J. Funct. Anal. 21 (1976), 209–243, specialized to a unimodular group.https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1236(76)90079-3

    Used in Where can the smaller representation be seen inside the larger one? · How does a bound on one column locate a translate of bounded matrix norm? · Why does the projected vector yield a positive diagonal period? · How much squared mass can one shifted summand carry? · How do identities of scalar functions recover a smooth column? · How do we find a smooth vector that sees the occurrence? · Which normalization identifies the projected coefficient? · How can a signed pairing detect every column? · When does one shifted representation fill the projected space?

  84. Spectral theorem for a compact self-adjoint operator

    For a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space the closed span of its nonzero eigenspaces is the orthogonal complement of its kernel. Each nonzero eigenspace has finite dimension. The quadratic form is the sum of the eigenvalues weighted by the squared coordinates in an orthonormal eigenbasis.

    A positive lower bound on the quadratic form at the projected vector forces a positive eigenvalue of the required size.

    MIT 18.102, Introduction to Functional Analysis, Lecture 22, Theorem 232.https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-102-introduction-to-functional-analysis-spring-2021/resources/lecture-22-the-spectral-theorem-for-a-compact-self-adjoint-operator/

    Used in Why does the projected vector yield a positive diagonal period?

  85. A linear change of variables in real volume

    On a finite-dimensional real vector space an invertible linear map A multiplies Lebesgue measure by |det A|. In an integral of f(Ax) with respect to the original variable x, substitution on the image therefore introduces the reciprocal factor.

    On the product of Hermitian matrix spaces the reciprocal Jacobian compares integrals on a compact set and its image.

    J. Hunter, Measure Theory, §2.8, Linear transformations.https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/measure_theory/measure_notes_ch2.pdf

    Used in Which determinant changes the volume?

  86. Volume under a linear automorphism over a local field

    On an additive vector space over a nonarchimedean local field, applying an invertible matrix to a measurable set multiplies its Haar volume by the normalized absolute value of the determinant. The pushforward measure of a fixed set gains the reciprocal factor.

    On each horizontal coordinate, multiplication by the conjugate scalar has determinant equal to the quadratic norm. That norm also acts on one central coordinate.

    H. Glöckner, Lectures on Lie groups over local fields, Lemma 1.5, p. 8.https://arxiv.org/pdf/0804.2234#page=8

    Used in Which density makes this product of measures left invariant? · What changes when the shell moves one step?

  87. Finite real covolume of an arithmetic subgroup

    Let G be a connected linear algebraic group over the rationals with trivial rational character group. An arithmetic subgroup of G has finite covolume in its real points for Haar measure.

    For each finite adelic lattice class, restriction of scalars expresses its archimedean stabilizer as an arithmetic subgroup. The conjugation of a unitary determinant rules out nontrivial rational characters.

    A. Borel and Harish-Chandra, Arithmetic Subgroups of Algebraic Groups, Theorem 9.4, Annals of Mathematics 75 (1962), p. 522.https://www.mathi.uni-heidelberg.de/~wienhard/retreat10/references/borel_harishchandra_2.pdf#page=39

    Used in Why the smaller unitary quotient has finite positive volume

  88. Complete reducibility for a compact group

    A finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of a compact Lie group splits as a sum of irreducibles. Averaging a positive Hermitian form gives an invariant inner product, so the orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace is invariant.

    The array carrying the derivative in one direction splits into compact types. On each type the Casimir acts by a scalar, which can then be summed over the orthogonal components.

    P. Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Corollary 35.2.https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-755-lie-groups-and-lie-algebras-ii-spring-2024/mit18_755_s24_lec_full.pdf#page=188

    Used in Which compact types can occur in one derivative? · How much of the weight gap survives?

  89. The product formula for a discrete-series formal degree

    For a regular Harish-Chandra parameter on U(p,q), with its Haar measure fixed, the formal degree is a common positive constant times the product of the pairwise parameter gaps in absolute value divided by the corresponding Weyl denominators.

    A shift of one coordinate changes only the factors touching that coordinate. Comparing with the same Haar measure cancels the common constant and gives the reciprocal-degree bound in the tensor moment.

    M. F. Atiyah and W. Schmid, A geometric construction of the discrete series for semisimple Lie groups, §5, p. 25, after (5.15).https://www.math.utah.edu/~ptrapa/math-library/schmid/atiyah-schmid.pdf#page=25

    Used in What does one lowering cost in formal degree? · How much squared mass can one shifted summand carry? · How does a single nonzero integral produce a bounded intertwiner? · When does one shifted representation fill the projected space?

  90. Cayley–Hamilton

    A square matrix over a commutative ring satisfies its own monic characteristic polynomial.

    After the power traces force the characteristic polynomial to be (T−1)ⁿ, evaluating at the rational matrix proves that subtracting the identity gives a nilpotent matrix.

    The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.16.1, Tag 00DX.https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DX

    Used in From the power traces to a distance from the identity · Why must an actual Galois element in every open coset have simple spectrum?

  91. Mass formula for a maximal definite Hermitian lattice

    For a totally definite Hermitian space over a quadratic extension of a totally real number field, the mass of the genus of a maximal lattice has a product formula. In the finite-unramified case used here the constant common to spaces of fixed rank is the mass of the orthonormal genus. A finite set of nonunimodular local factors accounts for the other maximal genera.

    The local factors at the bad places bound the mass of maximal enlargements. Counting smaller lattices inside these enlargements then gives the bound at an arbitrary discriminant order.

    W. T. Gan, J. P. Hanke and J.-K. Yu, On an exact mass formula of Shimura, Propositions 4.4 and 4.5, p. 110 (odd and even unitary ranks).https://web.math.princeton.edu/~jonhanke/Web-02/Mass-Formula-of-Shimura/shimura-mass.pdf

    Used in The genus mass at a fixed discriminant order · What is the total mass of the eligible perpendicular lattices? · How much mass can one set of bad primes carry?

  92. Factorization, norm and degrees of prime ideals

    Every nonzero proper integral ideal in a number ring factors uniquely into prime ideals. The absolute norm is multiplicative. For a rational prime p the sum of the products of ramification index and residue degree over the primes above p equals the field degree D. The prime of residue degree f has absolute norm pᶠ.

    Factoring off one prime above a chosen divisor of the norm gives at most D choices. Iterating bounds the number of possible bad ideals and hence the number of rational orbit representatives.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, §§3–4, particularly Theorem 3.34 and the definition of the ideal norm.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf

    Used in Which ideal records the isometry class of a rational subspace? · How many rational subspace orbits can one discriminant order require? · Why mark a maximal lattice before counting smaller ones? · How short a vector does every integral line contain? · Which sublattices of a line survive a discriminant cutoff? · Which rational hyperplanes share the determinant budget?

  93. The quantum comatrix identity

    For the matrix of elementary generators of gl(m) the ordered column determinant with consecutive unit shifts admits a cofactor expansion. The signed comatrix on the left times the shifted generating matrix on the right is the diagonal matrix of that determinant.

    Alternating the columns and expanding the last one gives an operator identity on smooth vectors. Specialization at a simple root then recovers the required tensor projection.

    A. I. Molev, Yangians and their applications, Definition 2.26 and Proposition 2.27, formulas (2.30)–(2.31), under the evaluation representation.https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0211288

    Used in Why do the columns of the differential minor have successive shifts? · Which side of the matrix does the comatrix multiply?

  94. The central character of the Capelli determinant

    For gl(m) with column parameters u, u−1, …, u−m+1, the full Capelli determinant has central coefficients. At highest weight μ, with coordinates numbered from zero, its scalar is the product of u+μⱼ−j.

    Converting the highest weight to the infinitesimal character gives the m distinct factors in the projector calculation.

    A. I. Molev, Sugawara Operators for Classical Lie Algebras, §4.6, formula (4.37) and Corollary 4.6.2.https://www.ams.org/bookstore/pspdf/surv-229-prev.pdf

    Used in How does evaluation select one shifted summand? · How much squared mass can one shifted summand carry?

  95. Signed interlacing for a discrete-series summand

    For the restriction from U(p,q) to U(p−1,q), a discrete series of the smaller group occurs discretely precisely when the two signed Harish-Chandra parameters satisfy the signed interlacing law. In the merged decreasing lists, consecutive entries from the same group have opposite signs and consecutive entries from different groups have the same sign, with signs interpreted for the positive line removed here.

    This branching criterion identifies the occurrence required by the period. The chapter explains the propagation of a known occurrence through a lowering of an ambient parameter and the recovery of an intertwiner from a nonzero coefficient.

    Hongyu He, On the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture for U(p,q), Definition 1 and Theorem 0.1, with the positive-line convention.https://www.math.lsu.edu/~hongyu/pub/ggp_hhe_final.pdf

    Used in Which signed parameters give a copy of the smaller representation? · Where can the smaller representation be seen inside the larger one? · Why does the trial vector give an actual discrete constituent? · How does the surviving coordinate give a copy of the lowered representation?

  96. Index of a rank-one ideal sublattice

    For a number ring R, a nonzero fractional ideal J and a nonzero integral ideal 𝔞, the additive index [J:𝔞J] equals the absolute norm of 𝔞. Every full sublattice ideal I contained in J is uniquely 𝔞J with 𝔞=IJ⁻¹.

    The discriminant of a line sublattice grows by the square of this index, so counting ideals up to a norm cutoff counts all eligible sublattices in each maximal line lattice.

    J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 3.32 and Proposition 4.2 on ideal norms and indices.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANTc.pdf#page=71

    Used in Which sublattices of a line survive a discriminant cutoff? · What is the total mass of the eligible perpendicular lattices?

  97. Brauer–Nesbitt in characteristic zero

    Two finite-dimensional semisimple representations of a group over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero are isomorphic if their characteristic polynomials coincide at every group element.

    Apply the assertion after adding the opposite character list to each odd-dimensional companion. The chapter proves it by simultaneous density on the simple constituents.

    P. Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory, Theorem 2.5(ii) and Theorem 2.17(i).https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf#page=24

    Used in How do good primes identify a character on the entire group? · How do three places above ℓ give one companion with the full local data? · How can a cohomological piece of unknown dimension determine rank m?

  98. Density of the compact-finite vectors

    In a continuous unitary representation of a compact Lie group, the Hilbert space is the closure of the sum of its finite-dimensional irreducible subrepresentations. The character projections onto compact types preserve smooth ambient vectors under a smooth ambient group action.

    Applied to a smooth ambient trial vector, compact approximation and the Casimir estimate together control the error of every smaller-block derivative.

    P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups, Lecture 4, Corollary 4.7.https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-757-representations-of-lie-groups-fall-2023/mit18_757_f23_lec04.pdf

    Used in How can a compact-finite trial vector retain the same error?

  99. Potential semistability of a de Rham representation

    Over a finite extension of ℚℓ, a finite-dimensional de Rham Galois representation with finite ℓ-adic coefficient field becomes semistable after a finite extension.

    For the residual de Rham constituent the attached Weil–Deligne representation can be compared with the corresponding summand of the odd-rank representation.

    L. Berger, Représentations p-adiques et équations différentielles, Inventiones Mathematicae 148 (2002), 219–284.https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0102179

    Used in Which local statements pass to the rank-n representation?

  100. Continuous functional calculus for a bounded self-adjoint operator

    Real continuous functions on a closed interval containing the spectrum act by self-adjoint operators, compatibly with sums, products and uniform limits. A nonnegative function gives a positive operator.

    The positive and negative parts of the bounded inverse shifted by one half have zero product and commute with the group.

    R. Melrose, Functional Analysis, Chapter 3, Theorem 3.5 and Remark 3.1.https://math.mit.edu/~rbm/18.102Sp20/Chapter3.pdf#page=30

    Used in A Casimir bound on every smooth vector of the cut

  101. Orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace

    Each vector of a Hilbert space has a unique decomposition into one vector in a given closed linear subspace and another in its perpendicular.

    Projection onto the closure of the range of the smooth quadratic operator proves that its range is dense.

    R. Melrose, Functional Analysis, Chapter 3, §9, Proposition 3.6.https://math.mit.edu/~rbm/18.102Sp20/Chapter3.pdf#page=7

    Used in A bounded inverse on the Hilbert space · Why is the partial trace a sum of ordinary squared norms? · When does one shifted representation fill the projected space?

  102. Local factors of an irreducible admissible automorphic representation

    An irreducible admissible smooth module for the finite-adelic Hecke algebra factors as a restricted tensor product of irreducible admissible local modules.

    At a split place the local factor is a representation of a general linear group. A vector fixed by its integral subgroup detects a spherical summand.

    D. Flath, Decomposition of representations into tensor products, Theorem 2 (p. 181). See also J. R. Getz, An introduction to automorphic representations, Theorem 7.5.https://sites.math.duke.edu/~jgetz/aut_reps.pdf#page=36

    Used in Why does a single automorphic vector give Satake data at almost every split place?

  103. Satake parameters for a spherical representation

    For an irreducible spherical representation of GLₙ over a nonarchimedean local field, the spherical Hecke character determines an unordered n-tuple of nonzero complex numbers in the chosen Satake normalization.

    This tuple supplies the source polynomial at a good split place before the two lists of auxiliary characters are added.

    I. Satake, Theory of spherical functions on reductive algebraic groups over p-adic fields, Theorems 2 and 3.https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1963__18__5_0.pdf#page=26

    Used in Why does a single automorphic vector give Satake data at almost every split place?

  104. The square of the Dirac operator on a compact type

    The square of the Dirac operator relates the full Casimir and the compact Casimir on the tensor with the exterior module. The chapter gives the scalar and the exterior correction for its chosen convention.

    The two halves vanish on a selected compact highest vector. The square then fixes the full Casimir eigenvalue on the terminal type.

    R. Parthasarathy, Dirac operator and the discrete series, Proposition 3.1 and its specialization in Proposition 3.2.https://www.math.utah.edu/~ptrapa/math-library/parthasarathy-dirac-operator.pdf#page=14

    Used in Which Casimir eigenvalue does the stopping type carry?

  105. The semisimple quotient of a pseudocharacter

    Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the quotient of the group algebra by the trace radical of a finite-degree pseudocharacter is a finite product of full matrix algebras. The trace on each surviving block is an integer multiple of its ordinary trace.

    This algebra realizes the limiting trace as a semisimple representation of the required rank. Its nondegenerate trace pairing also recovers matrix entries continuously.

    R. Rouquier, Caractérisation des caractères et pseudo-caractères, Journal of Algebra 180 (1996), Lemma 4.1 and §4.https://www.math.ucla.edu/~rouquier/papers/carcar.pdf#page=9

    Used in How does an odd-rank Hecke system give a Galois representation? · How does one recover unramifiedness at a specified place?

  106. Taylor’s formula with Lagrange remainder

    For a real function with m continuous derivatives on the closed interval between t and t+δ, the difference from its degree-(m−1) Taylor polynomial at t is bounded by |δ|ᵐ/m! times the supremum of its mth derivative in absolute value on that interval.

    Pairing a Hilbert-space Taylor remainder with its own unit direction yields the norm estimate for a noncompact group translate.

    MIT 18.014, Calculus with Theory, Chapter O, Theorem 2.https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-014-calculus-with-theory-fall-2010/04f26bc51297b857681b4c91df24c7b6_MIT18_014F10_ChOnotes.pdf

    Used in How do local Taylor expansions control an entire group translate?

  107. Finiteness and cohomological dimension of geometric étale cohomology

    For a smooth projective variety of dimension n over a number field and a prime ℓ, geometric étale cohomology with ℚℓ coefficients is finite-dimensional and vanishes in degrees greater than 2n. The natural absolute Galois action is continuous.

    The simultaneous Hecke eigenspace is taken inside a finite sum with a continuous Galois action.

    J. S. Milne, Lectures on Étale Cohomology, Theorems 15.1 and 19.2. For continuity see Brinon–Conrad, Example 1.2.3, linked in the passage.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/LEC.pdf#page=125

    Used in Which part of cohomology carries the auxiliary Hecke system?

  108. Crystalline summands and filtered de Rham periods

    A Galois-stable direct summand of a crystalline representation is crystalline. Its filtered de Rham periods form a filtered direct summand, and the dimensions of each graded piece add across a direct sum.

    Two split injections in opposite directions transfer crystallinity to the rank-m model and force all the specified filtration jumps to occur.

    O. Brinon and B. Conrad, CMI Summer School Notes on p-adic Hodge Theory, Theorem 5.2.1 and §6.3.https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/notes.pdf#page=68

    Used in How do the two injections recover the exact data at a prescribed prime? · Why do the filtration jumps survive a weighted approximation of traces?

  109. The holomorphic Lefschetz formula at transverse fixed points

    For a holomorphic self-map of a compact complex manifold with isolated nondegenerate fixed points, the alternating trace on cohomology of holomorphic a-forms is the sum at the fixed points of the trace on the ath exterior power of the cotangent pullback divided by det(I−A), where A is the derivative.

    The elliptic-curve example evaluates the two holomorphic degrees. The general geometric input for two correspondence maps is stated in the book.

    M. F. Atiyah and R. Bott, A Lefschetz fixed point formula for elliptic complexes II, Annals of Mathematics 88 (1968), 451–491, holomorphic case.https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1968/88-3/p04

    Used in Which part of cohomology carries the auxiliary Hecke system?

  110. Extension of an embedding inside a Galois extension

    If Ω/F is Galois and F⊆L⊆Ω, any F-embedding of L into Ω extends to an F-automorphism of Ω.

    An embedding of a field generated by finitely many Hecke coordinates determines one of the finitely many simultaneous conjugates of the whole system.

    J. S. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, Proposition 7.4.https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf#page=95

    Used in Why do all the original Hecke coordinates lie in one finite extension?

  111. Completeness of a finite-dimensional normed space over a complete field

    On a finite-dimensional vector space over a complete valued field every vector-space norm induces the same complete topology.

    The field generated by the original rational Hecke coordinates has bounded finite degree and is complete, so the trace-limit averages converge in this field.

    A. Sutherland, MIT 18.785, Fall 2016, Lecture 10, Proposition 10.6.https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2016fa/LectureNotes10.pdf

    Used in Why do all the original Hecke coordinates lie in one finite extension? · How does an odd-rank Hecke system give a Galois representation?

  112. Vanishing of nonzero cyclotomic twisted invariants

    Over a finite extension of ℚℓ, the completed algebraic closure has no nonzero element on which the absolute Galois group acts by a nonzero integral power of the cyclotomic character.

    A Galois-stable relation with minimal monomial support lies in a single column weight.

    O. Brinon and B. Conrad, CMI Summer School Notes on p-adic Hodge Theory, Theorem 2.2.7.https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/notes.pdf

    Used in How does a local filtration put a matrix in the tangent space of the global image?

  113. From de Rham jumps to the Hodge–Tate decomposition

    For a de Rham representation, the associated graded space of its filtered de Rham periods identifies with its graded Hodge–Tate periods. A jump of degree h corresponds to a completed coefficient line with cyclotomic twist −h.

    The multiplicities of the inducing embedding give the columns of the local comparison and the signs of the cocharacter exponents.

    O. Brinon and B. Conrad, CMI Summer School Notes on p-adic Hodge Theory, Example 6.3.1 and Proposition 6.3.2.https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/notes.pdf

    Used in How does a local filtration put a matrix in the tangent space of the global image?

  114. Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz for a maximal ideal

    A maximal ideal of a nonzero finitely generated algebra over an algebraically closed field has that field as its residue field.

    Inverting the product of finitely many tests before taking a residue field preserves all of the required inequalities.

    The Stacks Project, Theorem 10.34.1 (tag 00FV).https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00FV

    Used in Can the tangent matrix be chosen over the coefficient field? · What happens when a group element permutes the weight spaces?

  115. The radical of a finite-dimensional algebra

    The ideal annihilating every simple module is the largest nilpotent two-sided ideal of the algebra.

    Its image on the original representation has a stable complement and must vanish.

    P. Etingof et al., Introduction to representation theory, Lemma 2.8 and Proposition 2.11.https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/replect.pdf#page=26

    Used in What guarantees an inverse for a nonzero block?

  116. Elimination in an invertible matrix

    Over a field an invertible matrix can be reduced to a nonsingular diagonal matrix by adding multiples of other rows.

    Each row addition lifts to a transvection in the tangent-generated matrix algebra.

    MIT 18.700, Gaussian elimination, Theorem 4.8, with the row-addition pivot argument in the text.https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-700-linear-algebra-fall-2013/b144082f6883d02faeec26d7f708c63e_MIT18_700F13_gauss.pdf#page=16

    Used in Which part of the change of basis moves the weight spaces?

  117. Finiteness of the adelic class number

    For the connected unitary group over the number field, the rational points have finitely many classes modulo the archimedean group and the standard integral finite level. The same holds at each compact open finite level.

    A single bound over finitely many representatives controls every integral evaluation of an algebraic form.

    A. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Theorem 5.1.https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1963__16__5_0.pdf

    Used in Which evaluations keep a Hecke error small?

  2. Nontrivial zeta zeros

    For each complex s with ζ(s)=0, s ≠ −2(n+1) for all natural n, and s ≠ 1, Re s=1/2.

    Read the proof step

    For every positive natural modulus N, every complex Dirichlet character χ mod N and s in ℂ with Re s>1/2, (χ ≠ 1 or s ≠ 1) implies L(s,χ) ≠ 0.

  5. Zeros of primitive Dirichlet L-functions in the strip

    For every positive natural modulus N and every primitive complex Dirichlet character χ mod N, each zero s with 0 < Re s < 1 has Re s=1/2.
